profile.summary: Bacformer is a model of whole bacterial genomes. It takes the proteins of a genome, ordered by their coordinates on the chromosome and plasmids, embeds each one with a protein language model, and runs a transformer over those per-protein vectors so that every protein is represented in the context of the rest of the genome. The base size uses ESM-2 t12 35M embeddings in a 12-layer transformer of hidden size 480, was pretrained on about 1.3 million bacterial genomes and about 3 billion proteins, and is used for tasks such as strain clustering, operon identification, essential gene prediction and protein-protein interaction prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README opening paragraph and Requirements; model card opening and Architecture

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Every protein of a genome is embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector, so one protein is one token. Those tokens are fed in genomic order into a transformer of 12 layers and hidden size 480 for the base size, with rotary positional embeddings for order and learnable contig embeddings that mark which chromosome or plasmid a protein came from. Pretraining predicts the protein family of a masked or next protein out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input remains the exact protein sequence, so single-residue differences stay visible.
sections.source_locator: README opening paragraph; model card: Architecture

sections.title: Checkpoints in this family
sections.body: The README table lists eight checkpoints. It describes bacformer-masked-MAG and bacformer-causal-MAG as 26M parameter models pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, with a masked and an autoregressive objective; bacformer-masked-complete-genomes and bacformer-causal-complete-genomes as those two MAG models finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes; bacformer-large-masked-MAG and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes with the same text, a 300M parameter model pretrained on the MAG corpus with a masked objective; bacformer-causal-protein-family-modeling-complete-genomes as bacformer-causal-MAG finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes with protein-family tokens as input; and bacformer-for-essential-genes-prediction as bacformer-masked-complete-genomes finetuned on the essential-genes prediction task. The preprint gives the complete-genome set as 48,932 genomes. Bacformer Large has its own record.

sections.title: What it is used for
sections.body: The README names strain clustering, essential gene prediction, operon identification, protein-protein interaction prediction and protein function prediction, and ships tutorials for several of them. The preprint reports that the authors used the model to predict protein-protein interactions, uncover operon structure, infer phenotypic traits including antimicrobial resistance, and design template synthetic proteomes.

strengths.text: The genome, not the single protein, is the unit of modelling: each protein embedding depends on the other proteins present, which is what the authors report lets the model recover interactions and operon structure.

One pretrained model serves several bacterial genomics tasks: the README names strain clustering, essential gene prediction, operon identification, protein-protein interaction prediction and protein function prediction, with tutorials for several of them.
Code and the checkpoints read here are Apache-2.0 and the Hugging Face repositories are not gated, so the family can be used without an access request.
strengths.source_locator: Repository LICENSE; model card front matter; Hugging Face API gated field

strengths.text: Both a masked and an autoregressive variant are released at each stage, so the same architecture can be used for representation tasks and for generation of protein-family sequences.

limitations.text: A base protein language model is part of the pipeline: ESM-2 t12 35M for Bacformer and ESM-C for Bacformer Large, which must embed every protein before Bacformer runs.
Genomes are limited to 6,000 proteins in pretraining, so larger protein sets must be cut or split.

The install route expects PyTorch 2.2 or above with flash attention and the usage examples select a CUDA device, so a GPU machine is assumed; the README adds a troubleshooting path with a CUDA 12.1 conda environment.

No model card or Hugging Face metadata is saved here for two of the eight listed checkpoints, the protein-family generation model and the essential-genes finetune, so this record describes them only from the README table.

run_guide.summary: Install the bacformer package and compute contextual protein embeddings for a few protein sequences with a base-size Bacformer checkpoint.
prerequisites: Python 3.10, which the README names as the version Bacformer was developed in.
PyTorch 2.2 or above and flash attention, as the README install section asks for.
A CUDA GPU: the README usage examples set device to cuda:0.
Network access to Hugging Face for the Bacformer checkpoint and the ESM-2 t12 35M base model.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell:
pip install "torch>=2.2"
pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation
pip install bacformer
steps.explanation: The three install commands the README gives, in the order it gives them.

steps.title: Embed a few protein sequences
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM
from bacformer.pp import protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs

device = "cuda:0"
masked_model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("macwiatrak/bacformer-masked-MAG", trust_remote_code=True).to(torch.bfloat16).eval().to(device)

protein_sequences = [
    "MGYDLVAGFQKNVRTI",
    "MKAILVVLLG",
    "MQLIESRFYKDPWGNVHATC",
    "MSTNPKPQRFAWL",
]
inputs = protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs(
    protein_sequences,
    device=device,
    batch_size=128,
    max_n_proteins=6000,
)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = masked_model(**inputs, return_dict=True)
print(outputs.keys())
PY
steps.explanation: The README's load line for the masked MAG checkpoint and the toy example from the model card, wrapped in a shell heredoc. The final print of the output keys was added by Rewire so that the step prints something.

outputs: The keys of the model output. The sources describe the output as a last hidden state of shape (batch size, number of proteins plus special tokens, embedding dimension), which averaged over proteins gives one genome embedding.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and the model card and have not been executed by Rewire.
The sources do not state how much GPU memory Bacformer needs for inference.
flash-attn compiles against the local CUDA toolchain; the README gives a troubleshooting path with a clean conda environment and CUDA 12.1.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein sequence of a genome is first embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector per protein. Those vectors are the tokens of a transformer of 12 layers and hidden size 480, which attends over all proteins of the genome and so returns contextual protein embeddings. Position is encoded with rotary positional embeddings and learnable contig embeddings mark which chromosome or plasmid each protein came from. The pretraining head does not predict amino acids: it predicts a discrete protein family index out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input stays the exact protein sequence.

sections.title: What distinguishes this checkpoint
sections.body: The model card describes this checkpoint as a 27M-parameter transformer further pretrained on about 40 thousand complete genomes from NCBI RefSeq, starting from the matching metagenome-assembled-genome checkpoint. Its objective is autoregressive: the protein family of the next protein is predicted from the preceding proteins. It takes protein embeddings from ESM-2 t12 35M.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein sequence of a genome is first embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector per protein. Those vectors are the tokens of a transformer of 12 layers and hidden size 480, which attends over all proteins of the genome and so returns contextual protein embeddings. Position is encoded with rotary positional embeddings and learnable contig embeddings mark which chromosome or plasmid each protein came from. The pretraining head does not predict amino acids: it predicts a discrete protein family index out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input stays the exact protein sequence.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Architecture, Input embeddings and Transformer backbone

sections.title: What distinguishes this checkpoint
sections.body: The model card describes this checkpoint as a 27M-parameter transformer pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes covering more than 20 thousand bacterial species. Its objective is autoregressive: the protein family of the next protein is predicted from the preceding proteins. It takes protein embeddings from ESM-2 t12 35M.
sections.source_locator: Model card: opening section, Training Data and Training objective

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: A result should name the Hugging Face repository macwiatrak/bacformer-causal-MAG and the revision it used; this page was written from revision e4c8d6dc4decaa88729ce3853b1f329fee3b4960, which the Hugging Face API reported on 2026-11-27. The README table lists eight checkpoints. It describes bacformer-masked-MAG and bacformer-causal-MAG as 26M parameter models pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, with a masked and an autoregressive objective; bacformer-masked-complete-genomes and bacformer-causal-complete-genomes as those two MAG models finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes; bacformer-large-masked-MAG and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes with the same text, a 300M parameter model pretrained on the MAG corpus with a masked objective; bacformer-causal-protein-family-modeling-complete-genomes as bacformer-causal-MAG finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes with protein-family tokens as input; and bacformer-for-essential-genes-prediction as bacformer-masked-complete-genomes finetuned on the essential-genes prediction task. The README news list dates the Hugging Face release of Bacformer to 2025-05-15.

strengths.text: Each protein is represented in the context of the whole genome, so neighbouring and co-occurring genes influence its embedding; the authors report in the preprint that this raises zero-shot protein-protein interaction performance over the non-contextual base protein language model.
strengths.source_locator: Model card opening; preprint Results on protein-protein interactions

strengths.text: The input is the exact protein sequence, not a protein-family token, so single-residue differences between genomes are visible to the model even though pretraining predicts protein families.
Weights and code are both Apache-2.0 and the Hugging Face repository is not gated, so the checkpoint can be downloaded and used without an access request.
strengths.source_locator: Model card front matter; Hugging Face API gated field; repository LICENSE

limitations.text: The model does not read sequences by itself: protein embeddings must first be computed with the base protein language model ESM-2 t12 35M, so that model is part of any pipeline.
limitations.source_locator: README: Requirements; model card: Input embeddings

limitations.text: A genome is limited to 6,000 proteins in pretraining, so very large genomes or large protein sets have to be cut or split.
The install route the README gives expects PyTorch 2.2 or above with flash attention, and the usage examples select a CUDA device, so a GPU machine is assumed.
Pretraining predicts a protein family out of 50 thousand clusters rather than a protein sequence, so the pretraining head does not generate new sequences.

run_guide.summary: Install the bacformer package and compute contextual protein embeddings with the bacformer-causal-MAG checkpoint.
prerequisites: Python 3.10, which the README names as the version Bacformer was developed in.
PyTorch 2.2 or above and flash attention, as the README install section asks for.
A CUDA GPU: the usage examples in the sources set device to cuda:0.
Network access to Hugging Face, to download the bacformer-causal-MAG weights and the ESM-2 t12 35M base model.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell:
pip install "torch>=2.2"
pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation
pip install bacformer
steps.explanation: The three install commands the README gives, in the order it gives them.

steps.title: Load the checkpoint and embed a few proteins
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel
from bacformer.pp import protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs

device = "cuda:0"
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("macwiatrak/bacformer-causal-MAG", trust_remote_code=True).to(device).eval().to(torch.bfloat16)

protein_sequences = [
    "MGYDLVAGFQKNVRTI",
    "MKAILVVLLG",
    "MQLIESRFYKDPWGNVHATC",
    "MSTNPKPQRFAWL",
]
inputs = protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs(
    protein_sequences,
    device=device,
    batch_size=128,
    max_n_proteins=6000,
)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs, return_dict=True)
print(outputs.keys())
PY
steps.explanation: The toy example from the saved sources, wrapped in a shell heredoc. The load line is the one the model card gives for this checkpoint; the four toy protein sequences and the call to protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs are the ones the sources print, with the variable name kept consistent with the load line and a final print of the output keys added by Rewire so the step prints something.

outputs: The keys of the model output. The sources describe the output as a last hidden state of shape (batch size, number of proteins plus special tokens, embedding dimension), which averaged over proteins gives one genome embedding.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and the model card and have not been executed by Rewire.
The sources do not state how much GPU memory this checkpoint needs.
flash-attn compiles against the local CUDA toolchain, and the README's troubleshooting section describes a clean conda environment with CUDA 12.1 for that case.

profile.summary: bacformer-for-ppi-prediction is a Bacformer checkpoint whose configuration declares the model class BacformerForProteinProteinInteraction, that is a Bacformer encoder with a head for protein-protein interaction prediction. Bacformer itself treats a whole bacterial genome as a sequence of proteins in genomic order and computes an embedding for each protein that depends on the other proteins in the genome. The published model card for this repository is the automatically generated template and describes neither the training data nor the licence, so most of this page comes from the configuration file, the Hugging Face metadata and the repository README.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Bacformer embeds each protein of a genome with a base protein language model, averages the amino acid embeddings into one vector per protein and runs a transformer over those vectors in genomic order. This checkpoint's configuration declares 12 hidden layers, hidden size 480, 8 attention heads and a maximum of 6000 proteins per genome, and the model class is BacformerForProteinProteinInteraction with a single-label classification head.

profile.summary: Bacformer Large is the larger of the two Bacformer sizes. Like the base size it treats a whole bacterial genome as a sequence of proteins ordered along the chromosome and plasmids, but it embeds each protein with ESM-C 300M and runs a 30-layer transformer of hidden size 960 over those per-protein vectors, returning an embedding for each protein that depends on the rest of the genome. Two checkpoints are released: bacformer-large-masked-MAG, pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes, which is listed for complete genomes and whose Hugging Face metadata gives bacformer-large-masked-MAG as its base model.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card opening, What is new and Architecture; README: News and Requirements; Hugging Face API cardData.base_model for the complete-genomes checkpoint

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein of a genome is embedded with ESM-C 300M and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one 960-dimensional vector, so one protein is one token. The tokens are fed in genomic order into a 30-layer transformer of hidden size 960 that uses SwiGLU activations, rotary positional embeddings for order and learnable contig embeddings for chromosome and plasmid structure. Pretraining predicts the protein family of masked proteins out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input stays the exact protein sequence.
sections.source_locator: Model card: What is new in Bacformer Large, Architecture and Transformer backbone

sections.title: What distinguishes this size
sections.body: The card lists the differences from the base size: more than 300M parameters, SwiGLU activations, ESM-C 300M instead of ESM-2 as the base protein language model, no special tokens, and the forward argument renamed from token_type_ids to contig_ids. The Hugging Face safetensors index reports 431,765,841 parameters for both large checkpoints. The README says the release of Bacformer Large brought improved performance on downstream tasks.

steps.title: Embed a few protein sequences with Bacformer Large
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel
from bacformer.pp import protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs

device = "cuda:0"
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "macwiatrak/bacformer-large-masked-MAG", trust_remote_code=True
).to(device).eval().to(torch.bfloat16)

protein_sequences = [
    "MGYDLVAGFQKNVRTI",
    "MKAILVVLLG",
    "MQLIESRFYKDPWGNVHATC",
    "MSTNPKPQRFAWL",
]
inputs = protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs(
    protein_sequences,
    device=device,
    batch_size=128,
    max_n_proteins=6000,
    bacformer_model_type="large",
)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs, return_dict=True)
print('last hidden state shape:', outputs["last_hidden_state"].shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's Bacformer Large example, wrapped in a shell heredoc, with the comments removed.

profile.summary: bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes is one released checkpoint of Bacformer, a model that treats a whole bacterial genome as a sequence of proteins ordered along the chromosome and plasmids. Each protein is embedded with the base protein language model ESM-C 300M and the averaged embedding is used as one token, so the transformer returns, for every protein, a representation that depends on the other proteins in the same genome. This checkpoint was trained with a masked objective, predicting the protein family of masked proteins, on the MAG corpus of about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes and then about 40 thousand complete genomes from NCBI RefSeq.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein sequence of a genome is first embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector per protein. Those vectors are the tokens of a transformer of 30 layers and hidden size 960, which attends over all proteins of the genome and so returns contextual protein embeddings. Position is encoded with rotary positional embeddings and learnable contig embeddings mark which chromosome or plasmid each protein came from. The pretraining head does not predict amino acids: it predicts a discrete protein family index out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input stays the exact protein sequence.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Architecture, Input embeddings and Transformer backbone

sections.title: What distinguishes this checkpoint
sections.body: The model card describes this checkpoint as a 300M-parameter transformer further pretrained on about 40 thousand complete genomes from NCBI RefSeq, starting from the matching metagenome-assembled-genome checkpoint. Its objective is masked: 15 per cent of the proteins are masked and their protein families are predicted from the rest of the genome. It takes protein embeddings from ESM-C 300M.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: A result should name the Hugging Face repository macwiatrak/bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes and the revision it used; this page was written from revision 84f85c37a05e55559142b842c1569e265183b554, which the Hugging Face API reported on 2026-11-27. The README table lists eight checkpoints. It describes bacformer-masked-MAG and bacformer-causal-MAG as 26M parameter models pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, with a masked and an autoregressive objective; bacformer-masked-complete-genomes and bacformer-causal-complete-genomes as those two MAG models finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes; bacformer-large-masked-MAG and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes with the same text, a 300M parameter model pretrained on the MAG corpus with a masked objective; bacformer-causal-protein-family-modeling-complete-genomes as bacformer-causal-MAG finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes with protein-family tokens as input; and bacformer-for-essential-genes-prediction as bacformer-masked-complete-genomes finetuned on the essential-genes prediction task. The README row for this checkpoint repeats the MAG wording, while its model card describes further pretraining on about 40 thousand complete genomes. The README also records that a bug in the Bacformer Large code on Hugging Face was fixed on 2025-05-15 and that models downloaded or cached before that date should be downloaded again, which matters for this checkpoint.

steps.title: Load the checkpoint and embed a few proteins
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel
from bacformer.pp import protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs

device = "cuda:0"
encoder_model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("macwiatrak/bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes", trust_remote_code=True).to(torch.bfloat16).eval().to(device)

protein_sequences = [
    "MGYDLVAGFQKNVRTI",
    "MKAILVVLLG",
    "MQLIESRFYKDPWGNVHATC",
    "MSTNPKPQRFAWL",
]
inputs = protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs(
    protein_sequences,
    device=device,
    batch_size=128,
    max_n_proteins=6000,
    bacformer_model_type="large",
)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = encoder_model(**inputs, return_dict=True)
print(outputs.keys())
PY

profile.summary: bacformer-large-masked-MAG is one released checkpoint of Bacformer, a model that treats a whole bacterial genome as a sequence of proteins ordered along the chromosome and plasmids. Each protein is embedded with the base protein language model ESM-C 300M and the averaged embedding is used as one token, so the transformer returns, for every protein, a representation that depends on the other proteins in the same genome. This checkpoint was trained with a masked objective, predicting the protein family of masked proteins, on the MAG corpus of about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: opening section and Training Data; README opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein sequence of a genome is first embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector per protein. Those vectors are the tokens of a transformer of 30 layers and hidden size 960, which attends over all proteins of the genome and so returns contextual protein embeddings. Position is encoded with rotary positional embeddings and learnable contig embeddings mark which chromosome or plasmid each protein came from. The pretraining head does not predict amino acids: it predicts a discrete protein family index out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input stays the exact protein sequence.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Architecture, Input embeddings and Transformer backbone

sections.title: What distinguishes this checkpoint
sections.body: The model card describes this checkpoint as a 300M-parameter transformer pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes covering more than 20 thousand bacterial species. Its objective is masked: 15 per cent of the proteins are masked and their protein families are predicted from the rest of the genome. It takes protein embeddings from ESM-C 300M.

sections.body: A result should name the Hugging Face repository macwiatrak/bacformer-large-masked-MAG and the revision it used; this page was written from revision cb92cdf04e1b32993a19fdd9cf6f8f49efde2665, which the Hugging Face API reported on 2026-11-27. The README table lists eight checkpoints. It describes bacformer-masked-MAG and bacformer-causal-MAG as 26M parameter models pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, with a masked and an autoregressive objective; bacformer-masked-complete-genomes and bacformer-causal-complete-genomes as those two MAG models finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes; bacformer-large-masked-MAG and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes with the same text, a 300M parameter model pretrained on the MAG corpus with a masked objective; bacformer-causal-protein-family-modeling-complete-genomes as bacformer-causal-MAG finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes with protein-family tokens as input; and bacformer-for-essential-genes-prediction as bacformer-masked-complete-genomes finetuned on the essential-genes prediction task. The README also records that a bug in the Bacformer Large code on Hugging Face was fixed on 2025-05-15 and that models downloaded or cached before that date should be downloaded again, which matters for this checkpoint.

profile.summary: bacformer-masked-MAG is one released checkpoint of Bacformer, a model that treats a whole bacterial genome as a sequence of proteins ordered along the chromosome and plasmids. Each protein is embedded with the base protein language model ESM-2 t12 35M and the averaged embedding is used as one token, so the transformer returns, for every protein, a representation that depends on the other proteins in the same genome. This checkpoint was trained with a masked objective, predicting the protein family of masked proteins, on the MAG corpus of about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: opening section and Training Data; README opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein sequence of a genome is first embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector per protein. Those vectors are the tokens of a transformer of 12 layers and hidden size 480, which attends over all proteins of the genome and so returns contextual protein embeddings. Position is encoded with rotary positional embeddings and learnable contig embeddings mark which chromosome or plasmid each protein came from. The pretraining head does not predict amino acids: it predicts a discrete protein family index out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input stays the exact protein sequence.

sections.title: What distinguishes this checkpoint
sections.body: The model card describes this checkpoint as a 27M-parameter transformer pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes covering more than 20 thousand bacterial species. Its objective is masked: 15 per cent of the proteins are masked and their protein families are predicted from the rest of the genome. It takes protein embeddings from ESM-2 t12 35M.

The README table lists eight checkpoints. It describes bacformer-masked-MAG and bacformer-causal-MAG as 26M parameter models pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, with a masked and an autoregressive objective; bacformer-masked-complete-genomes and bacformer-causal-complete-genomes as those two MAG models finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes; bacformer-large-masked-MAG and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes with the same text, a 300M parameter model pretrained on the MAG corpus with a masked objective; bacformer-causal-protein-family-modeling-complete-genomes as bacformer-causal-MAG finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes with protein-family tokens as input; and bacformer-for-essential-genes-prediction as bacformer-masked-complete-genomes finetuned on the essential-genes prediction task. import torch

]

    max_n_proteins=6000,
)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = masked_model(**inputs, return_dict=True)
print(outputs.keys())
PY

profile.summary: gLM2 is a genomic language model that reads a stretch of genome as a mixture of two alphabets: protein coding regions as amino acids, and the intergenic sequence between them as nucleotides. Each element is prefixed with a strand token. It is a transformer encoder trained by masked language modelling on the OMG metagenomic corpus, and the authors say its representations carry functional information as well as coevolutionary signals in protein-protein interfaces and genomic regulatory syntax.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Model Description; model card: Model Description; Europe PMC abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: gLM2 is a transformer encoder trained with the masked language modelling objective. The input is a contig written as alternating coding and intergenic elements: coding elements as uppercase amino acids, intergenic elements as lowercase nucleotides, so the two alphabets cannot collide, and each element prefixed by <+> or <-> for the strand. The 650M checkpoint's config gives depth 33, dimension 1280, 20 heads, a SwiGLU feed-forward and a vocabulary of 37 tokens; the 150M checkpoint's config gives depth 30, dimension 640 and 10 heads. Pretraining used 315B tokens with a context length of 4096. An update in September 2024 raised the context from 2048 to 4096 tokens and changed intergenic tokenisation from BPE to per-nucleotide.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model Description, UPDATE(09/2024); model card: Model Description, Training Details; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are published: tattabio/gLM2_150M and tattabio/gLM2_650M. Both cards carry the same September 2024 update note, the same 315B pretraining tokens and the same 4096 context length, and their configs differ in size: depth 33 and dimension 1280 for 650M, depth 30 and dimension 640 for 150M. A result should name which checkpoint was used and its Hugging Face revision, because the September 2024 update changed both the context length and the intergenic tokenisation. This page read the 650M checkpoint at revision 3c4037ae and the 150M checkpoint at revision 93c88529.

prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and transformers.

steps.title: Extract embeddings for a contig
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained('tattabio/gLM2_650M', torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, trust_remote_code=True).cuda()
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('tattabio/gLM2_650M', trust_remote_code=True)

# A contig with two proteins and an inter-genic sequence.
# NOTE: Nucleotides should always be lowercase, and prepended with `<+>`.
sequence = "<+>MALTKVEKRNRIKRRVRGKISGTQASPRLSVYKSNK<+>aatttaaggaa<->MLGIDNIERVKPGGLELVDRLVAVNRVTKVTKGGRAFGFSAIVVVGNED"

# Tokenize the sequence.
encodings = tokenizer([sequence], return_tensors='pt')

# Extract embeddings.
with torch.no_grad():
    embeddings = model(encodings.input_ids.cuda(), output_hidden_states=True).last_hidden_state
PY

profile.summary: BioEmu-2 is a generative model from Microsoft Research that produces three dimensional all-atom structures for a biomolecular system given its chemical composition. Rather than returning a single predicted structure, it samples an ensemble of plausible structures by reverse diffusion, so a user can look at how a system moves between states; it can also propagate a set of sampled structures forward in time. The input is one or more biomolecular sequences, optionally with a multiple sequence alignment, contact conditioning and method conditioning, and systems may contain proteins, nucleic acids, ligands and other chemical components.
profile.summary_source_locator: MODEL_CARD.md: opening paragraph and Model summary table; README.md: Key features

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model card describes BioEmu-2 as a diffusion-based all-atom score model with approximately 500M parameters. Structures are generated by reverse diffusion from noise, conditioned on the chemical composition of the system and optionally on an alignment, on contacts between specific atoms and on a method label. Because sampling is generative, the same input can be sampled many times to give an ensemble rather than one answer, and the authors say structure prediction can be guided by user-supplied information about distances between specific atoms. The code also offers steering samplers that favour structures with chosen properties, and an implicit transfer operator mode that generates a structure a chosen lag time later.
sections.source_locator: MODEL_CARD.md: Model summary and Key model capabilities; README.md: Key features and Steer sampling

sections.title: What it was trained on
sections.body: The model card lists the training sets with the number of training sequences or systems in each. Experimental structures come from the PDB in the Boltz-1 preprocessing (189,745 systems). Seven sets of molecular dynamics trajectories generated inside Microsoft contribute between 170 and 7,164 systems each. The largest contributions are AI-predicted structures: 7,231,107 AFDB monomers, 753,271 AFDB homodimer multiconformation systems, 22,157 AFDB heterodimer systems and 50,651 Teddymer systems. The card states that training used only publicly available data and data generated in-house by Microsoft, and that the training dates were August to September 2026.
sections.source_locator: MODEL_CARD.md: Training data table and paragraph, Model summary table

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, named bioemu2-preview, which load_model downloads by default from the microsoft/bioemu2 repository on Hugging Face. The model card gives no version number for the model itself, states a release date of October 2026 and says the same checkpoint was used for every benchmark it reports. A result should therefore name the code commit, the checkpoint name and the Hugging Face revision; this page read code at commit 8d4a2b7238716a94543ceaf411dfe32f99c1ae7c and the Hugging Face repository at revision dd4b0c1b69984b68edcb6200a544213be4d75242. Sampling is stochastic, so a reproducible run must also fix the sampler and the number of samples; the checkpoint documentation shows the precision defaults, which can be changed to full precision.

strengths.text: It returns an ensemble rather than one structure, so different conformations of the same system can be compared.
Systems are not limited to single proteins: multi-chain complexes, nucleic acids, ligands and other chemical components are supported.
strengths.source_locator: MODEL_CARD.md: opening paragraph; README.md: Key features

strengths.text: Both code and the checkpoint are MIT licensed and the Hugging Face repository is not gated, so there is no access request to make.
Large systems can be sampled across several GPUs: context parallelism splits the pair representations over a square mesh of devices.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Sample large structures across multiple GPUs

limitations.text: Linux and an NVIDIA GPU are required; macOS and Windows are not supported, and the smallest device the developers tested the model on was an 80 GB A100.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: System requirements; MODEL_CARD.md: Technical requirements

limitations.text: Sampling frequencies are not calibrated probabilities: the model card says they must not be read as Boltzmann probabilities or quantitative free energies, and that binding affinity prediction is out of scope.
limitations.source_locator: MODEL_CARD.md: Known limitations and Out-of-scope use cases

limitations.text: Quality depends on the alignment and on how well the system is represented in the training data: the card expects worse results for shallow or poor alignments, including orphan proteins, engineered constructs and some viral proteins, and says performance on under-represented sequence classes is uncertain.

It is a research release. The card states it is not intended or validated for clinical or patient decisions and that commercial or real-world use is not recommended without further testing, and outputs should be treated as computational hypotheses.

run_guide.summary: Install BioEmu2 on a Linux GPU machine and sample eight equilibrium conformations of adenylate kinase from its PDB entry.
prerequisites: Linux with an NVIDIA GPU; macOS and Windows are not supported.
Python 3.12, 3.13 or 3.14. The developers tested and evaluated benchmark metrics with Python 3.12.
A GPU of compute capability 7.5 or newer for the cuda extra, or 7.0 with the cuda12 extra; the smallest device the developers tested was an 80 GB A100.
Network access: the checkpoint is downloaded from Hugging Face on first use.
At least four GPUs if context-parallel sampling is needed for a system that does not fit on one device.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/bioemu2.git
cd bioemu2
git checkout --detach 8d4a2b7238716a94543ceaf411dfe32f99c1ae7c
steps.explanation: The README's install commands are run from the repository root, so the clone and the checkout of the commit this page read were added here.

steps.title: Create and activate a virtual environment
steps.shell:
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
steps.explanation: The README recommends an isolated environment and gives these two commands for creating one from the repository root.

steps.title: Install with the CUDA extra
steps.shell: python -m pip install ".[cuda]"
steps.explanation: Installs BioEmu2 for GPUs of compute capability 7.5 or newer. On compute capability 7.0, such as a V100, the README gives the cuda12 extra with the PyTorch CUDA 12.6 index instead.

steps.title: Sample an equilibrium ensemble
steps.shell:
bioemu2 sample-equilibrium \
  --pdb-id 1AKE \
  --out outputs/adk
steps.explanation: The README's quick start command. It downloads the bioemu2-preview checkpoint on first use and samples eight equilibrium conformations of adenylate kinase into the output directory.

steps.title: Predict a single folded structure
steps.shell:
bioemu2 predict-structure \
  --pdb-id 1UBQ \
  --num-samples 1 \
  --out outputs/ubiquitin
steps.explanation: The README's second quick start command, for the structure prediction mode rather than ensemble sampling. Run bioemu2 --help to list all commands.

outputs: samples.xtc and topology.cif in each output directory, written by the sampling commands.
A cached copy of the bioemu2-preview checkpoint in the Hugging Face cache; the log reports where it was stored.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
Sampling is stochastic: repeated runs give different structures unless the sampler and seed are fixed.
The commands assume a supported Linux machine with an NVIDIA GPU; the README states macOS and Windows are not supported.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: AlphaGenome progressively downsamples DNA with convolutional blocks, then uses a transformer tower and pairwise interaction blocks to represent long-range context. A U-Net-style decoder restores sequence resolution using skip connections. Modality-specific heads predict one-dimensional genomic tracks, splicing outputs and two-dimensional contact maps.

The output consists of sampled complex structures; the default command produces five predictions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT-2 merges recurring DNA substrings into byte-pair tokens, then processes those tokens with a masked-language-model transformer. ALiBi supplies distance-dependent attention biases, while FlashAttention changes how attention is computed. The resulting contextual embeddings need an explicit pooling rule and prediction head for a downstream task.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESMFold predicts protein structures directly from amino-acid sequence using ESM-2 representations. ESM-2 sequence representations feed a folding trunk and structure module. The checked v1 configuration has 48 trunk blocks, eight structure-module blocks and up to four recycles. The documented inputs are protein amino-acid sequence; the ESMFold interface also accepts chains separated by a colon. The output consists of predicted PDB structure and confidence values.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens. Two graph encoders represent gene coexpression and Gene Ontology perturbation similarity. Perturbation embeddings are composed with gene embeddings, then a cross-gene network and gene-specific decoders predict expression changes. The documented inputs are single-cell expression data, perturbation labels and the graph resources used by the configured model. The output consists of predicted gene-expression responses and genetic-interaction analyses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MIMIC represents DNA, RNA, protein and associated molecular measurements in a shared multimodal model. Transformer encoder-decoder: 20 encoder layers and 12 decoder layers, width 1,536, rotary positional embeddings, mixed attention and five register tokens. The documented inputs are co-observed molecular modalities and optional text context, grouped into nucleic, protein and text tracks. The output consists of embeddings or generated modalities, such as residue solvent accessibility or splice-site classes.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProteinMPNN converts a supplied backbone into a graph whose edges encode interatomic distances. Message-passing layers update node and edge features, and an autoregressive decoder samples amino acids while conditioning on the backbone and previously assigned residues. Fixed residues, tied positions and chain choices change the design task and must accompany its result.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RhoFold+ predicts RNA three-dimensional structures from RNA sequence with alignment information. RNA-FM embeddings and MSA representations enter the Rhoformer transformer stack; a geometry-aware invariant-point-attention structure module predicts frames and torsion angles with recycling. The documented inputs are RNA FASTA (A, U, G, C), optionally a supplied MSA; an MSA is otherwise generated by the full workflow. The output consists of three-dimensional PDB models, predicted distograms, secondary structure and per-residue confidence.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-FM converts an RNA sequence into one token per nucleotide. Twelve transformer encoder blocks use self-attention to produce a 640-dimensional representation at each position. During pretraining, the model learns to recover masked nucleotides from their surrounding sequence. The resulting representations can be supplied to a separately specified downstream model; they are not, by themselves, a structure or functional prediction.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: scFoundation embeds gene identity and continuous expression together with source and target read-depth indicators. Its encoder processes only nonzero, unmasked genes. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpliceAI reads one-hot-encoded DNA through dilated convolutional residual blocks. Skip connections combine features at different depths, and a softmax layer assigns acceptor, donor or neither probabilities to the central positions. The 10kb version requires 5kb of sequence on each side of a scored position; variant scoring compares the reference and alternate predictions.

profile.summary: LangCell is a single-cell language model trained on pairs of single-cell transcriptomes and text descriptions of cell identity. It places cells and text in one shared feature space, so it can annotate cell types zero-shot by matching a cell against text descriptions of candidate types, as well as after few-shot training or fine-tuning.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Checkpoint; arXiv Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LangCell has a cell encoder and a text encoder. The cell encoder is initialised from a pre-trained Geneformer and takes Geneformer-style tokenised cells, with a [CLS] token whose embedding is projected into the shared space. The text encoder is initialised from PubMedBERT and has a cross-attention mode that scores whether a cell and a text match. Pre-training jointly optimises four losses: masked gene modelling, cell-cell contrastive learning, cell-text contrastive learning and cell-text matching. It runs in two stages: first the cell encoder alone with the first two losses, then all four.
sections.source_locator: arXiv Sections 3 and 4.1; README.md: Checkpoint

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is distributed as a Google Drive folder, split into five modules: text_bert, cell_bert, text_proj, cell_proj and ctm_head. cell_bert is a standard Hugging Face BertModel and can be used alone as LangCell-CE. The checkpoint has no version label or hash in the README, so a result should name the repository commit and the date the checkpoint was downloaded.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Checkpoint; Usage

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Cell identity understanding, mainly cell type annotation: zero-shot from text descriptions, few-shot, and fine-tuning of the cell encoder. Text descriptions of new cell types can be written following the OBO Foundry examples the authors provide.

profile.summary: scCello is a transcriptome foundation model for single-cell RNA-seq data. It reads a cell as a list of genes ordered by expression and outputs a cell representation (and masked-gene predictions). During pre-training it also uses each cell's cell-type label and the cell ontology graph, so that cells of the same or related types end up close together.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Overview; arXiv 2408.12373 Abstract and Section 2.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: scCello is a stack of transformer encoder layers. Each cell's genes are normalised and ranked by expression (rank value encoding, taken from Geneformer) and fed in as a sequence of gene tokens. Pre-training minimises four losses together: masked gene prediction as in BERT, an intra-cellular cell-type coherence loss that pulls cells of the same type together, an inter-cellular relational alignment loss that uses similarities between cell types computed on the cell ontology graph, and a regularisation term.
sections.source_locator: arXiv 2408.12373 Sections 2.1 to 2.5; Appendix D

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README names one pre-trained checkpoint on Hugging Face, katarinayuan/scCello-zeroshot. The README loads the same checkpoint both for zero-shot use and, with a classification head, for linear probing. The checkpoint repository holds config.json and pytorch_model.bin and no model card. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision, and the repository commit used to run it.

name: UCE (Universal Cell Embeddings)
description: Single-cell foundation model producing cell embeddings from protein-embedded gene tokens.

version.note: Checkpoint not named in the article text read

attributes.provenance_note: Model details as given in the cell-type annotation comparison, Table 1.

profile.summary: UCE (Universal Cell Embeddings) is a foundation model that maps single-cell RNA-seq profiles from any tissue or species into one shared embedding space. It takes raw counts plus protein language model embeddings of the genes, and outputs a cell embedding without any labelling, training or fine-tuning on the new dataset.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper Abstract and Fig. 1 legend; README.md: Output

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For each cell UCE draws a weighted sample of expressed genes (1,024 genes, with replacement). Each gene is represented by the ESM2 embedding of its protein product, so any protein-coding gene from any species can be represented from sequence. Genes are sorted by genomic location and grouped by chromosome with start and end tokens, then passed through a transformer. The cell embedding is the final-layer output of a CLS token. Training masks some expressed genes and asks a network, given the cell embedding and a gene's protein embedding, whether that gene was expressed.
sections.source_locator: Paper Fig. 1 legend; Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained models are on Figshare: 4layer_model.torch, which the script uses by default, and 33l_8ep_1024t_1280.torch, the 33-layer model from the paper. Embeddings from the two are not compatible with each other. Figshare article 24320806 is at version 5. A result should name the model file, the Figshare version and the repository commit.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Embedding a new dataset, Data; Figshare API response

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Zero-shot embedding of new single-cell datasets, for example to build integrated atlases or to transfer a cell type classifier to a new dataset. The authors used it to build the Integrated Mega-scale Atlas of 36 million cells.

strengths.text: Zero-shot: new datasets are embedded without labels, training or fine-tuning.
Genes are represented by protein embeddings, so the authors state any protein-coding gene from any species can be represented, including species not in the training data.
Code and weights carry permissive licences (MIT and CC BY 4.0), and the embedding script downloads the default model files itself.

limitations.text: Only 1,024 genes are sampled per cell, fewer than some cells express; the authors tie this to the quadratic cost of attention.
The 4-layer and 33-layer models give incompatible embeddings, and the paper's datasets were embedded with the 33-layer model.
Large downloads: the 33-layer model file is 5,686,283,829 bytes and the protein embeddings archive 2,735,410,523 bytes. The README sizes batches for an 80GB GPU.
Gene names must be symbols, not Ensembl IDs.

profile.summary: AlphaFold 3 predicts three-dimensional structures of complexes containing proteins, nucleic acids and other molecular components. It combines a Pairformer representation network with an atomic-coordinate diffusion model. This entry describes the model and local implementation; the hosted AlphaFold Server has a separate profile.
profile.summary_source_locator: Abstract; Model architecture; README: Installation and Usage

sections.title: Joint structure prediction
sections.body: Sequence, chemical and evolutionary features feed a Pairformer, which builds representations of individual tokens and their relationships. A diffusion module then predicts atomic coordinates. Separate heads estimate confidence. The paper describes 48 Pairformer blocks; the architecture models complexes jointly rather than treating every partner as a separately folded structure.
sections.source_locator: Main text: Model architecture; Fig. 1d and Fig. 2

sections.title: Training and evaluation context
sections.body: The standard model uses a structural training cutoff of 30 September 2021. The dedicated PoseBusters Methods section reports a separate model with a 30 September 2019 cutoff, although other training passages disagree (see limitations). Model seeds, templates, input information and ranking also affect the reported comparison; paper evaluation variants are not automatically identical to current downloadable weights.
sections.source_locator: Main paper Methods: Training regime, Inference regime and PoseBusters; supplement Section 5.2

sections.title: Local access
sections.body: The pinned repository provides inference code and a direct Google-hosted weights download. Its README is more current on access than the server FAQ, which still describes an application form. Code and model parameters have different licences; the server output terms should not be substituted for the local weights terms.
sections.source_locator: README: Obtaining Model Parameters and Licences; LICENSE; weights terms: Key things to know; FAQ: model access

sections.title: Training data and provenance
sections.body: Training combines experimental PDB structures with approximately 41 million predicted protein monomers, about 25,000 disorder-focused protein complexes and about 65,000 predicted RNA structures. The supplement also lists transcription-factor examples used during fine-tuning. Its sequence-search resources include UniRef90, UniProt, BFD/Uniclust30, MGnify, Rfam and RNAcentral. These resources have different versions and dates: the structural training cutoff is not a cutoff for every sequence database.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT-2 merges recurring DNA substrings into byte-pair tokens, then processes those tokens with a masked-language-model transformer. ALiBi supplies distance-dependent attention biases, while FlashAttention changes how attention is computed. The resulting contextual embeddings need an explicit pooling rule and prediction head for a downstream task.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESMFold predicts protein structures directly from amino-acid sequence using ESM-2 representations. ESM-2 sequence representations feed a folding trunk and structure module. The checked v1 configuration has 48 trunk blocks, eight structure-module blocks and up to four recycles. The documented inputs are protein amino-acid sequence; the ESMFold interface also accepts chains separated by a colon. The output consists of predicted PDB structure and confidence values.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: esmfold_v0 and esmfold_v1; v1 is the repository recommendation. Inference length is constrained by memory; the repository documents chunking and CPU offload. Backbone position settings do not alone establish the full folding pipeline limit.

profile.summary: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens.
profile.summary_source_locator: GEARS paper Methods: Overview, Gene coexpression graph encoder, GO graph, Cross-gene effects and gene-specific decoder; gears/model.py: GEARS_Model

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens. Two graph encoders represent gene coexpression and Gene Ontology perturbation similarity. Perturbation embeddings are composed with gene embeddings, then a cross-gene network and gene-specific decoders predict expression changes. The documented inputs are single-cell expression data, perturbation labels and the graph resources used by the configured model. The output consists of predicted gene-expression responses and genetic-interaction analyses.

profile.summary: MSAlign retrieves candidate molecules from tandem mass spectra by aligning pretrained molecular and spectral representations.
profile.summary_source_locator: MSAlign paper Section 3 Architecture and Training, Section 4 on splitting, and Section 5.1 Experimental Setting

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MSAlign retrieves candidate molecules from tandem mass spectra by aligning pretrained molecular and spectral representations. Frozen DreaMS and ChemBERTa encoders connected by lightweight MLP projections trained with a candidate-based contrastive objective. The documented inputs are MS/MS spectrum and a set of candidate molecular structures. The output consists of candidate-molecule retrieval scores in a shared representation space.

profile.summary: Nucleotide Transformer is a family of DNA encoders pretrained on human or multispecies sequence corpora.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/nucleotide_transformer.md: Model Variants and Sizes, Tokenization and How to use; Nucleotide Transformer paper Methods: Architecture, Pre-training datasets and Training

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Nucleotide Transformer is a family of DNA encoders pretrained on human or multispecies sequence corpora. Encoder-only transformers with 6-mer tokens; v1 uses learned positional encodings and v2 uses rotary positions and SwiGLU. The documented inputs are DNA sequences tokenized into 6-mers, with single-base handling of N and remainder bases. The output consists of contextual representations used in specified downstream prediction workflows.

sections.body: OpenFold is a trainable PyTorch implementation of AlphaFold 2 and AlphaFold-Multimer workflows. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Pangolin predicts splice-site strength and changes caused by genetic variants. Dilated convolutional network with 16 residual blocks and skip connections; separate probability and usage outputs for heart, liver, brain and testis. The documented inputs are VCF or CSV variants, reference FASTA and matching gene annotations; custom sequence inference is also available. The output consists of predicted increases/decreases in splice-site strength and their positions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProteinMPNN converts a supplied backbone into a graph whose edges encode interatomic distances. Message-passing layers update node and edge features, and an autoregressive decoder samples amino acids while conditioning on the backbone and previously assigned residues. Fixed residues, tied positions and chain choices change the design task and must accompany its result.

profile.summary: RNA-FM learns contextual representations of RNA nucleotides for downstream RNA analyses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-FM converts an RNA sequence into one token per nucleotide. Twelve transformer encoder blocks use self-attention to produce a 640-dimensional representation at each position. During pretraining, the model learns to recover masked nucleotides from their surrounding sequence. The resulting representations can be supplied to a separately specified downstream model; they are not, by themselves, a structure or functional prediction.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The nucleotide-based rna_fm_t12 and codon-based mrna_fm_t12 interfaces are distinct. The original RNA-FM paper sets a training input-length limit of 1,024 and describes a usable limit of 1,022 nucleotides. That limit should not be assigned to mRNA-FM without checking its separate configuration.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SegmentNT labels genomic elements at individual nucleotide positions using a pretrained DNA backbone. name: SpliceAI
description: Splicing effect prediction

profile.summary: SpliceAI annotates sequence variants with predicted splice acceptor and donor changes.
profile.summary_source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpliceAI reads one-hot-encoded DNA through dilated convolutional residual blocks. Skip connections combine features at different depths, and a softmax layer assigns acceptor, donor or neither probabilities to the central positions. The 10kb version requires 5kb of sequence on each side of a scored position; variant scoring compares the reference and alternate predictions.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper studies 80nt, 400nt, 2kb and 10kb receptive spans. Variant scoring averages five independently trained models; these are not five different assay results. SpliceAI-10k uses 5,000 flanking bases on each side. An input of length l + 10,000 produces predictions for l central positions; receptive span is distinct from maximum input length.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

description: Protein language model in the TAPE benchmark: two three-layer LSTMs with 1,024 hidden units for the forward and backward directions, pretrained by next-token prediction.

profile.summary: The TAPE LSTM baseline represents protein sequences using recurrent networks that read residues in both directions.
profile.summary_source_locator: tape/models/modeling_lstm.py: configuration and model classes; README.md: opening maintenance warning, Examples and Data; June 2019 TAPE preprint Sections 4.1,5 and AppendixA.3

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The TAPE LSTM baseline represents protein sequences using recurrent networks that read residues in both directions. Bidirectional recurrent protein encoder with three forward and three reverse LSTM layers in the default implementation. The documented inputs are amino-acid sequence in the tokenizer expected by the selected implementation. The output consists of residue/sequence representations and predictions from the chosen task head.

name: TAPE ResNet
description: Protein language model in the TAPE benchmark: a dilated residual network of 35 blocks, each with two convolutional layers of 256 filters, kernel size 9 and dilation rate 2, pretrained by masked-token prediction.

profile.summary: The TAPE ResNet baseline represents protein sequences using residual convolutional blocks before a task-specific prediction head.
profile.summary_source_locator: tape/models/modeling_resnet.py: configuration and model classes; README.md: opening maintenance warning, Examples and Data; June 2019 TAPE preprint Sections 4.1,5 and AppendixA.3

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The TAPE ResNet baseline represents protein sequences using residual convolutional blocks before a task-specific prediction head. The June 2019 preprint uses 35 residual blocks with two dilated convolutions each, 256 filters and kernel width 9. The later PyTorch defaults use30 layers and width 512. The documented inputs are amino-acid sequence in the tokenizer expected by the selected implementation. The output consists of residue/sequence representations and predictions from the chosen task head.

name: TAPE Transformer
description: Protein language model in the TAPE benchmark: a 12-layer Transformer with 512 hidden units and 8 attention heads (about 38 million parameters), pretrained by masked-token prediction.

profile.summary: The TAPE Transformer learns contextual protein representations using masked-residue pretraining and a task-specific prediction head.
profile.summary_source_locator: tape/models/modeling_bert.py: configuration and model classes; README.md: opening maintenance warning, Examples and Data; June 2019 TAPE preprint Sections 4.1,5 and AppendixA.3

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The TAPE Transformer learns contextual protein representations using masked-residue pretraining and a task-specific prediction head. The June 2019 preprint uses 12 transformer layers, width 512 and eight heads (38M parameters). The later PyTorch BertConfig defaults to width 768 and 12 heads; these are different configurations. The documented inputs are amino-acid sequence in the tokenizer expected by the selected implementation. The output consists of residue/sequence representations and predictions from the chosen task head.
sections.source_locator: tape/models/modeling_bert.py: configuration and model classes; README.md: opening maintenance warning, Examples and Data; June 2019 TAPE preprint Sections 4.1,5 and AppendixA.3

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: June 2019 TAPE preprint configurations and the later PyTorch package are distinct; the current README warns it is not an exact reproduction. The inspected default BertConfig sets max_position_embeddings to 8,096; this is an implementation default, not evidence that a historical TAPE checkpoint was trained at that length.

profile.summary: BERTax reads a DNA sequence and says which part of the tree of life it came from, without comparing it to a database of known genomes. It is a BERT model: the sequence is cut into overlapping three letter tokens and a transformer encoder reads them, and classification layers on top predict superkingdom, phylum and, in the released version, genus. The point of the method is novel organisms: when no close relative exists in a reference database, similarity search degrades, while BERTax works from the statistics of the sequence itself.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Significance, Introduction, Materials and Methods; README.md: Usage, Training BERTax models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Training has two steps. First a BERT encoder is pretrained without labels on genomic fragments of a fixed length of 1,500 nucleotides, each cut into 500 three letter tokens and presented as two sentences of 250 tokens. Then the model is fine-tuned for classification: the [CLS] token output goes to three taxonomy layers in what the authors call the all-in-one architecture, where each rank's prediction also sees the higher ranks. The authors compared flat, nested and all-in-one arrangements and found all-in-one best. Fine-tuning ran for at most 16 epochs with early stopping, and class weights per rank to stop the model favouring frequent classes. At prediction time each rank also has an unknown class, used when a sequence looks unlike any trained class.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Pretraining and Architectures, Results; README.md: Usage note on unknown

sections.title: What it can classify
sections.body: Four superkingdoms (archaea, bacteria, eukaryota and viruses), and a fixed list of phyla and genera that the README prints without giving counts. Anything outside those lists is likely to come back as unknown, and the authors say so plainly. The README also carries their recommendation to use BERTax for superkingdom and phylum, with genus possible but weaker, and points at the separate training repository for building a model that covers other taxa.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Compatible phyla and genera, Training BERTax models; Paper: Introduction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published tool is one model: the downloadable version, built on the all-in-one architecture, trained on what the paper calls the final model dataset, and the only version that predicts genus as well. The weights are a single file, big_trainingset_all_fix_classes_selection.h5, distributed through the repository's latest release, and the tool is also packaged as a conda package and a Docker image. The paper additionally describes models trained on a closely related and a distantly related dataset, used for its comparisons; those are not the released tool. A result should name the model file, the sequence splitting mode and the window settings, since long sequences are chunked and the chunk predictions are averaged by default.

profile.summary: DeepMicrobes assigns short metagenomic sequencing reads to a species or a genus. It reads a sequence as a bag of 12-mers, embeds them, passes them through a bidirectional LSTM with self-attention, and outputs a label with a confidence score; read level labels are then turned into an abundance profile. Its motivation is metagenome assembled genomes: species found by assembly have no curated place in a taxonomic tree, which standard classifiers need, and DeepMicrobes is trained directly on such genome collections instead.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction, Materials and Methods; document/prediction.md; README.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A read is tokenised into k-mers, with 12 as the length used unless stated otherwise, and complementary k-mers share one embedding vector, which is why the vocabulary files are described as merged. The embedded tokens go through a bidirectional LSTM and a multi-head self-attention layer, which the authors found to be the best of seven architectures they built; the others, kept in the repository, are a ResNet-like CNN, a CNN plus LSTM hybrid, Seq2species, and embed plus pool, CNN or LSTM variants. Reads are classified in pairs: the tutorial takes interleaved paired-end reads and the authors recommend paired-end mode as more accurate than single-end. The output per pair is a label and a confidence score, and a separate step turns those into a species or genus profile.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Materials and Methods; document/prediction.md; document/tfrecord.md: Prediction; DeepMicrobes-data README: Vocabulary

sections.title: Training data and compute
sections.body: The species model was trained on reads simulated from 2505 representative genomes of human gut species, most of them identified by metagenome assembly, together with the taxonomy above species level. Reads were simulated with ART using a HiSeq 2500 error model, paired-end with an insert size of 400 and a standard deviation of 50 bp, then trimmed from the 3 prime end to between 75 and 150 bp with equal probability, and each read labelled by its species or genus. A pair was treated as two single-end reads during training. Training used TensorFlow on an NVIDIA Tesla P40 24GB GPU, with 30 randomly sampled hyperparameter settings per architecture and the best chosen on an evaluation set.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, training set construction, implementation

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two things vary and must be named in any result: the taxonomic level, because the species and genus models are separate weight sets and the level flag has to match the weights, and the architecture, because the repository ships seven of them behind a --model_name option. The README also states that a new beta version is available, without a version number. No tag or release listing was saved, so whether a release carries the weights was not checked. The vocabulary file must match the k-mer length used, and the 12-mer vocabulary is the one the pretrained models use.

profile.summary: GeNet classifies shotgun metagenomic reads from raw DNA, without a similarity search against a reference database. It is a convolutional network: the bases of a read are embedded along with their positions, a ResNet style encoder reads them, and the output layers predict several taxonomic ranks at once, each rank's prediction able to see the one above it. The authors also use the network as a feature extractor, reporting that a linear model on top of its representations works for pathogen detection.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A read is turned into two embeddings, one for the base and one for its position, over a vocabulary of six symbols, and a one hot encoding is also built. A convolutional encoder follows, made of ResNet blocks that downsample when the block changes and double the filter count, with the number of blocks, the filter count and the filter size set by command line flags. The taxonomy is the part that distinguishes the method: the output has one group of units per rank and, with connect_softmax set, the softmax activations of the higher rank are fed into the next, so the hierarchy between labels is used during training. Class weights per rank are applied through a one hot mask over the units of that rank.
sections.source_locator: code/network.py: embeddings, resnet_block, build_conv_encoder, weights; code/genet_train.py: flags and Config; arXiv abstract

sections.title: Training configuration and data
sections.body: The defaults in the training script are one ResNet block, 128 filters in the first convolution, a filter size of 3 in the row dimension, 1024 fully connected units, a batch size of 64, a read length of 10000, an initial learning rate of 1.0 and a simulated quality score of 15. The flag help gives the acceptance probability as 10 to the power minus the score over ten, while the code computes one minus that value. The configuration also fixes a vocabulary of 6 and an output vocabulary of 100. The repository ships the NCBI taxonomy nodes file and three id lists, for the training microbes, the full set and a pathogen set, and the README says the first run downloads the required genomes from NCBI.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one code release and no published weights: training writes its own weights and tensorboard log into GeNet/saved_models. The repository has no licence file and the GitHub API returns a null licence field. A result must name the flags, because the architecture is built from them, and the id list used, since the training set is the csv file named by dataset_list. The sources read give no model card, no release tag and no checkpoint download. A third party benchmark, the MetageNN paper, reports retraining GeNet and extending its capacity to match their own model, so figures attributed to GeNet elsewhere may refer to that extended version rather than to the published configuration.

strengths.text: It uses the taxonomy during training rather than treating labels as flat, and the code exposes that as a switch: the higher rank's softmax can be connected to the next rank's output group.

The authors report competitive precision and good recall against Kraken and Centrifuge with orders of magnitude less memory, on datasets where a distribution shift occurs. These are their own claims in the abstract.

Its representations are reusable: the authors report over 90 per cent accuracy in a pathogen detection problem from a linear model on top of the learned features, and the repository ships the pathogen id list.

strengths.text: Getting started is short: one install script, one taxonomy extraction, one training command, and the genomes are fetched automatically on the first run.

limitations.text: No trained weights are released and there is no prediction script in the repository: the code provided is for training on the paper's dataset.

Training is set up for a GPU and long reads: the default read length is 10000 bases, which fixes the positional embedding matrix, and the script takes a GPU count.

name: MetageNN
description: Feed-forward neural network on 6-mer profiles of 1 kbp sequences sampled from reference genomes; long reads are split into 1 kbp chunks and classified by majority vote at genus level.

profile.summary: MetageNN assigns long sequencing reads to a genus. It does not align the read against a database: it counts short k-mers, 6-mers in the published setup, and feeds that profile to a neural network. The reason for using short k-mers is that they survive the high error rate of nanopore reads, which lets the model be trained on clean reference genome fragments and still work on noisy reads. Long reads are cut into 1 kbp chunks and the chunk predictions are combined by majority vote.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results, Methods; README.md: opening paragraph, Counting k-mers

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Training sequences of fixed length, 1 kbp in the published work, are sampled from reference genomes. Each sequence is turned into a profile of canonical 6-mer counts with the Phylopythia k-mer counting tool, and that vector is the model input: the settings file for the main database gives a k-mer dimension of 6144 and a layer width of 3000, trained for 500 epochs at a learning rate of 0.001 with class weighting and a batch size of 1024. At prediction time a long read is split into non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks, each chunk is classified, and a majority vote decides the read's genus, with ties broken by the highest mean probability and predictions below a probability of 0.5 left unclassified.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Counting k-mers, Settings; settings/MetageNN_settings_main_database.json; Paper: Methods, Results

sections.title: Databases and training
sections.body: Two reference sets are used. The small database holds 47 genomes, from which about 235,000 sequences of 1 kbp were sampled at 1x coverage for the fine-tuning experiments. The main database expands that about ten times by randomly adding RefSeq representative genomes, giving 516 genomes across 505 species and 311 genera; the model for it was trained at 8x coverage with validation on 200 sequences per genome, and its capacity was roughly doubled in neurons per layer. The paper reports about 17 million samples in that training set, four GPUs and convergence by early stopping after three days.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, database construction, training; settings/MetageNN_settings_main_database.json; git tree listing: data lists

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository is a training setup, not a packaged classifier: it holds one training script, two settings files (small and main database), the genome and isolate lists, and a Google Drive link for the small database 1x training set. No trained weights are published, and the README says the preprint is still to be released, while the published paper exists. What a result must name is the database, the coverage, the k-mer length and the settings file, since those are what differ between the two configurations; the k-mer counting command and the vocabulary dimension have to match each other.

strengths.text: Short k-mer profiles are the point: they are less affected by sequencing errors, so a model trained on clean genome fragments transfers to noisy long reads without long-read training data.

The authors report it as small and fast against the tools they compared: less than a quarter of the database storage of Kraken2, MEGAN-LR and MMseqs2, more than 7 times faster than MetaMaps and GeNet. These are their own figures.

The authors report better sensitivity when the reference database is incomplete, which is the case that matters for novel lineages, and they test it with reads from species deliberately left out of the database.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Conclusions; git tree listing: data lists

strengths.text: The record is reproducible in its inputs: the genome lists for both databases, the SRA accessions of the test isolates and the tuned hyperparameter files are all in the repository.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Data, Settings; git tree listing: data, settings

limitations.text: The authors call it a proof of concept, and say it is an alternative approach that can be optimised further rather than a finished tool.

No trained weights and no prediction script are published: the repository has a training script only, so using MetageNN means training it, and the paper's main database model took four GPUs and three days.
