profile.summary: Carbon-X is a 14.8 billion parameter chat language model that reads DNA and English in the same conversation. You paste raw DNA into a message and ask a question; it answers in English, for example whether a mutation is likely benign or pathogenic, which organism group a sequence comes from, or what the next bases are. It was built from the general-purpose Qwen3-14B model by adding DNA tokens and further training on DNA and biology text.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model Summary; Vocabulary extension

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNA and text share one token stream in one decoder, with no separate DNA encoder. A hybrid tokeniser keeps Qwen3's BPE vocabulary for text and encodes DNA as non-overlapping 6-mers, so one DNA token covers 6 base pairs; runs of at least 6 A, C, G or T bases are tagged as DNA automatically. Training had four stages. New DNA embeddings were first trained for about 10B tokens with the transformer frozen. The full model was then mid-trained on 302B tokens at sequence length 8,192, a mixture of 55% raw DNA, 20% English, 15% biology text and 10% instruction data. Supervised fine-tuning followed (3 epochs over 20 dataset subsets), then two rounds of GRPO reinforcement learning with code-checked rewards, all with thinking disabled.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Summary; Tokenizer; Training (Vocabulary extension, Mid-training, Supervised fine-tuning, Reinforcement learning)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The released model is HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X; this page read revision 17de8916. The training pipeline names two intermediate models, Carbon-X-Base (after mid-training) and Carbon-X-SFT (after fine-tuning), and GGUF quantisations exist for llama.cpp. All reported results used thinking disabled and the sampling defaults in generation_config.json (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20), so a result should name the revision, the model variant and any change to these settings. The training recipes, decontamination scripts and evaluation tasks are in the huggingface/carbon repository.

run_guide.summary: Install Transformers, load Carbon-X in bfloat16 on a GPU and ask it whether a variant is likely benign or pathogenic.
prerequisites: A CUDA GPU; the card says the weights fit on a single 80 GB GPU in bfloat16.
Transformers v5 or later, and PyTorch.
Hugging Face Hub access on first load (the tokeniser downloads its BPE vocabulary). The tokeniser is custom code loaded with trust_remote_code=True.
Weights and code are Apache-2.0 and not gated.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: pip install -U transformers
steps.explanation: The model card's install command. The card requires Transformers v5 or later.

steps.title: Ask a variant question
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda")

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": (
            "Reference: ATGGTGCATCTGACTCCTGAGGAGAAGTCTGCCGTTACTGCCCTGTGGGGCAAGG\n"
            "Variant:   ATGGTGCATCTGACTCCTGTGGAGAAGTCTGCCGTTACTGCCCTGTGGGGCAAGG\n\n"
            "Is this variant likely to be benign or pathogenic? Explain your reasoning."
        ),
    }
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    enable_thinking=False,
    return_tensors="pt",
    return_dict=True,
).to(model.device)

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's Python example, unchanged, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the weights on first run and keeps thinking disabled, as the developers recommend.

outputs: The model's English answer on whether the variant is likely benign or pathogenic, with its reasoning, printed to the terminal. Sampling uses the defaults in generation_config.json, so the text can differ between runs.
limitations: These commands were read from the model card and have not been executed by Rewire.
The snippet does not pin a Hugging Face revision; this page was written from revision 17de89165e25c49e7de4f845d0e5d464469de359.
The card also documents serving with vLLM (vllm serve HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X --trust-remote-code) behind an OpenAI-compatible API.

profile.summary: CodonBERT is a language model for the coding regions of mRNA, built by Sanofi for mRNA vaccine and therapeutic design. It reads a coding sequence codon by codon and outputs an embedding for each codon. These embeddings can be fine-tuned to predict properties such as protein expression and mRNA degradation, to help choose among the many mRNA sequences that encode the same protein.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results (first paragraph)

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CodonBERT is a BERT model of 12 bidirectional transformer encoder layers, each with 12 attention heads and hidden size 768. Each codon is one token: five symbols (A, U, G, C, N) in three positions give 125 codons, plus five special tokens, for a vocabulary of 130. The input is a pair of sequences joined by a separator, embedded with codon, position and segment embeddings. Pretraining combined two tasks: masked language modelling over codons, and sequence taxonomy prediction, in which the model predicts whether the two sequences come from the same one of 14 taxonomic categories. For downstream tasks, the embeddings feed additional trainable layers.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Model architecture'; Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained PyTorch model is released, as a single zip file (CodonBERT.zip, 954,923,856 bytes, last modified 8 May 2024) on a Sanofi download server rather than a versioned model hub, so the file has no revision identifier beyond its date. The repository holds pretraining and fine-tuning scripts, the NCBI IDs of all 10 million pretraining sequences, a held-out evaluation set, and the downstream datasets including an internal Sanofi set (MLOS.csv). A result should name the repository commit (451a1b16 read here) and the zip file's date or checksum.

strengths.text: Codon tokens match the unit that matters for coding sequence design, which the authors argue gives better representations.
The pretraining sequence IDs, evaluation split and downstream datasets, including a new internal dataset, are released with the code.
The authors report that CodonBERT outperforms previous mRNA prediction methods, including on a new flu vaccine dataset; this is their claim.

limitations.text: Code and weights are for academic research and non-commercial use by academic or non-profit organisations only.
Coding regions only: inputs must be codon sequences, so UTRs and non-coding RNA are outside its scope, and sequences over 512 codons were split into fragments in pretraining.
The environment is old: Python below 3.11, torch ^1.13.0 and transformers ^4.29.0, managed with Poetry.
The weights are a single zip on a company server with no version identifier, so a later change to the file would not be visible from the URL.

profile.summary: DeCodon is a generative language model for protein-coding DNA that works one codon at a time. Given an NCBI Taxonomy ID for an organism, it writes new coding sequences for that organism. It is the decoder half of the cdsFM suite, released with the encoder model EnCodon, and was pretrained on coding sequences from the NCBI Genomes database.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: introduction; Sequence Generation with DeCodon; bioRxiv abstract; config.json

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tokens are the 64 codons, 5 special tokens and one organism token per NCBI Taxonomy ID listed in the package's taxids.txt; config.json sets vocab_size 1736. DeCodon is loaded as a causal language model: its configuration marks it as a decoder with 12 hidden layers, 16 attention heads, hidden size 1024 and rotary position embeddings. To generate, the wrapper builds a prompt from the organism's taxonomy ID in angle brackets, so the model writes a sequence conditioned on the organism, and stops at the separator token. The same wrapper also offers embedding extraction and variant scoring.

Hugging Face counts 157,988,032 parameters in each, fewer than the 200M in the names. This page read decodon-200M at revision 5c5c3da1 and decodon-200M-euk at revision 89ce8d5c. profile.summary: EnCodon is a language model for protein-coding DNA that reads a coding sequence one codon at a time and returns a numerical embedding of it. The embeddings can be used as features or fine-tuned, and the package also scores codon variants by comparing model probabilities. It is part of the cdsFM suite, released with the generative model DeCodon, and was pretrained on coding sequences from the NCBI Genomes database.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: introduction; Sequence Embedding Extraction with EnCodon; bioRxiv abstract; cdsfm/encodon/_auto.py: score_variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each token is one of the 64 codons or one of 5 special tokens, and a start token and an end token are added around each sequence. EnCodon is loaded as a masked language model with rotary position embeddings. To embed a sequence, the wrapper runs the model, takes the hidden states of a chosen layer and averages them over the codon positions, leaving out the two special tokens. To score a variant, it compares the log probability of the alternative codon with that of the reference codon, either in the wild-type sequence or with the position masked.

profile.summary: GPN-MSA is a DNA language model that scores human single-nucleotide variants genome-wide. It reads a window of the human genome together with the aligned sequence of other vertebrates, and scores a variant by how much less likely the alternate allele is than the reference. Its developers now mark it as deprecated in favour of GPN-Star.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/gpn-msa.md, opening paragraph; model card title; cli.md, GPN section on the output score

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The published checkpoint is a 12-layer Transformer encoder (hidden size 768, 12 attention heads) trained as a masked language model. Each position is given the human nucleotide and the aligned nucleotides of the other species in the whole-genome alignment as auxiliary features, so the model predicts a masked human base from its sequence context and from what other vertebrates carry at the same site. A variant's score is the alternate-minus-reference log-likelihood ratio at its position, averaged over the forward and reverse-complement orientations. Negative values mean the alternate allele is less likely than the reference under the model.
sections.source_locator: config.json: architectures, num_hidden_layers, hidden_size, num_attention_heads, n_aux_features; cli.md: GPN and GPN-MSA sections on the output score; model card title

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One human checkpoint is published, songlab/gpn-msa-sapiens, trained on humans and 89 other vertebrates. The repository supports inference from it and no longer maintains GPN-MSA training or dataset construction. Inference needs a local alignment store whose target assembly, species count, species order and preprocessing match the checkpoint. Genome-wide hg38 scores are published as a dataset, so most uses do not need to run the model. A result should say whether it used the published scores or ran inference, and with which window size.

name: DNABERT-S
description: Species-aware DNA embedding model contrastively fine-tuned from DNABERT-2.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in Bůžková et al. 2026, Table 2.

profile.summary: DNABERT-S is a DNA embedding model that turns a DNA sequence into a single vector so that sequences from the same species end up close together. It starts from the DNABERT-2 genome foundation model and is further trained with contrastive learning on pairs of sequences from the same microbial species. The embeddings are meant for tasks such as species clustering, few-shot species classification and metagenomics binning, where many species have no reference genome.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README: 1. Introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT-S starts from the pretrained DNABERT-2 model and continues training it with contrastive learning on pairs of DNA sequences taken from the same species. Training follows a two-phase curriculum (curriculum contrastive learning): first a Weighted SimCLR objective pulls same-species sequences together and pushes different species apart, then a Manifold Instance Mixup (MI-Mix) objective mixes hidden representations at a randomly chosen layer to make harder examples. The resulting embedding, the mean of the last hidden states, can be clustered or fed to a simple classifier to separate species without reference genomes, for example in metagenomics binning.
sections.source_locator: Paper: abstract, Introduction, Section 3; README: 1. Introduction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one released checkpoint, zhihan1996/DNABERT-S, which this page read at revision 00e47f96. The repository provides the training and evaluation data through gdown links and the scripts used for training, clustering, classification and binning. The README pins transformers 4.27 and suggests uninstalling triton on GPUs other than the A100. The arXiv record has three versions, and the HTML full text read here carries a different title from the README (DNABERT-S: Pioneering Species Differentiation with Species-Aware DNA Embeddings). A result should name the checkpoint revision.

The packages in requirements.txt, including transformers==4.27 and torch. The README suggests uninstalling triton on GPUs other than the A100. The paper reports that the predictions in its species classification comparison took about 1 hour on 2 NVIDIA A100 GPUs; memory needs are not stated.

steps.title: Compute an embedding
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("zhihan1996/DNABERT-S", trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("zhihan1996/DNABERT-S", trust_remote_code=True)

dna = "ACGTAGCATCGGATCTATCTATCGACACTTGGTTATCGATCTACGAGCATCTCGTTAGC"
inputs = tokenizer(dna, return_tensors = 'pt')["input_ids"]
hidden_states = model(inputs)[0] # [1, sequence_length, 768]

# embedding with mean pooling
embedding_mean = torch.mean(hidden_states[0], dim=0)
print(embedding_mean.shape) # expect to be 768
PY

name: GENERATOR
description: Generative transformer decoder DNA language model family with 6-mer tokens and long context (98 kb in the first release, pretrained on eukaryotic DNA; the second version adds prokaryote variants), used for sequence generation, zero-shot variant effect scoring and as a source of embeddings for fine-tuning.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Named in Datta et al. 2026, Section 3, which cites Wu et al. 2025 for GENERATOR.

profile.summary: GENERator is a family of generative DNA language models that read DNA as six-base tokens and predict what comes next, like a text language model. The models handle long inputs (16,384 tokens, given as 98k base pairs in the first release) and are used to generate DNA sequences, score the effect of variants, and provide embeddings for classification tasks. The first release was trained on 386 billion nucleotides of eukaryotic DNA from RefSeq; the v2 series adds new eukaryote models and prokaryote models, at 1.2B and 3B parameters.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper Figure 1 caption, Section 4; v1 card; README

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENERator is a decoder-only transformer, built on the LLaMA framework, that predicts the next 6-mer token of a DNA sequence. Grouping six bases per token lets a 16,384-token window cover long stretches of DNA. The authors compared tokenizers for this autoregressive setting and found 6-mers best, with BPE close to random on their sequence recovery test. For the first release they trained only on gene-centric regions of eukaryotic RefSeq genomes rather than whole genomes, which gave lower loss for the whole-genome model but better downstream results for the gene-centric one. Training sequences start at a random offset of 0 to 5 bases so the model sees different 6-mer framings.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 2.2.1, 4.1, 4.3

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations. The first release (February 2025) has eukaryote models at 1.2B and 3B parameters. The v2 series (November 2025) adds new eukaryote models and prokaryote models at the same two sizes, described in a separate technical report on bioRxiv. The 1.2B configurations of the first release and v2 are identical; the v2 card adds a per-base sequence scoring function. The README asks users of the prokaryote models to re-download weights updated on 2026-07-06. A result should name the full checkpoint name, including v2 and eukaryote or prokaryote, and its Hugging Face revision. This page read GENERator-v2-eukaryote-1.2b-base at revision c41b0018 and GENERator-eukaryote-1.2b-base at revision 5e872c94. The paper gives the 1B model's pretraining compute as 11,776 A100-hours (368 hours on 32 GPUs) in Appendix B and as 11,793 A100-hours in its resource table (Table S16); the two figures conflict and the paper does not explain the difference. Table S16 gives 29,625 A100-hours for the 3B model.
sections.source_locator: README: News; v2 model card; paper Appendix B

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Decoder-only transformer based on the LLaMA framework with a 6-mer tokenizer. The 1.2B configuration (first release and v2 are identical): 26 layers, hidden size 2048, intermediate size 5632, 32 attention heads with 4 key-value heads, vocabulary 4128, RoPE theta 500000. The 3B configurations have 30 layers and hidden size 3072. The paper's Table S12 gives the same figures (26 and 30 layers, hidden size 2048 and 3072, 32 heads with 4 KV heads).

strengths.text: Long context for a transformer: 16,384 6-mer tokens, which the first-release card gives as 98k base pairs.
Fast generation by the authors' measurement: tens of times faster than Evo2 at comparable sizes on one L40S GPU.
Code and weights are MIT licensed and not gated, and the repository has scripts for variant effect prediction, sequence recovery, classification and fine-tuning.

prerequisites: Python 3.10, as the README states, and a CUDA GPU; the card example uses FlashAttention 2 and bfloat16. GPU memory needs are not stated.

steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/GenerTeam/GENERator.git

steps.title: Generate sequences
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-v2-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    attn_implementation="flash_attention_2",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
).cuda().eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-v2-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

# Define input sequences.
sequences = [
    "ATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCG",
    "ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGT"
]

# Truncate each sequence to the nearest multiple of 6
processed_sequences = ["<s>" + seq[len(seq)%6:] for seq in sequences]

# Tokenize the sequences
inputs = tokenizer(
    processed_sequences,
    add_special_tokens=False,
    return_tensors="pt",
    padding=True,
    padding_side="left",
).to("cuda")

# Generate the sequences
with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=32, do_sample=False)

# Decode the generated sequences
decoded_sequences = tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)

# Print the decoded sequences
print(decoded_sequences)
PY

name: Omni-DNA
description: Autoregressive transformer family pretrained on DNA by next-token prediction and then fine-tuned with added task tokens to solve several genomic tasks, including DNA-to-text and DNA-to-image mapping, in one model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Named in Datta et al. 2026, Section 3, which cites Li et al. 2025 for Omni-DNA.

profile.summary: Omni-DNA is a family of generative DNA language models, named by size from 20M to 1B parameters, that read a DNA sequence and predict the next token. After pretraining on multi-species genomes, a single model can be fine-tuned to answer several tasks at once, producing a class label, a text description of function, or image tokens from a DNA input. The base models can also be fine-tuned with a classification head like other genomic foundation models.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Figure 4; README Capabilities; Hugging Face API

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Omni-DNA works in two stages. First, decoder-only transformers based on OLMo are pretrained on DNA alone by next-token prediction. Then a model is fine-tuned on several tasks at once: the tokenizer vocabulary is expanded with new tokens for each task's outputs (class labels, text, or discrete image codes), and the model learns to generate the answer after the input sequence and a task description. To limit the shift in existing tokens caused by vocabulary expansion, the authors use a method they call Important Key Repetition together with NEFTune. Base models can also be fine-tuned in the usual way with a classification head.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Figure 4, Section 3; README: Capabilities

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Six base sizes and three fine-tuned 1B models are released on Hugging Face. The 116M and 1B models use non-parametric layer norm and the other four use RMSNorm. The repository's run.sh lists the commands used to replicate the paper's experiments, including classification fine-tuning and inference with the multi-task, DNA-to-text and DNA-to-image models. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read Omni-DNA-1B at revision 0ea9d54e.
sections.source_locator: Paper Section 3 (LayerNorm); README: Replicating Experiments

name: DNABERT
description: DNA language model with k-mer tokenisation.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Table 1.

profile.summary: DNABERT is a DNA language model that applies the BERT approach from natural language processing to genomic DNA. It reads a DNA sequence of up to 512 tokens, split into k-mers, and is pretrained on the human genome by predicting masked k-mers. Users fine-tune it with a small labelled data set to predict features such as promoters, splice sites and transcription factor binding sites, and can inspect its attention to find motifs and score variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: abstract, Methods 2.2.2; README

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT adapts the BERT language model to DNA. A sequence is cut into k-mers, each base joined with the bases that follow it, and these k-mers become the tokens. During pretraining on human genome sequences, the model sees contiguous spans of k-mers masked (about 15% of the input, raised to 20% for the last 20k of 120k steps) and learns to predict them, so it learns general patterns of DNA from unlabelled data. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned with a small labelled data set for a specific task. The repository adds tools to visualise attention, find motifs and score the effect of sequence variants with a fine-tuned model.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 2.1, 2.2.2; README: sections 5 to 7

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are four pretrained checkpoints, one for each k-mer size from 3 to 6, with the same architecture and settings. The paper reports results with k = 6 because it performed best, and says k = 3 to 6 gave very similar results. The README's download links have expired and point users to the Hugging Face copies. A result should name the k-mer size and the Hugging Face revision; this page read DNA_bert_6 at revision c56e67ea. The repository extends code from Hugging Face transformers and its README sets up a Python 3.6 environment with CUDA 10.0, and the README recommends checking out DNABERT-2 for newer work.

strengths.text: Code is Apache-2.0 and the repository covers the full cycle: pretraining, fine-tuning, prediction, attention visualisation, motif finding and variant scoring.
The authors report that a model pretrained on the human genome can be applied to other organisms after fine-tuning.
Four k-mer sizes are released, so users can choose the tokenisation; the authors found little difference between them.

limitations.text: Input is limited to 512 tokens; longer sequences must be split into pieces.
Trained on the human genome only; the sources read describe no multi-species pretraining. The authors point to DNABERT-2, trained on multi-species genomes, as the successor.
The software stack is old: the README environment uses Python 3.6, CUDA 10.0 and an NVIDIA GPU, and the original model download links have expired.
No licence is stated for the model weights on Hugging Face.

name: RNA-MSM
description: RNA language model pre-trained on multiple sequence alignments.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Table 1.

profile.summary: RNA-MSM is an RNA language model that reads a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of a target RNA and its homologues rather than a single sequence. It outputs a per-nucleotide embedding and attention maps, which the authors use to predict RNA secondary structure (base pairs) and solvent accessibility. The MSA must first be built with a homology search tool such as RNAcmap3.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: About The Project, Data Preparation; paper: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-MSM follows the protein MSA Transformer design: an embedding module with two learned position embeddings, one for the rows (sequences in the MSA) and one for the columns (positions), then 10 transformer blocks with 12 attention heads each and a 768-dimensional embedding. The authors cut the block count from 12 to 10 because of GPU memory. It was trained with the BERT masked language modelling objective, masking 20% of MSA tokens. The 120 attention maps (10 blocks by 12 heads) and the embedding of the query sequence are the outputs; separate downstream networks in the repository turn them into secondary structure and solvent accessibility predictions.
sections.source_locator: paper: Materials and methods; Figure 1 legend; README.md: Inference; RNA_MSM_Inference.py

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained checkpoint is released on Google Drive (RNA_MSM_pretrained.ckpt by the script's default path). The repository also carries trained downstream models for secondary structure and solvent accessibility, and the downstream datasets with their MSAs were released in July 2024. Results depend strongly on the MSA, so a result should name the checkpoint, the repository commit, and the homology search tool and settings used to build the MSA.

name: RNABERT
description: RNA language model pre-trained on small non-coding RNA.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Table 1.

profile.summary: RNABERT is a small RNA language model from Keio University that turns each base of a non-coding RNA sequence into a numerical vector (an embedding) that reflects its sequence context and secondary structure. It reads RNA sequences in FASTA format and outputs per-base embeddings, which the authors use to align RNAs by structure and to cluster them into RNA families.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction; README.md: Data processing, Earn embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each base gets a 120-dimensional token embedding plus a position embedding, and the sum passes through six Transformer layers. The output is a context-sensitive embedding for every base. Training alternates two tasks. In masked language modelling (MLM), some bases are hidden and predicted from the rest. In structural alignment learning (SAL), pairs of sequences from Rfam seed alignments are aligned using their embeddings, so that bases aligned in the reference alignment get similar embeddings. A structural alignment of two RNAs is then computed from the embeddings with the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Figure 2 caption; Introduction; Discussion

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained model file is offered, through a Google Drive link in the README, with no version number. The README says this model was trained on the full Rfam 14.3 dataset (about 400 nucleotides), while the paper describes MLM pre-training on 76 237 human small ncRNAs from RNAcentral and SAL training on Rfam alignments (TrainSet-A or TrainSet-B). Which of the paper's settings the download matches is not stated. A result should cite the repository commit and say that the Google Drive model was used.

name: RNAErnie
description: RNA language model with motif-aware pre-training.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Table 1.

profile.summary: RNAErnie is an RNA language model that turns an RNA sequence into embeddings for downstream prediction. During pretraining it uses known RNA motifs as prior knowledge and masks them at random, alongside the usual masked language modelling. Its developers fine-tune it for RNA sequence classification, RNA-RNA interaction prediction and RNA secondary structure prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The original RNAErnie is built on the ERNIE model in PaddlePaddle and pretrained with masked language modelling on RNAcentral sequences of up to 512 nucleotides. The released checkpoint combines the BERT, ERNIE and motif masking strategies. Downstream, the developers offer an optional two-stage, type-guided fine-tuning. For RNA secondary structure prediction the repository uses a folding module compiled from mxfold2. The authors' later PyTorch checkpoint is a BERT masked language model with 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and an 11-token vocabulary.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Pre-training, Extract RNA Sequence Embeddings, Downstream Tasks; config.json of the PyTorch checkpoint

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two lines of checkpoints. The original PaddlePaddle model from the paper, with masking-strategy variants and task-specific fine-tuned weights, is distributed through Google Drive folders linked from the README; an ad-hoc variant pretrained with an extra classification loss and a 1-epoch checkpoint are also linked. In June 2024 the developers trained a separate PyTorch model from scratch with a maximum length of 2048 on a newer RNAcentral release of about 31 million sequences, and published it on Hugging Face (now LLM-EDA/RNAErnie); its tokenisation differs slightly from the original. A result should say which of these checkpoints was used.

run_guide.summary: Set up the original PaddlePaddle RNAErnie environment and extract embeddings for three example RNA sequences with the pretrained checkpoint.
prerequisites: Conda, and a GPU: the environment installs paddlepaddle-gpu 2.3.2 and the example sets the device to gpu.

The pretrained checkpoint files (.pdparams and .json) downloaded by hand from the Google Drive folder linked in the README and placed in ./output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT so that output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT/checkpoint_final/ exists. The README does not state the folder layout inside the download.
The environment file pins Linux conda builds and a Tsinghua mirror channel, so it may not resolve on other platforms.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/CatIIIIIIII/RNAErnie.git
cd ./RNAErnie
git checkout --detach b5e4c1cfdc6f53101111823abaddcab00c43b0d3
steps.explanation: Clones the repository as in the README. The checkout line is added to pin the commit read for this page.

steps.title: Create and activate the environment

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate RNAErnie
steps.explanation: Creates the conda environment named RNAErnie with Python 3.8 and PaddlePaddle.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import paddle
from rna_ernie import BatchConverter
from paddlenlp.transformers import ErnieModel

# ========== Set device
paddle.set_device("gpu")

# ========== Prepare Data
data = [
    ("RNA1", "GGGUGCGAUCAUACCAGCACUAAUGCCCUCCUGGGAAGUCCUCGUGUUGCACCCCU"),
    ("RNA2", "GGGUGUCGCUCAGUUGGUAGAGUGCUUGCCUGGCAUGCAAGAAACCUUGGUUCAAUCCCCAGCACUGCA"),
    ("RNA3", "CGAUUCNCGUUCCC--CCGCCUCCA"),
]

# ========== Batch Converter
batch_converter = BatchConverter(k_mer=1,
                                  vocab_path="./data/vocab/vocab_1MER.txt",
                                  batch_size=256,
                                  max_seq_len=512)

# ========== RNAErnie Model
rna_ernie = ErnieModel.from_pretrained("output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT/checkpoint_final/")
rna_ernie.eval()

# call batch_converter to convert sequences to batch inputs
for names, _, inputs_ids in batch_converter(data):
    with paddle.no_grad():
        # extract whole sequence embeddings
        embeddings = rna_ernie(inputs_ids)[0].detach()
        # extract [CLS] token embedding
        embeddings_cls = embeddings[:, 0, :]
        print(names, embeddings.shape, embeddings_cls.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's embedding example, run from the repository root and wrapped in a heredoc; the commented-out FASTA line was dropped and a print of the names and tensor shapes was added.

outputs: Whole-sequence token embeddings and [CLS] embeddings for each batch of input sequences, held as Paddle tensors.

name: SpliceBERT
description: Pre-trained language model of precursor mRNA sequence.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Table 1.

profile.summary: SpliceBERT is a language model of primary RNA sequence, the full transcript including introns, trained on over 2 million sequences from 72 vertebrates. It reads up to 1024 nucleotides, one token per nucleotide, and outputs an embedding for each position. The authors use it to study RNA splicing: to find splice sites and branchpoints and to score whether a variant is likely to disrupt splicing.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, Methods, Discussion; README introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpliceBERT is a small BERT model trained by masked language modelling on primary RNA sequences, meaning whole transcripts including introns, from 72 vertebrate genomes. Each nucleotide is one token. The authors use its nucleotide embeddings and attention weights to study splicing: embeddings separate real splice sites from look-alike sites, and a score of how the model's predictions around a variant change (the paper's KL-context score) helps flag splice-disrupting variants. Fine-tuned, it predicts branchpoints and splice sites across species.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One Zenodo archive (record 7995778, version v0.1-alpha) holds three checkpoints that differ in training data and fragment length. The paper pretrained SpliceBERT in two stages, first on fixed 510 nt fragments and then, continuing from that model, on 64 to 1024 nt fragments (7 days on 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs, then 3 days on 4); it does not name the released folders. Most analyses in the paper use the vertebrate model and compare it with SpliceBERT-human. The repository has a download script and notebooks for each analysis section, and lists the package versions used (Python 3.9.7, transformers 4.24.0, PyTorch 1.12.1). A result should name the checkpoint folder (SpliceBERT.1024nt, SpliceBERT.510nt or SpliceBERT-human.510nt) and the Zenodo record.

run_guide.summary: Download the SpliceBERT weights from Zenodo and compute nucleotide embeddings and masked-nucleotide logits for one sequence with the Hugging Face transformers API.
prerequisites: PyTorch and Hugging Face transformers, installed by following their official installation pages; the README gives no pinned install command. The authors used Python 3.9.7, transformers 4.24.0 and PyTorch 1.12.1.
A Linux system with an NVIDIA GPU of at least 4 GB memory is recommended; CPU-only runs are possible but slow.
About 218 MB for models.tar.gz (217,605,407 bytes per Zenodo). Code is BSD-3-Clause; weights are CC BY 4.0.

steps.title: Download and unpack the weights
steps.shell: wget -c -O models.tar.gz https://zenodo.org/record/7995778/files/models.tar.gz?download=1 && tar -xzvf models.tar.gz
steps.explanation: The weights line from the repository's download.sh. It unpacks the three checkpoints; set SPLICEBERT_PATH in the next step to the folder of the one you want, for example SpliceBERT.1024nt.

steps.title: Compute embeddings and logits
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
SPLICEBERT_PATH = "/path/to/SpliceBERT/models/model_folder"  # set the path to the folder of pre-trained SpliceBERT
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoModelForTokenClassification

# load tokenizer
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(SPLICEBERT_PATH)

# prepare input sequence
seq = "ACGUACGuacguaCGu"  ## WARNING: this is just a demo. SpliceBERT may not work on sequences shorter than 64nt as it was trained on sequences of 64-1024nt in length
seq = ' '.join(list(seq.upper().replace("U", "T"))) # U -> T and add whitespace
input_ids = tokenizer.encode(seq) # N -> 5, A -> 6, C -> 7, G -> 8, T(U) -> 9. NOTE: a [CLS] and a [SEP] token will be added to the start and the end of seq
input_ids = torch.as_tensor(input_ids) # convert python list to Tensor
input_ids = input_ids.unsqueeze(0) # add batch dimension, shape: (batch_size, sequence_length)

# use huggerface's official API to use SpliceBERT
# get nucleotide embeddings (hidden states)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(SPLICEBERT_PATH) # load model
last_hidden_state = model(input_ids).last_hidden_state # get hidden states from last layer
hiddens_states = model(input_ids, output_hidden_states=True).hidden_states # hidden states from the embedding layer (nn.Embedding) and the 6 transformer encoder layers

# get nucleotide type logits in masked language modeling
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(SPLICEBERT_PATH) # load model
logits = model(input_ids).logits # shape: (batch_size, sequence_length, vocab_size)
PY
steps.explanation: The first part of the README's official-API example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. The README's lines that create fine-tuning heads are left out, because the sequence-classification line uses a class the example does not import. Replace the placeholder path, and use a real sequence of 64 to 1024 nt; the demo sequence is shorter than the model supports.

outputs: Tensors held in memory: the last-layer hidden states, the hidden states of the embedding layer and all six encoder layers, and masked-language-model logits of shape (batch_size, sequence_length, vocab_size). The example prints nothing.

name: SpTransformer
description: Task-specific transformer for tissue-specific splice site prediction.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Introduction.

profile.summary: SpliceTransformer (SpTransformer) predicts RNA splicing from genomic sequence alone. For each position in a pre-mRNA sequence it gives the probability of being a splice donor, a splice acceptor or neither, and how much the site is used in each of 15 human tissues. Comparing predictions for reference and variant sequence lets it score how a genetic variant changes splicing in each tissue.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Tissue-specific prediction of splicing; Fig. 1 caption. README: title paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpTransformer has two main modules. An encoder of stacked convolutional residual blocks (ResBlocks) reads one-hot encoded sequence; the paper uses two such encoders with identical structure. Their output feeds a Sinkhorn Transformer, an attention variant built for long sequences, with 256 channels, 8 attention heads (two of them local) per layer and eight layers, followed by a multi-layer perceptron. For a 9000 nt input it predicts the central 1000 nt, using 4000 nt of context on each side. The output is an N x 3 matrix for splice site class and an N x 15 matrix for tissue usage. Training ran in two stages: first the two encoders were trained separately, one on GTEx data and one on an extra mammalian dataset, with 12 epochs per stage.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, SpTransformer model structure; Data representation; Model training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository describes one trained model. Its weights are too large for GitHub; Git-LFS access was disabled in November 2024, and the weights are now a single Google Drive download placed in model/weights. The download has no version label, so a result can only name the repository commit (this page read b67a51da) and the date the weights were fetched. The authors note that outputs can differ slightly between GPU types for individual variants. The variant annotation script uses a 95% threshold for tissue specificity unless raw scores are requested, so a result should say which output mode was used.

Covers 15 human tissue classes only, defined by the GTEx-based training labels.

profile.summary: UTR-LM is a language model for the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of mRNA, the stretch before the coding sequence that strongly affects how well an mRNA is translated. It reads a 5' UTR sequence and, after fine-tuning, predicts mean ribosome loading, translation efficiency or mRNA expression level. Pretraining combines masked language modelling with labels computed from the sequence, such as secondary structure and minimum free energy.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md opening paragraph; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UTR-LM is built on a modified copy of the ESM-2 transformer code, shipped in the repository. The reported settings are 6 transformer layers, 16 attention heads and an embedding size of 128. Pretraining uses masked language modelling (MLM) and, in the recommended variants, also predicts the minimum free energy (MFE) and/or the secondary structure of the sequence. For downstream tasks the developers fine-tune the whole model and feed the [CLS]-token embedding to a predictor trained with Huber loss.

The README's own example pretraining command passes --heads 6 --embed_dim 16, which disagrees with the 16 heads and embedding size 128 listed under General Parameters and in the checkpoint file names. A result should name the exact checkpoint file and the repository commit. A runnable copy is also published as a CodeOcean capsule.

profile.summary: HyCell is a compact single-cell embedding model. It maps the raw counts of one human cell to a 512-dimensional embedding that is used as a frozen representation for clustering, integration across batches, annotation transfer and comparison of cell states; its decoder turns embeddings back into expected gene expression.
profile.summary_source_locator: Package README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A cell is an unordered set of gene tokens with no positional encoding. Each expressed gene contributes a learned gene embedding plus a small network applied to its log1p counts per 10,000. Up to 818 expressed genes enter, with measured zeros numbering a quarter of the expressed genes and a [CLS] token, at most 1,024 tokens. A six-layer transformer (width 256, four heads, SwiGLU) encodes the set and a linear projection of the final [CLS] state is the embedding. In training, a negative-binomial count decoder conditioned on learned dataset and donor codes reconstructs the profile, and a donor discriminator is trained against the encoder. The README says the 818 genes are the highest by value; the report says genes are sampled with probability increasing in expression when a cell expresses more. The sources do not reconcile the two.
sections.source_locator: Package README: Method; technical report Section 2

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint, hycell-16m version 0.1.0, ships inside the package (64 MB) with a sidecar recording its configuration and the SHA-256 of the weights; hycell info --verify checks it. The README states that on a CUDA GPU with flash-attn the package reproduces the report's embeddings bit for bit, and that PyTorch attention agrees up to rounding. A result should name hycell-16m, package version 0.1.0 and the weights hash.
sections.source_locator: weights.json; package README: Install, Reproducibility

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Frozen embeddings for clustering, batch integration, annotation transfer and comparing cells across donors and studies; decoding embeddings to expression; fine-tuning into a cell type annotator. The README advises reading donor-level properties such as sex or disease state from embeddings averaged per donor or sample.

description: SCimilarity is a single-cell embedding model trained with cell-type labels for searching an atlas for similar human cells.

profile.summary: SCimilarity is a model for searching large single-cell RNA-seq atlases for cells similar to a query cell. It takes a cell's normalised expression profile and outputs a 128-dimensional embedding in which similar cell states lie close together, so a query can be matched against a reference of 23.4 million cells, and cells can be annotated, without retraining on new studies.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.rst; paper Fig. 1 legend and Methods

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A fully connected encoder reduces 28,231 genes through hidden layers of 1,024, 1,024, 1,024 and 128 units; the 128-dimensional output is scaled to unit length, so embeddings lie on a hypersphere. Training combines a triplet loss, which uses Cell Ontology annotations to pull cells of the same type together and push different types apart, with a mean squared error reconstruction loss from a decoder that preserves finer variation. Training uses heavy dropout (40% on the input, 50% on hidden layers).

steps.title: Embed cells
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import scanpy as sc
from scimilarity import CellAnnotation
from scimilarity.utils import align_dataset, lognorm_counts

model_path = "/models/model_v1.1"
ca = CellAnnotation(model_path=model_path)
data_path = "/data/GSE136831_subsample.h5ad"
adams = sc.read(data_path)
adams = align_dataset(adams, ca.gene_order)
adams = lognorm_counts(adams)
adams.obsm["X_scimilarity"] = ca.get_embeddings(adams.X)
EOF

name: Stack
description: Stack is a single-cell foundation model that embeds sets of cells together and learns biology in context from the other cells of a sample.

attributes.access: Released weights, run by the HyCell report authors at default settings.

version.note: No checkpoint revision is printed.

attributes.provenance_note: Dong et al., 2026, as cited by the HyCell report. Created here because the store held no record of this published model; the store's Stack entries are challenge submissions, not the model.

profile.summary: Stack is a single-cell foundation model that reads a set of cells from one sample together, so each cell's representation is informed by the other cells in its context. It takes cell-by-gene count matrices and outputs cell embeddings; through in-context learning it can also generate expression profiles for a target cell population under a condition shown by unlabelled prompt cells, such as a drug or a different donor.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper Abstract; README.md introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Stack is an encoder-decoder with tabular attention: layers alternate between attention across cells and attention across genes. Genes are compressed into a small number of trainable gene-group tokens (100 by default), and the input is a cell set drawn from a single experimental sample. Pre-training uses a rectangular mask: a random list of genes is masked for all cells in a mini-batch, with a mask ratio sampled between 0.1 and 0.8, and the model reconstructs each cell's expression distribution. A post-training stage uses a frozen teacher (self-distillation) so the student learns to predict target cell distributions conditioned on prompt cells.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results and Methods; README.md: Model Architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are on Hugging Face. Stack-Large (bc_large.ckpt) is pre-trained on human scBaseCount for 10 epochs and has 217M parameters according to its card; the card points to the embedding tutorial. Stack-Large-Aligned (bc_large_aligned.ckpt) adds alignment on CellxGene 45M and Parse 10M PBMC for 8 epochs and points to the prediction tutorial. The paper reports configurations from 69 to 629 million parameters. A result should name the checkpoint file and Hugging Face revision.
sections.source_locator: Model cards; Hugging Face API responses; paper Results

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Embedding single-cell data, zero-shot prediction of unseen perturbation or observation profiles by in-context generation, and fine-tuning with a frozen teacher.

profile.summary: Tahoe-x1 (Tx1) is a family of single-cell foundation models, up to 3 billion parameters, pretrained on single-cell transcriptomes including the Tahoe-100M drug perturbation compendium. It takes single-cell expression data (genes by Ensembl ID) and outputs cell and gene embeddings, learned jointly with compound representations, for tasks such as gene essentiality, cell-type classification and perturbation response prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: Preprint abstract; README.md; model card

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tx1 is a transformer encoder pretrained with a masked-expression objective; the authors credit scGPT as inspiration for the architecture. Each gene token combines a gene embedding with a continuous expression encoding, and a CLS token gives the cell embedding. In the 3B configuration only, a chemical encoder adds a drug token (fp_dim: 2048, num_drugs: 378); the 1B and 70M configs have no chemical encoder block. The 3B configuration has 32 layers, model width 2560 and 20 heads; the 1B has 24 layers, width 2048, 16 heads; the 70M has 12 layers, width 512, 8 heads. Training uses FlashAttention on the MosaicML Composer and llm-foundry stack.
sections.source_locator: Abstract; model card: Model Details; model_config.yml files; README.md: Acknowledgements

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are released in one Hugging Face repository, in folders 70m-model, 1b-model and 3b-model, and on S3. The README calls them Tx1-70M (70M, context 1024), Tx1-1.3B (1.3B, context 2048) and Tx1-3B (3B, context 2048); the model card calls the middle one Tx1-1B with about 1.3B parameters. The README notes that the current code supports only FlashAttention without custom attention masks, while Tx1-1B and Tx1-70M were trained with the Triton backend and custom masks. A result should name the checkpoint folder, the Hugging Face revision and the repository commit.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Pre-trained Models, Training from Scratch; model card: Model Sizes; Hugging Face API response

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Cell and gene embeddings for cancer-relevant tasks: gene essentiality (DepMap), hallmark pathway recovery (MSigDB), cell-type classification and perturbation response prediction in held-out contexts; fine-tuning on new data.

name: TranscriptFormer
description: TranscriptFormer is a generative single-cell transcriptome model whose cell embeddings are used as representations.

attributes.access: Released weights, run by the HyCell report authors at default settings.

profile.summary: TranscriptFormer is a family of generative single-cell foundation models trained on up to 112 million cells from 12 species. It reads a cell's raw counts (genes by Ensembl ID) and models gene identities and expression levels jointly; its cell embeddings are used for cross-species cell type classification, disease state identification and transfer of annotations, and the generative model can be prompted for cell type-specific transcription factors and gene-gene interactions.
profile.summary_source_locator: Preprint abstract; README.md: Description

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: TranscriptFormer is a generative autoregressive joint model over genes and their expression levels in a cell, built on a transformer with coupled gene and transcript heads, expression-aware multi-head self-attention, causal masking and a count likelihood. The README says the non-trainable parameters come from frozen pretrained embeddings, that each model comes with protein embeddings for its training species, and that protein embeddings for new species can be generated with ESM-2. Cell embeddings are mean-pooled over the genes of a cell; contextual gene embeddings are the per-gene transformer outputs.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Description, Generating Protein Embeddings, Command-line Options

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three models are released: TF-Metazoa (12 species, 112 million cells), TF-Exemplar (human and four model organisms, 110 million cells) and TF-Sapiens (57 million human cells). They differ in trainable parameters and vocabulary size. Weights are downloaded from AWS S3 with the transcriptformer download command; no checksum or version label is given for them in the README. A result should name the model, the package version and the commit.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Description; Downloading Model Weights

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Zero-shot cell type classification in and across species, disease state identification in human cells, annotation transfer, and prompting for transcription factors and gene-gene relations. Out-of-distribution species can be embedded with protein embeddings for 24 species provided, or new ones generated with ESM-2.

profile.summary: CMLM designs an amino acid sequence for a protein backbone that is given to it (inverse folding). It is the non-autoregressive ProteinMPNN baseline of the ByProt codebase: a ProteinMPNN-style graph encoder and decoder trained by conditional masked language modelling, so at generation time it predicts every position at once from one categorical distribution rather than one residue after another. The released checkpoint is called protein_mpnn_cmlm and was trained on CATH 4.2.
profile.summary_source_locator: ByProt README.md: Example 1: Non-autoregressive (NAR) ProteinMPNN baseline, Pretrained model weights; HyInv report Appendix D.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is ProteinMPNN's message-passing encoder and decoder, trained with a conditional masked language modelling objective instead of left-to-right prediction. Generation uses the mask-predict strategy with one decoding iteration by default, so all positions are filled in a single parallel pass. The ByProt defaults make this explicit: max_iter is 1 and the strategy is mask_predict for ProtMPNN-CMLM, against 5 iterations and denoising for LM-Design. Sampling temperature defaults to 0, which makes the output deterministic.
sections.source_locator: ByProt README.md: flags for generation, Example 1: ProteinMPNN-CMLM; HyInv report Appendix D.1 and Table 5

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released: protein_mpnn_cmlm, trained on CATH 4.2, published in the Zenodo deposit 10046338 of 27 October 2023 alongside the LM-Design checkpoints. A result must name the decoding settings as well as the checkpoint, because the output depends on the number of iterations, the strategy and the temperature. The HyInv report ran it at its published setting, one parallel pass at temperature 0.1, and reports that regenerating the sequences reproduced the released scores to within 0.0022 scTM with all sequences identical.
sections.source_locator: ByProt README.md: Pretrained model weights; Zenodo files and publication_date; HyInv report Table 5

sections.title: What a third party reports
sections.body: The HyInv report used CMLM as one of ten published baselines on inverse folding panels. It states that the parallel decoders, CMLM among them, sample at much lower diversity than its own model and have the lowest scTM, and its table of paired differences puts HyInv ahead of CMLM by 0.048 scTM on average. These are the HyInv authors' figures for their own comparison, not Rewire's, and not the CMLM developers' claims.

steps.title: Design a sequence for one backbone
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from byprot.utils.config import compose_config as Cfg
from byprot.tasks.fixedbb.designer import Designer

# 1. instantialize designer
exp_path = "run/logs/fixedbb/cath_4.2/protein_mpnn_cmlm"
cfg = Cfg(
    cuda=True,
    generator=Cfg(
        max_iter=1,
        strategy='mask_predict',
        temperature=0,
        eval_sc=False,  
    )
)
designer = Designer(experiment_path=exp_path, cfg=cfg)

# 2. load structure from pdb file
pdb_path = "data/3uat_variants/3uat_GK.pdb"
designer.set_structure(pdb_path)

# 3. generate sequence from the given structure
designer.generate()

# 4. calculate evaluation metircs
designer.calculate_metrics()
PY

profile.summary: DPLM-2 is a protein language model that handles sequence and structure in one model. Backbone coordinates are turned into discrete tokens by a quantising structure tokeniser, so a protein becomes one token string of amino acids and structure tokens, and a discrete diffusion language model is trained over both. From that single model come sequence and structure co-generation, folding (structure from sequence), inverse folding (sequence from structure) and motif scaffolding. Checkpoints are released at 150M, 650M and 3B parameters, plus a bit-based variant.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: first paragraphs and Model Details

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The 650M checkpoint is an ESM-style transformer with 33 layers, hidden size 1280 and 20 attention heads, loaded by the class EsmForDPLM2. What makes it multimodal is the vocabulary: 8,229 tokens covering amino acids, structure tokens and special tokens. Structure tokens come from a separate structure tokeniser, published as airkingbd/struct_tokenizer, which also rebuilds a PDB file from tokens. Training is discrete diffusion over this joint vocabulary, and it starts from a pretrained DPLM sequence model, a warm-up strategy the authors use to carry evolutionary knowledge into structure modelling. The README adds that DPLM-2 does inverse folding by conditioning directly on structure tokens, where the earlier DPLM used an adapter on top of the language model.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Details; config.json; arXiv abstract; README.md: Structure-conditioned generation

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four checkpoints answered on Hugging Face: dplm2_150m, dplm2_650m, dplm2_3b and dplm2_bit_650m, the last being the finer-grained bit-based variant from the follow-up work the authors call DPLM-2.1. All are Apache-2.0 and none is gated. Decoding settings matter as much as the checkpoint: the README's inverse folding and folding commands use 100 iterations with deterministic unmasking and argmax sampling, and a July 2025 note says the default sampling strategy of DPLM-2 was changed to annealing@2.0:0.1. The HyInv report evaluated DPLM-2 3B at argmax decoding over 100 steps in BF16 autocast, and notes that with deterministic unmasking two designs of the same chain are almost always the same sequence.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Load Pretrained Models, News, Inverse Folding with DPLM-2; Hugging Face API ids; HyInv report Appendix D.1 and Table 5

sections.title: Training data
sections.body: Training uses experimental structures from the PDB together with AlphaFold2 predicted structures from SwissProt, published as the preprocessed dataset airkingbd/pdb_swissprot. The model is initialised from a pretrained DPLM checkpoint, and LoRA is used to keep the parameters from shifting far, with about 64,000 tokens per batch for 100,000 training steps. The bit-based variant uses the same data.

profile.summary: HyInv does inverse folding: given a protein backbone it proposes amino-acid sequences that should fold into it. The input is the N, C-alpha, C and O backbone atoms of a structure read from a PDB file; the output is a set of sequences, written as FASTA. It is a small graph network of 1,957,573 parameters that was trained first on natural and predicted structures and then by reinforcement learning against a structure predictor, and it ships as an installable Python package with its weights.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph, Usage, Layout; technical report Sections 2 and 2.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HyInv follows the message-passing encoder and decoder design of ProteinMPNN. Each residue is joined to its 48 nearest neighbours and the edges carry distance features that do not change with rotation or translation. The encoder has 4 layers of width 128 and runs once for a backbone; the decoder has 3 layers of the same width and predicts amino-acid distributions at the masked positions from the backbone and the residues already visible. Training had two stages: supervision that maximised the likelihood of the native sequence under a random residue order, then reinforcement learning whose reward was mostly the scTM between the predicted structure of a candidate sequence and the input backbone. At inference the model needs no protein language model, no structure predictor and no alignment.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: Sampling: draft and rewrite
sections.body: Sequences are not drawn in one pass. The positions are split at random into 8 fixed groups. A draft phase samples one group per round at temperature 0.6 starting from a fully masked sequence, and a rewrite phase then masks one group per round, keeps every other position visible, and resamples that group at temperature 0.34. Generating a design costs one encoder pass and 16 decoder passes. The authors report that separating the two temperatures gives a higher scTM at the same sequence diversity than sampling at a single temperature, by 0.0078 on CATH4.3 test and 0.0131 on RecentPDB, measured on an earlier checkpoint of the same run.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 3.1 and 3.2; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released: the reinforcement-learning version, which the technical report identifies as update 640 with draft temperature 0.6 and rewrite temperature 0.34, the setting used for every result in the report. The supervised checkpoint that preceded it is described but not released. A result should name the setting as well as the checkpoint, because the package offers three numerical paths. The default reference path is FP32 and reproduces its own output for the same seed, batch size, device type and PyTorch version; the exact path is accelerated FP32 and almost always returns the same sequences; the bf16 path is a different arithmetic and does not return the same sequences for the same seed. Batch size is part of the seed, because batch k uses seed plus k, and the CPU and GPU random streams differ.
sections.source_locator: Technical report Sections 3.2 and 5.1, Table 1; README.md Notes and Accelerated inference

strengths.text: Fast enough for library screening on one GPU: the authors measure 128 designs for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on an NVIDIA H20 with the bf16 path, and 10,000 designs for a 250-residue backbone in 2.11 s.
Needs nothing beyond the backbone at inference: no alignment, no protein language model and no structure predictor, and positions can be pinned so that a catalytic site or pocket is kept.

strengths.text: The developers report that on their five panels, with one panel scored by three structure predictors, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity. This is the authors' own evaluation.

limitations.text: Single chains only in intent. The authors state that HyInv targets single-chain backbones and name multi-chain interfaces and membrane environments as future work, although the command line accepts several chains.

The fast bf16 path does not reproduce the reference sequences, so a result must say which path produced it. The exact path reproduces them almost always: in a check of about 8,000 sequences one differed at one position.

limitations.text: The accelerated kernels were verified on one GPU only. The authors say they were verified with triton 3.3.1 on an H20 and should compile on other architectures but have not been checked there.

profile.summary: LigandMPNN designs amino acid sequences for a protein backbone that is given to it, and unlike earlier methods of its kind it also reads the non-protein atoms around that backbone: small molecules, nucleotides and metals. The input is a PDB file, the output a set of designed sequences with per-sequence confidence figures, and optionally packed side chain conformations so binding interactions can be inspected. The published package also serves ProteinMPNN, SolubleMPNN and two membrane-labelled models from the same code.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: first paragraph, Available models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Design is autoregressive over the backbone graph, in the manner of ProteinMPNN, with the ligand atoms added as context. The LigandMPNN checkpoints are built with 32 neighbour edges and 25 context atoms per residue, which is what the names ligandmpnn_v_32_005_25 and the like record. The atom context can be switched off with a flag, which the README offers as a way to see how much the ligand atoms move the amino acid probabilities, and side chain context can be switched on. A separate side chain packing checkpoint produces the side chain conformations.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Available models, examples 21 and 22, Side chain packing model; get_model_params.sh comments

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four LigandMPNN checkpoints are published, differing in the Gaussian coordinate noise used in training: 0.05, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.30 Angstrom. The same download script also fetches four ProteinMPNN checkpoints, four SolubleMPNN checkpoints, two membrane-labelled models and the side chain packing model, all from files.ipd.uw.edu. A result must name the checkpoint, the model type, the sampling temperature and the seed, since the README is explicit that no seed means a random seed and that running again gives different results. The default model type of run.py is ProteinMPNN, not LigandMPNN.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Available models, examples 1, 2 and 3; get_model_params.sh

sections.title: What is reported about it
sections.body: The preprint reports native backbone sequence recovery for residues that touch other molecules: 63.3 per cent against 50.4 per cent for Rosetta and 50.5 per cent for ProteinMPNN near small molecules, 50.5 against 35.2 and 34.0 near nucleotides, and 77.5 against 36.0 and 40.6 near metals. Separately, the HyInv report used LigandMPNN as one of ten published baselines on backbone-only inverse folding panels, where it is the strongest of the ten by average scTM (0.8555), and the smallest gap to HyInv (0.018 on average). These are their authors' figures, not Rewire's.

profile.summary: LM-Design designs an amino acid sequence for a protein backbone that is given to it (inverse folding). Rather than training a structure model from scratch, it takes an existing protein language model and implants a lightweight structural adapter into it, so the language model's knowledge of natural sequences is reused and given awareness of the fold. At generation time the sequence is refined over several passes. The released checkpoints are built on ESM-1b 650M and ESM-2 650M and trained on CATH 4.2, with one multichain checkpoint for complexes.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; ByProt README.md: Official implementation of LM-Design, Pretrained model weights

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A structural adapter is added to a frozen protein language model, which is what the authors call structural surgery. Generation is iterative: the ByProt defaults for LM-Design are five decoding iterations with the denoise strategy, against one iteration and mask_predict for the non-autoregressive ProteinMPNN baseline in the same repository. Sampling temperature defaults to 0, which makes the output deterministic; the README shows how to override it. The HyInv report describes the model's decoding as iterative denoising in five steps.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; ByProt README.md: flags for generation, Example 2; HyInv report Table 5

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three LM-Design checkpoints are published in Zenodo deposit 10046338 of 27 October 2023: lm_design_esm1b_650m on CATH 4.2, lm_design_esm2_650m on CATH 4.2, and lm_design_esm2_650m trained on the multichain data for complexes. Each archive is about 1.6 GB. The repository also holds experiment configurations for the ESM-2 series under configs/experiment/fixedbb, but only the 650M checkpoints are released. A result must name the base language model, the training data and the decoding settings, since five iterations at temperature 0 is not the same run as five iterations at temperature 0.1.
sections.source_locator: ByProt README.md: Pretrained model weights, Example 2; Zenodo files and publication_date

sections.title: What is reported about it
sections.body: The paper's abstract claims gains of 4 to 12 per cent in sequence recovery over the state of the art at the time, giving 55.65 per cent on CATH 4.2 and 56.63 per cent on CATH 4.3 for single chains and above 60 per cent for complexes. The repository's own worked example recovers 0.76 of the native sequence on one backbone, against 0.37 for the CMLM baseline. Separately, the HyInv report used LM-Design 650M as one of ten published baselines and puts its own model ahead by 0.044 scTM on average, while noting that LM-Design is among the parallel decoders that sample at lower diversity. All of these are their authors' figures, not Rewire's.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; ByProt README.md: Example 2 output; HyInv report Section 5.2 and Table 7

from byprot.utils.config import compose_config as Cfg
from byprot.tasks.fixedbb.designer import Designer

# 4. calculate evaluation metircs
designer.calculate_metrics()
PY

profile.summary: ProteinZero V2 designs amino acid sequences for a protein backbone that you supply. It starts from ProteinMPNN and improves it with online reinforcement learning: the model generates sequences, those sequences are folded by ESMFold and scored for structural agreement and predicted stability, and the reward is used to update the model. Two teaser checkpoints are released, for structures of up to about 100 residues.
profile.summary_source_locator: ProteinZero-V2/README.md: intro; README: ProteinZero

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The base model is ProteinMPNN, loaded with 128-dimensional node and edge features, three encoder and three decoder layers and 48 neighbours per residue. Reinforcement learning then trains it against rewards rather than a single supervised target: the V2 README names structural feedback from ESMFold and the fast change in folding free energy introduced in V1. V1 used GRPO; the V2 checkpoints were trained with PARPO, an algorithm the authors describe as aimed at exploring Pareto frontiers in multi-objective optimisation, and whose formulation is not yet published.
sections.source_locator: ProteinZero-V2/README.md: intro, Checkpoints; README: ProteinZero, ProteinZero V2

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two V2 checkpoints are released, differing only in which structure predictor gave the reward: proteinzero_v2_esmfold1.pt (ESMFold1) and proteinzero_v2_esmfold2.pt (ESMFold2). A result must name which of the two was used, the sampling temperature and the seed, since generation samples. They are described as teaser checkpoints, with full checkpoints and a paper to follow, so results may not be reproducible against later releases. The earlier ProteinZero V1 is a different model, built on InstructPLM.

profile.summary: AMPLIFY is a protein language model. It reads a protein amino acid sequence and returns per-residue and per-protein embeddings and masked-token logits, which can be used as features for property prediction or to suggest mutations. It comes in two sizes, 120M and 350M parameters, and the authors released the training code, data and checkpoints.
profile.summary_source_locator: model card: AMPLIFY; README: introduction; docs usage.rst: Inference

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: AMPLIFY is a transformer encoder trained with masked language modelling: 15% of residues are masked and the model learns to predict them. The layers use rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU activations and RMS normalisation, with no bias terms in the attention or feed-forward layers. Training ran in two stages. Stage 1 ran for 1,000,000 steps on sequences of up to 512 residues. Stage 2 extended the length to 2048 for 25,000 steps (120M) or 50,000 steps (350M). The authors frame the work around data quality rather than scale: they argue that sequence databases are a biased sample of the fitness landscape and built a curated training set, UR100P.
sections.source_locator: model card: Model Descritpion and Training Descritpion tables; README: introduction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four checkpoints are on Hugging Face and Zenodo: AMPLIFY_350M and AMPLIFY_120M are the final models, and AMPLIFY_350M_base and AMPLIFY_120M_base are the Stage 1 models, not extended beyond 512 residues. The two sizes differ in width and depth (640 hidden units and 24 layers against 960 and 32). The training datasets are also published, downloaded in December 2023 and processed with the repository's data pipeline. A result should name the checkpoint and the Hugging Face revision; this page read AMPLIFY_350M at revision 223e35e4. The repository code was read at commit 7fb657a6.

steps.title: Embed one protein
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModel
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from datasets import load_dataset

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("chandar-lab/AMPLIFY_350M", trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("chandar-lab/AMPLIFY_350M", trust_remote_code=True)
model = model.to("cuda")

dataset = load_dataset("chandar-lab/UR100P", data_dir="UniProt", split="test")

for sample in dataset:
    print("Sample: ", sample["name"], sample["sequence"])
    input = tokenizer.encode(sample["sequence"], return_tensors="pt")
    print("Input: ", input)
    input = input.to("cuda")
    output = model(input)
    print("Output: ", output)
    break
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's Get Started example, wrapped in a shell heredoc by Rewire with its comments removed. It downloads AMPLIFY_350M and one sample from the UR100P UniProt test split and runs one forward pass on the GPU.

outputs: The script prints the sample name and sequence, the token IDs, and the model output object for one UniProt test protein.
