profile.summary: Ankh is a family of protein language models with an encoder and a decoder, in the shape of a T5 model. You give it an amino-acid sequence and the encoder returns a vector per residue that can be used as a feature for another model, for example to predict secondary structure, localisation or solubility. The authors' stated aim was not scale but protein-specific optimisation: they ran over twenty experiments on masking, architecture and pretraining data to get the same or better results with fewer parameters than the larger models of the time. The later Ankh3 models add a second pretraining task, completing a sequence from its first half, so they can also generate the rest of a sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv 2301.06568 abstract; Ankh README opening lines and Usage; Ankh3 Large model card Model Details

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The published configuration of Ankh Base is a T5 encoder and decoder: 48 encoder layers and 24 decoder layers at model width 768, 12 attention heads, a feed-forward width of 3072, gated GELU activations and a vocabulary of 144 tokens. Word embeddings are not tied between encoder and decoder. For feature extraction the encoder is used on its own. Pretraining corrupts the sequence with sentinel tokens and asks the decoder to name the missing residues. Ankh3 adds a second task: the first half of the sequence goes to the encoder and the decoder generates the second half. Because Ankh3 was trained on both tasks, its inputs carry a prefix, NLU for representation extraction and S2S for sequence completion.
sections.source_locator: ankh-base config.json; Ankh3 Large model card Model Details and How to use

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository's model table names four loadable checkpoints: Ankh Large, Ankh Base, Ankh3 Large and Ankh3 XL, each with a Hugging Face repository. A result must name which of them it used, and should pin the revision, since the cards are updated in place; the revisions read here are d99cb6b9 for Ankh Base, 74b371db for Ankh Large and 2be09162 for Ankh3 Large. For Ankh3 there is a further choice inside the checkpoint: the card says the NLU prefix is used for the encoder representation and suggests trying the S2S prefix instead, because it can give better embedding quality, and the repository's own result tables report Ankh3 numbers separately for NLU and S2S. The tables also list a model called Ankh 2 Large, which has no loader and no Hugging Face link in the sources read.
sections.source_locator: Ankh README Models Availability and the secondary structure tables; Hugging Face API responses; Ankh3 Large model card How to use

sections.title: Downstream heads and licence
sections.body: The ankh package ships more than the language models. It also has small ConvBERT heads for binary classification, multi-class classification and regression, meant to sit on top of the embeddings, and a function that computes a pseudo-likelihood for a sequence. The datasets used in the original evaluation are listed as Hugging Face datasets, including secondary structure sets, DeepLoc, fluorescence and solubility. The licence is the thing to check before using any of this in a product: the pretrained models are released under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0, which the Hugging Face cards also declare, so commercial use is not permitted.
sections.source_locator: Ankh README Usage, Datasets Availability and License; Hugging Face API responses cardData

steps.shell: python -m pip install ankh

steps.title: Get embeddings from Ankh Large
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import ankh

model, tokenizer = ankh.load_ankh_large()
model.eval()

protein_sequences = [
  'MKALCLLLLPVLGLLVSSKTLCSMEEAINERIQEVAGSLIFRAISSIGLECQSVTSRGDLATCPRGFAVTGCTCGSACGSWDVRAETTCHCQCAGMDWTGARCCRVQPLEHHHHHH', 
  'GSHMSLFDFFKNKGSAATATDRLKLILAKERTLNLPYMEEMRKEIIAVIQKYTKSSDIHFKTLDSNQSVETIEVEIILPR',
]

protein_sequences = [list(seq) for seq in protein_sequences]

outputs = tokenizer(
  protein_sequences, 
  add_special_tokens=True, 
  padding=True, 
  is_split_into_words=True, 
  return_tensors="pt",
)
with torch.no_grad():
  embeddings = model(input_ids=outputs['input_ids'], attention_mask=outputs['attention_mask'])
print(embeddings.last_hidden_state.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's feature extraction example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. The import of torch and ankh and the final print were added, because the README snippet assumes them. Replace load_ankh_large with load_ankh_base for the smaller model.
steps.source_locator: Ankh README Usage, loading and feature extraction examples

steps.title: Or embed with Ankh3 Large through transformers
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5ForConditionalGeneration, T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch

sequence = "MDTAYPREDTRAPTPSKAGAHTALTLGAPHPPPRDHLIWSVFSTLYLNLCCLGFLALAYSIKARDQKVVGDLEAARRFGSKAKCYNILAAMWTLVPPLLLLGLVVTGALHLARLAKDSAAFFSTKFDDADYD"

ckpt = "ElnaggarLab/ankh3-large"

tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained(ckpt)

encoder_model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained(ckpt).eval()

nlu_sequence = "[NLU]" + sequence
encoded_nlu_sequence = tokenizer(nlu_sequence, add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors="pt", is_split_into_words=False)

with torch.no_grad():
  embedding = encoder_model(**encoded_nlu_sequence)
PY
steps.explanation: The Ankh3 Large model card's embedding example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. Note the NLU prefix and that T5Tokenizer must be used, not AutoTokenizer. The card suggests the S2S prefix may give better embeddings for some uses.

profile.summary: DPLM (diffusion protein language model) is a protein language model trained as a discrete diffusion model rather than by masked or autoregressive prediction. It generates protein sequences from scratch or from a partial sequence, and it can also be fine-tuned as a sequence representation model for predictive tasks. Three sizes are released (150M, 650M, 3B), along with a later multimodal family, DPLM-2, that generates structure and sequence together.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Overview, Key Features, Model Checkpoints; model card

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DPLM is pretrained with a generative self-supervised discrete diffusion objective over amino acid tokens, which the authors describe as generalising language modelling for proteins. Generation is iterative: the user asks for a length and a number of sequences and the model refines tokens over up to a set number of iterations. The released checkpoints use the ESM-2 transformer architecture (the model class is EsmForDPLM, with rotary position embeddings) and each config records the matching ESM-2 model as its base: facebook/esm2_t30_150M_UR50D, facebook/esm2_t33_650M_UR50D and facebook/esm2_t36_3B_UR50D. Beyond free generation, DPLM supports conditioning on a partial sequence (motif scaffolding), on a structure (inverse folding), and steering towards a secondary structure through classifier guidance.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Key Features, Generation Examples; config.json files

sections.title: The DPLM family
sections.body: The repository holds three families. DPLM (ICML 2024) models sequences. DPLM-2 (ICLR 2025) adds structure tokens and does sequence and structure co-generation, forward folding and inverse folding; it is initialised from a pretrained DPLM checkpoint and trained with LoRA on PDB and SwissProt structures. DPLM-2 Bit, from the 2025 design-space paper, predicts each bit of the quantised structure feature instead of the index. Seven checkpoints are listed: dplm-150m, dplm-650m, dplm-3b, dplm2-150m, dplm2-650m, dplm2-3b and dplm2-bit-650m. This page describes the sequence DPLM models named in the record.
sections.source_locator: README: Overview, Model Checkpoints, Training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: A result should name the checkpoint (dplm_150m, dplm_650m or dplm_3b), its Hugging Face revision, the code commit, and the sampling settings, above all the number of iterations (max_iter) and the sequence length. The repository changes behaviour over time: in July 2025 the developers changed the default sampling strategy of DPLM-2 to annealing@2.0:0.1. This page read the code at commit 8a2e15e5 and the checkpoints at revisions 49b7125a (150M), 7a7e651b (650M) and 53849d4a (3B).

profile.summary: E1 (Profluent-E1) is a family of protein language models that can read a query protein sequence on its own or together with homologous sequences retrieved for it. It outputs per-residue embeddings and amino acid probabilities (logits), which are used for zero-shot fitness and variant scoring, contact map prediction and as features for structural tasks. The developers present it as a drop-in replacement for the ESM family.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; README: introduction, Interactive Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: E1 is a masked language model (the released class is E1ForMaskedLM). In retrieval-augmented mode, homologous sequences are placed before the query, separated by commas, and the model attends across them with block-causal multi-sequence attention, so it can use family-specific evolutionary context without fine-tuning. The configuration has separate position encodings within each sequence and across the whole input, and uses global attention every third layer. The models were trained on four trillion tokens from the Profluent Protein Atlas, in BF16 precision. A `?` character marks a masked position.

steps.title: Run the model
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch

from E1.batch_preparer import E1BatchPreparer
from E1.modeling import E1ForMaskedLM

model = E1ForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("Profluent-Bio/E1-300m").to("cuda:0")
model.eval()

sequences = ["AAAAA?C", "MFCATEEKL,MCCASDF,MFCC?SEF"]
batch_preparer = E1BatchPreparer()
batch = batch_preparer.get_batch_kwargs(sequences, device="cuda:0")

with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=True):
    outputs = model(
        input_ids=batch["input_ids"],
        within_seq_position_ids=batch["within_seq_position_ids"],
        global_position_ids=batch["global_position_ids"],
        sequence_ids=batch["sequence_ids"],
        past_key_values=None,
        use_cache=False,
        output_attentions=False,
        output_hidden_states=False,
    )

logits: torch.Tensor = outputs.logits  # (B, L, V)
embeddings: torch.Tensor = outputs.embeddings  # (B, L, E)

print(logits)
print(embeddings)
PY

profile.summary: HyPLM-Flash is a masked protein language model of 652 million parameters. It reads one amino acid sequence, up to 8,190 residues in a single window, and returns a 1280-dimensional vector per residue, a pooled vector, or masked language model logits that can be turned into a zero-shot variant score. It keeps the 33 token alphabet and the output head of ESM-2, so it can stand in for ESM-2 in an existing pipeline, and it ships with its own GPU inference engine that uses INT8 matrix multiplication and padding-free batching.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report abstract and Section 2.1; README.md: Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: It is a bidirectional transformer encoder trained by masked language modelling: 15 per cent of residues are selected, 80 per cent of those replaced by a mask token, 10 per cent by a random amino acid and 10 per cent left as they are. Each of the 32 blocks puts RMSNorm before self-attention with per-head query and key normalisation and rotary positions, then before a SwiGLU feed-forward layer, each inside a residual connection. The output head is RoBERTa style: a dense layer, GELU, LayerNorm, then a linear map to 33 logits. The block weights were trained with the Muon optimiser and everything else with AdamW.
sections.source_locator: Report Section 2.1 and Section 2.2 (Objective and optimization); weights/config.json

sections.title: Training data and decontamination
sections.body: The corpus combines UniRef90 with the UniRef50 representatives it does not contain, MGnify90, the active entries of UniParc and the non-redundant isolate proteomes of JGI IMG. Sequences of 30 to 8,192 residues are kept, exact duplicates are removed across sources, and the sequences of the benchmarks used during development are removed by exact match, including all ProteinGym wild types and variants. That leaves 2.6 billion sequences, or 659 billion residues, sampled in proportion to length, so metagenomic and archival sequences supply about 80 per cent of the tokens. Pretraining covers 713 billion tokens on crops of up to 1,022 residues; a second stage of 13 billion tokens extends the crops to 8,190 residues and adds auxiliary structure objectives on 1.6 million chains, with those chains first filtered against the test proteins by MMseqs2. The auxiliary heads are used only during training.
sections.source_locator: Report Section 2.2: Data, Training stages, Training compute

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released, version 1.0.0 of the hyplm package, with the report dated 12 October 2026. The 2.6 GB of FP32 weights come as two shards from the repository's GitHub Releases under the tag hyplm-flash-weights; the download script merges them and checks the sha256 against ce7dcd4fc473dc334d869718a9a31149573893795db03c45efeb396e8b180ab1. A result must also name the precision, because the engine runs INT8 by default and BF16 on request. The developers state that zero-shot, structure, function and likelihood metrics agree within 0.01 between the two, while representations of variants of the same protein differ by about 1 per cent, so they advise BF16 when training regressors on such data.

steps.title: Score one mutation
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from hyplm import HyPLMEncoder

encoder = HyPLMEncoder.from_pretrained("weights")
sequence = "MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"
logits = encoder.logits(sequence, masks=[2])[0]         # [L, 33]; residue 3 is replaced by <mask> first
log_probs = logits[2].log_softmax(-1)
tokens = encoder.tokenizer.tokens                       # vocabulary order
score = log_probs[tokens.index("V")] - log_probs[tokens.index("T")]   # masked-marginal score of T3V
print(score)
PY

profile.summary: DeepAffinity predicts compound-protein affinity from a compound SMILES string and a structure property-annotated protein sequence (SPS), using pretrained recurrent seq2seq encoders followed by convolutional layers.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GRU seq2seq auto-encoders are first trained without labels on compound SMILES and protein SPS strings. In the unified RNN-CNN model, a 1D convolution and max-pooling layer is added after each encoder, the two outputs are concatenated and passed through two fully connected layers, and the whole pipeline is trained end to end with the pretrained encoders as initialisation. A separate RNN-CNN baseline keeps the encoders fixed.

profile.summary: hEvo is a family of DNA language models from MulinLab trained on haplotype sequences from human populations, so that the models see real human genetic variation rather than one reference genome. A model reads a DNA sequence of up to 1,024 nucleotides and returns one vector per nucleotide, plus masked-base predictions that can score a single-nucleotide variant as a log-likelihood ratio of the alternative against the reference allele. The authors use it for variant-effect scoring, regulatory annotation and population-genetic analysis.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Overview, Models; hEVO-base-o card: Model overview, Intended use

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hEvo is a bidirectional BERT-style masked language model with one token per nucleotide. Training has two stages. In Stage I the model learns representations by span masking on deduplicated haplotype windows drawn from population haplotypes. In Stage II the nucleotide prediction head is calibrated on contexts centred on variants. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant position is masked once and the log probability of the alternative allele minus that of the reference allele is taken from the same masked context; a positive value means the model prefers the alternative allele.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Two stages of learning, Models; hEVO-base-o card: Model overview, Single-nucleotide variant scoring

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists primary models hEvo-base and hEvo-large, and public-data variants hEvo-open-base and hEvo-open-large, which are published on Hugging Face as hEVO-base-o (87.1M parameters, 12 layers, hidden size 768) and hEVO-large-o (319.5M parameters, 16 layers, hidden size 1,280). Only the two -o checkpoints are linked for download, and both are gated. The -o models were pretrained separately on public 1000 Genomes Project and HGDP data. The README says hEVO-base-o matches the hEvo-open-base weights by file hash, and that hEVO-large-o has identical tensors to the hEvo-open-large checkpoint after conversion. The model cards pin a code and weights revision in their examples (fa613904 for base, 09541834 for large) and keep the card itself on main. A result should name the checkpoint and that revision.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "MulinLab/hEVO-base-o"
# Freeze the checkpoint and its custom code for reproducible inference.
REVISION = "fa6139047c21d92b58bd8eda49ea2f89a884e33c"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

load_options = dict(revision=REVISION, token=True, trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO, **load_options)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    use_frequency_embedding=False,
    use_flash_attention=False,
    **load_options,
)
assert config.use_frequency_embedding is False
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    config=config,
    attn_implementation="eager",
    dtype=torch.float32,
    **load_options,
).to(device).eval()

def encode_dna(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.strip().upper()
    if not 0 < len(sequence) <= config.max_position_embeddings:
        raise ValueError("Provide a sequence of 1 to 1,024 nucleotides.")
    if set(sequence) - set("ACGTN"):
        raise ValueError("DNA must contain only A, C, G, T or N.")
    encoded = tokenizer(sequence, return_tensors="pt", truncation=False)
    # This custom tokenizer returns 1D tensors for a single sequence.
    encoded = {
        key: value.unsqueeze(0) if value.ndim == 1 else value
        for key, value in encoded.items()
    }
    if "attention_mask" not in encoded:
        encoded["attention_mask"] = torch.ones_like(encoded["input_ids"])
    return {key: value.to(device) for key, value in encoded.items()}

sequence = "ACGTTGCATGTCGCATGATGCATGAGAGCT"
inputs = encode_dna(sequence)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_dict=True)
    token_embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [batch, length, hidden_size]

    # Optional: summarize the last-layer nucleotide embeddings by mean pooling.
    keep = inputs["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).to(token_embeddings.dtype)
    sequence_embedding = (token_embeddings * keep).sum(dim=1) / keep.sum(
        dim=1
    ).clamp_min(1)

print("Last-layer token embeddings:", tuple(token_embeddings.shape))
print("Mean-pooled sequence embedding:", tuple(sequence_embedding.shape))
EOF

profile.summary: hEVO-large-o is the larger of the two public checkpoints of hEvo, a DNA language model family from MulinLab trained on haplotype sequences from human populations. It reads a DNA sequence of up to 1,024 nucleotides and returns one 1,280-dimensional vector per nucleotide, plus masked-base predictions that can score a single-nucleotide variant as a log-likelihood ratio of the alternative against the reference allele. The -o checkpoints were trained on public 1000 Genomes Project and HGDP data.
profile.summary_source_locator: hEVO-large-o card: header, Model overview, Training data and objective; README.md: Overview

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hEVO-large-o is a bidirectional BERT-style masked language model with 16 transformer layers and hidden size 1,280, and one token per nucleotide with no boundary tokens. The family README describes two training stages: span-masked representation learning on deduplicated haplotype windows, then calibration of the nucleotide prediction head on variant-centred contexts. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant site is masked once and the alternative-allele logit minus the reference-allele logit at that site gives the log-likelihood ratio. Frequency embeddings are disabled in this checkpoint's configuration, so inference uses DNA sequence only.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "MulinLab/hEVO-large-o"
# Freeze the checkpoint and its custom code for reproducible inference.
REVISION = "09541834de8a063b09f9ddfebf06532c18bda53d"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

load_options = dict(revision=REVISION, token=True, trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO, **load_options)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    use_frequency_embedding=False,
    use_flash_attention=False,
    **load_options,
)
assert config.use_frequency_embedding is False
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    config=config,
    attn_implementation="eager",
    dtype=torch.float32,
    **load_options,
).to(device).eval()

def encode_dna(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.strip().upper()
    if not 0 < len(sequence) <= config.max_position_embeddings:
        raise ValueError("Provide a sequence of 1 to 1,024 nucleotides.")
    if set(sequence) - set("ACGTN"):
        raise ValueError("DNA must contain only A, C, G, T or N.")
    encoded = tokenizer(sequence, return_tensors="pt", truncation=False)
    # This custom tokenizer returns 1D tensors for a single sequence.
    encoded = {
        key: value.unsqueeze(0) if value.ndim == 1 else value
        for key, value in encoded.items()
    }
    if "attention_mask" not in encoded:
        encoded["attention_mask"] = torch.ones_like(encoded["input_ids"])
    return {key: value.to(device) for key, value in encoded.items()}

sequence = "ACGTTGCATGTCGCATGATGCATGAGAGCT"
inputs = encode_dna(sequence)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_dict=True)
    token_embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [batch, length, hidden_size]

    # Optional: summarize the last-layer nucleotide embeddings by mean pooling.
    keep = inputs["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).to(token_embeddings.dtype)
    sequence_embedding = (token_embeddings * keep).sum(dim=1) / keep.sum(
        dim=1
    ).clamp_min(1)

print("Last-layer token embeddings:", tuple(token_embeddings.shape))
print("Mean-pooled sequence embedding:", tuple(sequence_embedding.shape))
EOF

profile.summary: scRM (the single-cell read model) embeds single cells directly from raw sequencing reads, without a reference genome, gene annotation, count matrix or gene vocabulary. It takes paired 10x Chromium polyA FASTQ files, assembles each captured molecule from its reads, and learns a cell embedding from the base sequences; count matrices are used only as evaluation targets.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Architecture

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A Rust pipeline reads paired FASTQ files, trims R2, corrects cell barcodes against the CellRanger called-cell list, deduplicates UMIs without any gene partition, and assembles one consensus sequence per UMI (one captured mRNA) with a de Bruijn graph at k = 19. The molecules are written to an Arrow corpus sorted by cell and packed into windows of 16384 tokens. The Python model is hierarchical (bytes, contig, UMI, window, cell): a byte-level local transformer trunk, attention pooling at each level, and a global trunk over UMI slots, both LLaMA-style pre-norm stacks. Training combines masked base modelling, EMA-teacher terms at UMI and cell level, and a SIGReg regulariser.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three training arms are declared: S96, the flagship with global and local width 96, and S96ML and S96MA, mean-pooling ablations. The flagship recipe is fixed in code (arm S96, the corpora mouse_brain_5k, neuron_1k_v3, neurons_5k and sod1_spinal_cord, lambda 0.0196, seed 20260903, 8947 steps, 3000 training cells). Window length moves only on a ladder of 16384, 32768 and 49152 tokens, and runs at different rungs are different experiments. Checkpoints record the architecture hash and the regulariser. The sources do not offer a pretrained scRM checkpoint for download; the README's evaluation reads a checkpoint produced by training. A result should name the run, the arm, the seq_len rung and the commit.

git clone https://github.com/altoslabs/scRM
cd scRM
git checkout --detach 7afa21a788c8c9ee870e697e23e60954fc152c77

steps.title: Build a corpus
steps.shell:
target/release/scrm-corpus \
    --samplesheet <your samplesheet.csv> \
    --out $SCRM_PROJ/corpus_rel \
    --threads 32
steps.explanation: Replace the samplesheet and set SCRM_PROJ to your data root. This is the README's build command with one change: the README example writes to $SCRM_PROJ/corpus_v3, which REPRODUCE.md calls the predecessor root, while the release's corpus root is $SCRM_PROJ/corpus_rel, so --out points there. Each experiment is built into its own folder under --out and manifest.json is written last. The training launcher refuses a corpus that is not in the pinned digest file, so for the flagship the four pretraining corpora must match the pinned digests; REPRODUCE.md builds them with the per-dataset launchers that ./reproduce.sh --dry-run 2 prints, and the saved files do not say whether this direct command reproduces those digests.

steps.title: Train the flagship
steps.shell:
export SCRM_PROJ=/path/to/data-root
export SCRM_PY=/path/to/envs/scrm/bin/python
export SCRM_CORPUS_ROOT=$SCRM_PROJ/corpus_rel
export SCRM_REPO=$PWD
export SBATCH_PARTITION=<partition>
export SBATCH_ACCOUNT=<account>
export PYTHONPATH=model:eval:target/py
$SCRM_PY -m scrm_eval.registry --recipe armS96-c3k-sigreg-lam002-s20260903
sbatch model/jobs/arm_ablation.sbatch armS96-c3k-sigreg-lam002-s20260903
steps.explanation: REPRODUCE.md's hand path for the reported flagship, armS96-c3k-sigreg-lam002-s20260903 (seed 20260903). The registry command prints the recipe the launcher will use (the four pretraining corpora, seed 20260903, 8947 steps); the launcher writes $SCRM_PROJ/runs/<run>/latest.pt. SCRM_CORPUS_ROOT must be set because every launcher defaults to $SCRM_PROJ/corpus and arm_ablation.sbatch refuses against it. The README instead gives a direct python -m scrm_model.train command that reads $SCRM_PROJ/corpus/... and writes runs/armS96-c3k-sigreg-lam002; REPRODUCE.md gives that name to the seed-floor run (seed 20260817), while the README says train.py's defaults, including --seed, are the flagship's. The saved files do not settle which seed that README command would produce, so this step follows REPRODUCE.md.

profile.summary: ProtCell is a foundation model for single-cell proteomics, where assays such as CITE-seq and CyTOF measure different, limited protein panels. It takes a cell's protein abundance profile over whatever panel was measured and learns cell- and protein-level representations, used for cell annotation, batch integration, imputing unmeasured proteins and choosing compact protein panels.
profile.summary_source_locator: Preprint abstract; README.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each measured protein is represented by a protein-identity embedding from a shared protein codebook plus a continuous embedding of its abundance. A transformer encoder (in the CUDA configuration: 8 layers, model width 256, 8 heads, feed-forward size 2048) is pre-trained by masking abundances (masked ratio 0.15) and reconstructing them with a mean squared error loss; a CLS token feeds the decoder. Inputs are CITE-seq data normalised by CLR or CyTOF data with ARCSIN preprocessing.
sections.source_locator: Preprint abstract; README.md; configs/large-scale-new-10_config.yaml

The model was pre-trained on Moore Threads MTT S5000 GPUs; the sources do not explain how the _moore checkpoint differs. A result should name the checkpoint file and its SHA-256.

profile.summary: LncRFM is an RNA foundation model built for long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), whose function depends on both short sequence motifs and base pairing that can span thousands of nucleotides. It reads an RNA sequence and is pretrained to predict masked nucleotides, with masking guided by secondary structure; its encoder outputs can then be fine-tuned with a small task head for tasks such as lncRNA localisation, disease association or splice-site prediction. The authors also release the LncCorpus pretraining corpus and the LncBench benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; README.md: Model loading and inference, Downstream learning

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LncRFM is a hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder. Its state-space kernels build on Mamba, and its bidirectional backbone follows the Hydra and HydraRNA design. The model code requires a motif stem, a motif gate and a pair-aware bidirectional mixer. The released configuration has 12 layers of width 768, motif convolution kernels of sizes 3 and 7, and attention layers with 12 heads at positions 5 and 11. It is pretrained by masked language modelling, using a structure-aware masking collator adapted from RNAErnie2 and training data that records each base's pairing partner. The pretraining launcher uses FP32, sequences of 200 to 2,048 nucleotides and 300,000 steps.

The archive holds a folder lncrfm_pretrained with model.safetensors, model_config.json, the tokenizer files, a README and the licence. The model settings are loaded from model_config.json, which records global step 300000 and float32 precision. A result should name the Zenodo record and version and the repository commit.

steps.title: Predict a masked nucleotide
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
import json
import torch
from lncrfm import get_lncrfm, get_tokenizer

checkpoint = Path("checkpoints/lncrfm_pretrained")
options = json.loads((checkpoint / "model_config.json").read_text())["factory_kwargs"]
tokenizer = get_tokenizer(
    tokenizer_file=str(checkpoint / "tokenizer.json"),
    max_length=options["max_length"],
)
model = get_lncrfm(
    **options,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    from_pretrained=str(checkpoint),
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device="cuda",
).eval()

inputs = tokenizer("[CLS] A U G [MASK] C [SEP]", return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)
print(outputs.logits.argmax(dim=-1))
EOF
steps.explanation: The README's loading and inference example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It reads the model settings from the checkpoint and runs on CUDA.

outputs: test_model.py prints a PASS line for each check it runs, for example that the architecture and the checkpoint tensors match. The inference example prints the index of the most likely token at each input position, including the masked one.

profile.summary: LIMBER is an RNA language model for non-coding RNA. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and returns per-nucleotide embeddings and masked-token predictions, which the authors use for secondary-structure prediction, RNA family classification and mutational fitness scoring.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Overview and Quick start; preprint abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LIMBER stacks two kinds of layer in a repeating Transformer, Transformer, Mamba pattern. The Transformer layers use bidirectional self-attention, which relates any two positions directly; the authors link this to the long-range coupling that base pairing leaves in a sequence. The Mamba layers are selective state-space layers that process the sequence in order. The model is pretrained by masked language modelling: 15% of nucleotide positions are selected, and of those 80% are replaced by a mask token, 10% by a random nucleotide and 10% left unchanged. Tokenisation is one token per nucleotide over a 10-token vocabulary; T is mapped to U and any other symbol to N.
sections.source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Overview; Model zoo; Tokenization; Pretraining

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Five LIMBER sizes are released, from 10.2M to 664.3M parameters, with size-matched pure-Transformer and pure-Mamba models trained on the same data. The README counts 25 checkpoints in one Hugging Face repository, one subfolder per model, including data-fraction, training-epoch and shape ablations. A result should name the subfolder it used: LIMBER-macro, LIMBER-meso and LIMBER-nano differ in depth and width, not only in size. The Hugging Face repository was at revision d2d6ae6 when read on 2026-11-26.
sections.source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Model zoo; Hugging Face file listing at revision d2d6ae6

sections.title: What the authors report
sections.body: The authors fine-tuned LIMBER and each baseline themselves under one protocol. They report a median flexible F1 of 0.895 on bpRNA TS0 and 0.816 on Rivas TestSetB for LIMBER-macro, and 99.2% accuracy on the 13-class nRC benchmark. On IRES identification and 5'UTR mean ribosome load, RiNALMo-giga scores higher than LIMBER-macro on most metrics in the same tables. These are author-reported figures and are not yet recorded as results in this database.

import torch
from scripts.load_hybrid650 import load_hybrid, encode, embed

profile.summary: MirrorDNA is a very small DNA language model, 2.35M parameters for the main model, that learns its own way of splitting DNA into tokens. Its tokenizer is built so that a sequence and its reverse complement, the two strands of the same DNA, are always split into mirror-image pieces, so both strands get the same tokens. It is pretrained on the human genome and fine-tuned for DNA classification and regression tasks, giving features that either ignore strand or keep it, depending on the task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: opening paragraph, Intended use; Hugging Face API

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNA is double-stranded, so the same stretch can be read in either direction as its reverse complement. MirrorDNA learns how to cut a sequence into chunks (its tokens) with a symmetric boundary router built so that a sequence and its reverse complement are always cut into mirror-image chunks, whatever the parameter values. Both strands therefore get the same tokens. Bases pass through an encoder, the router chooses chunk boundaries and a transformer works on the chunks. A decoder produces per-base features at full resolution, from which the model computes its output logits; pretraining is masked language modelling with 15% of bases masked. For downstream tasks the model gives pooled features that do not depend on strand, or orientation-aware features for labels that do, such as promoters or splice sites.

profile.summary: The All-Atom Structure Tokenizer turns a three dimensional biomolecular structure into a short list of integers and back again. Its encoder reads an assembly of heavy atoms, with its chemical graph, and emits one integer per chemical unit (a protein residue, a nucleotide, or a single ligand atom or ion) from a vocabulary of 8,192 identifiers. A separate coordinate decoder takes those integers, the chemical inventory of the assembly and Gaussian noise and reconstructs atomic coordinates. It is published as a PyTorch reference implementation of the tokenizer described in a Scinetics technical report on AtomLM-9b; the authors' trained checkpoints are not distributed, so the released code starts from random parameters.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: opening paragraphs and Architecture table

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The atom graph joins all covalent bonds plus up to 32 intramolecular and 16 intermolecular spatial neighbours per receiver within 12 angstroms. An atom encoder of 8 scalar and vector blocks (256 scalar and 64 vector channels) feeds a unit encoder that pools inside each unit and then runs 4 full-assembly attention layers at width 512. An invariant readout projects scalars, vector norms, inner products and ordered signed volumes from 512 down to 5 values, and finite scalar quantisation with levels (8, 8, 8, 4, 4) maps those to mixed-radix identifiers 0 to 8191, trained with a straight-through estimator. The coordinate decoder is 12 unit transformer layers at width 768 plus 4 equivariant atom blocks at scalar width 256, and samples coordinates from centred Gaussian noise with 50 Heun steps by default. Decoding an identifier recovers the five discrete levels exactly, but the step from levels to coordinates is learned and stochastic.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Architecture table and the paragraph below it

sections.title: What the input must look like
sections.body: An assembly is a JSON record with three ordered arrays: units, each with a kind (protein, dna, rna, ligand, ion or modified), a component name, chain, molecule and chain-relative position; atoms, each with a unit index, element and atom-role name, and optional charge, aromatic flag and xyz coordinates in angstroms; and bonds, listed once each as a pair of atom indices with a bond order, where 4 means aromatic. The card is explicit that standardisation is the user's job: biological assembly expansion from PDB or mmCIF, ligand bond perception and chemical component dictionary standardisation are upstream preprocessing steps. Atom and unit ordering must be preserved between encoding and decoding, and the command line tool stores a fingerprint of the chemical records with the identifiers and checks it before decoding. A unit with no observed atoms gets the sentinel -1 from the encoder and needs a valid identifier supplied before sampling.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Molecular inputs; examples/peptide_ligand.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The package is version 0.1.0 and requires Python 3.10 or later with torch 2.4 or later; its only console script is atomtoken. This page read Hugging Face revision 4c231da23f4d3be880d9e0b9ab8a62e49d8477bd. No trained checkpoint is published, and the card warns that identifiers produced by different checkpoints need not have the same structural meaning, so a token list is only comparable within one checkpoint. The card also states that the repository does not reproduce the report's benchmark scores. Two training profiles are selectable, tiny and report, the latter being the default; a result must therefore name the profile, the checkpoint file and the decoder seed, since decoding is stochastic and deterministic only with a fixed noise seed.

strengths.text: The input schema is defined precisely, down to bond orders, formal charges, missing coordinates and the handling of inter-chain links, and a worked example file ships with the code.
It is not protein-only: units may be protein residues, DNA, RNA, ligand atoms, ions or modified components, so a mixed assembly can be tokenised in one pass.

The released tests cover the discrete bottleneck in detail, including all 8,192 identifiers, rotation and translation behaviour, chirality signs, missing coordinates and deterministic decoding with a fixed seed.
A short end-to-end example runs on the shipped data: train for two steps on the tiny profile, then encode and decode with that checkpoint.

limitations.text: There are no trained weights. Anything useful requires training the tokenizer yourself, and the card says the release does not reproduce the report's benchmark scores.

Token identifiers are not a shared vocabulary: the card states that identifiers from different checkpoints need not have the same structural meaning, so tokens cannot be compared across training runs.
No licence is stated anywhere in the sources read, so the terms for reusing the code are unclear.

profile.summary: BMRetriever-7B is a biomedical text embedding model for dense retrieval. It turns a query (with a one-sentence task instruction) or a passage into a 4096-dimensional vector, and relevance is scored as the dot product between query and passage vectors. It is the largest of four BMRetriever models and is built on the BioMistral 7B language model, further trained on biomedical corpora and instruction data.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Model Specifications, Model Usage; model card: Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BMRetriever starts from a pretrained language model (BioMistral for the 7B model), runs unsupervised pre-training on large biomedical corpora, then instruction fine-tuning on labelled datasets and synthetic pairs. At inference, each query is prefixed with a one-sentence task instruction, each passage with 'Represent this passage', and an end-of-sequence token is appended. The embedding is the final hidden state at the last token (last-token pooling). The 7B model is a 32-layer Mistral architecture with hidden size 4096.

sections.body: The family has four checkpoints on Hugging Face: BMRetriever-410M and 1B (Pythia backbones), 2B (Gemma) and 7B (BioMistral). The README reports the 7B model has the highest average scores of the four on the authors' retrieval tasks and applications. The instruction fine-tuning data, about 1.4M pairs, is released as BMRetriever/biomed_retrieval_dataset, and eval.py and prompt.py reproduce the BEIR experiments. A result should name the checkpoint, its Hugging Face revision (this page read 13e6adb9 for 7B) and the instruction text used for queries.

run_guide.summary: Load BMRetriever-7B from Hugging Face, embed two example queries and two passages, and print their dot-product similarity scores.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and Hugging Face transformers installed; the sources give no install command. The config was saved with transformers 4.37.2.
A CUDA GPU: the example moves inputs to 'cuda'. Memory needs are not stated; the weights are float32 with 7,110,660,096 parameters.
Weights and code are MIT licensed; the weights are not gated.

steps.title: Embed and score example texts
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("BMRetriever/BMRetriever-7B") 
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("BMRetriever/BMRetriever-7B") 

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

from torch import Tensor
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel


def last_token_pool(last_hidden_states: Tensor,
                 attention_mask: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    last_hidden = last_hidden_states.masked_fill(~attention_mask[..., None].bool(), 0.0)
    left_padding = (attention_mask[:, -1].sum() == attention_mask.shape[0])
    if left_padding:
        embedding = last_hidden[:, -1]
    else:
        sequence_lengths = attention_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1
        batch_size = last_hidden.shape[0]
        embedding = last_hidden[torch.arange(batch_size, device=last_hidden.device), sequence_lengths]
    return embedding

def get_detailed_instruct_query(task_description: str, query: str) -> str:
    return f'{task_description}\nQuery: {query}'

def get_detailed_instruct_passage(passage: str) -> str:
    return f'Represent this passage\npassage: {passage}'

# Each query must come with a one-sentence instruction that describes the task
task = 'Given a scientific claim, retrieve documents that support or refute the claim'
queries = [
    get_detailed_instruct_query(task, 'Cis-acting lncRNAs control the expression of genes that are positioned in the vicinity of their transcription sites.'),
    get_detailed_instruct_query(task, 'Forkhead 0 (fox0) transcription factors are involved in apoptosis.')
]

# No need to add instruction for retrieval documents
documents = [
    get_detailed_instruct_passage("Gene regulation by the act of long non-coding RNA transcription Long non-protein-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are proposed to be the largest transcript class in the mouse and human transcriptomes. Two important questions are whether all lncRNAs are functional and how they could exert a function. Several lncRNAs have been shown to function through their product, but this is not the only possible mode of action. In this review we focus on a role for the process of lncRNA transcription, independent of the lncRNA product, in regulating protein-coding-gene activity in cis. We discuss examples where lncRNA transcription leads to gene silencing or activation, and describe strategies to determine if the lncRNA product or its transcription causes the regulatory effect."),
    get_detailed_instruct_passage("Noncoding transcription at enhancers: general principles and functional models. Mammalian genomes are extensively transcribed outside the borders of protein-coding genes. Genome-wide studies recently demonstrated that cis-regulatory genomic elements implicated in transcriptional control, such as enhancers and locus-control regions, represent major sites of extragenic noncoding transcription. Enhancer-templated transcripts provide a quantitatively small contribution to the total amount of cellular nonribosomal RNA; nevertheless, the possibility that enhancer transcription and the resulting enhancer RNAs may, in some cases, have functional roles, rather than represent mere transcriptional noise at accessible genomic regions, is supported by an increasing amount of experimental data. In this article we review the current knowledge on enhancer transcription and its functional implications.")
]
input_texts = queries + documents

max_length = 512

# Tokenize the input texts
batch_dict = tokenizer(input_texts, max_length=max_length-1, padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors='pt')

# Important! Adding EOS token at the end
batch_dict['input_ids'] = [input_ids + [tokenizer.eos_token_id] for input_ids in batch_dict['input_ids']]
batch_dict = tokenizer.pad(batch_dict, padding=True, return_attention_mask=True, return_tensors='pt').to("cuda")

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**batch_dict)
    embeddings = last_token_pool(outputs.last_hidden_state, batch_dict['attention_mask'])

scores = (embeddings[:2] @ embeddings[2:].T)
print(scores.tolist())
PY

profile.summary: BulkFormer is a family of foundation models for human bulk RNA-seq. A model takes one expression profile per sample, covering about twenty thousand protein-coding genes, and returns either a single vector that represents the whole sample or a vector per gene plus recovered expression values. Those vectors are then used as frozen features for downstream prediction, for example disease classification, prognosis or drug response.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header and Choose a model; docs/original-paper.md: Abstract; docs/architecture.md; docs/models/atlas.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The two current models work differently. Atlas gives each gene a token that combines a learned identity embedding with a linear projection of log2(TPM + 1), then passes a CLS token and up to 4,096 selected gene tokens through 16 bidirectional transformer blocks of width 1,024 with 16 heads and SwiGLU feed-forward layers; the sample feature is the 1,024-dimensional CLS output taken before the projection head. Latest encodes all 19,973 gene positions at once: gene identity, a sinusoidal encoding of expression and a global expression MLP (19,973 to 2,560 to 768) are normalised separately and summed with fixed 1:1:1 coefficients, then a residual weighted graph convolution of hidden width 256 feeds a 12-layer Performer of width 768. A small network reads how much of the input is missing and applies a bounded gain and offset to the expression head.
sections.source_locator: docs/architecture.md; configs/atlas_model.json; configs/latest_model.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three generations sit in one repository. The publication family has five sizes: 37M, 50M, 93M, 127M and 147M parameters, with the authors recommending 147M where resources allow. The 2026-11-04 release added BulkFormer-Atlas (242.37M) and BulkFormer-Latest (154.55M), and on 2026-11-06 Latest moved to its final epoch-20 checkpoint. Each new model carries an immutable checkpoint ID: atlas-infonce-epoch10-update320000 and latest-20261106-epoch20-update148300. The repository is explicit that published PRIMO scores were produced by earlier checkpoints: Atlas appears as BulkFormer-variant, and the epoch-19 Latest as BulkFormer-V3Plus, whose scores do not evaluate the current download. A result should name the model, the checkpoint ID and the pooling protocol.

strengths.text: It is pretrained on bulk RNA-seq rather than single-cell data. The authors argue that the modality of the pretraining data matters and report that BulkFormer beat single-cell foundation models on five downstream tasks in their own evaluation.

import pandas as pd
from bulkformer import load_atlas, prepare_atlas_input, select_variable_genes, extract_atlas

profile.summary: BulkRNABert is a transformer language model for bulk RNA-seq data. It takes the expression levels of a fixed set of genes from one sample and returns embeddings of that sample. The embeddings are used to build downstream models for cancer-type classification and survival-time prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: PMLR abstract; README.md: 1. BulkRNABert; model card: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BulkRNABert is an encoder-only transformer. Each gene in the input is one token, and its expression value is binned and embedded together with a gene embedding. During pretraining, expression values are masked at random and the model learns to reconstruct them from the other genes, as in BERT. The released configuration has 4 transformer layers, an embedding size of 256, 8 attention heads, 64 expression bins and 19,062 genes. For a downstream task the authors either probe the learned embeddings or use parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
sections.source_locator: Model card: introduction; checkpoints/bulk_rna_bert_tcga/config.json; PMLR abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository ships three pretrained checkpoints in JAX: bulk_rna_bert_tcga (pretrained on TCGA), bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode (GTEx and ENCODE) and bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode_tcga (a mix of all three). It also ships a classification model for five TCGA cohorts used in an example notebook. The Hugging Face repository InstaDeepAI/BulkRNABert holds a PyTorch version for the transformers library, described as pretrained on TCGA, plus the JAX parameters. A result should name the checkpoint, the framework and the commit or Hugging Face revision; this page read the repository at commit bfdc2ab8 and the Hugging Face card at revision 4ee84d56.

sections.title: Input preparation
sections.body: The model expects expression values for a fixed list of genes, given in common_gene_id.txt, in a fixed order. The repository includes a script that turns raw RNA-seq files downloaded from the GDC portal into this format, using the unstranded TPM column in its example. The Hugging Face example applies log10(1 + x) to the expression values before tokenising and checks that the number of columns equals the model's gene count.

strengths.text: Weights for three pretraining datasets are released, so a user can compare a TCGA-only model with one trained on non-cancer tissue (GTEx and ENCODE) or a mix.
Code and weights are under Apache-2.0, and the Hugging Face weights are not gated.
The repository includes sample TCGA data, the gene list and a preprocessing script for raw GDC files, so the input format can be reproduced.

The authors report that it improves on previous methods for pan-cancer classification and survival analysis on TCGA, and that it transfers to unseen cohorts in survival analysis. This is the authors' own claim.

limitations.text: The input is a fixed list of 19,062 genes in a fixed order. Data from another gene annotation or platform must be mapped onto this list first.
The model gives embeddings, not predictions. Classification or survival needs a downstream model; only a five-cohort classifier and a pan-cancer survival checkpoint are shipped.

steps.title: Compute embeddings for the sample data
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import haiku as hk
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import pandas as pd

from multiomics_open_research.bulk_rna_bert.pretrained import get_bulkrnabert_pretrained_model
from multiomics_open_research.common.preprocess import preprocess_omic

# Get pretrained model
parameters, forward_fn, tokenizer, config = get_bulkrnabert_pretrained_model(
    model_name="bulk_rna_bert_tcga",
    embeddings_layers_to_save=(4,),
    checkpoint_directory="checkpoints/",
)
forward_fn = hk.transform(forward_fn)

# Get bulk RNASeq data and tokenize it
gene_expression_df = pd.read_csv("data/bulkrnabert/tcga_sample.csv")
gene_expression_array = preprocess_omic(gene_expression_df, config)
gene_expression_ids = tokenizer.batch_tokenize(gene_expression_array)
gene_expression_ids = jnp.asarray(gene_expression_ids, dtype=jnp.int32)

# Inference
random_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
outs = forward_fn.apply(parameters, random_key, gene_expression_ids)

# Get mean embeddings from layer 4
gene_expression_mean_embeddings = outs["embeddings_4"].mean(axis=1)
PY
steps.explanation: The README inference snippet, wrapped in a shell heredoc and run from the repository root. Replace bulk_rna_bert_tcga with bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode or bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode_tcga to use the other checkpoints.

outputs: An array of mean layer-4 embeddings, one row per sample in tcga_sample.csv, held in memory. The snippet prints nothing and writes no file.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The guide stops at embeddings. Classification or survival prediction needs a downstream model, as in the repository's example notebook.
Own data must first be converted to the model's gene list, for example with scripts/preprocess_tcga_rna_seq.py for GDC files.

profile.summary: Ladon is a foundation model for bulk RNA sequencing of tumours, built by the company Blank Bio. It learns from millions of RNA-seq profiles by reconstructing masked parts of isoform-level expression, and its embeddings are then used to predict patient survival, recurrence and response to treatment. The developers present it as a way to make RNA-based predictions that still hold in clinical trials and cohorts the model was not fitted on.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report page 1 (abstract); page 2, Introducing Ladon

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ladon is a transformer encoder-decoder of 3 billion parameters. It is pretrained self-supervised, by masked token reconstruction on isoform-level expression profiles, so it can learn from samples without outcome labels. For clinical use the developers then mid-train it with supervision to predict patient and tumour characteristics such as disease stage, age, tumour grade and genomic alterations, together with clinical outcomes. They then discard the prediction heads, freeze the encoder and fit simple outcome models, such as linear Cox survival models, on its embeddings. The report does not describe the layers, tokenisation or training corpus in more detail.
sections.source_locator: Report page 2, Introducing Ladon; page 11, Methods: Ladon representations; page 6; page 28, Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The report describes one model family and several adaptations of it (pretrained encoder, supervised mid-training with survival or response labels), and shows models of several sizes and training steps in its scaling figures, but names no released checkpoint. No weights, code or data release is listed with the report. On 2026-11-26 the GitHub organisation blankbio had 0 public repositories and the Hugging Face organisation BlankBio had 0 models and 0 datasets. Results from Ladon cannot be reproduced independently from public material.
sections.source_locator: Report pages 11, 41 to 42 (Figures 20 and 21, Methods: Reconstruction loss); GitHub org API; Hugging Face org overview

sections.title: Evaluation in the report
sections.body: Every result is reported on a setting not used for fitting: a held-out trial, another cohort or another platform. Survival models fitted on TCGA were applied unchanged to CPTAC and the reverse; the developers report Ladon ahead of differential gene expression signatures, BulkRNABERT and BulkFormer, and that adding Ladon to clinical covariates improved survival prediction in all 12 target cohorts. They also report better response prediction for immunotherapy than PD-L1 expression, recovery of isoform usage from gene-level counts (median Pearson r of 0.81 across 3,000 genes in held-out tumours), and cell-composition inference from single-cell references. All of these are the developers' own results in an unreviewed report.

name: CellPLM
description: Cell-level transformer foundation model pretrained on scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Primary reference: Wen et al., ICLR 2024.

profile.summary: CellPLM is a pre-trained transformer for single-cell transcriptomics that treats each cell as a token and a tissue (a set of cells) as a sentence, so it can model relations between cells. It takes gene expression for a set of cells and outputs cell embeddings; the repository's tutorials apply it to cell embedding, cell type annotation and spatial imputation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Preprint abstract; README.md; tutorials

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Instead of treating genes as tokens, CellPLM treats cells as tokens and tissues as sentences. It is pre-trained on single-cell and spatially resolved transcriptomic data so that it learns cell-cell relations, and it uses a Gaussian mixture prior on the latent space as an extra inductive bias. The shipped configuration names a flowformer encoder (4 layers, hidden size 1024), a gmvae latent module with 512 dimensions and 16 clusters, and a decoder module named nbmlp, trained with masking of 75% of nodes and 25% of features.
sections.source_locator: Preprint abstract; ckpt/20230926_85M.config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Checkpoints are on Dropbox and the authors say they may update them. The README names 20230926_85M as the latest version (dated 10/10/2023); the repository ships a config file of that name whose internal name field reads 20230926_75M_50M; the cell embedding tutorial loads 20231027_85M. The sources do not explain these differences. A result should name the checkpoint prefix exactly and the repository commit.

steps.title: Embed cells
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import anndata as ad
from CellPLM.utils import set_seed
from CellPLM.pipeline.cell_embedding import CellEmbeddingPipeline

PRETRAIN_VERSION = '20231027_85M'
DEVICE = 'cuda:1'
set_seed(42)

data = ad.read_h5ad('../data/gse155468.h5ad')
data.obs_names_make_unique()
pipeline = CellEmbeddingPipeline(pretrain_prefix=PRETRAIN_VERSION, # Specify the pretrain checkpoint to load
                                 pretrain_directory='../ckpt')
embedding = pipeline.predict(data, # An AnnData object
                device=DEVICE) # Specify a gpu or cpu for model inference
EOF

name: GenePT
description: Cell embeddings built from GPT text embeddings of gene descriptions, weighted by expression (GenePT-w variant).

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: GenePT builds gene and cell embeddings from text instead of training on expression data. Each gene's NCBI summary is embedded with an OpenAI text embedding model; a cell embedding is then either the expression-weighted average of its gene embeddings (GenePT-w) or the text embedding of the cell's gene names ordered by expression (GenePT-s). The embeddings feed gene-level and cell-level tasks such as gene property and cell type classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: What is GenePT?; paper Methods 3.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: About 33,000 genes were taken from the scGPT and Geneformer vocabularies and genes in the downstream datasets. Each gene's NCBI summary was embedded with text-embedding-ada-002, giving a 1,536-dimensional gene vector. For cells, counts are normalised to 10,000 per cell and log(1 + x) transformed. GenePT-w takes the expression-weighted average of the gene vectors and scales it to unit length. GenePT-s writes the expressed gene names in descending order of expression as a sentence and embeds that sentence. No model is trained on expression data.
sections.source_locator: Paper Methods 3.1; README.md

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The released artefact is a set of precomputed gene embeddings on Zenodo (record 10833191, one zip file). In March 2024 the authors added embeddings that include UniProt protein summaries and embeddings from the newer text-embedding-3-large model, alongside the original text-embedding-ada-002 ones. A result should state which summary file and which embedding model were used, since GenePT-w results depend on that choice.
sections.source_locator: README.md: News; Zenodo record

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Gene-level prediction tasks, gene-gene interaction analysis, cell type annotation and batch effect assessment, all shown as example notebooks.

name: Nicheformer
description: Transformer foundation model pretrained on dissociated and spatial transcriptomics.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Primary reference: Schaub et al., Nature Methods 2025.

profile.summary: Nicheformer is a transformer foundation model trained on both dissociated single-cell and image-based spatial transcriptomics from human and mouse. It turns each cell's expression into a ranked sequence of gene tokens, with tokens for species, modality and assay, and outputs a 512-dimensional cell embedding that can be fine-tuned or linearly probed to predict spatial labels and spatial composition.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper Abstract and Results

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Genes from human and mouse are merged into one vocabulary of 20,310 gene tokens, covering orthologous protein-coding genes and species-specific ones. Each cell's expression vector becomes a sequence of gene tokens ranked by expression, plus metadata tokens. A 12-layer transformer encoder with 16 attention heads, a feed-forward size of 1,024 and a 1,500-token context is pre-trained to predict masked tokens. The cell embedding is an aggregate of the gene token outputs. Spatial coordinates are not used in pre-training.

name: Novae
description: Graph attention foundation model for spatial transcriptomics domains.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Primary reference: Blampey et al., Nature Methods 2025.

profile.summary: Novae is a graph-based foundation model for spatial transcriptomics. It takes a spatial dataset at single-cell or spot resolution, builds a graph of neighbouring cells, and outputs a representation of each cell in its spatial context, which is used to assign spatial domains zero-shot across gene panels, tissues and technologies, with batch-effect correction built in.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; preprint abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Novae computes the spatial neighbours of each cell and learns cell representations with self-supervision on these graphs, a method adapted from SwAV. Representations are assigned to learned prototypes, which the documentation describes as elementary spatial domains; batch information is used only during training. The default human model's configuration sets 10 layers, 16 heads, hidden size 128, embedding size 512, output size 64 and 512 prototypes, with neighbourhood views of 2 hops.

The README announces a new improved model with a tutorial at a novae_scConcept page; it does not name the Hugging Face repository. A novae-test repository also exists. import novae

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: scELMo uses large language models to describe genes (or other features and cell metadata) in text and to embed those descriptions, then combines the embeddings with single-cell expression data to make cell embeddings. Without training a new model the cell embeddings support clustering, batch effect correction and cell type annotation; a small fine-tuned adaptor handles harder tasks such as perturbation analysis.

sections.title: How it works

A cell's embedding combines these feature embeddings with its expression profile. Unlike GenePT's arithmetic average, scELMo also offers a weighted average that uses expression levels as weights. In the fine-tuning framework, a light model (an adaptor) is trained on the gene embeddings and expression profiles.

The authors host precomputed embeddings, including gene embeddings from gpt4-o and drug embeddings from GPT 3.5, on a website. It adds a Mixture of Experts decoder that routes each sample to protocol-aware decoding of gene expression, samples training data in a spatially aware way, and uses a neighbourhood-based reconstruction objective to capture which cell states co-locate in tissue. At inference, embed_data returns an embedding per cell or spot.

name: scPRINT
description: Single-cell foundation model pretrained on CELLxGENE data for gene network inference and expression denoising.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Primary reference: Kalfon et al.

profile.summary: scPRINT is a transformer model for single-cell RNA-seq data, built mainly to infer gene networks. It takes the raw counts of a cell and can, without fine-tuning, denoise expression, produce a cell embedding, predict labels such as cell type, disease, sequencer, sex and ethnicity, and output a cell-specific gene network.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; FAQ; paper Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each gene in a cell is represented by the sum of three embeddings: its identity, its expression and its genomic location. The identity embedding is the ESM2 protein embedding of the gene's most common protein product. The paper says these gene embeddings can be frozen during training or used only for initialisation. A bidirectional transformer encodes the cell. Pre-training adds three losses together: denoising (recover a profile from a downsampled one), bottleneck learning (regenerate the expression profile from the cell embedding alone) and hierarchical label prediction. scPRINT generates a gene network by selecting and combining attention heads into a gene by gene matrix.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results: scPRINT; Fig. 1 caption

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The Hugging Face repository jkobject/scPRINT holds the checkpoints small-v1, small-v2, medium-v1, medium-v1.5 and large-v1, plus cell-transformer, esm-ft and many run-ID checkpoints under other_ckpts. The README uses medium-v1.5 in its examples. To reproduce the paper the README asks for version tag 1.6.4. The authors have since released scPRINT-2 in a separate repository. A result should name the checkpoint file, the Hugging Face revision and the package version.

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Zero-shot expression denoising, cell embedding, cell label prediction and gene network inference on human or mouse scRNA-seq, and fine-tuning for other analyses. The README says it can be used on organisms with a similar gene set; very different organisms need new gene embeddings and retraining.

name: Akita
description: Akita contact-map model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Akita predicts how a stretch of DNA folds in three dimensions. It takes just over one megabase of sequence, one-hot encoded, and returns a predicted contact map for that window, as log observed over expected values, for each of five cell types it was trained on. It is used for in silico work: saturation mutagenesis, interpreting eQTLs, predicting the effect of structural variants and comparing species.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract (Europe PMC record); params.json: model; targets.txt; explore_model.ipynb

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Akita is a convolutional network in two halves. A 1D trunk reads the one-hot sequence: a convolution block, then a tower of ten convolution and pooling blocks, then eight dilated residual blocks, which brings 1,048,576 bases down to 2,048 bp bins. A 2D head turns the 1D representation into a pairwise map (one_to_two with a mean operation), concatenates a distance encoding, symmetrises it, applies six dilated 2D residual blocks, crops the edges and reads off the upper triangle with a diagonal offset of 2. The final layer has five linear units, one per training dataset. Training used mean squared error with SGD, batch size 2, and reverse-complement and shift augmentation. The published model has 751,653 parameters, of which 746,149 are trainable.
sections.source_locator: params.json: model trunk and head_hic, train; keras_print.txt; explore_model.ipynb

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations. The published model is a single TensorFlow checkpoint, model_best.h5, trained on human Hi-C and micro-C mapped to hg38 at 2048 bp resolution, with params.json as its configuration. In 2021 the authors retrained Akita on human and mouse data together after a further hyperparameter search, splitting the genome into eight folds and training one model per held-out fold; those data and models sit in Google Cloud Storage under gs://basenji_hic/3-2021, with model file suffix 0 for human and 1 for mouse. A result should say which generation and, for the 2021 set, which fold and species. This page read the repository at commit 06ce5d38.

strengths.text: Small model, about 750 thousand parameters, and the authors say that once trained it gives rapid in silico predictions.
One forward pass gives maps for five cell types at once, so cell-type differences can be read from the same prediction.

Code, model configuration and a notebook that predicts from an arbitrary sequence are published in the Apache-2.0 Basenji repository, with scripts that download the weights and training data (no licence is stated for those files), and the repository also holds the training scripts.

It runs inside the Basenji codebase and is installed from requirements.txt or a conda environment, with TensorFlow installed separately, plus cooltools for the notebook. There is no pip package for Akita itself.

steps.title: Load the model and predict from a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import json, os, subprocess
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = '-1' ### run on CPU
import numpy as np
import pysam
from basenji import dna_io, seqnn

with open('params.json') as params_open:
    params = json.load(params_open)
    params_model = params['model']

seqnn_model = seqnn.SeqNN(params_model)
seqnn_model.restore('model_best.h5')
print('successfully loaded')

os.makedirs('./data', exist_ok=True)
if not os.path.isfile('./data/hg38.ml.fa'):
    print('downloading hg38.ml.fa')
    subprocess.call('curl -o ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz https://storage.googleapis.com/basenji_barnyard2/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)
    subprocess.call('gunzip ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)

fasta_open = pysam.Fastafile('./data/hg38.ml.fa')
seq = fasta_open.fetch('chr12', 115163136, 116211712).upper()
seq_1hot = dna_io.dna_1hot(seq)
test_pred_from_seq = seqnn_model.model.predict(np.expand_dims(seq_1hot,0))
print(test_pred_from_seq.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The notebook's cells for loading the model and predicting from sequence, stitched into one shell heredoc. The region chr12:115163136-116211712 is one of the notebook's own example test regions, which is 2^20 bases long. The makedirs line and the final print of the output shape are additions.

name: Puffin-D
description: Puffin-D transcription initiation model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Puffin-D is a deep learning model that predicts transcription initiation signals from DNA sequence. It takes 100 kbp of genome sequence and returns base-level predictions for ten tracks: five assays that map transcription start sites (FANTOM CAGE, ENCODE CAGE, ENCODE RAMPAGE, GRO-cap and PRO-cap) on each strand. It is the prediction-focused companion of Puffin, an interpretable model from the same authors.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; Puffin-D

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Puffin-D is a fully convolutional network. One-hot DNA passes through a stack of strided 1D convolutions that downsample the sequence by factors of 4, 4, 5, 5, 5 and 2, each followed by residual convolution blocks. Upsampling layers with skip connections then restore base resolution. This down-and-up pass is repeated a second time. A final 1x1 convolution with a softplus gives 10 non-negative output tracks at each position. Training details were not in the sources read.
sections.source_locator: puffin_D.py: classes ConvBlock and Puffin_D

sections.title: Puffin and Puffin-D
sections.body: The repository holds two models. Puffin is an interpretation-focused model that explains each transcription start site in terms of motifs and single bases, and works on short sequences with 325 bp padding on each side. Puffin-D is the deep learning model for prediction over 100 kbp. The README says Puffin-D gives better predictions when prediction is the main need.
sections.source_locator: README.md: introduction; Command line interface (CLI) Usage

profile.summary: DeepSTARR predicts how strongly a 249 base pair piece of DNA acts as an enhancer in Drosophila melanogaster S2 cells. It is a convolutional neural network with two outputs, one for developmental and one for housekeeping enhancer activity, trained on genome-wide UMI-STARR-seq measurements. Besides prediction, it is used to read out which nucleotides drive the predicted activity and so to study transcription factor motifs and their syntax.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: DeepSTARR, DeepSTARR model; preprint abstract; DeepSTARR.model.json: input layer and output layers

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The architecture is adapted from Basset: four convolutional layers, each followed by batch normalisation, a ReLU activation and max pooling, then two fully connected layers of 256 units and two single-unit output layers, Dense_Dev and Dense_Hk. The released model file gives 256 filters of width 7 in the first convolutional layer, then 60 of width 3, 60 of width 5 and 120 of width 3, with pooling size 2 throughout. The convolutional layers pick up local motifs and motif syntax; the fully connected layers combine them into one activity value per enhancer type. The model is a regression on measured UMI-STARR-seq activity, not a classifier.
sections.source_locator: README: DeepSTARR model; DeepSTARR.model.json: layers

sections.title: Interpreting the model
sections.body: The repository ships a second script that computes nucleotide contribution scores for a given sequence, separately for developmental or housekeeping activity, using DeepLIFT and SHAP. A Colab notebook runs the whole path end to end: training, contribution scores and TF-MoDISco motifs. The preprint states that the model learned TF motifs and higher-order syntax rules, including the effect of motif-flanking sequence and inter-motif distances, and that these rules were validated experimentally.
sections.source_locator: DeepSTARR/README.md: Interpreting DeepSTARR with nucleotide contribution scores, Tutorial; preprint abstract

name: Orca
description: Orca 3D genome structure model.

version.note: Family record

profile.summary: Orca predicts the three-dimensional folding of the human genome from DNA sequence alone. It takes a genomic sequence of up to 256 Mb and returns predicted contact matrices at nine scales, from 4 kb resolution within 1 Mb up to whole-chromosome distances. It is used to run in silico Hi-C experiments: to ask what a structural variant, a haplotype or a designed sequence would do to local and large-scale genome structure.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: What is Orca, What can I use Orca for; paper: Results, Sequence-based prediction of multiscale 3D genome interactions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Orca has a hierarchical sequence encoder and a cascade of decoders. The encoder turns a one-hot sequence into representations at nine resolutions, from 4 kb up to 1,024 kb. Each decoder predicts one 250 by 250 interaction matrix for a window of a given size, as a log fold change over a distance-based background. The decoders run from the top down: each lower level takes the sequence representation at its resolution, the prediction from the level above cropped and upsampled, and a pairwise distance encoding matrix. Encoder and decoders are convolutional with residual connections; each decoder has 112 convolution layers cycling through dilation factors 1 to 64. Predictions are symmetrised with their transpose and averaged between the forward and reverse-complement sequence. The encoder is also trained on an auxiliary task of predicting DNase-seq and ChIP-seq chromatin profiles.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Orca model architecture for multiscale 3D genome prediction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Orca is a framework with several models, not one checkpoint. Separate models were trained per dataset: H1-ESC and HFF from micro-C, and a cohesin-depleted HCT116 Hi-C model used for the compartment analysis. The README loads models by scale, named 1M, 32M and 256M, and offers the 1 Mb model as the faster option for sub-megabase screens. A result should name the cell-type model and the scale, and the repository commit, since the weights come as Zenodo resource tarballs rather than from a versioned model hub. The training code for the three stages is in the train directory.
