steps.title: Load the checkpoint through the package
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from gpn import register_auto_classes
from transformers import AutoModel

register_auto_classes("phylo")

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("songlab/PhyloGPN")
print(model.config)
PY
steps.explanation: The documentation's quick start, wrapped in a heredoc, with a print of the configuration added to confirm the load. This is one of two loading routes: the package registers the AutoClasses for you. Note that pip install gpn is not pinned to the commit read for this page.

steps.title: Score a batch of sequences
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

checkpoint = "songlab/PhyloGPN"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(checkpoint, trust_remote_code=True)

# Example data
seqs = [
    "TATAAA",
    "GGCCAATCT",
    "CACGTG",
    "AGGTCACGT",
    "GCCAGCC",
    "GGGGATTTCC"
]

# Output length is input length minus 480 (the receptive field size minus 1)
pad_token = tokenizer.pad_token
pad_size = 481 // 2
pad_sequence = lambda seq: pad_token * pad_size + seq + pad_token * pad_size
padded_seqs = [pad_sequence(seq) for seq in seqs]
input_tensor = tokenizer(padded_seqs, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)["input_ids"]

with torch.no_grad():
    padded_embeddings = model.get_embeddings(input_tensor)
    padded_logits = model(input_tensor) # These are log rate parameters for the F81 model

embeddings = []
logits = []

for i in range(len(seqs)):
    length = len(seqs[i])
    embeddings.append(padded_embeddings[i, :length])
    logits.append({})

    for k in "ACGT":
        logits[-1][k] = padded_logits[k][i, :length]

print(embeddings[0].shape, {k: v.shape for k, v in logits[0].items()})
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's example, wrapped in a heredoc, with a print of the first sequence's embedding and logit shapes added. It pads each sequence so that outputs cover every input position. This is the second loading route: it skips the gpn package and loads the checkpoint's own code with trust_remote_code, so it can be run instead of the previous step.

outputs: For each input sequence: a per-position embedding tensor, and a log rate parameter per position for each of A, C, G and T.

name: BPNet
description: BPNet convolutional architecture trained from scratch per task.

version.note: Family record; variants are on configurations

profile.summary: BPNet is a convolutional neural network that predicts transcription-factor binding from DNA sequence at single-base resolution. It reads a stretch of genomic sequence and predicts the strand-specific read profile and the total read count of a ChIP-nexus or ChIP-seq experiment over that region. It is not a pretrained model: users train a new BPNet on their own experiment, then interpret it to find the sequence motifs that drive binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: In the paper, the body of the network is a first convolutional layer of 64 filters of width 25 bp, followed by 9 dilated convolutional layers of 64 filters of width 3, with the dilation rate doubling at every layer and no pooling, so base resolution is kept. Two output heads per transcription factor sit on top: a deconvolutional layer that predicts the probability of a read at each position on each strand (profile shape), and a global average pooling layer with a fully connected layer that predicts the total read count. The loss is a multinomial negative log-likelihood for profile shape plus a mean squared error on log total counts. A control track is given as an extra input so that experimental bias is regressed out. After training, contribution scores and TF-MoDISco are used to extract motifs.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'BPNet predicts TF binding profiles from sequence'; Methods, BPNet architecture and loss function

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations of the code in the same repository. The original package that accompanied the paper is kept at the v0-final tag; it uses a `bpnet train` command, a dataspec.yml file and Python 3.6 with TensorFlow 1. The current master branch is described by its authors as the improved version and the one to use; it has separate `bpnet-train`, `bpnet-predict` and `bpnet-shap` commands, Python 3.7, and an example configuration with a 2114 bp input, a 1000 bp output profile, a first filter of width 21 and 8 dilated layers. The two generations use different defaults, so a result should name the code version (tag or commit), the architecture parameters file and the training data. The trained mouse ESC model from the paper (Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, Klf4) is published on Zenodo and on Kipoi as BPNet-OSKN.

steps.shell:
BASE_DIR=ENCSR000EGM
DATA_DIR=$BASE_DIR/data
MODEL_DIR=$BASE_DIR/models
REFERENCE_DIR=reference
CHROM_SIZES=$REFERENCE_DIR/hg38.chrom.sizes
REFERENCE_GENOME=$REFERENCE_DIR/hg38.genome.fa
CV_SPLITS=$BASE_DIR/splits.json
INPUT_DATA=$BASE_DIR/input_data.json
MODEL_PARAMS=$BASE_DIR/bpnet_params.json

bpnet-train \
        --input-data $INPUT_DATA \
        --output-dir $MODEL_DIR \
        --reference-genome $REFERENCE_GENOME \
        --chroms $(paste -s -d ' ' $REFERENCE_DIR/chroms.txt) \
        --chrom-sizes $CHROM_SIZES \
        --splits $CV_SPLITS \
        --model-arch-name BPNet \
        --model-arch-params-json $MODEL_PARAMS \
        --sequence-generator-name BPNet \
        --model-output-filename model \
        --input-seq-len 2114 \
        --output-len 1000 \
        --shuffle \
        --threads 10 \
        --epochs 100 \
        --batch-size 64 \
        --reverse-complement-augmentation \
        --early-stopping-patience 10 \
        --reduce-lr-on-plateau-patience 5 \
        --learning-rate 0.001

bpnet-predict \
        --model $MODEL_DIR/model_split000 \

name: SpeciesLM
description: Species-aware DNA language model (SpeciesLM).

version.note: Family record

profile.summary: SpeciesLM is a family of species-aware DNA language models for the non-coding regions that flank genes. A model reads the sequence before the start codon or after the stop codon of a gene, together with a token naming the species it came from, and predicts masked nucleotides. The published models give per-nucleotide probabilities and sequence embeddings, which the authors use to find regulatory motifs and to predict gene expression and mRNA half-life. The original models were trained on fungi; a later metazoa checkpoint is the one TraitGym scores on human variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and methods, Masked language modeling; README; TraitGym config/config.yaml: specieslm

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each model is a DNABERT transformer with 12 encoder blocks. Nucleotides are split into overlapping 6-mers before entering the model. During training, spans of overlapping 6-mers are masked and the model learns to reconstruct them by minimising cross-entropy. The species label is prepended to the sequence as an extra token whose embedding is learned. An agnostic version was trained without this token for comparison. To predict for a species not seen in training, the authors give the token of a closely related species (C. glabrata for the 3' model and K. africana for the 5' model). Sequence representations come from pooling hidden states; the tutorial notebook averages hidden layers from layer 8 onwards. The later metazoa checkpoint keeps the width, depth and head count but uses a rotary-embedding variant (model_type rotarybert) with its own modelling code loaded through trust_remote_code.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Masked language modeling; Fig. 1 legend; ModelUsage.ipynb: Parameters and Embedding Sequences; metazoa config.json and card

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two sets of weights exist. The paper's fungal models are four branches of one Hugging Face repository: species and agnostic models for the 3' region (300 bp after the stop codon) and for the 5' region (1000 bp before the start codon plus the start codon). This page read downstream_species_lm at revision 742e7928 and upstream_species_lm at revision 1052abf2, taken from the branch listing. A second set is published under the johahi account: specieslm-fungi-upstream-k1, specieslm-fungi-downstream-k1, specieslm-fungi-yeastss-upstream-k1 (the sources do not describe this one) and specieslm-metazoa-upstream-k6, read here at revision 744863be. TraitGym scores that metazoa checkpoint with a 2000 bp window, so a result on this record should name the account, the checkpoint and the revision; the fungal and metazoa weights are not interchangeable. The upstream models were trained with FlashAttention and converted to standard Hugging Face models, which the README says may give slight numerical instabilities in float32.

name: FlowDock
description: FlowDock: conditional flow-matching docking and affinity model built on ESMFold and NeuralPLexer components.

version.note: Family record; the evaluated setup is on the configuration

attributes.provenance_note: Model details as given in the PLABench paper, Table 1.

profile.summary: FlowDock predicts the three dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex and, at the same time, how strongly the ligand binds. The inputs are protein sequences and ligand SMILES strings, with no pocket and no multiple sequence alignment needed; the model first predicts an unbound protein structure with ESMFold, then moves it towards a bound structure. Each generated complex comes with a structural confidence score and a binding affinity value, and several ligands can be modelled at the same time.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Section 3 overview; README.md: Description, How to predict new protein-ligand complex structures and their affinities

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: FlowDock is a conditional flow matching model: it learns a path from an unbound (apo) protein structure to the bound (holo) structure, for any number of binding ligands. The protein side starts from an ESMFold structure, which the authors use as a surrogate prior, and the ligand side starts from a harmonic prior constrained by the bond graph of the given SMILES string. The network is the NeuralPLexer architecture, which encodes protein language model sequence embeddings and ligand SMILES strings and decodes contact maps that condition a flow ordinary differential equation for the coordinates. The authors fine-tune NeuralPLexer's score head with the flow matching objective, along with its other intermediate weights and heads, including a confidence head redesigned to predict binding affinity; NeuralPLexer's original confidence head stays frozen.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Section 3 Methods, structure parametrisation and optimisation

sections.title: Training data and compute
sections.body: Training used PDBBind-E, which the authors describe as an enhanced version of a PDBBind 2020 based training set: they collected 17 743 crystal complex structures from PDBBind 2020 and 47 183 structures from the Binding MOAD. The repository also ships preparation steps for DockGen and a PDB based van der Mers dataset, and a fine-tuning route on PLINDER, which it warns needs about an hour to download and about 750G of storage. The paper states that FlowDock was trained using only 4 80GB H100 GPUs for 1 week, which it contrasts with the 128 A100 GPUs for one month it attributes to Chai-1.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3 dataset curation, Section 4 results discussion; README.md: How to prepare data for FlowDock

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published weights are a tar archive on Zenodo record 15066450, and the commands in the README name two checkpoints from it: esmfold_prior_paper_weights.ckpt for fine-tuning and esmfold_prior_paper_weights-EMA.ckpt for evaluation and sampling. The pretrained NeuralPLexer weights are a separate download, from Zenodo record 10373581. A result should name the checkpoint, the prior type, the sampler and the number of steps, since those are all command line settings; the README's examples use prior_type=esmfold, sampler=VDODE, num_steps=40 and n_samples=5. The repository also ships a Dockerfile and points at a prebuilt image.

name: FLOWR.ROOT
description: FLOWR.ROOT: SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching model with joint structure, affinity and confidence heads.

version.note: Family record; the evaluated setup is on the configuration

attributes.provenance_note: Model details as given in the PLABench paper, Table 1.

profile.summary: FLOWR.root designs ligands inside a protein pocket and scores how strongly they would bind, with one model. Given a protein structure and a reference ligand that marks the pocket, it generates three dimensional ligands, and its affinity head predicts four endpoints (pIC50, pKi, pKd, pEC50) with a confidence estimate for the generated structure. The same model can instead score ligands you already have, and it can be adapted to a project's own compounds with low rank fine-tuning.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results overview; README.md: Predicting Binding Affinities, Generating Molecules from PDB/CIF; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is an SE(3)-equivariant flow matching framework: it learns to transport an initial ligand sample towards a plausible bound ligand in a given pocket, and the structure head, the affinity head and a pLDDT style confidence head share one backbone. Because structure and affinity are trained together, the affinity prediction can steer generation at inference time by importance sampling instead of calling an external scoring function. The architecture uses a pocket encoder and a ligand decoder with latent attention, 128 coordinate sets, a latent size of 64 and 32 attention heads. The paper gives about 33 million trainable parameters for its configuration, whose ligand decoder has width 384; the README puts the released joint affinity checkpoints at d_model 512, so the count is not tied to a released checkpoint. Training ran in three stages: pretraining on about 1.5B small molecule conformations and about 2.5M mixed fidelity protein-ligand complexes, refinement on the curated SPINDR and HiQBind co-crystal sets, then project specific adaptation with LoRA.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results overview, Methods architecture and training

sections.title: What it can be asked to do
sections.body: From a protein PDB or CIF file plus a reference ligand, the repository supports de novo pocket conditional generation, interaction and pharmacophore conditional sampling, scaffold hopping and elaboration, core growing, fragment growing, and local replacement of chosen atoms by substructure inpainting. A separate ligand only mode generates without a protein context, using its own checkpoint. Affinity prediction is a different entry point: it scores the ligand you give it and writes the scores back into an SDF file, and a multi ligand variant scores many ligands against one protein in a single job, averaging over several seeds.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Generating Molecules from PDB/CIF, Generating Molecules from SDF, Predicting Binding Affinities; Paper: Abstract; predict_aff.sl

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four checkpoints are published on Google Drive, and the paper says pretrained checkpoints are mirrored on Zenodo. flowr_root_v2.2.ckpt is the latest joint generation and affinity model, flowr_root_v2.ckpt is the model behind most results in the paper and is the one the authors name for reproduction, flowr_root_spindr_base.ckpt is a fully converged generation only model trained on SPINDR, and flowr_root_v2_mol.ckpt is the ligand only model. They differ in architecture flags, which must be passed by hand when warm starting: d_model 512 with no cross products and an affinity head for v2.2 and v2.1, d_model 384 with cross products and no affinity head for spindr and v2_mol. A result must therefore name the checkpoint, the flags and the seed; the README warns that a fixed seed gives different samples on CPU, MPS and CUDA.

Four affinity endpoints are predicted separately, pIC50, pKi, pKd and pEC50, rather than mixed into one score. The paper describes this as explicitly avoiding treating heterogeneous affinity labels as interchangeable.
The paper describes a small model, about 33 million trainable parameters for the configuration it reports, and the LoRA route adapts it with about 3.3M trainable parameters.

strengths.text: The release is unusually complete: MIT code with a locked dependency set, four checkpoints, datasets, SLURM scripts for generation, prediction, training and both fine-tuning routes, and a browser interface.

limitations.text: The authors say the joint affinity and generation model is not fully converged, because of computational constraints, and that clash count can be a problem on out of distribution data.
The affinity head is described as accurate in distribution only. For out of distribution data, such as in-series compounds, the authors say it should be combined with LoRA adaptation.

It needs a large GPU in practice: the README recommends a CUDA GPU with at least 40GB VRAM for inference, and says CPU inference takes minutes rather than seconds. Apple MPS is opt-in and unvalidated.

The checkpoints differ in architecture flags that are not read back from the file, so a warm start with the shipped training script fails unless the flags are changed by hand; the README states its shipped flags do not match flowr_root_v2.2.ckpt.

steps.title: Predict affinities for one protein and ligand
steps.shell:
uv run --no-sync python -m flowr.predict.predict_from_pdb \
    --pdb_file YOUR_PROTEIN.pdb \
    --ligand_file YOUR_LIGAND.sdf \
    --dataset YOUR_PROTEIN_NAME \
    --gpus 1 \
    --num_workers 12 \
    --seed 42 \
    --batch_cost 20 \
    --arch pocket \
    --pocket_type holo \
    --pocket_noise fix \
    --cut_pocket \
    --pocket_cutoff 7 \
    --ckpt_path /path/to/flowr_root_v2.2.ckpt \
    --save_dir ./predict-aff_seed-42
steps.explanation: This is the invocation from the repository's own scripts/predict_aff.sl, with its placeholder paths left to fill in, one seed instead of the script's loop over four, and its noise injection setting (coord_noise_std=0.1, passed as --coord_noise_scale) left out. profile.summary: MixingDTA predicts drug-target affinity: given a drug SMILES string and a protein sequence, it returns a continuous affinity value. It does not learn its own sequence representations. Instead it takes embeddings from two pretrained language models, MolFormer for the molecule and ESM3-open for the protein, and feeds them to a trained aggregation network called MEETA. A data augmentation step called GBA-Mixup then builds extra training pairs by interpolating the embeddings of neighbouring drugs and proteins, which is aimed at sparse regions of affinity space and at unseen drugs or proteins.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction, Figure 1 caption; README.md: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MEETA, the backbone, replaces the usual multi-head attention between drug and protein tokens with attention-free aggregation, which the authors say has linear rather than quadratic cost in sequence length and therefore lets them keep full drug and protein sequences instead of truncating them. The code implements this as a cross_AFT block with query, key and value projections in both directions, drug against protein and protein against drug, followed by a regression head that outputs a single value. The drug embeddings come from MolFormer-XL and the protein embeddings from ESM3-open with 1.4B parameters; everything in MEETA after those two encoders is trained. GBA-Mixup then samples a mixing ratio from a Beta distribution and interpolates the embeddings and labels of neighbouring drug-target pairs, where neighbours are defined by six perspectives. A meta-predictor finally combines the embeddings of the six encoders trained on those perspectives.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Methods 2.2 and 2.3, Figure 1 caption; model.py: cross_AFT, Regress, DTA; config.py: configuration; README.md: etc

sections.title: Training and the six perspectives
sections.body: Training runs in two stages. In the first, the MEETA model is trained once for each of six cases, which the configuration file names none, all pair, drug, protein, drug and protein, and reversed, and which differ in how neighbouring pairs are connected and whether mixup is applied. In the second stage the six trained encoders are combined by a meta-predictor. The defaults in the configuration are 500 epochs, batch size 64, AdamW with a learning rate of 5e-5, an embedding width of 256 and five splits. The datasets are DAVIS, KIBA, BindingDB_Kd and PDBbind_Refined, the first three taken from TDC and shipped in the repository as pickle files already split for five-fold cross validation. The paper reports five-fold cross validation on DAVIS and KIBA with a train, validation and test ratio of 6:2:2, and full strings without truncation.
sections.source_locator: config.py: cases, configuration; README.md: Processing datasets, Training; Paper: Methods 2.4.2; main.py: argument parser

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is no released set of MixingDTA weights. The README states that, because of storage limits, only the trained parameters for the DeepDTA version of MixingDTA are provided, on Google Drive, and the repository ships code for two backbones, MEETA and DeepDTA. A result should therefore name the backbone, the dataset, the case number or the integration stage, and the git commit, since all of those are command line or configuration choices. The maximum sequence length is a configuration value: 4200 by default, and the entry point raises it to 4700 together with other changes when the dataset is PDBbind_Refined.

name: GeoDock
description: GeoDock: geometric deep-learning protein docking framework.

version.note: No version printed

profile.summary: GeoDock predicts the structure of a two-chain protein complex from the structures of the two partners. It takes the sequences and structures of the docking partners, with no multiple sequence alignment, and returns a docked complex in which the residues are allowed to move, so conformational change on binding can be predicted rather than assumed away. The network is a multitrack iterative transformer, and the point of it is speed: the authors report an average inference time of under one second on a single GPU, which makes large-scale screening possible. On the DIPS test set they report a 43 per cent top-1 success rate, falling to 31 per cent after removing close homologs they found contaminating the standard training split.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: Abstract; README: header

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Conventional docking programs sample many candidate poses and rerank them, which is slow, and earlier deep learning dockers were faster but treated both partners as rigid bodies. GeoDock does neither. It is an iterative transformer over several tracks, taking the sequence and the structure of each partner, and it predicts the docked complex directly with residue-level flexibility. Because it takes structures rather than alignments, it fits the case where the individual structures are already known. The implementation depends on fair-esm, so language model embeddings of the sequences are part of the input pipeline. Inference is one call to a runner class with the two partner files.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint ships in the repository, geodock/weights/dips_0.3.ckpt, about 51.8 MB, and the notebook loads it by that path. The package is geodock version 1.0.4 with Python 3.7 or newer and dependencies pinned as minimums: torch 2.0.1, pytorch-lightning 1.8.6, einops 0.6.0, biotite 0.37.0 and fair-esm 2.0.0. The checkpoint name refers to DIPS, the training set, and the 0.3 suffix is not explained in the sources read. A result should name the checkpoint and the package version, and should say whether the DIPS training split was decontaminated, because the paper reports success rates of 43 and 31 per cent for the same model on the contaminated and cleaned splits.

strengths.text: Fast enough for screening: the authors report under one second per complex on a single GPU, against the heavy sampling and reranking of conventional docking.
No alignment needed. Only the two partner structures and their sequences go in, which suits cases where the monomer structures are already known.
Residues are allowed to move, so binding-induced conformational change can in principle be predicted rather than assumed absent, as in rigid docking.
The authors found and reported contamination in the standard DIPS split themselves, and give the lower success rate after cleaning it, which is the figure to compare against.

The flexibility is a foundation rather than a finished capability: the authors say binding-induced conformational change remains a challenge because training and evaluation data are limited.
Two partners only. Everything in the sources read, from the runner arguments to the output chains A and B, is a pairwise dock.

name: Graphinity
description: Graphinity: equivariant graph neural network predicting binding free-energy change from antibody-antigen structures.

version.note: No version printed

profile.summary: Graphinity predicts the change in antibody-antigen binding affinity caused by a mutation, the quantity written as delta delta G. It takes the structures of the wild-type complex and of the mutant, builds an atomic graph around the mutated site in each, passes both through an equivariant graph neural network, subtracts the two embeddings and reads out one number. The authors report Pearson correlations up to 0.87 on 645 experimental single-point mutations, then show that this reflects overtraining on a few hundred data points rather than a generalisable model. To find out how much data would be needed they built synthetic sets of 942,723 FoldX and 20,829 Rosetta Flex ddG values, and conclude that orders of magnitude more experimental data are likely required, with diversity mattering as well as volume.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: title, Abstract and Synthetic ddG Datasets; paper: Methods, EGNN architecture

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A structure goes in as a PDB file and becomes an atomic graph: non-hydrogen atoms are nodes, pairs of atoms less than 4 angstroms apart are edges, node features are a one-hot LibMolGrid atom type and edge features say whether the edge is within one binding partner or between the two. The graph is cut down to the neighbourhood of the mutated site: atoms on the mutated chain within 4 angstroms of the mutated residue, plus atoms on the partner chain within 4 angstroms of those. The network is three E(n) equivariant graph convolutional layers with a hidden dimension of 128. For a delta delta G prediction, the wild-type and mutant graphs are each passed through those layers and the embeddings subtracted, wild type minus mutant, before a final linear layer. Training used mean squared error, Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, dropout 0.2 on edges, weight decay 1e-16 and global max pooling as readout, for 500 epochs except on the large FoldX set where 10 epochs were used for cost.
sections.source_locator: paper: Methods, EGNN architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is no single released Graphinity model. The repository ships eight checkpoints from the data volume experiment, under example/ddg_synthetic/FoldX/varying_dataset_size/model_weights, each about 4.3 MB and named by the number of FoldX training examples it saw: subset_580, subset_900, subset_4500, subset_9000, subset_45000, subset_90000, subset_450000 and full_848597. They are illustrations of the data scaling question rather than a production predictor, so a result must name the checkpoint. The repository also keeps the experimental delta delta G datasets with their ten-fold cross-validation splits at CDR sequence identity cut-offs of 100, 90 and 70 per cent and a random split, under data/ddg_experimental. The environment is pinned hard, to Python 3.7.10, PyTorch 1.8.0 and PyTorch Geometric 1.6.3, with and without CUDA 10.2.

name: MochiBind
description: MochiBind: sequence-only pairwise antibody-antigen binding predictor using ESM-2 (esm2_t36_3B_UR50D) embeddings and a pairwise scoring module.

version.note: No version printed

attributes.provenance_note: Introduced in the MochiBind paper.

profile.summary: MochiBind predicts which of two antibodies binds a given antigen more strongly, from sequence alone. Antibody and antigen sequences are embedded with a pretrained protein language model, mean-pooled to one vector each, concatenated, projected into a shared latent space and scored by a small multilayer perceptron that outputs the relative binding strength of the pair. Pairwise scores for a large antibody pool are then turned into a global ranking, so the model is aimed at screening candidate antibodies rather than giving an absolute affinity. Because no structure is needed, it can be run over pools of thousands of antibodies on CPU.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Summary, Results introduction and STAR Methods, Method details

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each residue of the antibody and antigen sequences is embedded by ESM-2 (esm2_t36_3B_UR50D) with embedding dimension 2560. Mean pooling over residues gives one fixed-length vector per sequence; the antigen and antibody vectors are concatenated into a 5120-dimensional representation. A learnable projection layer of dimension 1024 maps that into a shared latent space, and a multilayer perceptron head with layers [256, 128, 64] predicts the relative binding strength between the two antibodies of a pair. Training minimises a mean squared error loss, so the model is pushed to get both the sign and the size of the affinity difference right, with learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, dropout 0.3, the Adam optimiser and early stopping after five epochs without an improvement in holdout loss. Pairwise predictions are turned into a global ranking with the TrueSkill algorithm.
sections.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Method details and Key resources table

sections.title: What it was trained on
sections.body: Training and evaluation use the AlphaBind dataset, which holds four antigen systems, each with thousands of experimentally characterised antibody candidates over a wide affinity range: AAB-PP489 (a single-chain variable fragment against human TIGIT), Pembrolizumab-scFv against PD-1, VHH72 (a camelid single-chain antibody against the SARS-CoV-1 receptor binding domain) and Trastuzumab-scFv against human HER2. The paper states that each antigen system contains approximately 30 000 antibody variants generated and validated with AlphaSeq. The released repository ships pretrained checkpoints for the four antigen systems, which the README lists as PEM, PP489, TRA and VHH72, together with sampled training, validation and test files from that data.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one release, the code deposited with the paper, and four checkpoints, one per antigen system. The repository is deliberately frozen: it states that the code is released solely for academic and scientific reproducibility and that pull requests are not accepted so the code stays exactly as it was used in the paper. A result should therefore name the commit and which checkpoint was used; this page read commit 0c693d815f7f0bf0a3dd5494205dca10fbc20c04. Full training is not reproducible from the repository alone: it expects precomputed ESM mean embedding files under a data_processed_esm_mean directory, which the user generates first.

strengths.text: No structures are needed, so large antibody pools can be screened: the paper reports scoring 200,000 pairs from 5,000 antibodies in about 13 s on CPU.
The trained part is small: a projection layer and a three-layer MLP on top of frozen language model embeddings, with an early stopping rule given in the paper.
Checkpoints and the sampled data are shipped together with the evaluation code for the structure-based baselines, so the paper's comparison can be repeated.

strengths.text: The authors report that MochiBind matched or beat the structure-derived baselines they tested, Boltz-2, GeoDock and Graphinity, on pairwise accuracy and retrieval; that is their own claim about their own model.

limitations.text: The licence is non-commercial: the repository, including the checkpoints, is CC BY-NC 4.0 and is described as released solely for academic and scientific reproducibility.
It ranks rather than measures: the model predicts the relative binding strength within a pair for one antigen, not an absolute affinity, and the ranking comes from a separate TrueSkill step.

limitations.text: The released checkpoints are per antigen system (PEM, PP489, TRA, VHH72), and the training data covers four antigens only, so coverage outside those systems is not demonstrated by the sources read.

profile.summary: GraphDTA predicts how strongly a drug molecule binds a target protein. The drug is given as a molecular graph rather than a string, and the protein as its amino acid sequence; the output is a single affinity value. The point of the method is the drug side: the authors argue that a graph is a more natural representation of a molecule than a SMILES string, and they encode it with a graph neural network while a one dimensional convolution reads the protein sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstractText, Summary; models/ginconv.py: GINConvNet

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The drug is turned into a graph of atoms with 78 features per node, and one of four graph networks encodes it: GINConvNet, GATNet, GAT_GCN or GCNNet. In GINConvNet, five GIN convolution layers of width 32 with batch normalisation are followed by sum pooling and a linear layer to a 128 wide drug vector. The protein sequence is mapped character by character to integers, cut or padded to 1000 positions, embedded with width 128, and passed through a single one dimensional convolution with 32 filters and a kernel of 8, then a linear layer to a 128 wide protein vector. The two vectors are concatenated and sent through dense layers of 1024 and 256 units to one output unit, trained with mean squared error.
sections.source_locator: models/ginconv.py: GINConvNet; create_data.py: seq_cat, max_seq_len; training.py: loss_fn; README.md: Source codes

sections.title: Data and training settings
sections.body: The repository ships the Davis and KIBA datasets, which the README says were downloaded from the DeepDTA repository, with the fold files that define the split. For Davis the preparation script converts the affinities to a log scale. Training runs for 1000 epochs with a batch size of 512 and Adam at a learning rate of 0.0005. Two scripts differ in how the best model is chosen: training.py keeps the model with the best mean squared error on the test data, following DeepDTA's practice, while training_validation.py holds out 20 per cent of the training data and selects on that instead.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The four drug encoders are the versions that matter: a result must say which of GINConvNet, GATNet, GAT_GCN and GCNNet was used, on which dataset, and with which of the two training scripts, because the selection rule differs between them. The code was read here at commit 6162245c6776684b391d30610850fe7077478435. The paper's availability statement says pre-trained models are at the repository; the file listing at this commit contains no model file, and the sources read do not explain the difference. A separate Zenodo deposit, doi 10.5281/zenodo.3603523, is given for the scripts and data behind the paper's statistical analysis.

profile.summary: PLM-GraphDTA keeps the drug side of GraphDTA, a graph neural network over the molecule, and replaces its protein encoder with a fixed embedding taken from a protein language model. One vector per protein is computed in advance, projected by a small stack of linear layers, concatenated with the drug vector and sent through dense layers to one affinity value. It is the code behind a study comparing many protein embedding types, so the embedding source is a command line choice rather than part of the model.
profile.summary_source_locator: models/plm_ginconv.py: PLM_GINConvNet; training.py: argument parser; GitHub API response: description

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The drug is a molecular graph with 78 features per atom, encoded by one of four GraphDTA style networks, here GIN, GAT, GAT_GCN or GCN, pooled by summation and projected to a 128 wide vector. The protein is not read as a sequence at all: a precomputed embedding, one vector per protein, is loaded from a json file and passed through linear layers with batch normalisation and ReLU, whose widths are set by the plm_layers argument. The two vectors are concatenated and sent through dense layers of 1024 and 256 units to a single output, trained with mean squared error and Adam. The input width of the protein branch is read from the embedding file itself, so changing the embedding type changes the first layer.
sections.source_locator: models/plm_ginconv.py: PLM_GINConvNet; training.py: embedding loading, optimiser

sections.title: Protein embeddings and splits
sections.body: The protein_embedding_type argument lists the embeddings the study compares: esm_320, esm_640, esm_1280, esmc_960, esmc_1152, deepfri_bp, deepfri_cc, deepfri_ec, deepfri_mf and prost_1024, with the number being the embedding width. The ESM script in the repository loads esm2_t30_150M_UR50D, takes the last layer's token representations and averages them over the residues to give one vector per protein. The repository also ships the fold files for several split regimes: setting1, drug_cold_1 to 5, protein_cold_1 to 5 and fully_blind_1 to 5, for the davis, davis_mutation and kiba datasets.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one code release and no published weights. The repository has no README and no licence file, and the GitHub API returns a null licence field. What a result must name is therefore the run configuration: the model (PLM_GINConvNet, PLM_GATNet, PLM_GAT_GCN, PLM_GCNNet, and the plain GraphDTA and ESM_GATNet baselines the script also imports), the dataset, the embedding type, the plm_layers widths, the fold setting and the seed. Seeding is implemented: with a seed given, the script sets deterministic algorithms and turns cudnn benchmarking off. Training runs 1000 epochs at batch size 512 and saves the model at the best training loss, then evaluates that model on the held out fold.

name: PiFold

profile.summary: PiFold designs an amino acid sequence for a protein backbone you supply: the inverse of structure prediction. It represents the backbone as a graph of residues, with features built by its own residue featurizer, and predicts all residues in one pass instead of one at a time. The authors report 51.66% sequence recovery on CATH 4.2 with inference about 70 times faster than autoregressive methods.
profile.summary_source_locator: ReadMe.md: Introduction, Framework; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The backbone is turned into a graph: each residue is a node, joined to its 30 nearest neighbours. A residue featurizer builds the node and edge features, including learnable virtual atoms meant to carry information that the real atom positions do not. Ten PiGNN layers then pass messages, mixing node, edge and global context. The decoder emits every residue at once, which is what makes it faster than autoregressive inverse folding models, and training optimises perplexity against the native sequence.
sections.source_locator: ReadMe.md: Framework; parser.py method parameters; main.py train; arXiv abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one method and one release. The Training&Data release, published 2023-03-05, carries a trained checkpoint.pth plus the cath4.2 and ts datasets, but the README does not document how to load it, so a PiFold result usually depends on a model someone trained or on the Colab notebooks. The code calls the method ProDesign, its earlier name, and main.py trains from scratch on CATH or TS50 with the defaults in parser.py (batch size 8, learning rate 0.001, up to 100 epochs, seed 111) before testing. A result should say which dataset split, which seed and which checkpoint or notebook it came from.

name: ProstT5
description: ProstT5 bilingual sequence and 3Di structure protein language model.

attributes.source_locator: Experimental design; Table 5 and 6 column headers

version.note: No checkpoint or version printed in the main text; parameters are in Supplementary Table S3, not retrieved. Tables 5 and 6 print ProstT5 under Structure; Experimental design names ProtT5 as the third structure embedding. Table label followed; Supplementary Table S3 not retrieved.

profile.summary: ProstT5 is a protein language model that translates between a protein's amino acid sequence and a one-letter-per-residue description of its 3D structure (Foldseek 3Di tokens). Given a sequence it can predict 3Di tokens ('folding'), given 3Di tokens it can propose sequences ('inverse folding'), and its encoder gives per-residue and per-protein embeddings of either. The authors use the predicted 3Di strings for fast structure-based search with Foldseek without computing 3D structures.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: introduction; model card: Model Description, Uses

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProstT5 is a T5 encoder-decoder initialised from ProtT5-XL-U50, a model trained with span corruption on protein sequences. Structures are written as Foldseek 3Di strings, which assign each residue one of twenty structural states. Training had two steps. First the model continued the span-denoising objective on both amino acid and 3Di sequences, to learn the new tokens without forgetting amino acids. Then it was trained to translate in both directions. A prefix token sets the direction: <AA2fold> for sequence to 3Di and <fold2AA> for 3Di to sequence. 3Di letters are written in lower case so they do not clash with amino acid letters.
sections.source_locator: model card: Model Description; paper: Figure 1 caption

sections.title: Training data
sections.body: The training set was built from AlphaFoldDB predictions: clusters were expanded with diverse members, then low-confidence predictions (pLDDT below 70), proteins shorter than 30 residues and highly repetitive 3Di strings were removed. The final set has 17M proteins, which gives 34M training samples because each protein is used in both translation directions. Training first truncated sequences to 256 residues and later extended to 512.

run_guide.summary: Install the Python libraries and compute residue and per-protein embeddings for one amino acid sequence and one 3Di string with ProstT5.
prerequisites: Python with pip.
A GPU is optional; the README says CPU works in full precision but is much slower.
Internet access to download Rostlab/ProstT5 from Hugging Face.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell:
pip install torch
pip install transformers
pip install sentencepiece
pip install protobuf
steps.explanation: Installs PyTorch, transformers and sentencepiece. The README says protobuf is needed with recent transformers versions to avoid an UnboundLocalError in the T5 tokenizer.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re
device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/ProstT5', do_lower_case=False)
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/ProstT5").to(device)
model.float() if device.type=='cpu' else model.half()

sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "strct"]
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]
sequence_examples = [ "<AA2fold>" + " " + s if s.isupper() else "<fold2AA>" + " " + s
                      for s in sequence_examples
                    ]

ids = tokenizer.batch_encode_plus(sequence_examples,
                                  add_special_tokens=True,
                                  padding="longest",
                                  return_tensors='pt').to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(
              ids.input_ids,
              attention_mask=ids.attention_mask
              )

emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,1:8] # shape (7 x 1024)
emb_1 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[1,1:6] # shape (5 x 1024)
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0) # shape (1024)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's embedding example, wrapped in a shell heredoc by Rewire with its comments shortened. It embeds the toy sequence PRTEINO (with <AA2fold>) and the toy 3Di string strct (with <fold2AA>) and mean-pools the first into a 1024-value vector.

outputs: Tensors in memory: residue embeddings of shape 7 x 1024 and 5 x 1024 and a per-protein embedding of 1024 values. The example prints nothing.

profile.summary: ProtTrans is a family of protein language models from Rostlab, trained on unlabelled protein sequences from UniRef and BFD. The models take an amino acid sequence and return per-residue vectors (1024 values each for ProtT5-XL), which are averaged for a per-protein vector; those vectors are then used as the only input to small supervised models for tasks such as secondary structure or subcellular localisation. The family covers six architectures, and ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is the one the authors recommend.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Quick Start, Models Availability; model card: Model description, Intended uses

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each model is a standard NLP transformer trained on protein sequences with no labels. The authors trained two autoregressive models (Transformer-XL and XLNet) and four autoencoder models (BERT, Albert, Electra and T5). ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 follows the t5-3b shape, with model width 1024, 24 encoder and 24 decoder layers and 32 heads, but is trained with a Bart-like masked language modelling objective rather than T5 span denoising, masking 15% of amino acids. Sequences are uppercased, the rare amino acids U, Z, O and B are mapped to X, and residues are separated by single spaces. For feature extraction the authors recommend the encoder side only.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model description, Preprocessing; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists ten checkpoints on Hugging Face and Zenodo: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50, ProtT5-XL-BFD, ProtT5-XXL-UniRef50, ProtT5-XXL-BFD, ProtBert-BFD, ProtBert, ProtAlbert, ProtXLNet, ProtElectra-Generator-BFD and ProtElectra-Discriminator-BFD. There is also Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc, a half-precision encoder-only copy of ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 used in the README example. The training corpus differs between the UniRef50 and BFD variants, so a result must name the checkpoint. The Hugging Face API responses carry no parameter counts and no licence field, so the revision is the only version handle; this page read prot_t5_xl_uniref50 at revision 973be27c.

prerequisites: Python with pip, PyTorch and the transformers library.
A GPU is optional; the README says CPU needs full precision and is much slower.

steps.shell:
pip install torch
pip install transformers
pip install sentencepiece
pip install protobuf

steps.title: Embed two sequences
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc', do_lower_case=False)
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc").to(device)

if device == torch.device("cpu"):
    model.to(torch.float32)

sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "SEQWENCE"]
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]

ids = tokenizer(sequence_examples, add_special_tokens=True, padding="longest")

input_ids = torch.tensor(ids['input_ids']).to(device)
attention_mask = torch.tensor(ids['attention_mask']).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)

emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,:7] # shape (7 x 1024)
emb_1 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[1,:8] # shape (8 x 1024)
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0) # shape (1024)
print(emb_0.shape, emb_0_per_protein.shape)
PY

name: AIDO.RNA
description: AIDO.RNA RNA language model family.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: AIDO.RNA is a family of RNA foundation models from GenBio AI; its Hugging Face repositories and current code use the name GB.RNA. The models read an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and turn it into embeddings that a downstream model can use, for tasks such as RNA secondary structure prediction, mRNA-related prediction and RNA function prediction. The largest model has 1.6 billion parameters and was trained on 42 million non-coding RNA sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: 1.6B model card: opening paragraph; Hugging Face API id

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The models are encoder-only transformers pretrained with a masked language modelling (MLM) objective: parts of the sequence are hidden and the model learns to predict them. The 1.6B model has 32 layers, hidden size 2,048, feed-forward size 5,440 and 32 attention heads, with a vocabulary of 16 tokens. The 650M model's configuration has 33 layers, hidden size 1,280, intermediate size 3,392 and 20 attention heads. Both configurations use rotary position embeddings and SwiGLU activations. Users normally adapt a backbone to a task through GenBio's ModelGenerator framework, which offers embedding, sequence-level and token-level classification, and regression heads.
sections.source_locator: 1.6B model card: Model architectural details, How to Use; config.json of 1.6B and 650M

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository documentation lists seven RNA backbones: gb_rna_1b600m, gb_rna_1b600m_cds, gb_rna_650m, gb_rna_650m_cds, gb_rna_300m_mars, gb_rna_25m_mars and gb_rna_1m_mars. GB.RNA-1.6B and GB.RNA-650M were trained on non-coding RNA. GB.RNA-1.6B-CDS and GB.RNA-650M-CDS are domain-adapted versions for coding sequences, whose Hugging Face metadata name the base models. The three MARS models were trained on 886 million RNA sequences from the MARS database. The Hugging Face repositories read are named GB.RNA rather than AIDO.RNA, and the sources read do not explain the difference. The model cards call the backbones aido_rna_1b600m and aido_rna_650m, while the pinned repository uses gb_rna_ names. A result should name the checkpoint, its Hugging Face revision and the backbone name used; this page read GB.RNA-1.6B at revision cea90e53 and GB.RNA-650M at revision efaf4af4.

name: BiRNA-BERT
description: BiRNA-BERT RNA language model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: BiRNA-BERT is an RNA language model that turns an RNA sequence into embeddings for downstream prediction tasks. It can read a sequence either one nucleotide at a time, for fine-grained tasks such as secondary structure prediction, or as compressed byte-pair tokens, so that long RNAs can be processed without cutting them short. It is a 117M-parameter transformer encoder trained on about 36 million non-coding RNA sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; model card opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BiRNA-BERT is a BERT-style transformer encoder trained with the MosaicBERT framework. It uses ALiBi relative positional encoding instead of fixed position embeddings, which lets it handle sequences longer than those seen in training. Its main idea is dual tokenisation: the same model is trained by masked language modelling on both byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokens, with a vocabulary of 4096, and single-nucleotide (NUC) tokens. BPE compresses long sequences so they fit in memory, while nucleotide tokens keep the per-base detail needed for tasks such as secondary structure prediction. With the released tokenizer, an unspaced sequence is split into BPE tokens and a space-separated sequence into nucleotide tokens.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results (first paragraph), Methods (tokenisation); model card: Usage

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The main checkpoint is buetnlpbio/birna-bert, used with the tokenizer buetnlpbio/birna-tokenizer. The paper also trained BPE-Only-BERT and NUC-Only-BERT as controls, and the buetnlpbio account lists bpe-only-rna-bert and nuc-only-rna-bert. The README warns that the current version is substantially updated and suggests re-analysing data processed with earlier versions. The README's own embedding example loads a different model name, Lancelot53/birnabert-2ep, while the model card loads buetnlpbio/birna-bert; the sources do not explain the difference. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision (this page read revision 35bceaf6) and say whether BPE or nucleotide tokenisation was used.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import transformers
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-tokenizer")

config = transformers.BertConfig.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-bert")
mysterybert = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-bert",config=config,trust_remote_code=True)
mysterybert.cls = torch.nn.Identity()

# To get sequence embeddings
seq_embed = mysterybert(**tokenizer("AGCTACGTACGT", return_tensors="pt"))
print(seq_embed.logits.shape) # CLS + 4 BPE token embeddings + SEP

# To get nucleotide embeddings
char_embed = mysterybert(**tokenizer("A G C T A C G T A C G T", return_tensors="pt")) 
print(char_embed.logits.shape) # CLS + 12 nucleotide token embeddings + SEP
PY

name: Genos
description: Human-centric mixture-of-experts genomic model trained on human de novo assemblies with a 1 Mb context, which models sequence at single-nucleotide resolution and predicts effects of noncoding variants on RNA expression.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Genos genomic foundation model family; listed in ViroBench Table 9 as a mixture-of-experts transformer.

profile.summary: Genos is a family of DNA language models for the human genome from the Genos Team in Hangzhou, China (GitHub and Hugging Face organisation BGI-HangzhouAI). It reads DNA one base at a time, with inputs of up to about one million bases, and is trained to predict the next base. Its internal representations (embeddings) are used for tasks such as classifying genomic elements, predicting variant effects and, after fine-tuning, predicting RNA-seq coverage from DNA sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Methods; README_en.md: Model Architecture, Notebook Usage Examples

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Genos is a decoder-style Transformer with a mixture-of-experts feed-forward layer. Each base (A, T, C, G or N) is one token. Every layer has grouped-query attention, with 16 heads sharing 8 key-value groups, and rotary position embeddings for long contexts; a router sends each token to 2 of 8 expert networks. A final linear layer gives the probability of the next base, which is the training objective. Pre-training mixed sequence lengths of 8,192, 32,768, 131,072 and 1,024,000 bp. For downstream use the paper names three modes: embedding extraction, sequence generation and fine-tuning.

sections.body: Three models are released, each as a Hugging Face checkpoint and a Megatron-LM checkpoint: Genos-1.2B and Genos-10B, trained on human genomes, and Genos-10B-v2 (released 2025-12-18), which adds about 60 billion bases of East Asian genomes, non-human primate genomes and other mammalian genomes, mixed 1:1 with the human corpus. Genos-10B-v2 was trained on 6286B tokens against 2200B for Genos-10B, so results from the two are not interchangeable. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision. The README also announces Gengram (2026-01-30) as a separate model in its own repository.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

# Specify model path
model_path = "/path/to/your/local/Genos-1.2B" # Replace with local model path

# Load tokenizer and model
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path)

# Load locally downloaded Genos weights
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_path,
                                  output_hidden_states=True,
                                  torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
                                  trust_remote_code=True,
                                  attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" # Use flash_attention
  )
model.cuda() # Load model to GPU
model.eval() # Switch model to inference mode

import random

# Randomly select a specific number of bases
bases = ['A', 'T', 'G', 'C']
seqs = random.choices(bases, k=8192)
# Generate input base sequence
text = ''.join(seqs)

# Encode text
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")

# Load data to GPU
inputs = {k: v.cuda() for k, v in inputs.items()}

# Model inference
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)

# Get hidden states from all layers
hidden_states = outputs.hidden_states  # Tuple containing hidden states from each layer

# Iterate through embeddings from each layer and display key information
for i, layer_embedding in enumerate(hidden_states):
    print(f"Layer {i} embedding ({layer_embedding.shape}): {layer_embedding[0, 0, :10]}")
    print("-" * 50)
PY
steps.explanation: The code cells of the official embedding notebook, steps 1 to 6, joined into one heredoc. Two print lines that only show the input were left out. Replace /path/to/your/local/Genos-1.2B with the folder from the previous step.

name: LucaVirus
description: LucaVirus unified nucleotide-protein language model for viruses.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: LucaVirus is a language model for viruses that reads both nucleotide sequences (DNA or RNA) and protein sequences in one model. It was trained on OpenVirus, a corpus of 15.7 million viral sequences, and outputs per-token and per-sequence embeddings. These embeddings are used, or the model is fine-tuned, for tasks such as viral sequence classification, protein fitness prediction and antibody-antigen binding prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: title, 2. PreTraining Data, 4. Downstream Tasks; model card: Usage; paper: Results

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LucaVirus is an encoder-only Transformer with about 1 billion parameters. It was initialised from the weights of LucaOne, a general biological foundation model, then reduced to 12 transformer layers with a context window of 3072 tokens. The default checkpoint's config gives hidden size 2560, 20 attention heads and one vocabulary for nucleotides and amino acids. Pretraining combines masked language modelling with seven supervised tasks. Three are sequence-level (order taxonomy for nucleotide and protein sequences, and UniProt functional keywords for proteins) and four are token-level (gene prediction on nucleotides, and homologous superfamily, conserved domain and active site annotation on proteins). The user tells the tokenizer whether an input is a gene (DNA or RNA) or a protein. In the paper, downstream tasks train a small head (attention pooling, a fully connected layer and a prediction head) on frozen LucaVirus embeddings.
sections.source_locator: paper: Results, LucaVirus: a unified model; README.md: 3. PreTraining Tasks; config.json; model card: Usage

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Five LucaVirus checkpoints are listed on Hugging Face under LucaGroup: default-step3.8M, prot-step3.8M, gene-step3.8M, mask-step1.4M and mask-step3.8M. The repository's training scripts describe the variants: one trained only with the masked language modelling task, one only on viral gene (DNA and RNA) data and one only on viral protein data. The repository's own embedding script downloads checkpoints from the authors' FTP server, while the Hugging Face checkpoints are loaded through the lucavirus package (version 1.1.1). A result should name the checkpoint and its revision; this page read the default checkpoint at revision 207da019. The README gives two figures for the LucaOne starting checkpoint: step 1,760,000 in its pretraining section and step=17600000 or 36000000 in its training scripts section. The paper says the pretrained weights, downstream models and training data are also on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.15703216).

The training corpus is viral only and covers all known viral taxa and hosts from all three domains of life, and it has been released on Hugging Face.

run_guide.summary: Install the lucavirus package and compute an embedding for one nucleotide sequence with the default Hugging Face checkpoint.
prerequisites: Python with pip. The model card pins lucavirus==1.1.1, tokenizers==0.19.1 and transformers==4.41.2.
The card's code uses a CUDA GPU if available and the CPU otherwise. The authors recommend large-memory GPUs such as A100, H100 or H200 for long sequences.

steps.title: Embed a nucleotide sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import lucavirus
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

model_id = "LucaGroup/LucaVirus-default-step3.8M"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    task_level="token_level",
    task_type="embedding",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model.to(device)
model.eval()

nucleotide_sequence = "ATGCGTACGTTAGC"
nucleotide_inputs = tokenizer(
    nucleotide_sequence,
    seq_type="gene",
    return_tensors="pt",
    add_special_tokens=True
)
new_nucleotide_inputs = {}
for item in nucleotide_inputs.items():
    new_nucleotide_inputs[item[0]] = item[1].to(device)
nucleotide_inputs = new_nucleotide_inputs

with torch.no_grad():
    nucleotide_outputs = model(**nucleotide_inputs)
    nucleotide_last_hidden = nucleotide_outputs.last_hidden_state
    mean_nucleotide_embedding = nucleotide_last_hidden[:, 1:-1, :].mean(dim=1)
print(f"Nucleotide Embedding Shape: {nucleotide_last_hidden.shape}")
print(mean_nucleotide_embedding)
PY

name: MP-RNA
description: MP-RNA RNA language model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: MP-RNA is an RNA foundation model that reads an RNA sequence one base at a time and produces representations for downstream prediction. It was pretrained on plant transcriptomes from over 1,000 species with objectives that include predicting secondary structure and repairing single-base mutations. It is aimed at tasks that need per-base resolution, such as RNA secondary structure prediction and mutation detection, and the authors also apply it to DNA tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model Description, Training Data; paper Section 3

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MP-RNA is a transformer encoder that reads RNA one base at a time. It is pretrained with three combined objectives: masked RNA language modelling, single nucleotide mutation repair (5% of sites are mutated and the model learns to correct them), and secondary structure prediction. Structure labels come from ViennaRNA. To limit noise from these computed labels, the authors keep the 10% of samples with the lowest expected calibration error for incremental pretraining, and append structures to the sequence in 10% of masked language modelling examples. After pretraining, the model is fine-tuned or used for tasks such as secondary structure prediction, mutation detection and repair, and DNA genomic tasks.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 3.1 to 3.3; model card: Model Description

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper describes two sizes, MP-RNA-52M and MP-RNA-186M, both pretrained on four RTX 4090 GPUs over one month. This page read one checkpoint, yangheng/MP-RNA; its configuration (32 layers, dimension 720) and parameter count match the 186M version. The paper states that only MP-RNA-186M received incremental pretraining and that the incrementally pretrained 52M model will not be released. Whether any other MP-RNA checkpoint is public was not checked. The paper and card link to github.com/yangheng95/OmniGenomeBench; the code repository read here is yangheng95/OmniGenBench, and no saved file shows how the two addresses are related. Its README's examples use OmniGenome models and list MP-RNA as one supported model. A result should name the Hugging Face revision; this page read revision 0a727ebb.

name: OmniReg-GPT
description: OmniReg-GPT generative genomic foundation model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: OmniReg-GPT is a generative DNA foundation model for long human genomic sequences. It reads DNA tokenised into subword units and was pretrained to predict the next token on 20 kb windows of the human T2T genome. Its embeddings are fine-tuned for regulatory tasks such as histone marks, promoters and enhancers, gene expression, chromatin accessibility and 3D chromatin contacts, and it can generate candidate enhancer sequences from a prompt.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Training procedure; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OmniReg-GPT is a decoder-only transformer trained with next-token prediction. DNA is tokenised with the BPE tokenizer from GENA-LM (vocabulary 32,000). The network has 12 local blocks, where each window of tokens attends to itself and the preceding window, and 2 global blocks that build a whole-sequence representation. The authors say this reduces attention cost from quadratic to linear in sequence length. It uses rotary position embeddings and FlashAttention. For downstream tasks a single vector is taken as the mean of all token embeddings.

The paper reports a 270 million parameter model and also mentions a 138 million parameter variant with hidden dimension 768 in its memory comparison; the Zenodo record does not say which variant the file is. The code is also archived on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.16933275), and downstream datasets are in Zenodo record 14883459. A result should name the repository commit and the Zenodo weights record; this page read commit 7cae626d.

name: RiNALMo
description: RiNALMo RNA language model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: RiNALMo is an RNA language model that reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and produces a numerical representation of each position. It was pretrained on 36 million non-coding RNA sequences by learning to fill in masked nucleotides, and the representations are then fine-tuned for tasks such as RNA secondary structure prediction and splice site prediction. The largest model has 650M parameters; smaller 148M and 33.5M versions are also released.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Methods; README: About

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RiNALMo is an encoder-only transformer trained by masked language modelling: 15% of tokens in each training sequence are selected, most are replaced with a mask token, and the model learns to reconstruct them. It uses rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU feed-forward layers and FlashAttention-2. Training sequences were sampled once per cluster per epoch to keep batches diverse. For downstream use, the per-nucleotide representations or the classification token embedding feed a task head; the authors fine-tuned it for secondary structure prediction, splice site prediction, mean ribosome loading and ncRNA family classification.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; README: Usage

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three pretrained sizes are published on Zenodo: giga (650M), mega and micro. Their parameter counts differ slightly between the paper, the README and the Zenodo description. The 650M model was pretrained on seven 80 GB A100 GPUs for 2 weeks. Fine-tuned giga weights and the train_<task>.py scripts allow the paper's downstream evaluations to be rerun. The Python loader in the repository downloads only giga-v1. A result should name the size, whether pretrained or fine-tuned weights were used, and the Zenodo record (15043668).

import torch

DEVICE = "cuda:0"

name: ViroCaduceus
description: Caduceus-architecture model pretrained on viral sequences by the ViroBench authors (in-house model).

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: ViroCaduceus is a DNA language model built by the ViroBench authors to test whether a virus-enriched pretraining corpus helps nucleotide models on viral tasks. It takes a Caduceus backbone and trains it on ViroBlend (also spelt ViroBland), a 216 Mbp mix of human, multi-species and viral sequence. Given a DNA sequence it returns hidden states, which the benchmark pools into embeddings for viral taxonomy and host classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card; paper section 4.2.4; get_embedding.py

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ViroCaduceus uses the Caduceus (Mamba-DNA) architecture. The paper describes it as Caduceus-PS adapted with the same ViroBland pretraining used for the authors' ViroHyena models. The released file is a set of backbone weights. To use it, the demo script loads the Caduceus-Ph base model from kuleshov-group, then overlays the ViroCaduceus weights from pytorch_model.bin. It tokenises the sequence, takes the last hidden layer and mean-pools over non-special tokens to give one embedding per sequence. In ViroBench the backbone is frozen and a light supervised head is trained on top for classification.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model details, Files; paper section 4.2.4; get_embedding.py; README: Unified protocol

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, YDXX/ViroCaduceus; this page read revision 91cee313. The paper also calls it Caduceus-ViroBench. Its sources disagree on the base: the paper says Caduceus-PS, while the model card and the demo script use Caduceus-Ph. The repository's config.json is a HyenaDNA configuration (d_model 32, 2 layers), which does not match a Caduceus model with d_model 256, so a result should name the revision and the base model used to load the weights. The demo script only applies the ViroCaduceus weights if YDXX/ViroCaduceus/pytorch_model.bin exists on disk relative to where it runs; otherwise it silently returns the unmodified base model.

name: ViroHyena
description: Hyena-architecture nucleotide model pretrained on viral sequences by the ViroBench authors (in-house model).

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: ViroHyena is a small family of nucleotide language models built on the Hyena architecture by the authors of the ViroBench viral genomics benchmark. They were pretrained on ViroBlend, a 216 Mbp corpus that mixes human reference, multi-species and viral sequences. The models take nucleotide sequences and serve as baselines in ViroBench for viral taxonomy and host classification from embeddings and for likelihood-based genome modelling.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card introduction; ViroBench README: benchmark description and evaluation protocol

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ViroHyena uses the HyenaDNA model type: stacked Hyena layers over a nucleotide vocabulary of 12 tokens and a maximum of 8192 positions. The four checkpoints differ in width and depth, from d_model 128 with 2 layers to d_model 1024 with 20 layers. The cards tag the models for text generation. In ViroBench, classification is done with the backbone frozen: a sequence embedding is extracted and a small MLP head is trained on it. Generation diagnostics score likelihood in bits per base and test completion of coding sequences.

name: ChemBERTa
description: ChemBERTa molecular language model.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: ChemBERTa is a family of transformer language models trained on SMILES strings, the text notation for molecules. Given a SMILES string, a model returns embeddings that can be fine-tuned or used as features for molecular property prediction. ChemBERTa-2, the version cited by the benchmark source, is pretrained on up to 77M PubChem compounds with either masked language modelling or multi-task regression.
profile.summary_source_locator: ChemBERTa-2 abstract and Methods

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ChemBERTa-2 uses the RoBERTa transformer implementation in Hugging Face. Masked language modelling (MLM) masks 15% of SMILES tokens and trains the model to recover them; multi-task regression (MTR) trains it to predict 200 molecular properties computed with RDKit from the SMILES. The vocabulary is at most 591 tokens and sequences at most 512 tokens. The authors searched 50 configurations of 5M to 46M parameters on a 5M-compound set, then trained selected ones on 10M and 77M compounds. They report that MTR pretraining gives better downstream results but trains more slowly.
sections.source_locator: ChemBERTa-2 Methods and Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper compares MLM and MTR models pretrained on 5M, 10M and 77M compounds, alongside the original ChemBERTa, and says the trained models are open-sourced. The DeepChem/ChemBERTa-77M-MLM checkpoint on Hugging Face is a 3-layer RoBERTa masked language model (hidden size 384, 12 heads, vocabulary 600) with no model card. MassSpecGym in the Wild also used a checkpoint published under a different Hugging Face account, Derify/ChemBERTa_augmented_pubchem_13m (43,963,205 parameters, Apache-2.0, trained on an augmented 13M PubChem set). A result should name the exact Hugging Face repository and revision.
sections.source_locator: ChemBERTa-2 Table 1 and Discussion; Hugging Face API and config; Derify card; MassSpecGym in the Wild Appendix A.4

sections.title: Use in the benchmark source
sections.body: MassSpecGym in the Wild (an existing source on this record) did not evaluate ChemBERTa as a spectrum model. It used ChemBERTa encoders to show a shortcut in the MassSpecGym retrieval candidates: a frozen ChemBERTa-2 encoder (Derify/ChemBERTa_augmented_pubchem_13m) aligned with DreaMS spectrum embeddings, and a spectrum-blind classifier fine-tuned from DeepChem/ChemBERTa-77M-MLM. Because true molecules kept non-canonical SMILES while decoys were RDKit-canonicalised, these models could rank the true molecule first from formatting alone; MassSpecGym v1.5 canonicalises all SMILES by default.
sections.source_locator: MassSpecGym in the Wild Section 5.1 and Appendix A.4

name: ChemFormer
description: ChemFormer molecular language model.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: Chemformer is a BART-style transformer language model for chemistry that reads and writes SMILES strings. It is pretrained to reconstruct original SMILES from corrupted or randomised ones, and then fine-tuned for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as reaction and retrosynthesis prediction or for property prediction. Inputs are SMILES strings; outputs are predicted SMILES or property values.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md introduction; paper abstract and Section 2

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each molecule is written as a non-canonical SMILES string, randomly modified, tokenised and embedded with sinusoidal positions. A bidirectional encoder reads the modified string and an autoregressive decoder is trained with cross-entropy to output the original SMILES. After pretraining, the weights are fine-tuned for each task. Chemformer (base) uses the original Transformer sizes: model dimension 512, feed-forward 2048, 6 layers, 8 heads, about 45M parameters. Chemformer-Large has about 230M.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 2 and 2.1-2.4, Table 1

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds the code for three Chemformer papers and has been replaced by AiZynthModels, which includes an updated Chemformer. Public pretrained models and datasets are on a Box share; checkpoints from older versions need a key renamed (vocab_size to vocabulary_size) before use with the current code. The paper pretrained base and Large models on about 100 million ZINC-15 SMILES. A result should name the checkpoint file and the code version.
sections.source_locator: README.md introduction; paper Section 2.1

sections.title: Use in the benchmark source
sections.body: MassSpecGym in the Wild (an existing source on this record) did not evaluate Chemformer as a spectrum model. It built a two-stage retrieval pipeline on a frozen ChemFormer BART encoder (d = 512, 6 layers, 8 heads, 523-token vocabulary) paired with a trained spectrum encoder, and showed that it reached over 63% hit rate@1 by exploiting a SMILES canonicalisation difference between true molecules and decoys in the MassSpecGym candidates.
