name: DiffMS
description: DiffMS: formula-conditioned discrete diffusion model that generates molecules from spectra via a MIST encoder.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: DiffMS generates candidate molecular structures from a tandem mass spectrum (de novo structure elucidation). It takes an MS/MS spectrum and the molecule's chemical formula, encodes the spectrum with a formula transformer, and uses a discrete graph diffusion model to build molecular graphs with the right heavy atoms. It outputs a set of sampled candidate structures.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv 2502.09571v2 abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The encoder is the MIST formula transformer, which embeds spectrum peaks labelled with formulas and neutral losses. The decoder is a discrete graph diffusion model adapted from DiGress: it denoises an adjacency matrix over a fixed set of heavy atoms taken from the known formula, and hydrogens are placed implicitly. The decoder is pretrained on 2.8M fingerprint-molecule pairs (2048-bit Morgan fingerprints, radius 2) from DSSTox, HMDB, COCONUT and MOSES; the encoder is pretrained on the finetuning data (NPLIB1 or MassSpecGym); then the whole model is finetuned with the denoising cross-entropy loss.
sections.source_locator: Paper: abstract, Section 3, Appendix A

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Pretrained end-to-end models and decoders are on Zenodo record 23542112 (published 2026-10-21, MIT, files diffms_checkpoints.tar.gz and msg_preprocessed.tar.gz). MIST encoder checkpoints are on a separate Zenodo record, in four variants (CANOPUS or MassSpecGym, with or without synthetic training spectra), with training code in coleygroup/MIST. The MassSpecGym in the Wild paper reports that the MIST attention code as first published in the MIST and DiffMS codebases mishandled padding in batched inputs, and that a commonly reused MIST checkpoint from DiffMS could not be reproduced. A result should name the checkpoint files, the MIST encoder variant and the code commit.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Pretrained Checkpoints; Zenodo record; MassSpecGym in the Wild Section 6.1

sections.title: Use in benchmarks
sections.body: MassSpecGym in the Wild (an existing source on this record) lists DiffMS in its updated MassSpecGym de novo leaderboard and also uses it for generative retrieval. It shows that changing metric settings on identical DiffMS predictions changes the scores, and recommends keeping metric code consistent with the MassSpecGym reference implementation.

name: FOAM
description: Formula-constrained graph genetic algorithm that evolves candidate molecules, seeded from PubChem formula matches and DiffMS samples, and ranks them by ICEBERG-simulated spectral similarity to the observed MS/MS spectrum.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

attributes.provenance_note: Listed in MassSpecGym in the Wild Table 9 as FOAM (DiffMS + PubChem).

profile.summary: FOAM (Formula-constrained Optimization for Annotating Metabolites) proposes molecular structures for an unknown tandem mass spectrum by optimisation rather than by a single trained generator. Given the spectrum and the molecular formula, it starts from seed structures with that formula, evolves them with a formula-constrained graph genetic algorithm, and keeps the candidates whose ICEBERG-simulated spectra best match the observed one. Seeds can come from PubChem or from other models such as DiffMS.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md introduction; paper abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: FOAM first retrieves seed structures that match the formula (from PubChem, with the true structure excluded in evaluation, or from another tool). ICEBERG simulates the spectrum of each candidate, candidates are scored by similarity to the observed spectrum, and the best form a mating pool. A graph genetic algorithm then applies crossover and mutation that keep the formula fixed, and the loop repeats until a budget of ICEBERG calls is used. A multi-objective variant adds a penalty on structural complexity. FOAM has no trained weights of its own; the learned part is the ICEBERG simulator.
sections.source_locator: Paper Section 2 and Figure 1; README.md

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Reproduction configs are in configs/final, for NIST'20 (7,500 calls) and MassSpecGym with PubChem and DiffMS seeds. The MassSpecGym ICEBERG checkpoints (msg_gen.ckpt and msg_inten_cosine.ckpt) and the PubChem and DiffMS seed caches are on Zenodo record 18502041 (CC-BY-4.0, published 2026-02-06). The NIST'20 ICEBERG weights and NIST spectra are not public. A result should name the config, the seed sources, the call budget and the ICEBERG checkpoints.

name: FRIGID
description: FRIGID diffusion-based molecular generation model from mass spectra.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: FRIGID generates candidate molecular structures from a tandem mass spectrum (de novo structure elucidation). A MIST encoder predicts a molecular fingerprint from the spectrum, and a masked diffusion language model generates molecules as SAFE strings conditioned on that fingerprint and the chemical formula. An optional refinement loop simulates spectra of the candidates with the ICEBERG forward model and re-generates the parts that do not match.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction, Overview

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Stage 1 (FRIGID-base): a MIST encoder predicts a 4096-bit radius-2 Morgan fingerprint; its active bits are embedded and passed through 3 self-attention layers, and the precursor formula is encoded as per-element counts; both enter every Transformer block through cross-attention. The backbone is a 12-layer BERT-style masked diffusion language model (hidden size 896, 14 heads) over BPE-tokenised SAFE strings, and an NGBoost model predicts the sequence length from the formula. Stage 2: candidates are ranked against the predicted fingerprint, ICEBERG simulates their spectra, peaks that appear in simulation but not in the experiment flag inconsistent atoms, and those tokens are re-masked and re-denoised over several rounds. The code is adapted from NVIDIA's GenMol.
sections.source_locator: README.md: How It Works, Model Architecture Details

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README reports that earlier MIST encoders for MassSpecGym were trained with synthetic spectra of PubChem molecules chosen to resemble test formulas, which used test-set information. The encoders were replaced (MIST 2M-aug for NPLIB1, MIST 4M-aug for MassSpecGym), the evaluations repeated, and the earlier results marked as superseded: for example FRIGID on MassSpecGym fell from 18.29% to 9.05% top-1 accuracy. The updated release (Zenodo record 23543494, 2026-10-21, Apache 2.0) holds DLM.ckpt and four ICEBERG checkpoints; MIST encoders come from a separate Zenodo record. The paper read is arXiv v3 (25 Oct 2026). A result should state which MIST encoder was used, whether refinement was applied and how many rounds.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Important note, Results, Data and checkpoint setup; Zenodo record; paper

sections.title: Use in benchmarks

For its own augmentation experiments it trained MIST encoders with a modified MIST implementation that it links to the MIST-FRIGID branch of the FRIGID repository.

name: ICEBERG
description: ICEBERG forward spectrum simulation model, used for retrieval by scoring candidates against simulated spectra.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: ICEBERG predicts the tandem mass spectrum (MS/MS) of a molecule by simulating how it breaks apart in collision-induced dissociation. Given a molecular structure, collision energy and polarity, it generates plausible fragments and predicts their intensities, giving a spectrum. Its main use is ranking candidate structures for an unknown spectrum by how well their simulated spectra match.
profile.summary_source_locator: ICEBERG 2.0 preprint abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ICEBERG has two stages. ICEBERG-Generate builds a pruned fragmentation graph (a DAG) by learning which atoms break off, allowing up to three atom-breaking steps and six bond breakages; its training labels come from the MAGMa algorithm, which enumerates fragmentations and matches them to observed peaks. ICEBERG-Score takes the fragment graph, uses a GNN with instrument parameters to embed fragments and the parent molecule, and a set transformer to predict fragment intensities, which are merged into a spectrum. Version 2.0 added collision energy and polarity as inputs, contrastive fine-tuning and charge migration.
sections.source_locator: ICEBERG 2.0 preprint: Results and Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: ICEBERG 1.0 (Goldman et al., arXiv 2304.13136) is archived on the iceberg_1.0 branch; ICEBERG 2.0 (Wang et al. 2025) is on the iceberg_2.0 branch; the main branch holds ICEBERG 2.1, which the README calls about three times faster with official NIST'23 support, alongside the newer GLACIER model. Open MassSpecGym-trained ICEBERG 2.1 weights (msg_all and msg_simulation) are shared on Dropbox; NIST-trained weights are given only to NIST licence holders on request. ICEBERG 1.0 was evaluated on NPLIB1 and NIST20. A result should name the ICEBERG version and the training data of the weights.
sections.source_locator: README.md: update notes, ICEBERG 2.1, Demo

sections.title: Use in the benchmark source
sections.body: MassSpecGym in the Wild (an existing source on this record) trained two ICEBERG models with the ms-pred code: a leakage-free one on the MassSpecGym training set and an adversarial one that also saw the test set, to show how synthetic spectra from a forward model can leak test information into MIST training. It also reports ICEBERG forward-model retrieval on the full MassSpecGym test split, imputing missing collision energies, and says MassSpecGym v1.5 releases officially retrained data-safe versions of ICEBERG and other components.

name: MADGEN
description: MADGEN mass-spectrum-guided de novo molecule generation.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: MADGEN (Mass-spec Attends to De Novo Molecular GENeration) generates molecular structures from a tandem mass spectrum in two stages. First it retrieves the molecule's core scaffold (its Murcko ring framework) by ranking candidate scaffolds against the spectrum; then a spectrum-guided generative model adds the remaining atoms and bonds, using the chemical formula to fix which atoms are present. It outputs sampled candidate molecules.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv 2501.01950v4 abstract and Section 3

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Stage 1 treats scaffold retrieval as ranking: contrastive learning aligns spectra (with their formula) with candidate Murcko scaffolds, and the top-ranked scaffold is chosen; an oracle retriever that is given the true scaffold is used to measure stage 2 alone. Stage 2 starts from the scaffold and the formula's atoms and generates the missing bonds with a Markov bridge process adapted from RetroBridge, using attention to bring spectral information into every step. The generator is a 5-layer graph transformer. The paper gives 50 diffusion steps in one passage and a 100-step Markov bridge in its training details; the README samples with --n_steps 100.
sections.source_locator: Paper abstract and Sections 3.1-3.2

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained generators are released on Zenodo record 17115068 (CC-BY-4.0): msgym.ckpt (MassSpecGym) and canopus.ckpt (CANOPUS), together with processed data, predicted scaffold rankings and scaffold-retrieval datasets. The NIST23 model and data are not public because NIST is licensed. The paper read is arXiv v4 (29 Apr 2025), published at ICLR 2025. A result should say whether the predictive or the oracle scaffold retriever was used, because the gap is large.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Pre-trained Models, Data Preparation; Zenodo record; paper

name: MolForge
description: MolForge fingerprint-to-molecule decoder, used with a MIST spectrum encoder.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: MolForge is a set of transformer models that translate a molecular fingerprint back into a molecule, written as SMILES or SELFIES. The input is the list of set bits of a structural fingerprint (for example ECFP4) and the output is a decoded molecular string. In mass spectrometry work it is used as the second stage of de novo structure generation: a spectrum encoder such as MIST predicts a fingerprint, and MolForge decodes it into candidate structures.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Prediction & Demo; paper Model overview; Neo et al. abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MolForge treats fingerprint-to-molecule conversion as translation. The fingerprint's set bits are tokens on the source side and SMILES or SELFIES tokens on the target side, each with its own vocabulary file (ECFP4_vocab_sp and smiles_vocab_sp in the README demo). A later paper that reuses MolForge describes its SMILES tokenizer as SentencePiece. The model is a standard encoder-decoder Transformer: six encoder and six decoder layers with eight attention heads, 512-dimensional attention and 2048-dimensional feed-forward layers, with layer normalisation before each sub-layer. Each fingerprint and output representation pair is a separate model, trained with a negative log-likelihood loss on two GPUs for up to 500 K steps. Decoding is greedy or beam search.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Model overview, Training; README.md: Prediction & Demo

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The authors trained one model per fingerprint and output representation; the README's results table covers 15 fingerprint encodings including MACCS, Avalon, RDK4, atom pairs, topological torsions, ECFP0 to ECFP4, FCFP2, FCFP4 and atomic environments. Checkpoints are shared as two Google Drive archives: the top-performing models and all other models. The demo loads saved_models/ECFP4_smiles_checkpoint.pth. A result should name the fingerprint, the output representation (smiles or selfies), the checkpoint and the decoding method.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Prediction & Demo, Result

sections.title: Use with mass spectra and in benchmarks
sections.body: Neo et al. (2025) paired a MIST spectrum encoder with a MolForge decoder, thresholded fingerprint bit probabilities, and reported top-1 31% and top-10 40% on MassSpecGym. The MassSpecGym in the Wild paper (an existing source on this record) retrained MolForge decoders on 2.5M, 10M and 50M molecule corpora with the public MolForge code and a 4096-bit Morgan fingerprint preset, paired with a freshly trained MIST encoder. It reports that the earlier MIST + MolForge results were inflated by a batched-inference problem with a reused MIST checkpoint: top-1 accuracy was 31.75% with batch size 24 and 10.73% after correction, and it marks the inflated figures as not valid.
sections.source_locator: Neo et al. abstract; MassSpecGym in the Wild: Appendix (MolForge Training and Inference Configuration), Section 6.1.2, Table 4

name: MS-BART
description: MS-BART spectrum-to-molecule generation model.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: MS-BART generates molecular structures from tandem mass spectra by treating the task as translation between token sequences. A MIST encoder first turns the spectrum into a predicted molecular fingerprint; MS-BART reads the fingerprint bits as tokens and writes the molecule as a SELFIES string, using one vocabulary for both. It is pretrained on 4 million simulated fingerprint-molecule pairs, fine-tuned on experimental spectra and then aligned with chemical feedback.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Sections 3.1-3.2; README.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The backbone is BART-base trained from scratch. Inputs are fingerprints predicted by MIST and binarised with a threshold (0.2 for NPLIB1, 0.11 for MassSpecGym); outputs are canonical SELFIES from a 185-token vocabulary. Pretraining combines three span-denoising tasks and one fingerprint-to-molecule translation task on 4M simulated pairs built from MassSpecGym's unlabelled molecules, excluding molecules close to the test fold. The model is then fine-tuned on MIST fingerprints of experimental spectra, and finally aligned with a chemical feedback step that favours molecules closer to the reference.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 3.1-3.4, Implementation, Appendix

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The original release on Figshare (article 30393544, CC BY 4.0, published 2025-10-19) holds, for CANOPUS and MassSpecGym, the final model weights, pretrained models, MIST checkpoints and preprocessed data. The current README also supports alternative MIST encoders from FRIGID for the fingerprint step, and notes known path and variable errors in its evaluation scripts. A result should state the MIST encoder, the fingerprint threshold and which stage (pretrained, fine-tuned or aligned) was evaluated.

name: MSNovelist
description: MSNovelist de novo structure generation from fingerprints.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: MSNovelist generates candidate molecular structures de novo from a tandem mass spectrum. SIRIUS and CSI:FingerID first predict the molecular formula and a molecular fingerprint from the spectrum; an encoder-decoder recurrent neural network then writes SMILES strings that fit the fingerprint and formula, and candidates are ranked by how well they match the predicted fingerprint. The authors now point users to SIRIUS 6, where MSNovelist is integrated.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Results; README.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MSNovelist splits the problem in two. CSI:FingerID maps the spectrum to a high-dimensional molecular fingerprint, and SIRIUS predicts the formula. Instead of searching a database with the fingerprint, an RNN generates structures: the fingerprint and formula are encoded into a starting state, and a three-layer LSTM decoder writes the SMILES character by character, in analogy to image captioning. Because the generator learns from structures rather than spectra, it was trained on 1,232,184 structures from HMDB, COCONUT and DSSTox, with simulated fingerprint errors added. Candidates are ranked by a modified Platt score against the predicted fingerprint.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results and Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published version depended on SIRIUS 4.4.29, whose backend no longer runs, so the Docker workflow in the README is marked obsolete. MSNovelist was integrated into SIRIUS 6 and retrained there on new SIRIUS 6 data; the repository is mostly that backend and cannot be used directly without retraining on other fingerprint data. A mist branch, merged into the repository, has early work on using predicted 4096-bit Morgan fingerprints. A result should say whether it used the published model, the SIRIUS 6 version, or a retrained model on another fingerprint (such as MIST + MSNovelist).

name: Neuraldecipher
description: Neuraldecipher fingerprint-to-molecule decoder.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: Neuraldecipher reverse-engineers extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs) back to molecular structures. A feed-forward network maps an ECFP to a continuous molecular descriptor (CDDD), and the pretrained CDDD decoder of Winter et al. turns that descriptor into a SMILES string. It was built to test whether shared fingerprints can reveal confidential structures; in mass spectrometry work it has been used as a fingerprint-to-molecule decoder after a spectrum encoder.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Section 2; MassSpecGym in the Wild Table 9

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The Neuraldecipher is a standard feed-forward network with fully connected layers. Its input is an ECFP of length k (binary or count); its output is a point in the 512-dimensional CDDD space. It is trained to minimise the distance between predicted and true CDDD vectors (optionally with a cosine loss). The fixed CDDD decoder, an RNN with three stacked recurrent layers, then decodes the vector to SMILES; using it means the Neuraldecipher does not have to learn SMILES syntax itself.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 2 and 2.1; README.md: Training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository ships one trained model: ECFP6 with 1024 bits, trained on the cluster split (models/1024_final_model_cs_gpu/weights.pt), evaluated in source/evaluation.ipynb. Parameter files for other ECFP settings are in params/. The CDDD decoder comes from a separate repository and must be installed in the same environment. A result should state the ECFP length, radius, binary or count form, and the split.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Evaluating the trained model, Repository structure; models/ listing

sections.title: Use in the benchmark source
sections.body: MassSpecGym in the Wild (an existing source on this record) lists MIST + Neuraldecipher, which pairs a MIST spectrum-to-fingerprint encoder with Neuraldecipher, in its updated MassSpecGym de novo leaderboard with 0.00% top-1 accuracy. name: Spec2Mol
description: Spec2Mol spectrum-to-molecule generation model.

version.note: Family record; the setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: Spec2Mol recommends molecular structures from tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) alone. An encoder turns a set of four spectra of a compound (positive and negative mode, low and high collision energy) into an embedding, and a decoder pretrained on about 135 million molecules turns that embedding into SMILES strings. It is modelled on speech-to-text systems.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Methods; README.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The decoder comes from a SMILES autoencoder with GRU encoder and decoder, pretrained on about 135 million PubChem and ZINC-12 molecules to translate between molecular representations. The spectra encoder is trained to predict that autoencoder's embedding from four spectra per compound: [M+H]+ and [M-H]- precursors at 35% and 130% NCE. Structures are produced either directly, by sampling several SMILES from the decoder and keeping valid ones, or indirectly, by retrieving database structures close to the embedding.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds one trained spectra encoder (spectra_encoder.pt) and the decoder model, vocabulary and config (decoder/models/), plus sample spectra and a sample embedding file. The encoder was trained on the NIST Tandem Mass Spectral Library 2020, a commercial dataset. A result should state whether the direct or indirect strategy was used and, for MassSpecGym, how the four-spectrum input was formed.

name: AlphaPeptDeep
description: AlphaPeptDeep modular Transformer fragment intensity predictor (about 1.8M parameters).

version.note: Family record; the retrained setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: AlphaPeptDeep (package name peptdeep) is a Python framework for predicting properties of peptides from their sequence. Its built-in pretrained models take a peptide sequence, its modifications, precursor charge, collision energy and instrument type, and predict the MS2 fragment intensities, the retention time and the collision cross section. The usual output is a predicted spectral library, for example built from a FASTA file, for use in peptide identification.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: About; paper: abstract and introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The MS2 model is built on four transformer layers with a hidden size of 256. For each peptide of length n it outputs intensities for (n-1) cleavage positions and eight fragment types: singly and doubly charged b and y ions and their modification-associated neutral losses. The retention time and collision cross section models are smaller: a CNN layer followed by two bidirectional LSTM layers. Modifications are represented by their chemical composition, so a modification the model has not seen can still be encoded. Training intensities are normalised by the highest matched intensity in each spectrum, so predictions lie between zero and one. The authors stress transfer learning: refining a pretrained model takes minutes and is possible without a GPU.
sections.source_locator: paper: Fig. 2 caption, MS2 model, Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The pretrained models are not versioned as separate checkpoints on the page: peptdeep downloads a single pretrained_models.zip from the repository's pre-trained-models release when it is first used, and the settings file names its URL in model_url. The MS2 model has several variants selected by model_type, which can be generic, phos, hla or digly, and separate releases exist for other labels, for example dimethyl-labelled peptides. External model files can be given instead with external_ms2_model, external_rt_model and external_ccs_model. A result should name the peptdeep version and the model type; this page read the repository at commit 8e9eba6e.
sections.source_locator: README: install-models, export-settings, Other pre-trained MS2/RT/CCS models

sections.title: How the benchmark used it
sections.body: PepSpecBench describes AlphaPeptDeep as a modular Transformer of about 1.8M parameters and retrained it, with the other five baselines, on the benchmark data under backbone-disjoint splits. That figure and those results therefore describe the benchmark's own retrained model, not the pretrained model shipped with peptdeep, whose MS2 model the paper states has 3,988,974 parameters.

name: FastSpel
description: FastSpel lightweight linear spectrum predictor (about 50K parameters), used as a lower-bound reference.

version.note: Family record; the retrained setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: FastSpel predicts the fragment intensities of a tryptic peptide measured by higher-energy collisional dissociation, so that a spectral library can be generated or peptide-spectrum matches rescored. It takes a list of precursors, each with a modified sequence, a precursor charge and a collision energy, and returns the non-zero predicted b and y ion intensities with their m/z values. Instead of a neural network it fits a separate multistep linear regression for each peptide length, charge and collision energy, which makes it fast and its parameters readable.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: abstract, Description of FastSpel Prediction Method; download page: Spectral library generation

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For each combination of peptide length, precursor charge and collision energy, FastSpel fits a multistep linear regression that maps a binary encoding of the peptide sequence to the fragment intensity profile. Peptides are built from the 20 common amino acids plus oxidised methionine, so the encoding uses 21 symbols, and fragments are predicted up to charge min(3, precursor charge). The model is effectively hundreds of small separate models: the paper says 350 length, charge and collision energy triplets were trained. Because the relation is linear, the authors read the fitted coefficients and find known fragmentation rules such as the proline effect.
sections.source_locator: paper: Description of FastSpel Prediction Method, Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code is a Python package distributed from the group's own site, not from GitHub or PyPI. The FTP folder it links to holds one file, fastspel-0.1.0.tar.gz, and the page's install commands name that same version. The page says it was last updated on 2 September 2026. A result should name the package version and the collision energy used, because a separate model is fitted per collision energy and only the six trained values are accepted.
sections.source_locator: paper: closing paragraph; download page: Installation; FTP listing

sections.title: How the benchmark used it
sections.body: PepSpecBench calls FastSpel a linear model of about 50K parameters and uses it as a lower-bound reference, with its output projected into the benchmark's shared fragment layout. All six baselines, FastSpel among them, were retrained on the benchmark data under backbone-disjoint splits, so that parameter figure and those results describe the benchmark's retrained model rather than the released package.

strengths.text: Prediction is fast on CPU only: the authors report one million precursors in under 5 s on a single CPU core, and hundreds of times faster than Prosit, PeptDeep and MS2PIP in their own test.
The fitted coefficients can be read directly, and the authors use them to recover known fragmentation rules such as the proline effect.
Retraining is cheap: the authors say less than 40 s per collision energy, so the method can be refitted for other instruments, CID data or non-tryptic peptides.
The package installs with pip and needs only numpy, scipy, pandas and h5py, with a command line tool and a Python function for use inside other code.
strengths.source_locator: download page: Installation, Spectral library generation

limitations.text: It predicts no retention time or ion mobility, only fragment intensities, so rescoring features that need retention time have to come from elsewhere.
Scope is narrow: tryptic HCD data only, b and y ions only, unmodified peptides or oxidised methionine only, and the authors say it is not trained for timsTOF instruments.
limitations.source_locator: paper: FastSpel Limitations, Methods; download page: Spectral library generation

limitations.text: A separate model is fitted per length, charge and collision energy, so a precursor outside the trained combinations or at an untrained collision energy falls back to the nearest trained value.
No licence is stated for the code or the fitted model, and the package is served from a group web page rather than a code host, so there is no commit to pin.

name: PredFull
description: PredFull residual CNN full-spectrum predictor with squeeze-excitation (about 8.2M parameters).

version.note: Family record; the retrained setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: PredFull predicts a complete tandem mass spectrum for a peptide, not only the b and y fragment ions. The input is a table of peptides with precursor charge, fragmentation type (HCD or ETD) and normalised collision energy; the output is an MGF file of predicted peaks. The model is a residual convolutional network that predicts intensity in mass bins of 0.1 Th up to m/z 2000.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: introduction, Method, Input format, Usage; predfull.py: hyperparameters

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PredFull treats the spectrum as a vector of mass bins rather than a list of named fragment ions. The script sets a bin width of 0.1 Th and a spectrum dimension of 20000 bins, which covers m/z up to 2000. The network is built from residual convolutional blocks, with coordinate channels added to the convolutions so position information is available, and it is trained on over 2 million experimental spectra. Predicted peaks weaker than one thousandth of the strongest peak are dropped as noise.
sections.source_locator: README: introduction, Method, Important Notes; predfull.py: hyperparameters and imports

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One trained model file is distributed, pm.h5, downloaded from a Google Drive folder linked in the README and placed in the repository folder. The README's update history shows the model changed over time: non-tryptic peptides were supported from May 2020, oxidised methionine from May 2021 and peptides of any length from May 2022. Only one model file is offered, so a result should name the date it was downloaded and the repository commit; this page read the repository at commit fc3641e0. The README also warns the model does not load correctly with TensorFlow earlier than 2.3.0.

name: Prosit
description: Prosit GRU encoder-decoder fragment intensity predictor (about 2.5M parameters).

version.note: Family record; the retrained setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: Prosit is a neural network that predicts the MS2 fragment intensities and the indexed retention time (iRT) of a peptide. The input is a list of peptide sequence, precursor charge and collision energy; the output is a predicted spectrum, written as a MaxQuant style msms.txt, an msp library or a generic text file. It is used to build spectral libraries and to rescore peptide-spectrum matches. The original implementation runs as a server in a Docker container and needs a CUDA GPU.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Two models are loaded side by side: one for fragment intensities and one for iRT. A peptide is encoded over an alphabet of the 20 common amino acids plus oxidised methionine, so 21 symbols, with cysteine always treated as carbamidomethylated. The intensity model covers y and b ions up to fragment charge 3, with no loss, water loss and ammonia loss variants, for up to 29 cleavage positions. Prediction runs behind an HTTP server: a posted peptide list is converted to numpy arrays, both models predict, and the result is written in the requested output format.

name: Prosit Transformer
description: Prosit Transformer fragment intensity predictor (about 86M parameters).

version.note: Family record; the retrained setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: Prosit Transformer predicts MS2 fragment intensities for a peptide using a transformer instead of the recurrent network of the original Prosit. It takes a peptide sequence with its precursor charge and collision energy and predicts the intensities of the six common ion series (singly, doubly and triply charged b and y ions). It is built by putting a prediction head on TAPE, a transformer trained on protein sequences, and fine-tuning it on the Prosit training data.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: abstract, Architecture, Results

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: TAPE is a transformer autoencoder trained on Pfam protein sequences to fill in a missing residue. It has 12 attention layers of 768 hidden units and encodes the peptide into a 512-dimensional embedding. A Prosit-specific transformer with the same settings but nine attention layers decodes the combined embedding. A separate metadata layer, a two-layer perceptron of width 512, takes seven inputs: a six-dimensional one-hot charge state and the collision energy. Its output is combined with the peptide embedding before the decoder, and a two-layer prediction layer follows the decoder. Predicted negative intensities are set to zero, and ions that cannot exist for a peptide, because the charge or the length is too low, are set to -1 and excluded from similarity measurements.
sections.source_locator: paper: Architecture, Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code is in the first author's repository, which has no licence file and no release. It installs with pip install -e . and uses the TAPE training command, and the README's notes say that downloading trained models is still a to-do, so no weights are published there. The training data are the Prosit HDF5 files from figshare, converted to LMDB; the paper says the converted LMDB files were deposited on figshare as well. A result therefore has to state which model the author trained and with which config file; the repository's example config is config/prositTransformer.json. This page read the repository at commit 36d788f5.

name: UniSpec
description: UniSpec attention-based fragment dictionary model (about 12M parameters).

version.note: Family record; the retrained setup is on the configuration

profile.summary: UniSpec predicts the full set of fragment ion series for a peptide, not only b and y ions, and is sensitive to the collision energy. The input is a spectrum label: sequence, charge, modifications and collision energy. The output is a predicted intensity for each entry of a fixed fragment dictionary, written out as an msp spectral library. The released model, UniSpec23, ships in the repository with its dictionary and accessory files.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: UniSpec; model_config.yaml; predict.yaml: write_msp label types

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UniSpec predicts into a fixed dictionary of fragment ions rather than a binned spectrum. The released model config has 9 blocks, an embedding size of 256, 38 input channels, a sequence length of 40 and an output dimension of 7919, which is the size of the fragment dictionary. Attention head sizes are 16, 16 and 64, and the last filter width is 512. The training config has an option CEembed for embedding the collision energy; in the released UniSpec23 config it is false. A dictionary usage criteria file and ion statistics from training ship beside the checkpoint and are used when a prediction is written.
sections.source_locator: saved_models/unispec23/model_config.yaml; Train.yaml: model_config; model folder listing

sections.body: One trained model is released, saved_models/unispec23, holding the checkpoint ckpt_epoch16_0.9263 of about 59.8 MB with its dictionary, model config, criteria, modifications list and training ion statistics. The prediction config is preset to those paths. Koina also hosts a version of UniSpec that returns the top 200 predicted peaks by intensity, which is not the same output as the local model, so a result should say which was used. The training and evaluation datasets are not in the repository: the configs point to a Zenodo download. This page read the repository at commit 60574023.

name: AttentiveFP
description: Attentive fingerprint graph network.

version.note: The tables name the model without a release version

profile.summary: AttentiveFP (Attentive FP) is a graph neural network for molecular property prediction. It reads a molecule as a graph of atoms and bonds and learns a fixed-length vector for the whole molecule, a neural fingerprint, using a graph attention mechanism over node and edge features; that vector is then mapped to the property being predicted. It is a molecular architecture rather than a protein model, and it appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained it as a baseline on protein tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: PubMed abstract 31408336; metadata.yml: description; DeepProtein full text, Structural-based learning

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A molecule is represented as a graph whose nodes are atoms and whose edges are bonds. Attention layers update the node and edge embeddings, and a readout step pools the node embeddings into one vector for the molecule, which a predictor head turns into the target property. The authors report that the learned features are interpretable and that feature visualisation suggests the model picks up nonlocal intramolecular interactions from the task it was trained on. In the DeepProtein benchmark the model is configured with three AttentiveFP layers, an AttentiveFP readout and node and edge embedding dimension 64.
sections.source_locator: PubMed abstract 31408336; DeepProtein full text, GNN variants

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark trained AttentiveFP as one of its graph baselines. It does not call the authors' own code: its encoder wraps the AttentiveFPGNN and AttentiveFPReadout classes of the dgllife library, and the benchmark records DGLlife 0.3.2 in its software configuration. The benchmark also states that since its protein inputs are two dimensional, it adds edge information with edge featurisers for some graph networks. A result quoted against AttentiveFP on a protein task therefore describes a model the benchmark trained, not a checkpoint released by the AttentiveFP authors.
sections.source_locator: encoders.py: class DGL_AttentiveFP; DeepProtein full text, Software configuration and Figure 1 caption

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The official repository is a Code Ocean capsule export (licence dated 2019) with no version number and no trained weights: it ships the model code and Jupyter notebooks for drug discovery datasets. A result must therefore name the code commit and the training script used, not a checkpoint. This page read the repository at commit dda6708342ffe255ded73c459ad64214a4615542. For a protein result, name instead the benchmark library and encoder that produced it; the DeepProtein README states that its legacy graph encoders, DGL_AttentiveFP among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.

name: ChemLLM-7B
description: ChemLLM-7B chemistry large language model, prompted for protein property questions.

version.note: The tables name the model without a release version

profile.summary: ChemLLM-7B-Chat is a chat language model for chemistry. It is built from InternLM2-Base-7B by instruction tuning, first on a general question and answer corpus and then on a mixture of that corpus with 7 million chemistry question and answer pairs assembled from chemical databases. It answers chemistry questions in text and accepts molecule notations such as SMILES. It is in this database because the DeepProtein benchmark prompted it for protein properties without fine-tuning it, not because its developers designed it for proteins.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: title and System Prompt Best Practice; paper: ChemLLM, a large language model for chemistry; DeepProtein: large language models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ChemLLM is a chat language model, not a protein model. It starts from InternLM2-Base-7B and is instruction tuned in two stages. The first stage uses Multi-Corpus, 1.7 million question and answer pairs collected from Hugging Face, to build general language ability. The second stage mixes ChemData, 7 million instruction tuning question and answer pairs built from chemical databases with a template method, with Multi-Corpus again, so that chemical knowledge is added without losing general ability. The released config is an InternLM2 causal language model with 32 layers, hidden size 4096 and 32 attention heads.
sections.source_locator: Paper: ChemLLM, a large language model for chemistry; ChemData; config.json

sections.title: What it is built for
sections.body: The developers describe ChemLLM as a model for chemistry and molecule science, able to hold a dialogue about chemical tasks. The card's recommended system prompt says the model accepts SMILES strings, prefers to answer with IUPAC names, writes reactions as SMARTS and also accepts SELFIES. Nothing in the model's own sources describes protein sequence tasks. Its appearance in this database comes from the DeepProtein benchmark, which prompted it for protein properties and reports that it was not fine-tuned for them.
sections.source_locator: Model card: title and System Prompt Best Practice; DeepProtein: large language models

run_guide.summary: Install transformers, then load ChemLLM-7B-Chat and generate an answer to one question with the settings the card gives.
prerequisites: Python with the transformers package and torch.
A CUDA GPU: the card's example moves the inputs to cuda and loads the model in float16 with device_map auto.
Enough memory for a 7.7 billion parameter model in half precision, as the Hugging Face parameter count gives its size.
Willingness to run the modelling code shipped in the weights repository, since the example passes trust_remote_code.

steps.title: Install transformers
steps.shell: pip install transformers
steps.explanation: The install line the card gives before its usage example.

steps.title: Load the model and ask one question
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
import torch

model_name_or_id = "AI4Chem/ChemLLM-7B-Chat"

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name_or_id, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map="auto",trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name_or_id,trust_remote_code=True)

prompt = "What is Molecule of Ibuprofen?"

inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")

generation_config = GenerationConfig(
    do_sample=True,
    top_k=1,
    temperature=0.9,
    max_new_tokens=500,
    repetition_penalty=1.5,
    pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id
)

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, generation_config=generation_config)
print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
PY
steps.explanation: The card's usage example, wrapped in a shell heredoc and otherwise unchanged. It downloads the weights on first use. For a chemistry dialogue the card recommends wrapping the prompt in the InternLM2 chat template and adding its suggested system prompt.

outputs: The decoded reply printed to standard output.

name: Deep Prot-T5
description: DeepProt-T5: Prot-T5-XL fine-tuned per task, introduced by the DeepProtein authors.

version.note: The tables name the model without a release version

profile.summary: DeepProt-T5 is a set of protein property predictors made by the DeepProtein authors. They took Prot-T5-XL, an existing protein language model, and fine-tuned it separately on each task of their benchmark, so there is one checkpoint per task rather than a single general model. Each checkpoint takes a protein sequence and returns the prediction for its task, for example a stability value, a subcellular location or a per-residue epitope label. The authors report it as the strongest entry in their own benchmark on several tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Fine-tuned models; Deep Prot-T5

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DeepProt-T5 is not a new architecture. The DeepProtein authors took Prot-T5-XL, a 3B parameter protein language model from ProtTrans, and fine-tuned it separately on each of their benchmark datasets with the Hugging Face trainer. The difference from their other protein language model runs is that the upstream weights are updated during training rather than frozen, which they call dynamic rather than fixed embeddings. Each task therefore has its own checkpoint, and together they form the series the paper calls DeepProt-T5.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; DeepProtein framework, Deep Prot-T5

sections.title: Training setup the authors report
sections.body: For the DeepProt-T5 fine-tunes the paper gives a learning rate of 0.00002 for every model and a batch size of 10, chosen to avoid memory errors, against a default of 0.0001 and batch size 32 for the library's other sequence models. The maximum number of training epochs for all models is 100. The fine-tuning ran on two 24 GB NVIDIA RTX 3090 cards.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Training setup; Hardware configuration

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one checkpoint per benchmark task rather than a single model. The paper and the README both say the fine-tuned models are released in the Hugging Face collection jiaxie/protlm. When that collection was read through the API on 2026-11-26 its item list was empty, so no individual checkpoint could be pinned to a revision, and the per-task parameter counts and sizes could not be read. A result should name the task, the seed (the paper uses 7, 42 and 100) and the library commit; the code is at github.com/jiaqingxie/DeepProtein, read here at commit 63247833.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Fine-tuned models, Availability and implementation; README: News; collection API response

sections.title: What the authors claim for it
sections.body: The abstract says the DeepProt-T5 series reaches the best reported performance on four of the benchmark tasks and is competitive on six others. In the results text the authors say their DeepProt-T5 models improved on the original Prot-T5 models on six tasks, named as Beta-lactamase, Solubility, SubCellular, PPI_Affinity, CRISPR and Fold. These are the authors' own claims about their own benchmark.

strengths.text: The authors report that these fine-tunes beat the frozen Prot-T5 embeddings on six named tasks of their own benchmark: Beta-lactamase, Solubility, SubCellular, PPI_Affinity, CRISPR and Fold.
The authors' stated purpose is to spare users the fine-tuning run, since a trained checkpoint exists for each benchmark task.
The surrounding library is open under MIT, with documented one-line training commands, dataset loaders and Colab notebooks, including one for inference with DeepProtT5 models.

limitations.text: The released weights could not be pinned: the Hugging Face collection the authors name listed no items when read on 2026-11-26, so there is no checkpoint name, revision, size or licence to record.

No licence is stated for the fine-tuned weights in the paper, the README or the Hugging Face collection, so redistribution terms are unknown.
Fine-tuning the model needs real hardware and small batches: the authors used two 24 GB RTX 3090 cards and had to drop the batch size to 10 to avoid memory errors.

name: Graphormer

version.note: The tables name the model without a release version

profile.summary: Graphormer is a transformer architecture for graphs, published by Microsoft Research for molecule modelling. It takes a graph, such as a molecule, and encodes the graph's structural information into a standard Transformer. The released package is a training toolkit for graph-level prediction tasks rather than one fixed model; it appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained a Graphormer layer as a baseline on protein tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph; arXiv abstract; DeepProtein full text, GNN variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Graphormer keeps the standard transformer blocks and adds encodings that put the graph structure into the model: the paper describes structural encoding methods, which the benchmark paper summarises as spatial, centrality and edge encoding. The authors also give a mathematical characterisation of the expressive power of the architecture and argue that with these encodings many popular graph neural network variants are special cases of Graphormer. The package builds on a pinned fairseq revision, so training and inference run through the fairseq command line.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; DeepProtein full text, Graphormer paragraph; README.md: Containerized legacy environment

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark trained Graphormer as one of its graph baselines. It does not use the Microsoft package: its encoder imports GraphormerLayer from DGL, wraps it with a linear projection and max pooling, and the benchmark states that for simplicity and scalability on large graphs it deployed only one Graphormer layer with ReLU activation, node embedding dimension 64 and LayerNorm after the MLP layers. A protein result against the name Graphormer is therefore a single DGL Graphormer layer the benchmark trained, not a Microsoft Graphormer checkpoint.
sections.source_locator: DeepProtein full text, Graphormer paragraph; encoders.py: class Graphormer

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository is at version 2.0, released in December 2021, and its README states that pretrained models on PCQM4M and PCQM4Mv2 are available and that advanced pretrained versions are available only on Azure Quantum Elements. The README gives no download address for the pretrained models, so a result should name the code commit, the task script and the checkpoint path used. This page read the repository at commit c55f56923c2d7cd654161a6c84b28a2db65b5f3d. For a protein result, name the benchmark library instead; the DeepProtein README says its legacy graph encoders, Graphormer among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.

strengths.text: The repository ships a container that pins the legacy fairseq, Python and CUDA stack the code needs, with a verification script, so the environment can be rebuilt years after release.
It supports the dataset interfaces of PyG, DGL, OGB and OCP, so existing graph datasets can be used without conversion code.

The authors report competition results for the architecture: first place in the quantum prediction track of the OGB Large-Scale Challenge (KDD Cup 2021) and a win in the Open Catalyst Challenge, both claims made by the developers in their README.

limitations.text: The code is on a legacy stack. The container pins Python 3.9, PyTorch 1.9.1 and CUDA 11.1 user space libraries, and the README states this is a reproducibility environment, not a claim of compatibility with current releases.

The better pretrained models are not open: the README says advanced pretrained versions are available exclusively on Azure Quantum Elements, and gives no download address for the PCQM4M models it does mention.
Multi-node training is out of scope for the supported setup, and the GPU path needs the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.
The benchmark result does not measure the published model. DeepProtein ran a single DGL Graphormer layer for scalability, and has since dropped that encoder from its version 2 runtime.

profile.summary: LlaSMol-Mistral-7B is a chemistry language model: Mistral-7B-v0.1 with a LoRA adapter trained on SMolInstruct, a dataset of 14 small molecule tasks and more than three million instruction samples. It answers questions about molecules in text, with chemical content marked by tags such as SMILES and IUPAC, covering name conversion, property prediction, molecule captioning and generation, and reaction prediction. It is in this database because the DeepProtein benchmark prompted it for protein properties without fine-tuning it; its own developers describe no protein task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: body; paper: Abstract; README: Tasks and Examples; DeepProtein: large language models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LlaSMol-Mistral-7B is Mistral-7B-v0.1 with a LoRA adapter trained on SMolInstruct, an instruction tuning dataset of 14 chemistry tasks and more than three million samples. The released repository holds the adapter only, about 84 MB, not a full set of weights: the adapter config gives rank 16, alpha 16, dropout 0.05 and the seven projection modules it adapts. Queries and answers use tags that mark the type of each piece of content, for example SMILES, IUPAC, MOLFORMULA, NUMBER and BOOLEAN, and the repository code canonicalises any SMILES wrapped in its tags.
sections.source_locator: Model card: body; adapter_config.json; paper: Abstract; README: Usage note; Hugging Face file listing

sections.title: What it is built for
sections.body: The README groups the trained tasks into four types: name conversion between IUPAC names, SMILES and molecular formulae; property prediction on the ESOL, LIPO, BBBP, ClinTox, HIV and SIDER datasets; molecule captioning and generation from a description; and chemical reaction tasks, forward synthesis and retrosynthesis. All of these are small molecule tasks. Protein sequences are not among them. The record exists because the DeepProtein benchmark prompted the model for protein properties, wrapping the sequence in PROTEIN tags, without fine-tuning it.
sections.source_locator: README: Tasks and Examples; DeepProtein: large language models

The paper reports Mistral as the best base model for chemistry tasks. Each repository holds a LoRA adapter, so a run must name both the adapter revision and the base model it was applied to; this page read osunlp/LlaSMol-Mistral-7B at revision 044d6124 over mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1. The code is at github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/LLM4Chem, read here at commit 43ab5fcc, and includes the three step evaluation scripts for SMolInstruct.

name: MPNN
description: Message passing neural network over the protein graph.

version.note: The tables name the model without a release version

profile.summary: MPNN, the message passing neural network, is a general family of graph neural networks rather than a single trained model. A molecule or other graph is read as nodes and edges; the model learns a message passing algorithm and an aggregation procedure that compute a function of the whole graph, which is mapped to the property being predicted. The name appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained an MPNN as a baseline on protein tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; DeepProtein full text, GNN variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: In the paper's framework, the model learns a message passing algorithm and an aggregation procedure that compute a function of the whole input graph. Unlike the simpler graph convolution and graph attention baselines, an MPNN uses edge features as well as node features. In the DeepProtein configuration the readout is Sum and Max and the node and edge embedding dimension is 64, with the number of message passing steps set by the encoder's num_timesteps argument.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; DeepProtein full text, MPNN paragraph; encoders.py: class DGL_MPNN

sections.title: What has been released
sections.body: An open source implementation of the paper is at github.com/brain-research/mpnn under the Apache 2.0 licence. Its README states that it contains only the model class definition and some unit tests, that a dataset reader and basic trainer were planned for a future release, and that it is not an official Google product. It also notes that the default hyperparameters give reasonable performance on all targets but that the numbers in the paper came from a separate hyperparameter search with 50 trials per target. There are no trained weights.
sections.source_locator: README; LICENSE

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark did not use the brain-research/mpnn reference code. Its encoder imports MPNNGNN from the dgllife library and adds a Sum and Max readout and a linear layer to the predictor dimension. A protein result reported against the name MPNN is therefore a dgllife message passing network that the benchmark trained on that task. The DeepProtein README states that its legacy graph encoders, DGL_MPNN among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.
sections.source_locator: encoders.py: class DGL_MPNN; DeepProtein Readme.md, target_encoding row; DeepProtein full text, Software configuration

It is a framework rather than one model: the paper recasts several earlier graph networks into one framework, and at least two implementations exist, the brain-research reference code and the dgllife one the benchmark used.

name: PAGTN
description: Path-augmented graph transformer network.

version.note: The tables name the model without a release version

profile.summary: PAGTN, the path-augmented graph transformer network, is a graph neural network for molecular property prediction. Instead of only aggregating from immediate neighbours, it computes features of the paths between pairs of atoms and uses them to build global attention layers, so that distant parts of a molecule can influence each other directly. The authors trained it on quantum chemistry, physical chemistry and biochemistry property datasets; the name appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained it as a baseline on protein tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README.md: opening lines; DeepProtein full text, PAGTN paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The authors' starting point is that graph convolution networks rely on local aggregation and so can miss higher-order graph properties. The repository precomputes shortest paths in the molecular graph as a preprocessing step, and the paper uses path features in molecular graphs to build global attention layers. The repository's training script exposes the path length as a flag, with a maximum path length of 3 in the published command, along with position and ring embeddings, a hidden size of 160 and two attention heads. In the DeepProtein configuration the model is five PAGTN layers with LeakyReLU activation and node embedding dimension 64.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; README.md: preprocessing and training commands; DeepProtein full text, PAGTN paragraph

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark did not use the authors' repository. Its PAGTN encoder imports PAGTNGNN from the dgllife library and adds a weighted sum and max readout and a linear layer to the predictor dimension. The benchmark groups PAGTN with the graph transformers it added because, it says, graph transformers have recently shown their power in protein function prediction. A protein result against the name PAGTN is therefore a dgllife path-augmented network the benchmark trained, not a checkpoint from the authors.
sections.source_locator: encoders.py: class PAGTN; DeepProtein full text, Structural-based learning

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository has no releases, no version number and no trained weights: it ships the model code, the preprocessing script, the training script and the data and splits used in the paper as data.zip, plus the scripts that generated the published results. A result must therefore name the commit and the training flags used; this page read commit 4fd3606d49e81ebbe009aa9c69add16bd092d4d1. The README also gives two other model types behind the same script, a local variant selected with -mask_neigh and a convolutional network selected with -model_type conv_net, so a result must say which was run. For a protein result, name the benchmark library instead; the DeepProtein README says its legacy graph encoders, PAGTN among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.

run_guide.summary: Set up the authors' conda environment, compute the shortest paths for a dataset and train the path-augmented transformer on it.
prerequisites: Conda, with the rdkit channel available.
A CUDA 10.0 GPU machine for the -cuda flag in the training command.
A dataset directory; the repository ships the paper's data and splits in data.zip.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/benatorc/PA-Graph-Transformer.git
cd PA-Graph-Transformer
git checkout --detach 4fd3606d49e81ebbe009aa9c69add16bd092d4d1
steps.explanation: The README gives no clone command, so the clone and the checkout of the commit this page read were added here. The remaining steps are copied from the README.

steps.title: Create the environment
steps.shell:
conda create -c rdkit -n prop_predictor rdkit
source activate prop_predictor
conda install pytorch torchvision cudatoolkit=10.0 -c pytorch
conda install scikit-learn tqdm
steps.explanation: The four commands the README gives for its conda environment, in order. The README notes the set up can differ slightly by system.

steps.title: Put the repository on the Python path
steps.shell: export PYTHONPATH=path_to_repo:
steps.explanation: Taken from the README as printed; replace path_to_repo with the checkout directory.

steps.title: Compute the shortest paths
steps.shell: python preprocess/shortest_paths.py -data_dir path_to_data
steps.explanation: The preprocessing step that produces the path features the model attends over. Replace path_to_data with the dataset directory, for example one unpacked from data.zip.

steps.title: Train the path-augmented transformer
steps.shell:
dataset=path_to_dataset
python train/train_prop.py -cuda \
    -data $dataset -loss_type mse \
    -max_grad_norm 10 -batch_size 50 -num_epochs 100 \
	-output_dir output_test/sol_transformer -n_rounds 10 \
	-model_type transformer -hidden_size 160 \
	-p_embed -ring_embed -max_path_length 3 -lr 5e-4 \
	-no_share -n_heads 2 -d_k 80 -dropout 0.2
steps.explanation: The README's command for the transformer model, copied as printed, including its tab indentation. Adding -mask_neigh runs the local variant, and -model_type conv_net runs the convolutional network instead.

outputs: Training output written under the directory given by -output_dir, for 100 epochs over the chosen dataset.
Shortest-path files for the dataset, written by the preprocessing step.

description: ProtT5 protein language model, as named in the resource-usage table.

profile.summary: ProtT5 is a protein language model from the ProtTrans project. It reads one amino acid sequence and returns a vector for every residue, which can be averaged into a single vector for the whole protein. Those vectors are then used as the input to a smaller predictor, or the model is fine-tuned on a labelled task. The ProtTrans authors report that for per-residue prediction these embeddings beat methods that use evolutionary information, without any database search. The record here is the Prot-T5 line in the DeepProtein benchmark, which ran Prot-T5-XL-UniRef50.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model description and Intended uses; paper: Abstract; DeepProtein: section on protein language models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is built on the t5-3b architecture: an encoder-decoder Transformer with 24 encoder layers, 24 decoder layers, model dimension 1024 and 32 attention heads in the released config. Unlike the original T5, which denoises spans, it was pre-trained with a BART-like masked language modelling objective that masks 15 per cent of the amino acids. The tokenizer is per-residue with a vocabulary of 21 symbols, the sequence is upper-cased, the rare residues U, Z, O and B are mapped to X, and training sequences were cut or padded to 512 tokens. Training started from the ProtT5-XL-BFD checkpoint rather than from scratch.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model description, Training procedure, Pretraining; config.json

sections.title: What it is used for
sections.body: The developers offer the model for feature extraction or as a starting point for fine-tuning. They say fine-tuning can be more accurate than using it as a fixed feature extractor, and that for feature extraction the encoder-side embeddings should be used rather than the decoder's. All reported ProtT5-XL-U50 results in the paper come from encoder embeddings, measured in half precision, and the developers report no loss from half precision. The repository also ships a script that writes per-residue or per-protein embeddings for a FASTA file.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Intended uses and limitations; README: Quick Start, Important note on ProtT5-XL-UniRef50

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: ProtT5 is one line in a larger ProtTrans family. The README lists ProtT5-XL-UniRef50, ProtT5-XL-BFD, ProtT5-XXL-UniRef50 and ProtT5-XXL-BFD, alongside ProtBert, ProtBert-BFD, ProtAlbert, ProtXLNet and two ProtElectra models, each with a Hugging Face and a Zenodo download. The paper gives 3B parameters for the XL size and 11B for the XXL size. For ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 the weights repository holds three checkpoint files at the revision read here: pytorch_model.bin, pytorch_model_600k.bin and pytorch_model_723k.bin, each about 11.3 GB, so a result should name both the revision and which file was loaded. The README also points at a half-precision encoder-only repository, Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc, which its quick start example loads instead.

That paper names the checkpoint as Prot-T5-XL-UniRef50, says it is based on T5-3B, gives the embedding dimension as 1024, and used it with fixed embeddings as well as fine-tuning it per task to make their own DeepProt-T5 models.

run_guide.summary: Install the three packages the README names, then produce per-residue and per-protein ProtT5 embeddings for two short sequences.
prerequisites: Python with torch, transformers and sentencepiece, as the README installation section lists.
The README notes that a change in the T5 tokenizer can raise an error about sentencepiece_model_pb2, fixed by installing protobuf.
A GPU is optional. The README example falls back to CPU, and says half precision is GPU only and that CPU use is much slower.
Disk space for the checkpoint: each weights file in Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_uniref50 is about 11.3 GB, and the half-precision encoder repository used in the quick start is smaller.

steps.title: Install the packages
steps.shell:
pip install torch
pip install transformers
pip install sentencepiece
pip install protobuf
steps.explanation: The first three lines are the README installation block. The fourth is the fix the README gives for the T5 tokenizer error.

steps.title: Embed two sequences
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc', do_lower_case=False)
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc").to(device)
if device == torch.device("cpu"):
    model.to(torch.float32)
sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "SEQWENCE"]
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]
ids = tokenizer(sequence_examples, add_special_tokens=True, padding="longest")
input_ids = torch.tensor(ids['input_ids']).to(device)
attention_mask = torch.tensor(ids['attention_mask']).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)
emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,:7]
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0)
print(emb_0.shape, emb_0_per_protein.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: This is the README quick start example, wrapped in a shell heredoc with a print of the two shapes added so the step produces visible output. It loads the half-precision encoder-only repository that the README itself uses, not the full encoder-decoder checkpoint.

steps.title: Embed a FASTA file instead
steps.shell: python prott5_embedder.py --input sequences/some.fasta --output embeddings/protein_embeddings.h5 --per_protein 1
steps.explanation: The repository's own embedding script, as the README gives it. It writes an HDF5 file of per-protein embeddings; drop the per_protein flag for per-residue embeddings. The script lives in the Embedding folder of the repository at commit 27c02f07.

outputs: Step two prints the shape of the per-residue embedding matrix for the first sequence and of its per-protein mean vector; the README annotates these as 7 x 1024 and 1024.
Step three writes an HDF5 file of embeddings for every sequence in the FASTA input.

name: Prot-T5-XL
description: ProtT5-XL protein language model.

version.note: The tables name the model without a release version

profile.summary: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 (ProtT5-XL-U50, often just ProtT5) is a protein language model from the ProtTrans project. It reads a single amino acid sequence, with no alignment, and produces a 1024-value embedding for each residue, which can be averaged into one embedding per protein. These embeddings are used as features for downstream predictors, or the model is fine-tuned, for tasks such as secondary structure and subcellular localisation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model description, Intended uses; README: Quick Start; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is based on the t5-3b encoder-decoder model and was pretrained self-supervised on raw protein sequences. Unlike the original T5, which used span denoising, it was trained with a BART-like masked language modelling objective: 15% of amino acids are masked, 90% of those replaced by a mask token and 10% by a different random amino acid. Sequences are uppercased, rare amino acids U, Z, O and B are mapped to X, and each residue is one token. The configuration has 24 layers, hidden size 1024 and 32 attention heads. For feature extraction the developers recommend the encoder output rather than the decoder.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model description, Preprocessing, Intended uses; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two Hugging Face checkpoints hold ProtT5-XL-UniRef50: the full encoder-decoder model (Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_uniref50) and an encoder-only half-precision copy (Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc), which the README's quick start uses. The developers report the same downstream performance from both. Sibling ProtT5 models trained on BFD, and XXL variants, are separate checkpoints. ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 was initialised from ProtT5-XL-BFD rather than trained from scratch. A result should name the checkpoint, its revision (this page read 973be27c and 94a6abc0) and whether the encoder output was used.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

# Load the tokenizer
tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc', do_lower_case=False)

# Load the model
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc").to(device)

# only GPUs support half-precision currently; if you want to run on CPU use full-precision (not recommended, much slower)
if device == torch.device("cpu"):
    model.to(torch.float32)

# prepare your protein sequences as a list
sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "SEQWENCE"]

# replace all rare/ambiguous amino acids by X and introduce white-space between all amino acids
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]

# tokenize sequences and pad up to the longest sequence in the batch
ids = tokenizer(sequence_examples, add_special_tokens=True, padding="longest")

input_ids = torch.tensor(ids['input_ids']).to(device)
attention_mask = torch.tensor(ids['attention_mask']).to(device)

# generate embeddings
with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)

# extract residue embeddings for the first ([0,:]) sequence in the batch and remove padded & special tokens ([0,:7]) 
emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,:7] # shape (7 x 1024)
# same for the second ([1,:]) sequence but taking into account different sequence lengths ([1,:8])
emb_1 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[1,:8] # shape (8 x 1024)

# if you want to derive a single representation (per-protein embedding) for the whole protein
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0) # shape (1024)
PY
steps.explanation: The README quick start, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the encoder-only checkpoint and computes embeddings for two short example sequences.

outputs: Per-residue embeddings of shape 7 x 1024 and 8 x 1024 for the two example sequences, and a 1024-value per-protein embedding for the first, held in memory. The snippet prints nothing.

name: ProtBert
description: ProtBert protein language model.

version.note: The tables name the model without a release version

profile.summary: ProtBert is a protein language model with the BERT architecture, trained only on protein sequences with a masked language modelling objective: 15 per cent of the amino acids in a sequence are hidden and the model learns to put them back. It takes an uppercase amino-acid sequence, written with a space between residues, and returns either predictions for the masked positions or a vector per residue, 1024 numbers wide, that can be used as a feature for another model. The developers say it can be used for feature extraction or fine-tuned on a downstream task, and that fine-tuning was more accurate on some tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: ProtBert model, Model description, Intended uses & limitations, How to use; config.json

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The architecture is BERT, declared in the config as BertForMaskedLM with 30 hidden layers, a hidden size of 1024, 16 attention heads, an intermediate size of 4096 and a vocabulary of 30 tokens. Unlike the original BERT there is no next-sentence prediction, because each protein sequence is treated as a complete document. Masking follows the original recipe: 15 per cent of amino acids are chosen, 80 per cent of those are replaced by the mask token, 10 per cent by a different random amino acid and 10 per cent left as they are. Sequences are uppercased and split with single spaces, and the rare letters U, Z, O and B are mapped to X. Training ran on one TPU Pod V3-512 for 400,000 steps, 300,000 at sequence length 512 with batch size 15k and 100,000 at length 2048 with batch size 2.5k, with the Lamb optimiser at learning rate 0.002.
sections.source_locator: config.json; model card Model description, Preprocessing and Pretraining

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two BERT checkpoints exist in the ProtTrans family and they differ in their training corpus: ProtBert, trained on UniRef100, and ProtBert-BFD, trained on BFD. A result should say which one, since the ProtTrans README reports different downstream numbers for them, for example 75 against 76 on CASP12 three-state secondary structure. Each is published both on the Hugging Face hub and on Zenodo, and neither is gated. The Hugging Face revisions read here are 7a894481acdc12202f0a415dd567f6cfdb698908 for ProtBert and 6c5c8a55a52ff08a664dfd584aa1773f125a0487 for ProtBert-BFD. The wider ProtTrans release also holds ProtT5, ProtAlbert, ProtXLNet and ProtElectra models, which are different architectures and not covered here.

Anyone redistributing or building a product on the weights should read the Academic Free License itself rather than assume the repository's MIT terms apply to them.

from transformers import BertModel, BertTokenizer
