profile.summary: ESMC (ESM Cambrian) is a family of protein language models that read an amino acid sequence and return per-residue representations and masked-residue predictions. The models are trained on billions of protein sequences, so the representations can be used as features or fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as variant effect prediction or protein engineering. Three sizes are published, with approximately 300M, 600M and 6B parameters; the 6B model also serves as the frozen backbone of the ESMFold2 structure predictor and of a set of sparse autoencoders released for interpretation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model Details and Parameters; README.md: ESMC section

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESMC is a transformer trained with masked language modelling over protein sequences. The model card states it uses pre-layer normalisation, rotary position embeddings and SwiGLU activations, with no biases in the linear layers or layer norms. The 6B model has 80 layers; the card's parameter table gives 30 layers for the 300M variant and 36 for the 600M. Training ran in two stages: one million steps at a context length of 512 with metagenomic data at 64 per cent of the mixture, then 500,000 steps at a context length of 2048 with metagenomic data reduced to 37.5 per cent. Beyond the final layer, hidden states from all layers can be returned, and pretrained sparse autoencoders decompose the 6B model's hidden states into interpretable features.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Architecture, Parameters, Training Procedure and Usage; README.md: ESMC Sparse Autoencoders

sections.title: Sizes and what they were trained on
sections.body: The card's table gives three scales: ESMC-300M with 30 layers and 1.26e22 training FLOPs, ESMC-600M with 36 layers and 2.17e22, and ESMC-6B with 80 layers and 2.37e23. The Hugging Face metadata gives exact counts from the stored tensors: 332,997,184 parameters for ESMC-300M, 575,036,992 for ESMC-600M and 6,352,005,184 for ESMC-6B. Training sequences come from UniRef, MGnify and the Joint Genome Institute, clustered at 70 per cent sequence identity into 83M, 372M and 2B clusters respectively. All three variants are described as publicly released, and none of the three repositories is gated.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Parameters, Model Variants and Training Data; Hugging Face API responses

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two generations of weights exist under the same name. The December 2024 weights, esmc-300m-2024-12 and esmc-600m-2024-12, were released in the esm package format; their card now says they are kept for backwards compatibility and recommends the Hugging Face compatible weights at biohub/ESMC-6B, biohub/ESMC-600M or biohub/ESMC-300M instead. Benchmark results that name ESM-C 300M or ESM-C 600M were produced with the older repositories. The developer organisation has also been renamed: requests for EvolutionaryScale repositories now resolve to biohub ones. A result should therefore name the repository, the revision and which generation of weights was used; this page read biohub/ESMC-600M at revision 5e366569e675ad5ae3512f66bf0b53ffe80ee83e and the legacy card at revision 7f10b20ae75017b2dbc884070e03434515709a8d.

steps.title: Run ESMC on one sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

GFP = "MSKGEELFTGVVPILVELDGDVNGHKFSVSGEGEGDATYGKLTLKFICTTGKLPVPWPTLVTTFSYGVQCFSRYPDHMKQHDFFKSAMPEGYVQERTIFFKDDGNYKTRAEVKFEGDTLVNRIELKGIDFKEDGNILGHKLEYNYNSHNVYIMADKQKNGIKVNFKIRHNIEDGSVQLADHYQQNTPIGDGPVLLPDNHYLSTQSALSKDPNEKRDHMVLLEFVTAAGITHGMDELYK"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("biohub/ESMC-600M")

inputs = tokenizer(GFP, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)

with torch.inference_mode():
    output = model(**inputs)

print(f"logits shape: {tuple(output.logits.shape)}")
PY

name: DeepFoldRNA
description: DeepFoldRNA: RNA structure prediction from deep self-attention networks with gradient-based folding.

version.note: Family record; the version run is on the configuration

attributes.provenance_note: Model details as given in the RNA 3D structure benchmark, Table 1.

profile.summary: DeepFoldRNA predicts the 3D (tertiary) structure of an RNA from its sequence alone. It builds a multiple sequence alignment and secondary structure prediction for the input RNA, uses a deep self-attention network to predict distance and angle restraints, and then folds the chain by gradient-based simulation. The output is all-atom models in PDB format, before and after refinement.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; README.txt: Running instructions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The pipeline has four stages. First, rMSA builds an MSA and PETfold predicts secondary structure; SPOT-RNA-1D predicts torsion angles. Second, a neural network with 48 MSA transformer blocks, 4 single-sequence blocks and 2 pair blocks, run for 4 recycling cycles, predicts restraints: binned distances from 2 to 40 Angstrom, inter-residue orientation angles and torsion angles. Third, gradient-based folding simulations build the structure from these restraints. Fourth, SimRNA and QRNAS refine the full-atom model. The authors note that the restraints do not include base atoms, so the unrefined model has slightly better backbone RMSD but worse base pairing than the refined one.
sections.source_locator: README.txt: Installation step 2; Running instructions; network/config.py

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The stand-alone program is Version 1.0, dated 03/28/2022. The network weights are stored in the repository under network/parameters, in four folders (model_1, model_1_2, model_2, model_2_2) of three weight files each. By default the program makes 6 models with different network parameters, or 3 if --generate_all_models is False. Results also depend on the sequence databases used for MSA generation. A result should name the commit (this page read 0c2c1925), the model number and whether the refined or unrefined model was used. A web server is also available.

name: DRfold
description: DRfold: ab initio RNA structure prediction that combines end-to-end learning with deep geometrical potentials.

version.note: Family record; the version run is on the configuration

attributes.provenance_note: Model details as given in the RNA 3D structure benchmark, Table 1.

profile.summary: DRfold predicts the 3D (tertiary) structure of an RNA from its nucleotide sequence alone, without a multiple sequence alignment. Deep learning models trained on solved RNA structures predict both coarse nucleotide positions and inter-nucleotide geometry; these are combined into an energy function that guides structure assembly. The output is a refined all-atom model in PDB format.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods: Feature preparation and embedding; README: Example

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DRfold encodes the sequence as one-hot vectors (A, U, G, C and N for unknown) and adds secondary structure predicted by RNAfold and PETfold as pair features. A stack of 48 transformer blocks, extended from AlphaFold2's Evoformer, updates sequence and pair representations, with 3 recycles. Two kinds of model are trained. End-to-end models use a structure module with invariant point attention to place each nucleotide as a rigid three-bead unit (C4', P and glycosidic N). Geometry models predict inter-nucleotide geometry restraints. Both outputs are combined into a hybrid energy potential that is minimised to assemble a coarse-grained structure. Arena rebuilds full atoms and OpenMM refines the model.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Feature preparation and embedding; RNA transformer network; RNA structure module); Results on refinement

sections.title: Training data
sections.body: The training set holds 3864 unique RNAs from the PDB deposited before 2021. Test structures deposited in or after 2021, and their sequence cluster members, were excluded from training. Training crops were limited to under 200 nucleotides because of GPU memory (a single Nvidia A40 GPU). The training and test sets are available for download from the authors' website.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results (benchmark set description); Discussion of large RNAs

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The GitHub repository does not include the trained models; they are downloaded separately as DRfold_models.zip from the Zhang group website. A run uses 6 end-to-end models and 3 geometry models; the final model is DPR.pdb. A result should name the repository commit (this page read 9586990c) and the date the model archive was downloaded, since the archive has no version number in the sources read.

name: NuFold
description: NuFold: RNA 3D structure prediction method built on the AlphaFold architecture with RNA-specific inputs.

version.note: Family record; the version run is on the configuration

attributes.provenance_note: Model details as given in the RNA 3D structure benchmark, Table 1.

profile.summary: NuFold predicts the full-atom 3D structure of a single RNA chain from its sequence. It takes the sequence, a multiple sequence alignment and a predicted secondary structure, and outputs ranked structure models as PDB files. It adapts the AlphaFold2 network to RNA, with a nucleobase-centred representation that lets the ribose ring take flexible shapes.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results (overview); README: Running NuFold

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: NuFold keeps the three-part AlphaFold2 layout. An input module reads the sequence, an MSA from the rMSA pipeline and a secondary structure predicted by IPknot. Evoformer blocks embed the MSA and pairwise information. A structure module builds the 3D model, and the steps are repeated in recycling rounds to refine it. Instead of amino acids, the network uses seven letter types: the four nucleotides, unknown, gap and masked. The network predicts the translation and rotation of each base frame plus a set of torsion angles, which the nucleobase centre representation turns into full-atom coordinates. Training added self-distillation data from bpRNA-1m to the small set of PDB structures.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, NuFold overview and Fig. 1; Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README publishes one checkpoint, global_step145245.pt, downloaded from kiharalab.org, and runs it with the config preset initial_training. The paper also describes variants trained for analysis, such as smaller 24-block Evoformer models and models trained with less self-distillation data; the README does not publish these. The code is archived on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.14498624). NuFold was trained with PyTorch 1.10.0+cu111 and tested with 2.0.1+cu117. A result should name the commit, the checkpoint file and the MSA source, because the paper reports that metagenome MSAs and more recycling change accuracy; this page read commit f77d34af.

name: RosettaFoldNA
description: RoseTTAFoldNA (RF2NA): three-track network that predicts protein and nucleic acid structures and complexes.

version.note: Family record; the version run is on the configuration

attributes.provenance_note: Model details as given in the RNA 3D structure benchmark, Table 1.

profile.summary: RoseTTAFoldNA (also called RF2NA) predicts the three-dimensional structure of proteins, RNA and DNA, alone or bound together in complexes. It takes the sequence of each chain, builds multiple sequence alignments and template searches, and outputs an atomic model in PDB format with per-residue confidence (predicted lDDT) and predicted aligned error. It extends the RoseTTAFold protein structure network to nucleic acids.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README: Inputs, Expected outputs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RoseTTAFoldNA uses the three-track design of RoseTTAFold, which refines three representations together: the sequence (1D), pairwise distances between residues (2D) and atom coordinates (3D). The authors extended each track to nucleic acids. The 1D track gains 10 tokens for the four DNA and four RNA nucleotides plus unknown DNA and unknown RNA. The 2D track models base-base and base-amino acid interactions. The 3D track places each nucleotide with a frame on its phosphate group and 10 torsion angles. The network has 36 three-track layers and four refinement layers. It was trained on protein monomers and complexes, RNA monomers and dimers, and protein-RNA and protein-DNA complexes from the PDB, with a generalised all-atom FAPE loss, and inputs include MSAs of related protein and nucleic acid sequences.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, paragraphs on architecture (Fig. 1) and training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists v0.2, dated 13 April 2023, with updated weights (RF2NA_apr23.tgz) for better homodimer-DNA prediction and DNA sequence recognition, MSA pipeline bug fixes and support for paired protein/RNA MSAs. The run script loads network/weights/RF2NA_apr23.pt. The sources do not say which weights the paper's results used. Predictions also depend on the sequence and template databases, which the README downloads at fixed versions for UniRef30 (2020_06) and the PDB templates (pdb100_2021Mar03) but from the current release for Rfam and RNAcentral. A result should name the weights file, the repository commit (this page read f761af28) and the database versions.

strengths.text: One network handles protein-only, RNA-only, protein-RNA and protein-DNA structures, including complexes.

Each prediction comes with confidence estimates (per-residue lDDT and predicted aligned error). The authors report that confident predictions are considerably more accurate than other methods they compared; this is their claim.
Code is MIT licensed and the full pipeline, from MSA generation to the final model, is in the repository.

limitations.text: Setup is heavy: the README downloads UniRef30 (46G), BFD (272G), NCBI nt (151G), RNAcentral (12G) and other databases, and the environment needs CUDA (pytorch-cuda 11.7) and DGL.
The authors say most failures come from poor prediction of single subunits, typically large multidomain proteins, large RNAs (over 100 nt) and small single-stranded nucleic acids.
Training used PDB structures from before May 2020, and the authors point to limited nucleic acid training data.
No licence is stated for the weights file.

name: trRosettaRNA
description: trRosettaRNA: MSA and pair representations fed into the RNAformer transformer, followed by 3D folding.

version.note: Family record; the version run is on the configuration

attributes.provenance_note: Model details as given in the RNA 3D structure benchmark, Table 1.

profile.summary: trRosettaRNA predicts the full-atom 3D structure of an RNA from its sequence. It takes a multiple sequence alignment and a secondary structure, uses a transformer network to predict inter-nucleotide distances, orientations and backbone torsion angles, and then folds a 3D model by energy minimisation in Rosetta. The output is a PDB file.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; package README: Overview, Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For a query RNA, an MSA is built (with rMSA, or Infernal against RNAcentral) and a secondary structure is predicted with SPOT-RNA. These are turned into an MSA representation and a pair representation, which also carries direct couplings from the MSA and the secondary structure probability matrix. A transformer called RNAformer, similar to the Evoformer in AlphaFold2, updates both representations. A single pass has 48 blocks, cycled 4 times. It outputs probability distributions for 1D torsion angles and 2D distances, contacts and orientations. These are converted into restraints that, with physics-based Rosetta energy terms, guide energy minimisation to full-atom models; the package generates several decoys and keeps the one with minimum energy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Overview of trRosettaRNA; Methods, Preparation of input data, RNAformer, 3D structure folding; package README: Step 2

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two releases of the standalone package are named. Version 1.0 is the version used in the Nature Communications paper, downloadable from the lab website. Version 1.1, on Zenodo (record 10616895, 2024-02-03), adds support for custom secondary structure files. The package ships one RNAformer checkpoint, params/model_1, used by default. For its benchmarks the paper trained separate models on date-filtered training sets to avoid leakage; those are not described as released. A result should name the package version, the MSA tool and database, and the secondary structure source, since the authors report sensitivity to secondary structure quality.

strengths.text: Fully automated: in CASP15 and RNA-Puzzles blind tests the authors report its predictions for natural RNAs were competitive with the top human predictions.
Code and model files are on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, and a web server is available for users who do not want to install it.
Version 1.1 accepts a user-supplied secondary structure (dot-bracket, ct or SPOT-RNA probabilities), so SPOT-RNA can be replaced by another predictor or a known structure.

limitations.text: The authors state that accuracy depends on the quality of the predicted secondary structure, is limited on novel RNAs, and that synthetic RNAs remain hard.
Needs an MSA built separately (Infernal or BLASTN against NT or RNAcentral are recommended) and converted to A3M.
Installation pulls in PyRosetta and a separate Python 3.6 TensorFlow 1.14 environment for SPOT-RNA. Most run time (over 95%) is the CPU-bound 3D folding step.

description: Genome-scale nucleotide language model pretrained on over 110 million prokaryotic gene sequences and fine-tuned on SARS-CoV-2 genomes to model viral evolution and identify variants.

version.note: Family record

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the RNAGym fitness leaderboard.

profile.summary: GenSLM (genome-scale language model) is a family of autoregressive language models that read DNA coding sequence as codons, three nucleotides per token. The foundation models were pretrained on over 110 million prokaryotic gene sequences, and a SARS-CoV-2 model was fine-tuned on 1.5 million viral genomes to track the virus's evolution and pick out variants of concern. The released code computes sequence embeddings and generates new sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction, contributions; Figure 1 caption. README: Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GenSLMs are generative pre-trained transformers (GPT-style causal language models) with a codon-level tokeniser. The released foundation models load GPT-NeoX architecture files (the 25M file declares GPTNeoXForCausalLM with 8 layers, hidden size 512 and 8 attention heads) and a 69-token codon vocabulary, and were trained at four sizes from 25 million to 25 billion parameters with a maximum sequence length of 2,048 tokens on individual genes from BV-BRC. The 25M and 250M models were then fine-tuned on SARS-CoV-2 genomes with sequence length 10,240 tokens; the larger sizes ran out of GPU memory at that length. The paper also describes a hierarchical model in which a diffusion model guides a codon-level transformer to cover whole genomes; the README points to a separate repository for it.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Sec. 5 model training. inference.py: GenSLM.MODELS. README: Diffusion Model

sections.body: The inference code names five model IDs: genslm_25M_patric, genslm_250M_patric, genslm_2.5B_patric and genslm_25B_patric (foundation models, 2,048 tokens) and genslm_25M_covid (SARS-CoV-2 model, 10,240 tokens). Each ID maps to a fixed weight file name, for example patric_25m_epoch01-val_loss_0.57_bias_removed.pt. Weights are downloaded from a Globus endpoint; the README warns that files fetched before 3 May 2023 have a name space issue and should be downloaded again. The COVID model's weights are available on enquiry. A result should name the model ID, the weight file name and the repository commit (this page read 6622c47e).

prerequisites: Python with pip. The README example uses a GPU when present, else CPU. The sources do not state memory needs.
The weight file patric_25m_epoch01-val_loss_0.57_bias_removed.pt from the Globus endpoint.
Code is MIT. No licence is stated for the weights.

steps.shell: pip install git+https://github.com/ramanathanlab/genslm@6622c47e8d9f00a1e8b8c4e30b78e6d702d2b883
steps.explanation: The README's install command, with @<commit> added to pin the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Download the weights
steps.shell:
# From the Globus endpoint
# https://app.globus.org/file-manager?origin_id=25918ad0-2a4e-4f37-bcfc-8183b19c3150&origin_path=%2F
# download patric_25m_epoch01-val_loss_0.57_bias_removed.pt into the current directory.
steps.explanation: A manual Globus transfer. The file name is the one the inference module expects for genslm_25M_patric, and the module looks in the current directory by default.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import numpy as np
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from genslm import GenSLM, SequenceDataset

model = GenSLM("genslm_25M_patric")
model.eval()
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model.to(device)

sequences = [
    "ATGAAAGTAACCGTTGTTGGAGCAGGTGCAGTTGGTGCAAGTTGCGCAGAATATATTGCA",
    "ATTAAAGATTTCGCATCTGAAGTTGTTTTGTTAGACATTAAAGAAGGTTATGCCGAAGGT",
]
dataset = SequenceDataset(sequences, model.seq_length, model.tokenizer)
dataloader = DataLoader(dataset)

embeddings = []
with torch.no_grad():
    for batch in dataloader:
        outputs = model(
            batch["input_ids"].to(device),
            batch["attention_mask"].to(device),
            output_hidden_states=True,
        )
        emb = outputs.hidden_states[-1].detach().cpu().numpy()
        emb = np.mean(emb, axis=1)
        embeddings.append(emb)

embeddings = np.concatenate(embeddings)
print(embeddings.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README embedding example wrapped in a shell heredoc. The model_cache_dir argument (a Colab Google Drive path in the README) is dropped so the default, the current directory, is used; comments are removed and the final bare expression is wrapped in print().

outputs: An array of averaged last-layer embeddings; the README shows shape (2, 512) for the two example sequences.

name: Orthrus
description: Mamba RNA encoder trained contrastively so that splice isoforms and orthologous transcripts have similar embeddings, used to predict mature mRNA properties.

version.note: Family record

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the RNAGym fitness leaderboard.

profile.summary: Orthrus is a family of RNA foundation models that turn a full mature mRNA transcript into an embedding. It was pretrained so that splice isoforms of the same gene, and transcripts of orthologous genes across mammals, get similar embeddings. The embeddings are used, directly or after fine-tuning, to predict mRNA properties such as RNA half-life and ribosome load.
profile.summary_source_locator: Preprint abstract; README: Model Overview

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Orthrus uses a Mamba encoder, a state-space model whose memory grows linearly with sequence length, so it can read whole mRNAs. The input is a per-base track matrix: four one-hot nucleotide tracks, plus in the 6-track models a coding sequence track (1 at the first base of each codon) and a splice track (1 at the last base of each exon). Pretraining is contrastive: the model maximises embedding similarity between pairs of transcripts formed from splice isoforms and orthologues. One released checkpoint adds a masked language modelling objective. The model returns a mean-pooled embedding per transcript, or per-position hidden states.

Three pre-publication checkpoints sit under quietflamingo. The GitHub README still describes the earlier 4-track base and 6-track large models loaded from local Lightning checkpoint files. A result should name the Hugging Face repository and its revision; this page read orthrus-4-track at revision 1326c689 and orthrus-6-track at revision 4994263c.

prerequisites: Python 3.10 in a mamba or conda environment, as the model card recommends.
A CUDA GPU: the Mamba kernels require CUDA. GPU type and memory are not stated.
Code and weights are MIT licensed; the weights are not gated.

steps.title: Create the environment
steps.shell:
mamba create -n orthrus python=3.10
mamba activate orthrus
steps.explanation: Creates and activates a Python 3.10 environment, as in the model card.

steps.title: Install PyTorch, transformers and the Mamba kernels
steps.shell:
pip install 'torch>=2.2' 'transformers<4.46' 'huggingface_hub>=0.24' safetensors
pip install causal-conv1d==1.2.0.post2 --no-build-isolation --no-cache-dir
pip install mamba-ssm==1.2.0.post1 --no-build-isolation --no-cache-dir
steps.explanation: The model card pins the Mamba kernel versions for the published checkpoints.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "antichronology/orthrus-4-track",
    trust_remote_code=True,
).to(device).eval()

sequence = (
    "TCATCTGGATTATACATATTTCGCAATGAAAGAGAGGAAGAAAAGGAAGCAGCAAAATATGTGGAGGCCCA"
    "ACAAAAGAGACTAGAAGCCTTATTCACTAAAATTCAGGAGGAATTTGAAGAACATGAAGTTACTTCCTCC"
)
oh = model.seq_to_oh(sequence).unsqueeze(0).to(device)  # (1, L, 4)
lengths = torch.tensor([oh.shape[1]], device=device)

with torch.no_grad():
    emb = model.representation(oh, lengths, channel_last=True)
# emb.shape == (1, D)
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's load and pooled-representation snippets, joined and wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the weights and runs custom model code from the Hugging Face repository (trust_remote_code).

name: RNAGenesis
description: RNA model trained on non-coding RNAs that combines a BERT-style encoder with a diffusion-guided decoder to represent, predict structure for and design functional RNA sequences.

version.note: Family record

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the RNAGym fitness leaderboard.

profile.summary: RNAGenesis is an RNA foundation model that handles sequence representation, structure prediction and sequence design in one framework. A BERT-style encoder, pretrained with masked RNA modelling on non-coding RNAs, turns an RNA sequence into embeddings; a query-based compression step maps those into a short latent code, and a diffusion model generates new latent codes that a decoder turns back into sequences. It is used both to score or classify RNAs after fine-tuning and to design new ones, such as aptamers and CRISPR sgRNA scaffolds.
profile.summary_source_locator: Preprint abstract; README: Overview, Encoder Checkpoint for Embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The repository's pretraining configuration for the stage-one encoder uses single-nucleotide embeddings of width 1,280, six parallel convolutional layers with kernels 3 to 13 whose outputs are summed with those embeddings, and 32 bidirectional Transformer blocks with 20 attention heads, RoPE and SwiGLU feed-forward layers. Training is masked RNA modelling: 30% of positions are selected and the loss is cross-entropy on those positions only. The repository notes that masking happens before the convolutional embeddings, so the masked bases cannot leak through the convolutions. No source read says which configuration the released Zenodo and Hugging Face weights use. The repository tree also holds two files whose names contain 6layers_16heads_128embedsize. For generation, the encoder output is compressed into a latent code, a diffusion model samples new latent codes, and a decoder produces sequences. Sampling can be steered at inference time by a classifier gradient or by beam search.
sections.source_locator: PRETRAIN.md: Architecture and objective; preprint abstract; README: Inference Pipeline; repository tree: models/autoencoder/encoder/checkpoints/Pretrained

sections.title: What it is used for
sections.body: Two routes are documented. For understanding tasks, the pretrained encoder is fine-tuned: the repository's example adds LoRA adapters, averages the valid nucleotide embeddings and trains an MLP head for 13 ncRNA classes. For design, generation.py samples sequences from a diffusion checkpoint, with aptamer and sgRNA checkpoints given as examples, optionally with classifier guidance or beam search. A separate module fine-tunes the encoder for 3D structure prediction.

name: 3UTRBERT
description: 3UTRBERT, a BERT language model pretrained on 3' UTR sequences.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: 3UTRBERT is an RNA language model for 3' untranslated regions (3'UTRs), the stretch of an mRNA after the coding sequence that carries many regulatory signals. It is a BERT model pre-trained on human 3'UTR sequences, read as overlapping k-mer tokens, and then fine-tuned to predict RNA-binding protein sites, m6A modification sites and where an mRNA sits in the cell. Its attention scores can be used to highlight regions with likely regulatory function.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: 3UTRBERT is the encoder part of a Transformer: token embeddings of dimension 768 plus positional embeddings pass through twelve stacked Transformer layers, each with multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward layer. Sequences are split into overlapping k-mer tokens. It was pre-trained as a masked language model: 15% of the k-mers are masked, in contiguous spans of k tokens so that a masked k-mer cannot be read off its neighbours, and the model learns to restore them; next sentence prediction was dropped. For downstream use, the model is either fine-tuned end to end on short labelled sequences, or frozen and used to extract embeddings for longer sequences.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Experimental Section, Architecture of 3UTRBERT and pre-training; Results 2.1

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four pre-trained checkpoints are linked from the README, for 3-mer, 4-mer, 5-mer and 6-mer tokens. The paper says they share the same architecture and training settings. The 3-mer checkpoint is a single zip file of 322227069 bytes on figshare. Fine-tuning and prediction must use the tokenizer that matches the checkpoint (rna3 to rna6). A result should name the k-mer checkpoint, its figshare version, and the fine-tuning data.

name: AIDO.RNA
description: AIDO.RNA RNA foundation model (650M and 1.6B parameter checkpoints).

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: AIDO.RNA is a family of RNA foundation models from GenBio AI; its Hugging Face repositories and current code use the name GB.RNA. The models read an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and turn it into embeddings that a downstream model can use, for tasks such as RNA secondary structure prediction, mRNA-related prediction and RNA function prediction. The largest model has 1.6 billion parameters and was trained on 42 million non-coding RNA sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: 1.6B model card: opening paragraph; Hugging Face API id

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The models are encoder-only transformers pretrained with a masked language modelling (MLM) objective: parts of the sequence are hidden and the model learns to predict them. The 1.6B model has 32 layers, hidden size 2,048, feed-forward size 5,440 and 32 attention heads, with a vocabulary of 16 tokens. The 650M model's configuration has 33 layers, hidden size 1,280, intermediate size 3,392 and 20 attention heads. Both configurations use rotary position embeddings and SwiGLU activations. Users normally adapt a backbone to a task through GenBio's ModelGenerator framework, which offers embedding, sequence-level and token-level classification, and regression heads.
sections.source_locator: 1.6B model card: Model architectural details, How to Use; config.json of 1.6B and 650M

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository documentation lists seven RNA backbones: gb_rna_1b600m, gb_rna_1b600m_cds, gb_rna_650m, gb_rna_650m_cds, gb_rna_300m_mars, gb_rna_25m_mars and gb_rna_1m_mars. GB.RNA-1.6B and GB.RNA-650M were trained on non-coding RNA. GB.RNA-1.6B-CDS and GB.RNA-650M-CDS are domain-adapted versions for coding sequences, whose Hugging Face metadata name the base models. The three MARS models were trained on 886 million RNA sequences from the MARS database. The Hugging Face repositories read are named GB.RNA rather than AIDO.RNA, and the sources read do not explain the difference. The model cards call the backbones aido_rna_1b600m and aido_rna_650m, while the pinned repository uses gb_rna_ names. A result should name the checkpoint, its Hugging Face revision and the backbone name used; this page read GB.RNA-1.6B at revision cea90e53 and GB.RNA-650M at revision efaf4af4.

name: BiRNA-BERT
description: BiRNA-BERT RNA language model with adaptive nucleotide and BPE tokenisation.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: BiRNA-BERT is an RNA language model that turns an RNA sequence into embeddings for downstream prediction tasks. It can read a sequence either one nucleotide at a time, for fine-grained tasks such as secondary structure prediction, or as compressed byte-pair tokens, so that long RNAs can be processed without cutting them short. It is a 117M-parameter transformer encoder trained on about 36 million non-coding RNA sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; model card opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BiRNA-BERT is a BERT-style transformer encoder trained with the MosaicBERT framework. It uses ALiBi relative positional encoding instead of fixed position embeddings, which lets it handle sequences longer than those seen in training. Its main idea is dual tokenisation: the same model is trained by masked language modelling on both byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokens, with a vocabulary of 4096, and single-nucleotide (NUC) tokens. BPE compresses long sequences so they fit in memory, while nucleotide tokens keep the per-base detail needed for tasks such as secondary structure prediction. With the released tokenizer, an unspaced sequence is split into BPE tokens and a space-separated sequence into nucleotide tokens.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results (first paragraph), Methods (tokenisation); model card: Usage

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The main checkpoint is buetnlpbio/birna-bert, used with the tokenizer buetnlpbio/birna-tokenizer. The paper also trained BPE-Only-BERT and NUC-Only-BERT as controls, and the buetnlpbio account lists bpe-only-rna-bert and nuc-only-rna-bert. The README warns that the current version is substantially updated and suggests re-analysing data processed with earlier versions. The README's own embedding example loads a different model name, Lancelot53/birnabert-2ep, while the model card loads buetnlpbio/birna-bert; the sources do not explain the difference. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision (this page read revision 35bceaf6) and say whether BPE or nucleotide tokenisation was used.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import transformers
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-tokenizer")

config = transformers.BertConfig.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-bert")
mysterybert = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-bert",config=config,trust_remote_code=True)
mysterybert.cls = torch.nn.Identity()

# To get sequence embeddings
seq_embed = mysterybert(**tokenizer("AGCTACGTACGT", return_tensors="pt"))
print(seq_embed.logits.shape) # CLS + 4 BPE token embeddings + SEP

# To get nucleotide embeddings
char_embed = mysterybert(**tokenizer("A G C T A C G T A C G T", return_tensors="pt")) 
print(char_embed.logits.shape) # CLS + 12 nucleotide token embeddings + SEP
PY

name: DGRNA
description: DGRNA long-context RNA foundation model with bidirectional Mamba2 attention.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: DGRNA is a pretrained RNA language model built for long RNA sequences. It is built mainly from bidirectional Mamba2 layers rather than the Transformer layers of earlier RNA language models, a choice the authors make to handle long sequences efficiently, and was trained on 100 million RNA sequences. Given RNA sequences, the released code returns a per-position representation that can be used for downstream tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: About; bioRxiv abstract; DGRNA/mamba2_pretrained.py: MambaLMHeadModel.forward

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tokens are embedded and passed through pairs of Mamba2 blocks: one reads the sequence forwards and one reads it reversed. A linear layer merges each pair's outputs. After the last pair, one multi-head attention layer with 32 heads and rotary embeddings is applied, followed by a final normalisation. The model is built on the ESM and Fairseq code bases and uses an ESM-1b style alphabet. The released forward pass returns the hidden states, not token logits. The sources read do not describe the pretraining objective.

name: ERNIE-RNA
description: ERNIE-RNA RNA language model with structure-enhanced representations.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: ERNIE-RNA is a pretrained RNA language model that learns from RNA sequence alone but is given a hint about which bases could pair. It is a modified BERT model whose attention is biased by possible base pairs, trained on 20.4 million non-coding RNA sequences. Given RNA sequences up to 1024 nucleotides, it returns sequence and per-base embeddings and attention maps; the repository also ships fine-tuned heads for secondary structure, 3D closeness and 5' UTR mean ribosome load prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Fig. 1, Discussion; README: Embedding Extraction, Secondary structure prediction, 3D Closeness Prediction, UTR MRL prediction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ERNIE-RNA follows the BERT design: 12 transformer blocks, each with 12 attention heads over a 768-dimensional token embedding, about 86 million parameters in total. Its change is an all-against-all pairwise bias added to the attention scores, which gives the model prior knowledge of which bases could pair. It was pretrained with masked language modelling: about 15% of nucleotide tokens are replaced and the model predicts them with a cross-entropy loss. The authors report that the attention maps of the pretrained model already capture secondary structure without fine-tuning.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, The architecture and pre-training of ERNIE-RNA; Methods, pre-training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained checkpoint is released (ERNIE-RNA_pretrain.pt), together with fine-tuned checkpoints: six for secondary structure prediction, each tied to a training set (bpRNA-1m, RNAStralign, RIVAS, RNA3DB, a frozen bpRNA-1m model used for bpRNA-new, and bpRNA-1m plus RNAStralign), one for 3D closeness and one for UTR mean ribosome load. All are downloaded from a Google Drive folder with no version tags. A result should name the checkpoint file, the dataset_name used for structure prediction, and the repository commit; this page read commit 43bc06de.

name: GenerRNA
description: GenerRNA autoregressive generative RNA language model.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: GenerRNA is a generative language model that writes new RNA sequences. It is a decoder-only transformer, the same style as GPT, trained on millions of natural RNA sequences so that it can sample sequences it has never seen. It takes no structure, label or alignment as input: either sample from it as it is, or fine-tune it on a family or a function first.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: GenerRNA; model card: Model Summary; paper: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GenerRNA is a decoder-only transformer of 350 million parameters: 24 layers with a model dimension of 1280, the same shape as GPT-2-medium. It is trained to predict the next token, with no labels. Sequences are split by a byte-pair encoding tokenizer with a vocabulary of 1024, so one token covers several nucleotides. The context window is 1024 tokens, about 4000 nucleotides. In preprocessing, U was replaced with T and ambiguity codes were kept. Generation is sampling: sampling.py writes new sequences from a checkpoint and a tokenizer.
sections.source_locator: paper: 2.1 Model architecture, 2.2 Pre-training data preparation; model card: Model Details; README.md: Usage

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints exist. The Hugging Face repository pfnet/GenerRNA holds model_updated.pt, which the card recommends and calls the longer-context model trained on deduplicated data, and keeps the original model under experiment_data/historical_version/ as four split parts with its own tokenizer. The GitHub repository pfnet-research/GenerRNA opens by saying it is not the newest version and points to Hugging Face. Each checkpoint has its own tokenizer directory, and they must be paired correctly. A result should name the checkpoint file, its tokenizer and the Hugging Face revision; this page read revision 43efbbd0.

name: LAMAR
description: LAMAR RNA foundation model pretrained on mammalian genome and transcriptome sequences (2k and 4k context checkpoints).

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: LAMAR is an RNA language model from the Shanghai Institute of Nutrition and Health (CAS) for studying how RNA processing is regulated. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and returns an embedding for each nucleotide; fine-tuned versions predict splice sites, translation efficiency from 5' UTRs, mRNA degradation from 3' UTRs and internal ribosome entry sites (IRES). It was pre-trained on about 15 million genome and transcript sequences from 225 mammals and 1569 viruses.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model weights; README.md: Compute embeddings; paper: Methods, Model architecture

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LAMAR is a bidirectional Transformer encoder with 12 layers, each with 12 attention heads and a feed-forward size of 3072, and rotary position embeddings. Each nucleotide is one token. During pre-training a portion of nucleotides (15%) is masked and the model predicts them from the surrounding sequence. The code builds the model with an ESM-style model class, EsmModel, from the repository's own LAMAR package. For a downstream task, a task-specific prediction head is placed on the final embeddings and the model is fine-tuned, either with the encoder frozen or with all parameters updated.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture; Results; Table 1; README.md: Compute embeddings

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pre-trained models exist: LAMAR-2k (context up to 2048 tokens) and LAMAR-4k (up to 4096 tokens), each saved at training step 250,000. Four fine-tuned models are also published: SpliceSitePred, UTR5TEPred, UTR3DegPred and IRESPred. All six sit in one Hugging Face repository, zhw-e8/LAMAR, as safetensors files under folders named for the run, so a result should give the folder name and the Hugging Face revision. The README's embedding example passes the architecture as arguments that override the base configuration file, which describes a different ESM-2 model (30 layers, hidden size 640); a user must keep those overrides.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from LAMAR.modeling_nucESM2 import EsmModel
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoTokenizer
from safetensors.torch import load_file, load_model
import torch


seq = "ATACGATGCTAGCTAGTGACTAGCTGATCGTAGCTG"
model_max_length = 1026
device = torch.device("cuda:0")
# instance tokenizer and config
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("tokenizer/single_nucleotide/", model_max_length=model_max_length)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    "config/config_150M.json", vocab_size=len(tokenizer), pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
    mask_token_id=tokenizer.mask_token_id, token_dropout=False, positional_embedding_type='rotary',
    hidden_size=768, intermediate_size=3072, num_attention_heads=12, num_hidden_layers=12
)
# intance the model and load pretrained weights
model = EsmModel(config)
weights = load_file('pretrain/saving_model/mammalian80D_4096len1mer1sw_80M/checkpoint-250000/model.safetensors')
weights_dict = {}
for k, v in weights.items():
    new_k = k.replace('esm.', '') if 'esm' in k else k
    weights_dict[new_k] = v
model.load_state_dict(weights_dict, strict=False)
model = model.to(device)
# Compute embeddings
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    inputs = tokenizer(seq, return_tensors="pt")
    input_ids = inputs['input_ids'].to(device)
    attention_mask = inputs['attention_mask'].to(device)
    outputs = model(
        input_ids=input_ids,
        attention_mask=attention_mask
    )
    embedding = outputs.last_hidden_state[0, 1 : -1, :]
print(embedding.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's embedding example, run from the repository root in a heredoc, with a final print of the embedding shape added.

outputs: A tensor of per-nucleotide embeddings for the input sequence, without the special start and end tokens; the added print shows its shape.

name: MP-RNA
description: MP-RNA RNA language model.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: MP-RNA is an RNA foundation model that reads an RNA sequence one base at a time and produces representations for downstream prediction. It was pretrained on plant transcriptomes from over 1,000 species with objectives that include predicting secondary structure and repairing single-base mutations. It is aimed at tasks that need per-base resolution, such as RNA secondary structure prediction and mutation detection, and the authors also apply it to DNA tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model Description, Training Data; paper Section 3

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MP-RNA is a transformer encoder that reads RNA one base at a time. It is pretrained with three combined objectives: masked RNA language modelling, single nucleotide mutation repair (5% of sites are mutated and the model learns to correct them), and secondary structure prediction. Structure labels come from ViennaRNA. To limit noise from these computed labels, the authors keep the 10% of samples with the lowest expected calibration error for incremental pretraining, and append structures to the sequence in 10% of masked language modelling examples. After pretraining, the model is fine-tuned or used for tasks such as secondary structure prediction, mutation detection and repair, and DNA genomic tasks.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 3.1 to 3.3; model card: Model Description

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper describes two sizes, MP-RNA-52M and MP-RNA-186M, both pretrained on four RTX 4090 GPUs over one month. This page read one checkpoint, yangheng/MP-RNA; its configuration (32 layers, dimension 720) and parameter count match the 186M version. The paper states that only MP-RNA-186M received incremental pretraining and that the incrementally pretrained 52M model will not be released. Whether any other MP-RNA checkpoint is public was not checked. The paper and card link to github.com/yangheng95/OmniGenomeBench; the code repository read here is yangheng95/OmniGenBench, and no saved file shows how the two addresses are related. Its README's examples use OmniGenome models and list MP-RNA as one supported model. A result should name the Hugging Face revision; this page read revision 0a727ebb.

name: PlantRNA-FM
description: PlantRNA-FM RNA foundation model pretrained on plant transcriptomes.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: PlantRNA-FM is an RNA language model for plants. It was pretrained on transcript sequences from 1,124 plant species, together with predicted secondary structure and labels for the 5' UTR, coding sequence and 3' UTR. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and outputs per-nucleotide embeddings, which the authors fine-tune for tasks such as genic region annotation and translation efficiency, and use to find RNA sequence and structure motifs linked to translation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results 'PlantRNA-FM integrates 1,124 plant transcriptomes'; Methods 'RNA tokenization'; Discussion; README: Inference

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PlantRNA-FM is an encoder-only transformer with 12 layers and an embedding dimension of 480. Each nucleotide is one token, and positions are encoded with rotary position embedding. Pretraining used three objectives together: masked nucleotide modelling, in which 20% of nucleotides in each sequence are selected for masking and reconstructed; prediction of the RNA secondary structure, which the authors annotated with ViennaRNA (RNAfold); and classification of each nucleotide into CDS, 5' UTR or 3' UTR. For a downstream task the authors replace the output layer and fine-tune the model. To find motifs, they use the model's attention contrast matrix with unsupervised hierarchical clustering.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Model architecture', 'RNA tokenization', 'Pretraining strategies of PlantRNA-FM', 'Fine tuning of downstream tasks'; README: Model Overview

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, yangheng/PlantRNA-FM on Hugging Face; this page read it at revision 5e7baf4e. The model card points users to a newer model from the same group, OmniGenome-186M, also trained on OneKP; it is a separate model and not described here. The sources disagree on some details. The paper and model card describe 24 attention heads, while the published config.json sets 20. The GitHub README says the model handles up to 512 nucleotides, while the paper says pretraining used 512 and fine-tuning allowed up to 1,026 tokens, the model card says up to 1026 nucleotides, and config.json sets max_position_embeddings to 1026. A result should name the Hugging Face revision. The GitHub repository holds the fine-tuning datasets and task scripts; the paper says training and inference code is in the Hugging Face repository.

name: ProtRNA
description: ProtRNA RNA language model adapted from a protein language model.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: ProtRNA is an RNA language model made by adapting a protein language model, ESM-2, to RNA sequences. The authors' idea is that information learned from the much larger body of protein sequences can transfer to RNA, where sequences are fewer and less conserved. It takes RNA sequences and returns per-nucleotide embeddings, which the repository uses for secondary structure, protein-RNA interaction and mean ribosome loading prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Abstract, Inference, Evaluation; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtRNA starts from the ESM-2 protein language model and is trained further on RNA by a cross-modality transfer learning strategy. In the released code the model keeps the ESM-2 vocabulary of amino acids and appends lower-case RNA tokens (a, u, g, c, x), so the same alphabet holds both kinds of sequence. Input RNA is lower-cased, T is mapped to u, and any other character becomes x. The pretrained model built by the loader has 33 layers, embedding dimension 1280 and 20 attention heads. Embeddings from layer 33 feed separate prediction heads for each downstream task. The sources read do not describe the RNA training objective or data in detail.
sections.source_locator: README: Abstract, Inference; pretrained.py load_pretrained_model; protrna/data.py Alphabet.from_architecture and _to_rna_vocab

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained language model is released, ProtRNA_pretrained.h5, as TensorFlow weights on Zenodo record 14795554. The same record holds task heads: four RotaFormer secondary structure heads trained on different datasets and selected under different metrics, protein-RNA interaction heads for 17 RBPs in HeLa cells, and a mean ribosome loading head (the last two in PyTorch). The README notes that an earlier version of the paper scored secondary structure with the authors' own metrics and keeps a script for that. A result should name the Zenodo record, the head file and the repository commit; this page read commit 991037d6. The preprint has two bioRxiv versions, and the bioRxiv record links a published version, DOI 10.1016/j.cels.2025.101371.

name: RFamLlama
description: RFamLlama autoregressive RNA language model trained on Rfam families (base and large).

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: RFamLlama is a generative RNA language model conditioned on RNA family. Given an Rfam family ID as a prompt tag, it writes new RNA sequences of that family; the same model can also score sequences for zero-shot fitness prediction. It was trained on sequences from over 4,000 RNA families, each labelled with a family tag.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card introduction; workshop abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RFamLlama is a decoder-only Llama model for causal (next-token) language modelling over a 22-token vocabulary. Each training sequence is preceded by a control tag naming its family. A prompt has the form <|bos|> <|tag_start|> family number <|tag_end|> <|5|>, where the family number is the Rfam ID without the RF prefix; the model then writes the sequence, which ends at the <|3|> token. The developers report that the family tags improve zero-shot fitness prediction; the sources read do not say how a fitness score is computed.
sections.source_locator: config.json (base); model card usage code; abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are published: RFamLlama-base (8 layers, hidden size 512, 31,488,512 parameters) and RFamLlama-large (10 layers, hidden size 768, 88,523,520 parameters). Both use the same tokenizer and prompt format. Generation is sampled (do_sample=True), so a result should name the checkpoint, its revision and the sampling settings.

steps.title: Generate sequences for one Rfam family
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
# generation
from transformers import LlamaForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, pipeline
import torch
import sys

model_url = "jinyuan22/RFamLlama-base"
model = LlamaForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_url, torch_dtype=torch.float16)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_url)

device = torch.device("cuda:0") if torch.cuda.is_available() else torch.device("cpu")

pipe = pipeline("text-generation", model=model, device=device, tokenizer=tokenizer)

tag = "RF00005"
txt = f"<|bos|> <|tag_start|> {tag[2:]} <|tag_end|> <|5|> "
all_outputs = []
outputs = pipe(txt, num_return_sequences=10, max_new_tokens=300, repetition_penalty=1, top_p=1,temperature=1, do_sample=True)

for i, output in enumerate(outputs):
    seq = output["generated_text"]
    seq = seq.split("<|5|>")[1].split("<|3|>")[0]
    print(f">{i}\n{seq}")
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. Replace RF00005 with another Rfam ID, or the model URL with jinyuan22/RFamLlama-large, to change family or size. It downloads the latest revision.

outputs: Ten sampled sequences printed in FASTA style, with headers >0 to >9.

name: RiNALMo
description: RiNALMo RNA language model (micro, mega and giga checkpoints).

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: RiNALMo is an RNA language model that reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and produces a numerical representation of each position. It was pretrained on 36 million non-coding RNA sequences by learning to fill in masked nucleotides, and the representations are then fine-tuned for tasks such as RNA secondary structure prediction and splice site prediction. The largest model has 650M parameters; smaller 148M and 33.5M versions are also released.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Methods; README: About

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RiNALMo is an encoder-only transformer trained by masked language modelling: 15% of tokens in each training sequence are selected, most are replaced with a mask token, and the model learns to reconstruct them. It uses rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU feed-forward layers and FlashAttention-2. Training sequences were sampled once per cluster per epoch to keep batches diverse. For downstream use, the per-nucleotide representations or the classification token embedding feed a task head; the authors fine-tuned it for secondary structure prediction, splice site prediction, mean ribosome loading and ncRNA family classification.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; README: Usage

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three pretrained sizes are published on Zenodo: giga (650M), mega and micro. Their parameter counts differ slightly between the paper, the README and the Zenodo description. The 650M model was pretrained on seven 80 GB A100 GPUs for 2 weeks. Fine-tuned giga weights and the train_<task>.py scripts allow the paper's downstream evaluations to be rerun. The Python loader in the repository downloads only giga-v1. A result should name the size, whether pretrained or fine-tuned weights were used, and the Zenodo record (15043668).

profile.summary: RNA-km is a language model for non-coding RNA sequences, built to predict RNA secondary structure, including pseudoknots, without training on labelled structures. It reads a single RNA sequence and returns a 1024-value representation per nucleotide and attention maps. In the paper, the attention maps are turned into base pairs with a minimum-cost flow algorithm.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; README.md: Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-km is a transformer encoder with 12 layers and model width 1024; the code sets the feed-forward width to four times the model width and uses relative position biases instead of absolute positions. Its token vocabulary covers A, T, C, G and X; the script converts U to T and other letters to N. It was trained by self-supervision on 23 million ncRNA sequences, using a k-mer masking strategy. A pair head projects the per-nucleotide representations to pairwise features. For structure prediction the paper uses the attention maps with a minimum-cost flow algorithm; that algorithm is not part of the repository files read.

profile.summary: Uni-RNA is a pre-trained language model for RNA sequences from DP Technology. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Uni-RNA is a Transformer encoder with a masked-language-model head: the masked-LM class outputs, for each position, logits over the token vocabulary. The released configurations use 64-dimensional attention heads, a GELU feed-forward layer three times the hidden size, rotary position embeddings and a vocabulary of 10 tokens; in the L16 upload these are four special tokens (<pad>, <eos>, <cls>, <mask>) and the letters N, A, T, C, G and U. The last hidden layer gives per-position embeddings that can be used directly or fine-tuned for a downstream task. The training data and pre-training details are described in the preprint, whose full text was not read here.

name: AlphaFold 2
description: Deep-learning protein structure prediction model evaluated in this comparison.

profile.summary: AlphaFold 2 predicts the three-dimensional structure of a protein from its amino acid sequence. It first searches sequence databases to build a multiple sequence alignment and find structural templates, then runs a neural network that reasons jointly over the alignment and over pairs of residues, and finally outputs atomic coordinates with a per-residue confidence score. This repository is the inference pipeline, and it also includes AlphaFold-Multimer for predicting complexes of several chains.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: AlphaFold; Installation; AlphaFold output; paper, introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The pipeline has two halves. First, standard search tools, which the paper names as jackhmmer and HHBlits, build a multiple sequence alignment from the sequence databases, and templates are taken from homologous structures where available. Then the network runs: a trunk of 48 Evoformer blocks that passes information between the alignment representation and a pairwise representation of residue relationships, followed by a structure module that gives each residue an explicit rotation and translation and so places the atoms. The whole network is applied several times over, feeding its own output back in, which the authors call recycling. A relaxation step with Amber then fixes local geometry, and the five models are ranked by predicted LDDT.
sections.source_locator: paper, Inputs and data sources, AlphaFold network; README: AlphaFold output

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: A result must name three things: the code version, the parameter set and the databases. The presets are monomer, monomer_casp14, monomer_ptm and multimer. The parameter sets are dated tar files, and the README explains how to go back to the 2022-03-02 (v2.2.0) or 2022-01-19 (v2.1.0) multimer weights. The v2.3.0 technical note says the current multimer weights were fine-tuned with a new training cutoff of 2021-09-30, keeping the same model architecture. The databases that the download scripts fetch are not the CASP14 versions, and the README lists the exact CASP14 database releases for anyone reproducing that work. Some targets have high run-to-run variance over random seeds. The authors call AlphaFold-Multimer a work in progress that is not expected to be as stable as the monomer system, and it also needs the UniProt database.
sections.source_locator: README: Running AlphaFold; Using deprecated model weights; Note on CASP14 reproducibility; technical_note_v2.3.0.md

sections.title: What it costs to run
sections.body: The README is specific about the setup. Linux only, up to 3 TB of disk for the databases (556 GB to download, 2.62 TB unpacked) and an NVIDIA GPU; larger proteins need more GPU memory. The reduced_dbs preset asks for 8 CPU cores, 8 GB of RAM and 600 GB of disk. The reference machine was 12 vCPUs, 85 GB of RAM and one A100. Prediction alone, excluding the database searches, took 4.9 s for 100 residues and 18,824 s for 5,000 residues on one A100.

profile.summary: RoseTTAFold All-Atom predicts the structure of a biomolecular assembly from its parts. Inputs are given per chain: protein sequences as FASTA, nucleic acid strands as DNA or RNA FASTA, small molecules as SDF files, plus covalent bonds between a protein chain and a small molecule. The output is a PDB file with predicted lDDT in the B-factor column and a separate PyTorch file of confidence metrics, of which the developers' main one is pae_inter, the mean error of protein residues with respect to atom frames together with atom coordinates with respect to protein frames. They warn that the model is not accurate for all cases and say the error estimates are there to let users tell the good predictions from the bad, with pae_inter below 10 expected to mean a high quality dock.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Inference Configs Using Hydra and Understanding model outputs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Inference is driven by Hydra configuration files: a job inherits the base configuration and adds one entry per chain under protein_inputs, na_inputs, sm_inputs and covale_inputs. Alignments and templates are built by a script against UniRef30, BFD and a 2021 March snapshot of PDB100. The network settings in rf2aa/config/inference/base.yaml, the only model configuration in the sources read, sit under the key legacy_model_param and describe a RoseTTAFold style stack: 4 extra blocks, 32 main blocks and 4 refinement blocks, with MSA channels 256, full MSA channels 64, pair channels 192 and template channels 64, and SE(3) transformer layers of 32 channels and 2 degrees for structure refinement. It uses atom frames, chirality and Lennard-Jones terms. At inference the loader keeps up to 128 latent and 1,024 total alignment sequences and 4 templates, and recycles 4 times by default. The developers recommend keeping the defaults because they match the training task, but say raising MAXCYCLE to 10 gives better results on hard cases.
sections.source_locator: base.yaml: loader_params and legacy_model_param; README: Inference Configs Using Hydra and Setup

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One released checkpoint, RFAA_paper_weights.pt, downloaded from files.ipd.uw.edu and named as checkpoint_path in the default configuration. The sources read list no other weights, and the developers say they will share new models as they create them. Reproducibility also depends on the databases, which are pinned by name: UniRef30_2020_06, BFD, and PDB100 at 2021 March 03, plus legacy BLAST 2.2.26. A result should name the checkpoint, the repository commit, the MAXCYCLE setting and the database versions, and should state whether signalp6 was installed, since the Docker route leaves it out for licensing reasons and the predictions then do not use it.

name: Chroma
description: Diffusion-based protein backbone generation method evaluated in Scaffold-Lab (released 2023-11).

version.note: Table 1 gives a release date and repository, not a version

profile.summary: Chroma is a generative model that designs proteins: it samples all-atom structures of single chains and complexes, and the matching sequences, by reversing a diffusion process. The user can sample freely or steer the sampling with composable conditioners for symmetry, substructure, shape, fold class or a text caption. It can also redesign the sequence and side chains of a structure given to it.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README: introduction, Sampling, Design, Conditioners

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Chroma uses a diffusion process designed to match the conformational statistics of polymer ensembles: structures are corrupted towards collapsed polymer noise and a network learns to denoise them. The denoiser is a random graph neural network with long-range connectivity, inspired by N-body algorithms, which scales sub-quadratically with the number of residues, plus a layer that solves for a global structure from predicted inter-residue geometries. A second graph-based design network generates sequence and side chains, and conditional random fields are used for the sequence. Conditioners are PyTorch modules that transform the state or add energy, and the total energy is backpropagated so that any composition of them can be sampled with annealed Langevin dynamics.
sections.source_locator: Paper abstract and Fig. 1 caption; README: introduction, Conditioners, Conditioner API

sections.title: Design modes and conditioners
sections.body: The design network is diffusion-aware: it was trained to predict sequence and side chains not only for natural structures at diffusion time t=0 but for noisy structures at all times. The design_t parameter therefore trades exact design (t=0.0) against robust design in a neighbourhood of the target backbone (t=0.5, the repository default), which the developers report improves one-shot refolding. Predefined conditioners cover symmetry, substructure, shape, secondary structure, domain class (Pfam, CATH, taxonomy), text captions and subsequence constraints, and new ones can be written as small PyTorch modules.
sections.source_locator: README: Design, Conditioners, Note on Conditioners

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper describes two versions of the model, v.0 and v.1, used for its large unconditional sample sets, and notes an overrepresentation of alpha helices in v.1 under low-temperature sampling. The code is on GitHub and on PyPI as generate-chroma; the weights are downloaded at run time from Generate Biomedicines with a registered access token, so a result should name the code commit or package version, the weights the run downloaded, and the sampling settings (design_t, langevin_factor, inverse_temperature, sde_func). This page read the code at commit 501f474a.

strengths.text: One model covers both generation and design: unconditional and conditional sampling of monomers and complexes, plus sequence redesign and side-chain packing of a given structure.
Conditioners compose, so symmetry, substructure, shape, class and text constraints can be combined without retraining, and new ones are a few lines of PyTorch.
strengths.source_locator: README: Conditioners, Conditioner API; paper abstract

strengths.text: Sampling is sub-quadratic in the number of residues; the README says large complexes can be generated in a few minutes on a commodity GPU.

The developers' claim, from the paper abstract: 310 designed proteins were characterised experimentally, were highly expressed and folded, and two crystal structures agreed with the samples to about 1.0 angstrom backbone RMSD.

limitations.text: The weights are not open: an access token is required and the Chroma Parameters License limits free use to academic and non-profit users, with commercial use by arrangement.
Generation under restraints can be hard to integrate: the developers warn that the effective energy landscape can become rugged and advise caution with new conditioner combinations.
Sample statistics are not neutral: the paper reports an overrepresentation of alpha helices in the later version under low-temperature sampling, and refolding success falls for longer proteins.
The published paper's results used exact design at t=0.0, while the repository now defaults to t=0.5, so repository defaults do not reproduce the paper's design mode.

name: FrameDiff
description: Diffusion-based protein backbone generation method evaluated in Scaffold-Lab (released 2023-03).

version.note: Table 1 gives a release date and repository, not a version

profile.summary: FrameDiff generates new protein backbones from noise. It represents each residue as a rigid body (a frame: a position and an orientation in 3D) and runs a diffusion model over those frames. The output is a set of monomer backbone structures in PDB format at the requested lengths, which can then be given sequences with a design tool such as ProteinMPNN.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Inference

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The authors develop a diffusion model on SE(3), the space of rotations and translations, applied to one frame per residue. Noise is added separately to translations (an R(3) diffuser) and rotations (an SO(3) diffuser), and a network learns the SE(3) equivariant score used to reverse the noise. In the released configuration the score network has 4 blocks of invariant point attention layers with 8 heads and a 2-layer sequence transformer, node embedding 256 and edge embedding 128. The repository keeps a modified fork of OpenFold. FrameDiff does not rely on a pretrained structure prediction network. Sampling uses 500 steps by default.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; config/base.yaml: diffuser and model; config/inference.yaml: diffusion; README: Third party source code

sections.body: The repository holds two weight files. weights/paper_weights.pth gives the ICML paper results and is loaded by default. weights/best_weights.pth is a fine-tuned model produced after a bug fix in the rotation score, dated 27 June 2023 in the README. Matching configs are config/icml_published.yaml and config/base.yaml. The authors report preliminary designability of 0.29 for the published settings and 0.34 for base.yaml; those are their numbers. A result should name the weight file and the config used. This page read the repository at commit 53359d71.

name: Genie
description: Diffusion-based protein backbone generation method evaluated in Scaffold-Lab (released 2023-01).

version.note: Table 1 gives a release date and repository, not a version

profile.summary: Genie generates new protein backbones with a diffusion model. It represents a structure as a cloud of oriented residues: noise is added to and removed from the alpha carbon coordinates, while the network reasons over Frenet-Serret frames built from the backbone geometry, which give each residue a position and an orientation. Sampling runs the reverse diffusion for 1,000 steps and writes alpha carbon coordinates, with no sequence input. The published models were trained from scratch on filtered SCOPe domains or on AlphaFold predictions of SwissProt, and the authors report designability, diversity and novelty against RFdiffusion, FrameDiff and other generators. The model is small, 4.1 million parameters against RFdiffusion's 59.8 million.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: title, Sections 2.2, 2.3, 3.2 and Datasets; README: header and Sampling

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The forward process adds Gaussian noise to the alpha carbon coordinates of a domain over a fixed variance schedule with 1,000 steps. The network is trained to predict the noise added at each step, following the usual denoising diffusion objective, so training reduces to fitting that noise prediction model. What makes the representation asymmetric is that the input is a point cloud while the reasoning is frame based: Frenet-Serret frames are constructed from the backbone geometry of the noised structure, giving each residue an orientation as well as a position, which the authors call equivariantly diffusing oriented residue clouds. The architecture uses pair transform layers, with triangular attention switched off in the shipped configuration. At sampling time the noise vector can be multiplied by a constant factor, in the manner of low temperature sampling, which trades designability against diversity.
sections.source_locator: paper: Sections 2.2, 2.3, Loss and 3.2; weights/scope_l_256/configuration

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The weights ship inside the repository rather than on a model hub. At the commit read here there are three sets, each with its own configuration file: weights/scope_l_128 with epoch=49999.ckpt, weights/scope_l_256 with epoch=29999.ckpt, and weights/swissprot_l_256 with epoch=99.ckpt. The names match the paper's variants: a model trained on SCOPe with a maximum length of 128, and the two long models, Genie-SCOPe and Genie-SwissProt, both with the maximum sequence length set to 256. The shipped configuration for scope_l_256 sets maximumNumResidues to 256, five pair transform layers, no triangular attention and a learning rate of 1e-4. A result should name the weight folder, the checkpoint epoch, the repository commit and the sampling noise scale, since that scale changes the output distribution.

strengths.text: The designability evaluation is included, not left to the reader: a script sets up a ProteinMPNN and ESMFold pipeline and a second script scores a directory of samples.

limitations.text: Short proteins only. The released models cap at 128 or 256 residues, set in the configuration as maximumNumResidues.

Sampling is long: the reverse process runs 1,000 diffusion steps, and sampling time in the paper is reported as a function of those steps and the protein length.
The README's weight loading snippet names a file, weights/genie_l_128_epoch=49999.ckpt, that does not exist at the commit read; the checkpoints live in per-model subfolders instead.

profile.summary: MassFormer predicts the tandem mass spectrum (MS/MS) of a small molecule from its structure. It takes a molecule (as SMILES) plus spectrum metadata such as precursor adduct and collision energy, and outputs a binned spectrum. Predicted spectra can be used to identify compounds by comparing them with measured spectra.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; arXiv 2111.04824v3 Section 2.1 and abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MassFormer adapts the Graphormer graph transformer. Node and edge embeddings are taken from the molecular graph, the graph transformer models relationships between all atoms, and a readout gives one embedding for the molecule. This embedding is combined with metadata (precursor adduct, collision energy) and passed to an MLP that outputs a binned spectrum. The transformer and input embeddings are initialised from a Graphormer model pre-trained on PCQM4Mv2 (about 4 million molecular graphs with simulated HOMO-LUMO gaps), then the whole model is fine-tuned on MS/MS spectra.
sections.source_locator: arXiv 2111.04824v3: Section 2.1, Figure 1, Section 4.4

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository is the original implementation that accompanies the arXiv preprint (three versions; v3 dated 1 May 2023) and the Nature Machine Intelligence paper. The models in the manuscript were trained on the NIST 2020 MS/MS library, and NIST does not allow their parameters to be redistributed, so no manuscript checkpoints are released. The one public checkpoint is a demo model trained on MoNA with an InChIKey split (checkpoints/demo.pkl, from Zenodo record 8399738). Configs are provided to retrain on NIST and MoNA, including models at 1.0 Da and 0.1 Da bin sizes. A result should state the config file, the training data and whether NIST was used.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Running the Demo, Checkpoints for Models from the Manuscript, Training a Model on All of the Data

sections.title: Use in benchmarks
sections.body: The FlexMS benchmark paper (an existing source on this record) describes adapting the MassFormer predictor design (an MLP with bidirectional prediction and a learned gate) as one of three predictor heads that it pairs with different molecule embedders.
