name: MolMS
description: Point-cloud molecular spectrum predictor, used as a predictor head in FlexMS.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: 3DMolMS (called MolMS in the FlexMS benchmark) predicts the tandem mass spectrum (MS/MS) of a compound from its 3D conformation. It takes a molecule with its precursor type and collision energy, generates a 3D conformation, encodes the atoms as a point set, and outputs a binned spectrum. The learned molecular representation can also be fine-tuned for retention time and collision cross section prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; Bioinformatics paper abstract and Sections 2.1-2.3; FlexMS Section 3.2

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A 3D conformation is generated with the ETKDG algorithm in RDKit. Each atom becomes a point with its x, y, z coordinates and RDKit atom attributes, and bonds are represented by neighbouring vectors. In the paper, an encoder of six 3D molecular convolution layers (64 to 1024 dimensions) produces representations that are concatenated with metadata into a 2048-dimensional vector, and a decoder of five fully connected layers with residual blocks outputs the spectrum. By default spectra are binned at 0.2 resolution over m/z 0 to 1500, giving 7500 bins. Release v1.4.0 changed the encoder to aggregate over the covalent bond graph and replaced the decoder with a bidirectional head, so the current checkpoints are not the paper's architecture.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 2.2-2.3; README.md: Latest release

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The package molnetpack has had many releases since v1.0.0 (2023-06-30). Notable changes: training data enlarged with MoNA and Waters QTOF data (v1.1.0), an Orbitrap MS/MS model (v1.1.6), an E(3)-invariant encoder (v1.3.1) and the bond-graph encoder with a bidirectional head (v1.4.0, 2026-08-11), for which all four checkpoints (QTOF, Orbitrap, RT, CCS) were retrained from geometric pretraining on ChEMBL. Release v1.4.0 has five zip assets, including a pretraining checkpoint. v1.4.0 checkpoints embed their training config and loading refuses mismatches; older checkpoints only give a warning. A result should name the package version and the checkpoint (qtof or orbitrap).
sections.source_locator: CHANGE_LOG.md; GitHub release v1.4.0; docs checkpoints.rst

sections.title: Use in benchmarks
sections.body: The FlexMS benchmark paper (an existing source on this record) describes adapting the MolMS decoder design (fully connected layers with residual blocks) as one of three predictor heads that it pairs with different molecule embedders.

name: NEIMS
description: Neural electron-ionization mass spectrum predictor, used as a predictor head in FlexMS.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: NEIMS (Neural Electron-Ionization Mass Spectrometry) predicts the electron ionization (EI) mass spectrum of a small molecule. It takes a molecule, turns it into a count-based circular fingerprint, and outputs a spectrum with an intensity for every integer m/z bin. The aim is to add predicted spectra to a reference library so that molecules missing from the library can still be matched.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Methods; README.md: Introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Molecules are mapped to additive (count) ECFP fingerprints of length 4096 and radius 2, computed with RDKit, and passed to a multilayer perceptron. The tuned MLP has seven layers of 2000 nodes with residual connections, ReLU and dropout 0.25. The output is adjusted for physical effects of ionisation: besides a forward prediction, a reverse prediction mode is added, because the authors found forward prediction struggles with large fragments from neutral losses, and the two are combined (bidirectional prediction). The model is written in TensorFlow.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Spectral Prediction, Adjustments for Physical Phenomena), Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one published model and one set of pretrained weights, linked from the README. When Rewire requested that weights URL anonymously on 2026-11-27, Google Cloud Storage returned an Access denied error, so the pretrained weights could not be confirmed as available. The repository is archived on GitHub. The train, validation and test molecules are provided in training_splits (InChIKey and SMILES). The paper's models were trained on 240 942 spectra from the NIST 2017 main library, which is not distributed with the code, so retraining the published model needs a NIST licence. A result should state whether it used the released weights or a retrained model, and on what data.

profile.summary: DeepVariant is a germline variant caller: it finds SNPs and small indels in a person's sequencing reads. It takes reads aligned to a reference genome, turns the reads around each candidate site into a pileup image, classifies that image with a convolutional neural network, and writes the calls to a VCF or gVCF file. Trained models are provided for short-read, long-read and other sequencing technologies, all trained on human data.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and notes; paper title

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DeepVariant runs as three programs. make_examples reads the aligned reads and the reference and writes a multi-channel tensor for each candidate site. All models use six base channels (read base, base quality, mapping quality, strand, whether the read supports the allele, and whether the base matches the reference); Illumina models add an insert size channel and PacBio and ONT models add a haplotype channel. call_variants classifies each tensor with a convolutional network and is the only step that uses a GPU. The usage guide's section on changes since the 2016 precisionFDA challenge says the model moved to the Inception-v3 architecture; the sources read do not state the architecture of the v1.10 models. postprocess_variants sorts the results, combines multi-allelic records and writes a VCF, and optionally a gVCF. Genotypes are limited to hom-ref, het and hom-alt.
sections.source_locator: deepvariant-details.md: Inputs and outputs, Updates since the precisionFDA challenge; quick start: Notes on GPU image; README.md: notes

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: DeepVariant is released as numbered versions; the README read is for v1.10, with Docker image google/deepvariant:1.10.0. Each release bundles its models inside the Docker image, selected with --model_type: WGS, WES, PACBIO, ONT_R104 or HYBRID_PACBIO_ILLUMINA. Model files for all releases are also kept in a public Google Cloud bucket. Training data change between releases, so a result must name the release version and the model type.

run_guide.summary: Pull the DeepVariant 1.10.0 Docker image, download the small test bundle and call variants in a 10 kb region of chromosome 20.
prerequisites: A Unix-like machine with the AVX instruction set and Docker (the quick start installs docker.io with apt).
No GPU needed; a GPU image exists for the call_variants step.
Network access to Docker Hub and storage.googleapis.com.
Code is BSD-3-Clause; no separate licence for the models is stated.

steps.title: Get the Docker image
steps.shell:
BIN_VERSION="1.10.0"

sudo apt -y update
sudo apt-get -y install docker.io
sudo docker pull google/deepvariant:"${BIN_VERSION}"
steps.explanation: Copied from the quick start. The models are inside the image.

steps.title: Download the test bundle
steps.shell:
INPUT_DIR="${PWD}/quickstart-testdata"
DATA_HTTP_DIR="https://storage.googleapis.com/deepvariant/quickstart-testdata"

mkdir -p ${INPUT_DIR}
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam.bai
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta.fai
steps.explanation: A subset of the quick start's download lines: the BAM, its index, the reference FASTA and its index, which the run step uses. The quick start also downloads truth files for evaluation with hap.py.

steps.title: Call variants
steps.shell:
OUTPUT_DIR="${PWD}/quickstart-output"
mkdir -p "${OUTPUT_DIR}"

sudo docker run \
  -v "${INPUT_DIR}":"/input" \
  -v "${OUTPUT_DIR}":"/output" \
  google/deepvariant:"${BIN_VERSION}" \
  /opt/deepvariant/bin/run_deepvariant \
  --model_type=WGS \
  --vcf_stats_report=true \
  --ref=/input/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta \
  --reads=/input/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam \
  --regions "chr20:10,000,000-10,010,000" \
  --output_vcf=/output/output.vcf.gz \
  --output_gvcf=/output/output.g.vcf.gz \
  --intermediate_results_dir /output/intermediate_results_dir \
  --num_shards=1
steps.explanation: Copied from the quick start. run_deepvariant runs make_examples, call_variants and postprocess_variants in turn.
steps.source_locator: deepvariant-quick-start.md: Run DeepVariant with one command

outputs: In quickstart-output: output.vcf.gz and output.g.vcf.gz with their .tbi indexes, output.visual_report.html, and the intermediate_results_dir directory.

name: ModernGENA
description: BERT-style DNA language model built on the ModernBERT backbone with a 32k BPE vocabulary.

attributes.access: Checkpoints for ModernGENA base and large on Hugging Face (DNA language models collection)

version.note: Family record; sizes are on configurations

profile.summary: ModernGENA is a DNA language model that adapts the ModernBERT encoder to genomic sequences. It reads DNA split into byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokens and was pretrained by masked language modelling on 443 vertebrate genome assemblies. It outputs token embeddings that are fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as sequence classification or per-token regression; the authors present it as an efficient baseline for future DNA model work.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Tokenization, Pretraining corpus; GENA_LM examples README

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ModernGENA is a BERT-style encoder built on ModernBERT. The model card lists RoPE positional embeddings, hybrid local and global attention, pre-norm transformer blocks, GeGLU feed-forward layers and end-to-end unpadding, with FlashAttention for faster inference on compatible hardware. In the published configurations, local attention covers 128 tokens and every third layer uses global attention. Input DNA is tokenised with the 32k BPE vocabulary from GENA-LM over the symbols A, T, G, C and N. Pretraining used masked language modelling on intervals sampled from -16 kbp to +8 kbp around each transcription start site, on both strands, to reduce the weight of simple repeats.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Technical features, Tokenization, Pretraining corpus; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are released on Hugging Face: ModernGENA base (22 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads) and ModernGENA large (28 layers, hidden size 1024, 16 attention heads). Both use the same tokenizer, the same pretraining corpus description and a vocabulary of 32768 tokens. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read base at revision 7036ebb6 and large at revision 01de8202. The paper says the full implementation and configuration are released; the fine-tuning examples the card links to live in the GENA_LM repository.

name: CPA
description: Perturbation-response model the authors benchmarked against (main text paragraph 2); the authors say it was not designed to predict the effects of unseen perturbations (main text paragraphs 16 and 20).

attributes.source_locator: Main text paragraphs 2, 16 and 20; Methods 'Software versions and parameters'

version.note: Family record; the version is on the configuration

profile.summary: CPA (Compositional Perturbation Autoencoder) is a deep generative model that predicts how single cells respond to drugs and genetic perturbations, alone or in combination. It is trained on a perturbation dataset of single-cell expression with perturbation, dose and covariate labels, and predicts expression for unseen combinations of perturbations, doses and cell types, with interpretable perturbation and covariate embeddings.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper Abstract and synopsis; README.md: What is CPA?

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: An encoder network decomposes each cell's expression into additive latent embeddings for its basal state, the observed perturbations and the observed covariates. An adversarial discriminator is trained against the encoder so the basal state carries no perturbation or covariate information, which lets embeddings be recombined at prediction time. Perturbation embeddings are scaled by a neural network of the dose or time. A decoder maps the recombined latent state back to expression.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results and Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: CPA learns from a given single-cell perturbation dataset; the README's preprocessing recipe prepares the user's own dataset for it. The current implementation is the cpa-tools package in theislab/cpa, whose hyperparameter tuner is based on the scvi-tools optimiser; datasets and pre-trained models are in a Google Drive folder linked from the README. The paper's analyses are in a separate reproducibility repository. A result should name the package version or commit, the training dataset and the hyperparameters.
sections.source_locator: README.md; paper Data availability

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Predicting responses to unseen drug and gene combinations and doses, transferring perturbation effects to unseen cell types, estimating dose-response curves, and removing batch effects in latent and expression space.

steps.title: Preprocess your dataset
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import scanpy as sc
# adata: your perturbation AnnData with perturbation and dosage in adata.obs
sc.pp.filter_cells(adata, min_counts=100)
adata.layers['counts'] = adata.X.copy()
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4, exclude_highly_expressed=True)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(adata, n_top_genes=5000, subset=True)
EOF
steps.explanation: The README's preprocessing recipe wrapped in a heredoc by Rewire. It does not load data: add your own line that creates adata, and save the result with adata.write_h5ad.

name: scBERT
description: Single-cell foundation model, published as a pretrained deep language model for cell type annotation (reference 4); not designed for perturbation prediction and used here with a linear decoder (main text paragraph 2).

profile.summary: scBERT is a pretrained deep language model for annotating cell types in single-cell RNA-seq data. It is first pre-trained on large amounts of unlabelled scRNA-seq data to learn gene-gene interactions, then fine-tuned on a labelled reference; the fine-tuned model takes a normalised expression profile and outputs the cell type of each cell, and can flag novel cell types by thresholding prediction confidence.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction, Usage; preprint abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: scBERT follows BERT's pre-train and fine-tune approach with a Performer encoder. Expression values are binned into a small number of tokens (num_tokens, default 7 in the README) and combined with a gene embedding; predict.py uses Gene2vec encoding for genes by default and a sequence of 16906 genes plus one. The default encoder has 6 layers, 10 heads and a 200-dimensional embedding. For annotation a classifier head is trained on top during fine-tuning.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Guidance for hyperparameter selection; predict.py; preprint abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained checkpoint is offered through a Weixin Drive link, with no version label or checksum. Users fine-tune it on their own labelled data, so every annotation result depends on the fine-tuning data. predict.py sets bin_num to 5 by default and builds the model with num_tokens = bin_num + 2 = 7, which matches the README's default num_tokens of 7 (the README calls this the number of bins). A result should name the repository commit, the checkpoint source and the fine-tuning data.

sections.body: Cell type annotation of scRNA-seq data after fine-tuning, including detection of novel cell types; research use only, not for clinical use.

review.method_note: Independent review pass. Both pinned artifacts were re-downloaded and their SHA-256 checked against the source records, the mutable abstract page included, and both matched. A pdftotext -layout run (poppler 26.08.0) on the refetched PDF is byte for byte the contents of the archived gzipped text layer, so the archive is provably derived from the pinned bytes. npm run batch -- check-values reproduced the extractor's figures exactly (64 in_cell, 11 in_row, 6 locator_not_parsed, no wrong_column and no overclaimed_in_row) and wrote the same value-check.tsv. All 81 results were then re-read by review/recheck_tables.py, written for this pass and using neither extract/parse_tables.py nor extract/check_tables.py: it takes each table's column spans from the character offsets of that table's own printed header line, assigns every numeric token on a body line to the column whose header centre is nearest, and matches cells to records through each result's source_locator text rather than its ID, checking printed_value, numeric_value, the printed spread and the system the result's evaluation names. Two negative controls confirmed it fails on a swapped pair of values and on a cell shifted into the neighbouring column. A manual check of 16 cells covered column assignment in all three tables, including Table 2's unlabelled PerturbPFN score line, Table 1's third label and value pair on each of its three rows, and Table 3's middle columns. The printed overall score was re-derived as the equal-weight mean of each row's three normalised columns. The 54 descriptive records were read against Sections 2 to 5, Appendices A to E and Tables 4 to 8 of the pinned PDF.
review.reviewer_note: Claude review agent (independent of the extractor); no human review claimed. Transcription was checked against the pinned source; nothing was reproduced and no value was recomputed.

attributes.training_data: Prior-predictive synthetic episodes only: modular scale-free gene graphs of 40 to 60 genes, synthetic drug families with Hill-type dose-response strengths, and zero-inflated log-normal observations with SERGIO noise; no real perturbation responses are used for training (Section 2.3, Appendix A, Tables 4 and 5).

profile.summary: PerturbPFN predicts how cells respond to chemical perturbations whose targets are unknown. Given observed responses to other perturbations as context, it infers a latent gene graph, sparse intervention targets and intervention strengths, and propagates them through a causal (SCM) decoder to predict expression under a new perturbation. It is trained only on simulated perturbation episodes and has no released code or weights.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv Abstract and Section 2

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PerturbPFN follows the prior-data fitted network (PFN) approach: a transformer is pre-trained on synthetic tasks so that at test time it predicts in context, without gradient updates. Each synthetic episode samples a modular, scale-free gene regulatory network, drug-like perturbations with sparse targets and Hill-type dose-response strengths, and zero-inflated log-normal observations with SERGIO noise. The model infers context interventions and an episode-level graph, predicts the query's targets and strengths with dedicated heads, and generates expression through a modulated SCM decoder in topological order. Training uses multi-task losses on the synthetic graph, target, strength and outcome labels.
sections.source_locator: arXiv Sections 2.3 and 2.4; Fig. 1

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper reports one selected checkpoint, taken at step 3100 of a 3500-step run, with 14.98M parameters, used for all reported results. No code or weights were found: on 2026-11-27 a GitHub repository search for perturbpfn returned a total count of 0 and Hugging Face model searches for perturbpfn and perturb-pfn returned empty lists. The paper's results cannot be reproduced from public artefacts.

profile.summary: AlphaFold-Multimer predicts the structure of a protein complex. It is the multi-chain mode of AlphaFold v2: the input is a FASTA file holding every chain of the complex, alignments are built against several sequence databases, and the system returns coordinates together with per-residue and per-pair confidence estimates, pTM and predicted aligned error. Five trained parameter sets are shipped, and by default each is run with five random seeds, giving 25 predictions that are ranked. It is the same code base as single chain AlphaFold, selected with one flag, and the developers call the multimer implementation a work in progress that is less stable than the monomer system.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Model parameters and Running AlphaFold-Multimer; config.py: MODEL_PRESETS

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The pipeline has two halves. First a data pipeline searches genetic databases to build alignments and find templates: BFD, MGnify, PDB70, the PDB in mmCIF format, UniRef30, UniRef90, and for the multimer mode also PDB seqres and UniProt. Then the neural network predicts the structure, and the multimer models carry heads for a distogram, masked MSA, experimentally resolved atoms, predicted aligned error and predicted lDDT. The current weights come from the v2.3.0 update: the same architecture and training method as the AlphaFold-Multimer paper, fine tuned on PDB structures up to 2021-09-30 instead of 2018-04-30, with the training crop raised from 384 to 640 residues, the number of chains used at training raised from 8 to 20, and the maximum number of alignment sequences raised from 1,152 to 2,048 for three of the five models. The self-distillation set was also rebuilt from clustered MGnify with a looser cluster filter.
sections.source_locator: README: Genetic databases; technical note: whole document; config.py: heads

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The default multimer preset names five models, model_1_multimer_v3 through model_5_multimer_v3, and the parameter file for them is alphafold_params_2022-12-06.tar. Two older generations remain usable but deprecated: the v2.2.0 weights from alphafold_params_2022-03-02.tar, selected by changing _v3 to _v2 in the multimer presets, and the v2.1.0 weights from alphafold_params_2022-01-19.tar, selected by removing _v3. The code applies version-specific differences to the configuration, mostly for numerical stability. Reproducibility also depends on the database snapshot: the README warns that PDB seqres and the PDB mmCIF files must be from exactly the same date or template search for multimers can fail, and prediction uses a max_template_date cutoff given on the command line. A result should therefore name the parameter tar, the model preset, the number of seeds per model and the template date.
sections.source_locator: config.py: MODEL_PRESETS and the version difference comment; README: Model parameters, Using deprecated model weights, Updating existing installation and Running AlphaFold-Multimer

sections.title: When to prefer it
sections.body: The developers give a rule. The v2.3.0 multimer models are expected to be preferred whenever the stoichiometry of the complex is known, including for structures known to be monomeric. Where the stoichiometry is unknown, for instance in genome-scale prediction, single chain AlphaFold is likely to be more accurate on average, unless the chain runs to several thousand residues. For very large or difficult targets they suggest raising the number of seeds per model to 20, which is not the default because of the cost.

profile.summary: IntelliFold predicts the all-atom structure of a biomolecular complex from its sequences, in the manner of AlphaFold 3. The current release, IntelliFold-2, takes an AlphaFold 3 style JSON input listing the chains and ligands, runs a Pairformer trunk and a diffusion sampler, and writes predicted coordinates with confidence scores. The developers report it on FoldBench against AlphaFold 3, Boltz, Chai-1 and Protenix, with the gains concentrated in antibody-antigen interfaces and protein-ligand co-folding. Code and weights are Apache-2.0 and the weights are hosted on Hugging Face; a hosted server runs a further variant that is not released.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Inference and License; release note: Introduction and Benchmark Performance

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: IntelliFold follows the AlphaFold 3 design: a Pairformer trunk over token representations feeding a diffusion module that generates all-atom coordinates. The release note describes what changed in version 2. The latent representations inside the Pairformer blocks were widened, which the authors say both raises capacity and improves hardware utilisation. The atom attention mechanism was reformulated for consistency between training and inference, and atom-level tokenisation is applied stochastically. The diffusion sampler was fine tuned with Proximal Policy Optimization, treating the sampler as a stochastic policy, which the authors say reduces unstable or low-quality trajectories. Training used a focal-loss style reweighting that puts more gradient on hard examples, and the Protein Data Bank was reprocessed with an updated pipeline alongside a larger self-distillation dataset. The release note calls PPO-enhanced sampling and the difficulty-aware loss exclusive to IntelliFold-2-Pro, the server-only variant, so the released IntelliFold-2 and IntelliFold-2-Flash weights do not include them. At inference an optional steering mode adds, at every denoising step, the gradient of a set of differentiable physical potentials covering bond lengths and angles, clashes, chirality, planarity, van der Waals overlap, covalent connections and symmetric chain repulsion.
sections.source_locator: release note: Key Technical Changes; README: Inference, steering paragraph; release note: model variants list

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three variants of version 2 exist, and only two are released. IntelliFold-2-Flash has 12 standard Pairformer blocks and is offered for academic use and fine tuning; IntelliFold-2 has 48 widened Pairformer blocks with latent space scaling and is the most accurate released model; IntelliFold-2-Pro adds PPO-enhanced sampling and difficulty-aware loss and runs only on the developers' server. The Hugging Face repository holds intellifold_v0.1.0.pt from the first release, intellifold_v2.pt, intellifold_v2_flash.pt, and the JAX conversion intellifold_v2.bin.zst with intellifold_v2_fourier.npz, at the revision read here. Since June 2026 the repository runs version 2 on the AlphaFold 3 JAX engine, vendored at version 3.0.3, and the JAX weights were converted from the PyTorch checkpoint with convert_ifv2_to_jax.py. A result should name the variant, the weight file, the engine and whether steering was on, because steering changes the sampler.

profile.summary: OpenFold3 is an open reproduction of AlphaFold 3 by the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University and the OpenFold consortium. It predicts the structure of a biomolecular complex from its sequences, covering standard and non-canonical protein, RNA and DNA chains together with small molecules, and it writes coordinates in mmCIF with per-sample confidence files. Unlike most reproductions it also ships the training code and the training datasets, including a 13 million sequence distillation set, so the model can be retrained from scratch. The published versions are research previews: the model is called OpenFold3-preview and the developers say the final model is still in development.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Features, Datasets and Upcoming; technical report: Introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model follows the AlphaFold 3 design and input features, which the developers set out to reproduce bitwise. Alignments are built either from the ColabFold server or with JackHMMER and hhblits following the AlphaFold 3 protocol, and templates can be supplied for protein monomers. Training follows the AlphaFold 3 supplementary information. For OpenFold3-preview2 that meant 155,000 steps in total, split into 131,500 steps of initial training, 8,000 steps of fine-tuning stage 1 and 15,500 steps of fine-tuning stage 2, on 256 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Unlike AlphaFold 3 the team skipped the third fine-tuning stage and trained the PAE confidence head from the start. Inference can use kernel acceleration through cuEquivariance and DeepSpeed4Science, spread one job across several GPUs, and run in a low memory mode.
sections.source_locator: README: header, Features; technical report: Model Updates, Training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three parameter sets are documented, each tied to a range of software releases. The current default is openbind-2025-06-30-174k, file of3-ob-2025-06-30-174k.pt, at 174,000 training steps, trained with what the README calls the forthcoming OpenFold3 architecture and a June 2025 training cutoff. The two earlier sets are marked deprecated: openfold3-p2-155k, file of3-p2-155k.pt, at 155,000 steps, and openfold3-p1, file of3_ft3_v1.pt, at 78,000 steps. Older parameters need an older release, for example pip install openfold3 < 0.5 for the preview2 weights, and setup_openfold must be rerun after changing version. A result must therefore name both the parameter set and the package version. The repository cites itself as version 0.4.2 with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19001000, and the packaging file carries a fallback version of 0.5.1.

name: Borzoi
description: Model trained to predict RNA-seq coverage from DNA sequence.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Borzoi is a neural network that predicts RNA-seq coverage, the read depth along genes in different cell types and tissues, directly from DNA sequence. It takes a 524 kb stretch of human or mouse genome and outputs predicted coverage for thousands of experiments in 32 bp bins. Comparing predictions for the reference and the variant sequence gives scores for a variant's effect on gene expression, splicing and polyadenylation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README.md: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Borzoi is a supervised model, not a language model: it is trained to reproduce measured coverage tracks. It uses the core Enformer architecture, a tower of convolution and pooling blocks followed by self-attention blocks at 128 bp resolution, then a U-net that upsamples back to 32 bp resolution. The training targets are RNA-seq coverage from ENCODE and GTEx plus the Enformer training data (CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq). Variant effects are computed from the difference between predicted coverage for the reference and the alternate sequence, summarised by statistics such as logSED for gene expression, COVR for polyadenylation and nDi for splicing.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Main, model description; README.md: introduction; legacy score_variants tutorial

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published model is four replicates trained with identical data splits, each distributed as a human and a mouse .h5 weight file. The authors report that an ensemble of the four replicates generally performed better than any single replicate. A separate collection of smaller Mini Borzoi models, trained on subsets of data types or with architecture changes, is also published. The repository has legacy and latest data transforms; the README says the legacy transforms are similar to those used in the manuscript. A result should say which replicates were used, whether they were averaged, and which transform was applied.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model Availability, Mini Borzoi Models, Tutorials; paper: Methods; legacy tutorial notes

name: Caduceus
description: Self-supervised DNA language model pretrained on human genomic sequence.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Caduceus is a family of DNA language models for long human genomic sequences. It reads DNA one base at a time, looking both upstream and downstream, and is built so that a sequence and its reverse complement are treated consistently. The pretrained models output masked-base predictions and per-base embeddings that can be fine-tuned or used as features, for example for variant effect prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Details; README: eQTL SNP Variant Effect Prediction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Caduceus builds on the long-range Mamba block. The authors extend it to a BiMamba component that reads a sequence in both directions, and to a MambaDNA block that is also reverse-complement (RC) equivariant. The published checkpoints have hidden dimension 256 and 16 MambaDNA layers and were pretrained as masked language models on the human reference genome. In the RC-equivariant Caduceus-PS model the hidden state is twice the width of a non-equivariant model, and the card says to run a downstream model on the hidden state and its reverse complement, or average them, to get RC-invariant outputs.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Details; README: Using Caduceus with Hugging Face

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists two pretrained checkpoints on Hugging Face. Caduceus-Ph was trained with reverse-complement data augmentation. Caduceus-PS is RC equivariant by design and needs no augmentation. Both were trained on sequences of length 131k with model size 256 and 16 layers, for 50k steps at batch size 8. A result should name the checkpoint (Ph or PS) and its Hugging Face revision; this page read PS at revision d89eeb85 and Ph at revision b0477522. The repository also holds the training code used to reproduce the paper's pretraining and fine-tuning experiments.

name: Enformer
description: Convolution and Transformer model trained to predict genomic tracks from sequences of up to about 200 kb.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3; Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Enformer is a neural network that predicts gene expression and other genomic signals directly from DNA sequence. It reads about 200 kb of sequence and predicts 5,313 human (or 1,643 mouse) tracks, such as CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq signal, in 128 bp bins across the central 114,688 bp. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate sequences gives variant effect scores, and precomputed scores are published for common 1000 Genomes variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Methods, Model architecture; README.md: Pre-computed variant effect predictions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Enformer is a supervised model trained to reproduce measured genomic tracks. It has three parts: seven convolutional blocks with pooling that reduce 196,608 bp to 1,536 positions of 128 bp each, eleven transformer blocks that let distant positions exchange information, and a cropping layer followed by pointwise convolutions into separate human and mouse output heads. The transformer layers use relative positional basis functions and give a receptive field that reaches elements up to 100 kb away. It was trained jointly on human and mouse data from the Basenji2 dataset, with the input extended to 196,608 bp.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and Training; Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained model is published, at https://tfhub.dev/deepmind/enformer/1, with code to load its weights into the Sonnet Enformer module for fine-tuning. The README's inference example passes 393,216 bp, of which the model uses only the central 196,608 bp. Precomputed SAD and SAR variant scores on hg19 and their top 20 principal components are published for frequent 1000 Genomes variants. The paper also describes fine-tuning the model on human data. A result should state the model URL and version, whether published scores were used, and the genome build.

strengths.text: Long receptive field: the authors report it reaches regulatory elements up to 100 kb away, against 20 kb for the earlier Basenji2 and ExPecto models.
Predicts thousands of cell-type and assay-specific tracks at once, for human and mouse.

The software is pinned to old versions (TensorFlow 2.5.0 in requirements.txt, 2.4.1 in the README text, Python 3.8 in the test instructions), and the usage notebook expects a GPU.

name: GENA-LM
description: Transformer DNA language models in BERT-base, BERT-large and BigBird variants.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: GENA-LM is a family of transformer DNA language models for reading long genomic sequences, up to 36,000 base pairs in its sparse-attention versions. It takes DNA split into variable-length tokens and returns sequence representations that are fine-tuned for tasks such as promoter, splice site, enhancer and chromatin profile prediction. Most models were trained on the human T2T genome, and species-specific and multispecies models also exist.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Materials and methods (Sequence tokenization); README_previous_generation.md: Pre-trained models, Downstream tasks

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENA-LM models are BERT-style transformer encoders trained as masked language models. DNA is first split by a Byte-Pair Encoding tokenizer with a dictionary of 32 000 tokens, so one token covers several bases; the paper reports a median token length of 9 bp. BERT models use pre-layer normalisation. Three models reach 4096 tokens (about 36,000 bp): two use DeepSpeed sparse attention with rotary position embeddings, and bigbird-base-t2t uses the Hugging Face BigBird implementation. The paper also describes fine-tuning with a recurrent memory mechanism to process even longer segments.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sequence tokenization, Abstract; README_previous_generation.md: Pre-trained models

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository table lists eight pretrained checkpoints: five BERT models of 512 tokens (4500 bp) and three BigBird-style models of 4096 tokens (36000 bp). They differ in depth (12 or 24 layers), in the data used for the tokenizer and for training (T2T only, T2T with 1000 Genomes SNPs, or with multispecies data), and in which chromosomes were held out. The paper also names yeast, fly and Arabidopsis models. Fine-tuned checkpoints for promoters and splice sites are kept as branches of the Hugging Face repositories. A result should name the checkpoint, the branch if any, and the Hugging Face revision; this page read gena-lm-bert-base-t2t at revision 4f1352bd. The developers have since released a successor family, modernGENA, in the same repository.

Several training-data choices are released side by side, including human-only, multispecies and taxon-specific models for yeast, Arabidopsis and Drosophila.

name: GPN
description: Masked DNA language model; variant effects scored by single-nucleotide masking.

attributes.source_locator: Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: GPN (Genomic Pretrained Network, also called GPN-SS) is a DNA language model that learns from unaligned genome sequences alone. Given a 512-bp DNA window with some positions masked, it predicts the nucleotide at each masked position. Its main use is to score genetic variants without labels: the score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele. The published model was trained on Arabidopsis thaliana and seven other Brassicales genomes.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/gpn.md introduction; paper Fig. 1 caption; model card title

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN is a convolutional neural network, not a transformer. The masked DNA sequence is one-hot encoded with single nucleotides as tokens, then passed through 25 convolutional blocks. Each block has a dilated convolution and a feed-forward layer, with residual connections and layer normalisation; the embedding dimension stays at 512. Training is masked language modelling: 15% of positions are masked and predicted with a cross-entropy loss. To score a variant, only the variant position is masked, and the score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele. The authors down-weighted repetitive elements in the loss; the card records a repeat weight of 0.1.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Fig. 1 caption; model card: Some hparams

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The songlab-cal/gpn repository now covers four model families: GPN, GPN-MSA, PhyloGPN and GPN-Star. This page is about single-sequence GPN. Its published checkpoint is songlab/gpn-brassicales, which uses a seven-token DNA tokenizer. The same family also has an animal promoter model (songlab/gpn-animal-promoter) and a sorghum gene-expression model fine-tuned from gpn-brassicales. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read gpn-brassicales at revision eb9c35d0. The paper analyses are kept in an archive branch, and the maintained training recipe is in recipes/gpn_training. Note that the existing benchmark source (Tang et al. 2025) did not use gpn-brassicales: it evaluated a custom GPN pre-trained on the human reference genome.

strengths.text: Needs only a reference genome: the authors say the model can be applied to any species with one, without functional genomics data.
Single-nucleotide tokens make variant scoring direct: one position is masked and the two alleles compared.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods; Fig. 1 caption

strengths.text: Maintained package with a command-line tool for variant scoring, logits and embeddings, MIT licensed code and weights.

limitations.text: The published checkpoint is a plant model (Arabidopsis and seven other Brassicales). For other species, a user needs another checkpoint or must train one.
The context window is 512 bp, so it sees only local sequence around a variant.
The variant scorer accepts only biallelic SNVs, and the score is raw and uncalibrated.
The authors trained each model on GPUs (about 4 days on 4 NVIDIA A100 80 GB). The sources give no minimum hardware for inference; inference defaults to FP32 on any device.

run_guide.summary: Install the gpn package with inference extras, load the published GPN checkpoint, and score SNVs from a table against a reference genome.
prerequisites: Python 3.13, which the package supports.
For CUDA, install PyTorch with the official PyTorch installer before or alongside GPN. The sources state no GPU type or memory for inference.
Your own inputs: a variants table (for example variants.parquet) of biallelic SNVs with one-based pos, and the matching reference genome FASTA. The published checkpoint is for Brassicales genomes.
Code and weights are MIT licensed. The weights are not gated.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: pip install "gpn[inference]"
steps.explanation: Installs the gpn package with the file-backed inference commands. The PyPI release is not pinned to the commit read here.

steps.title: Load the published checkpoint
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from gpn import register_auto_classes
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM

register_auto_classes("ss")

model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("songlab/gpn-brassicales")
PY
steps.explanation: The GPN quick-start snippet from the documentation, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the gpn-brassicales weights and loads them as a masked language model.

steps.title: Score variants
steps.shell:
gpn ss vep \
  --input-path variants.parquet \
  --genome-path genome.fa.gz \
  --window-size 512 \
  --model-path songlab/gpn-brassicales \
  --output-path scores.parquet \
  --per-device-eval-batch-size 64
steps.explanation: The documented variant scoring command. variants.parquet and genome.fa.gz are the user's own files; positions are one-based and the reference allele must match the genome.

outputs: scores.parquet, with one row per input variant. Its score column is the raw, uncalibrated alternate-minus-reference log-likelihood ratio averaged over both strands; negative values mean the alternate is less likely.

name: HyenaDNA
description: DNA language model pretrained on the human reference genome with context lengths of 32 kb to 1 Mb.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3; Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: HyenaDNA is a family of DNA language models that read very long stretches of genome one base at a time, up to 1 million bases in the largest model. It was pretrained on the human reference genome by predicting the next base, and it outputs per-base embeddings that can be fine-tuned for tasks such as finding regulatory elements or classifying species.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Intro; model card: Model & Training Overview; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HyenaDNA replaces attention with a stack of Hyena operators, which use input projections, implicit long convolutions and gating and scale sub-quadratically with sequence length. Each layer has a global receptive field. A single-character tokenizer with a vocabulary of the 4 nucleotides plus special tokens keeps single-base resolution. The model is causal: it is pretrained by next-nucleotide prediction on the human reference genome (HG38), and the inference script pads on the left for that reason.

name: Sei
description: Supervised sequence model built from residual dilated convolutions and pretrained on 21,907 chromatin profiling datasets.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3; Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Sei is a deep learning model that reads a 4-kb human DNA sequence and predicts the probability of 21,907 chromatin profiles (transcription factor binding, histone marks and chromatin accessibility) at its centre. Those predictions are then summarised into 40 sequence classes, such as promoter, cell type-specific enhancer or Polycomb-repressed, which give a score for a sequence or for the effect of a variant.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results (model) and Methods; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The Sei model has three parts: a convolutional network with parallel linear and nonlinear paths, residual dilated convolution layers that widen the receptive field without losing resolution, and a B-spline basis layer that reduces 256 spatial bins to 16 before fully connected output layers. It was trained with Selene in PyTorch as a multi-label classifier: for each 4-kb region, the label is whether the centre base overlaps a peak in each of the 21,907 profiles. The authors then predicted 30 million genome positions at a 100-bp step, reduced the predictions with PCA and clustered them with Louvain community detection. The 40 largest clusters are the sequence classes. A sequence's class score is a projection of its chromatin predictions onto each class vector; for variants the score is alt minus ref, with histone predictions adjusted for nucleosome occupancy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and training, Sequence classes; README: Sequence class prediction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one released Sei model, published on Zenodo (record 4906996, dated 2021-06-07) as a 3,281,639,255-byte archive. The repository download script fetches it, with a resources archive holding hg19 and hg38 FASTA files. Whole-genome sequence class annotations for hg38, and for hg19 lifted over from hg38, are in a separate Zenodo record, and the authors recommend these annotations over raw sequence class scores for reference genome sequences. The training configuration is in train/train.yml. A result should name the repository commit and the Zenodo model record; this page read commit 1e16bff9.

strengths.text: Covers a wide set of regulatory signals in one model: 21,907 profiles spanning about 1,000 DNA-binding proteins, 77 histone marks and chromatin accessibility in more than 1,300 cell lines and tissues.

The 40 sequence classes give a compact, interpretable summary of a sequence or variant effect, grouped as promoter, enhancer, CTCF, TF binding, Polycomb, heterochromatin, transcription and low signal.

name: TREDNet
description: Two-phase CNN for enhancer prediction and variant prioritisation, developed by the group of the senior author of the comparison that evaluated it.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: TREDNet predicts whether a 2,000 base pair stretch of human DNA acts as an enhancer, and how much a single-nucleotide variant changes that prediction. It works in two stages: a first convolutional network turns the one-hot encoded sequence into 1,924 predicted epigenomic signals (DNase I hypersensitivity, histone modifications and transcription factor binding), and a second, smaller network turns that vector into an enhancer probability for one tissue or cell line. Released phase two models cover pancreatic islets, HepG2 and K562.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, TREDNet: A DL Model for Enhancer Prediction; README: Phase one, Phase two; Kipoi phase one model.yaml: schema

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Phase one is a multitask convolutional classifier in the style of DeepSEA, Beluga and DanQ. It takes a one-hot encoded 2,000 base window and outputs 1,924 values, one per epigenomic feature. Phase two is a smaller convolutional network trained on enhancer regions, but each region is first passed through phase one and so is represented by the 1,924-value vector rather than by its sequence. Phase two can be a single-output classifier for one tissue or a multitask classifier over several. Chromosomes 8 and 9 were held out of training and used for testing.
sections.source_locator: README: Phase one, Phase two; paper: Results; Kipoi model.yaml files: schema, info

sections.title: Scoring variants and regions
sections.body: The repository's score_variant.py reads a VCF, needs an hg19 FASTA, and writes a tab-separated file. With -score-iep it builds the 2,000 base reference and alternate sequences centred on the SNP, predicts both, and scores the variant as the larger probability times the absolute difference between the two. With -score-delta it takes the 2,000 base window around the variant, substitutes every other base at each position from 990 to 1010, averages the drop from the reference prediction at each position and divides by the median absolute value, writing the resulting list of values. Separately, the paper reports saturated mutagenesis across whole enhancers, which it calls enhancer damage (ED) scores, and defines peaks and dips in them as enhancer damaging regions (EDRs) and enhancer strengthening regions (ESRs). A second module, peak_detection/annotate.py, performs what the README calls PAS/DAS detection from a file of precomputed deltas.
sections.source_locator: README: Run the command, Run PAS/DAS detection; score_variant.py: generate_scores; paper: Figure 1 legend

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Zenodo record 6463875 holds four TREDNet weight files: one phase one model and three phase two models (islets, HepG2, K562). The record also holds six smaller PAS and DAS weight files, annotation and enhancer BED files, and a README. The same weights are registered in the Kipoi database, where each entry pins the weight URL and an MD5 checksum. The Kipoi entries declare python 3.9 with keras 2.8 and tensorflow 2.8, while the repository's requirements.txt pins keras 2.1.2 and tensorflow 1.4.1, so a result should say which route and which versions were used, along with the phase two cell name.

profile.summary: RFD4-Proteina designs proteins and biomolecular complexes, generating sequence and all-atom structure together rather than a backbone to be sequenced later. The design is specified either as an annotated CIF structure or as a short YAML condition spec, which can fix a motif, name hotspots, hold a binding target or a ligand, or constrain features such as burial and hydrogen bonds. One model covers monomers, protein and DNA binders, antibodies and nanobodies, enzyme motif scaffolding and small molecule pockets, and it can also refine an existing design by partial diffusion or search over generation paths scored by structure prediction oracles. It is a flow matching model in the latent space of a frozen autoencoder, so generation always loads two matched checkpoints. Code and weights are BSD 3-Clause, from the Baker Lab and NVIDIA GenAIR.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Try it now and Key features; model card: opening paragraph and At a glance; checkpoints reference: Types of checkpoints

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Two components are always loaded together. The autoencoder is frozen and unified: one encoder and decoder covering proteins, nucleic acids, DNA and modified residues, with 32 latent channels per residue and a residue vocabulary of 147 classes, trained to 400,000 steps. The denoiser is a flow matching latent model that generates in exactly that latent space, which is why the pair cannot be mixed across releases: the developers say mixing a flow model with a different autoencoder produces nonsense rather than an error. The released denoiser is a pretrained base at step 320,000 with a rank-32 LoRA fine-tune merged in, and by default it conditions the decoder on its own sequence readout during inference. Sampling runs 60 steps, with the trunk recycled a varying number of times per step: the three released presets, low, medium and high, come to 120, 180 and 300 trunk passes, medium being the default. Reward-guided search branches and prunes candidates at points in that schedule, scored by a refolding oracle such as OpenFold3.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The current release is the 2026-10-19 pair: rfd4-proteina-flow-release-2026-10-19 as the denoiser and rfd4-proteina-ae-release-2026-10-19 as the autoencoder, published under the stable names flow_checkpoints/rfd4_proteina_flow-ema.ckpt and ae_checkpoints/rfd4_proteina_ae-ema.ckpt, with SHA-256 sidecars and a release manifest. It supersedes the 2026-10-15 pair, which shared the architecture, and an earlier pair with a 16-dimensional latent and a 33-class vocabulary which is incompatible. The pretrained base and the LoRA adapter are published separately under base/ and adapter/, and the root bundle is exactly the two merged. The published checkpoints carry EMA weights and hyperparameters only, which is enough for inference or fine-tuning but not to resume a training run. Per release-checkpoints.json the released flow checkpoint is 1,751,488,703 bytes against 3,511,389,403 for its full training checkpoint, and the autoencoder 1,029,340,246 against 3,095,456,721. The model card states 1.74 GB and 4.21 GB for the flow pair, which does not match its own manifest: 4,211,265,195 bytes is the full size of a different file, flow_checkpoints/rfd4_proteina_flow_pretrain-ema.ckpt, and 1,742,660,596 is the size of model.safetensors. Reproducibility comes from pinning: configs/inference.yaml names the Hub repository and the revision, from_pretrained takes a revision argument, and the documentation tells users not to hard-code filenames anywhere else.

sections.title: What the developers claim, and how they qualify it
sections.body: The model card reports design efficiency as structurally distinct computational passers per GPU-hour, including generation and evaluation, on four internal benchmarks: 71.60 on 24 protein binder targets against 13.24 for the best comparator, 112.25 on 77 small-molecule binder targets against 15.48, 91.18 on 37 atomic motif enzyme targets against 26.02, and 41.97 on three DNA binder targets against 9.46. The developers attach three qualifications themselves. The numbers were measured on the previous release pair in a frozen benchmark of 9 October 2026 and have not been re-measured on the current checkpoints. The conditioning differs between methods in some comparisons, and only three DNA targets are included. And computational passers do not establish experimental activity.

strengths.text: One model and one input format cover many design tasks: monomers, protein and DNA binders, antibodies and nanobodies, enzyme motif scaffolding and small molecule pockets.
Sequence and all-atom structure are generated together, so a design does not need a separate inverse folding step to get a sequence.

strengths.text: The release is unusually well pinned: a manifest with source filenames, sizes and SHA-256 checksums, stable aliases, a revision to pass to from_pretrained, and a single configuration file named as the runtime source of truth.

run_guide.summary: Install from PyPI with uv, describe a PD-L1 binder in a short YAML spec, and generate with the released weights from the Hugging Face Hub.
prerequisites: Linux x86_64, Python 3.12, an NVIDIA GPU from the tested list and a CUDA 13-compatible driver. macOS and Windows are not supported.
About 7 GB for the environment and about 1.7 GB for the weights bundle, cached under HF_HOME.
Network access to the Hugging Face Hub. The repositories are public, so no token is needed; a restricted repository needs HF_TOKEN or hf auth login.
Nothing extra for generation. Refolding metrics and reward-guided search need an AlphaFold 2 or OpenFold3 environment, installed separately.
BSD 3-Clause terms for the model, the weights and the code; the optional refolding images have their own terms.

steps.title: Install pip, uv and the package
steps.shell:
pip install "pip @ https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/3f/06/3e4420302363fbb71be3c7f35ce042f54bfca330e3e66b3a2e3c4cca579f/pip-26.2.2-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=fd7f4dfa8190e014013b9f08f3e973f4e4c26ffd179a204895533a7254813a70"
pip install "uv>=0.13.4"
uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install "rfd4-proteina[all-cuda13]"
steps.explanation: The README's pip quick start, in its order. The first line pins pip 26.2.2 from a hash-pinned URL because older pip releases still trust a compromised certificate authority; the CUDA extra also brings the fused cuEquivariance kernels the model loads.

steps.title: Describe the design
steps.shell:
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RosettaCommons/RFD4-Proteina/main/docs/examples/inputs/5o45_cropped.cif.zst
cat > binder.yaml <<'EOF'
binder:
  input: 5o45_cropped.cif.zst
  contig: "50-120, /0, A17-131"
  conditions: {C_CRDGRP: {1: [{select: "sel('A/*/*/[N,CA,C,O]')"}]},
               C_SEQ: {true: [{select: "sel('A')"}]}}
EOF
steps.explanation: The README's example: download the PD-L1 target structure and write the condition spec that asks for a 50 to 120 residue binder to it. JSON with the same keys also works.
steps.source_locator: README: Quick start with pip and Run the model

steps.title: Generate
steps.shell: rfd4-generate inference_experiment=quickstart inputs=binder.yaml out_dir=./runs/first
steps.explanation: The README's generation command. The quickstart preset skips scoring and the torch.compile warm-up so a first run finishes quickly, and should be dropped for larger runs.

steps.title: Optional: pin the weights explicitly
steps.shell:
rfd4-generate hf_ckpt_path=nvidia/RFD4-Proteina \
    inference_experiment=quickstart inputs=binder.yaml out_dir=./runs/hf
steps.explanation: The README's Hub route, which loads the released pair from the Hub with no local checkpoints and no DATA_PATH. The README writes inputs=design.yaml; the name is changed here to the binder.yaml written in the earlier step. Add hf_ckpt_revision to pin an exact commit for reproducibility.
steps.source_locator: README: Hugging Face and Python; checkpoints reference: Downloading

steps.title: Optional: the same from Python
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import rfd4_proteina as rfd4

model = rfd4.Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina")
rfd4.generate(model, overrides=["inference_experiment=quickstart", "inputs=binder.yaml", "out_dir=runs/hf"])
PY
steps.explanation: The README's Python API example, wrapped here in a shell heredoc and pointed at the YAML file written above. from_pretrained also takes a revision argument.

The weights bundle cached in the Hugging Face cache, about 1.7 GB.

The quickstart preset omits scoring, so the designs come out unscored; rfd4-evaluate and a refolding environment are a separate step.
The repository clone route with make setup is the developers' recommended path and also offers the AlphaFold environments; the pip route above is the shortest one and leaves those out.

name: CI-SpliceAI
description: SpliceAI reimplementation retrained on a collapsed isoform set of manually curated GENCODE HAVANA splice sites from all chromosomes.

version.note: Release or checkpoint not printed

profile.summary: CI-SpliceAI predicts whether a DNA variant disrupts RNA splicing. It keeps the SpliceAI deep convolutional network design but retrains it on manually curated GENCODE splice sites, with all isoforms of a gene collapsed into one, and on all chromosomes. Given a VCF file and a human reference genome, it reports for each variant the predicted gain or loss of acceptor and donor sites and where they occur.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction; README: Differences to SpliceAI, Output

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CI-SpliceAI uses the SpliceAI design: five deep convolutional neural networks that label every nucleotide as acceptor, donor or neither, using 10,000 nucleotides of flanking context. For training, GENCODE v37 (GRCh38) transcripts with automated (level 3) annotation were removed, and all remaining splice sites of a gene were merged into one collapsed isoform. Sequences were cut into 15,000-base windows, each predicting 5,000 central nucleotides. The training procedure was reimplemented from SpliceAI, with categorical cross-entropy and the Adam optimiser. The five trained networks are packed into one frozen graph. To score a variant, the tool predicts on the reference and the variant sequence and reports the change (delta score) for acceptor and donor gain and loss.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Methods, Splice site recognition; Algorithmic comparison on variant data; Train README: aggregate.py

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper trained the model twice: on SpliceAI's 19 training chromosomes, for a fair comparison, and on all chromosomes, which is the final model shipped in the annotation package as the frozen file CI-SpliceAI.pb. At the commit read, setup.cfg gives package version 1.2.1, while PyPI serves 1.2.2 as the latest release. A result should name the cispliceai package version and the annotation table used (grch38 by default, or grch37).

strengths.text: Runs on CPU with a plain pip install; the README says GPU setup is only worth it for more than about 50 variants.
The annotation tool scores all variants, including multi-nucleotide variants, and analyses all overlapping genes.

Training data, training code, the comparison code and the curated variant set are released. On the authors' set of 1,316 functionally tested variants, they report about 92% accuracy for CI-SpliceAI against about 91% for SpliceAI.

steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from cispliceai.model import CISpliceAI
from cispliceai.data import DNAPreprocessor

model = CISpliceAI()

# you can run multiple sequences in a batch
# you can input sequences of varying length, but it's your responsibility to ensure that the batch fits on memory!
# The sequences here are only an example, you should upload much longer slices to get sensible results
predictions = model.predict([
  DNAPreprocessor.onehot_and_pad('CTTCCTCTCCTCCTGCCCCACCTTCCTCTCCTCCTGCCCCACCAGAACCGGGGGCGGCTGGCAGACAAGAGGACAGTCGCCCTGCCTGCC'),
  DNAPreprocessor.onehot_and_pad('CTCCTCCTGCCCCACCAGAACCGGGGGCGGCTG'),
])

# Get acceptor and donor scores for the two sequences
acceptor_prob_1 = predictions[0][:, 1]
donor_prob_1 = predictions[0][:, 2]

acceptor_prob_2 = predictions[1][:, 1]
donor_prob_2 = predictions[1][:, 2]
PY

profile.summary: OpenSpliceAI predicts splice sites from DNA sequence. It is a PyTorch reimplementation of SpliceAI that scores every position as a donor site, an acceptor site or neither, and can also score how genetic variants change splicing. It ships a human model retrained on GRCh38 with MANE annotations, models for four other species, and tools to train new models.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction, Key Features; paper: Results

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OpenSpliceAI keeps the SpliceAI design: a deep residual convolutional neural network that reads one-hot encoded DNA. In the 10,000 nt model the input passes through an initial Conv1D layer and 16 residual units with skip connections, then a softmax gives, for each position, the probability of donor, acceptor or neither. Smaller variants use fewer residual units (12 for 2000 nt, 8 for 400 nt). The input is padded with 5000 Ns on each side. For each flanking length five models were trained with different random seeds, and their outputs are averaged as an ensemble. The variant subcommand computes delta scores that measure how a variant changes splice site strength.
sections.source_locator: paper: Figure 1, figure supplement 1; Figure 2; Methods; README.md: What OpenSpliceAI Does

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The human model, OSAI-MANE, was released at four flanking lengths (80, 400, 2000 and 10000 nt), each as five checkpoint files (Model 1 to 5). The authors strongly recommend the 10000 nt model; the others are for experimental and research use. Species models exist for mouse, zebrafish, honey bee and thale cress. The README at the commit read shows version v.0.0.7. A result should name the species model, the flanking length, whether the five-model ensemble or a single seed was used, and the package version.

profile.summary: SpliceAI2 is a deep learning model from Illumina that predicts RNA splicing from genomic sequence. It reads about 200 kb of DNA around a gene and predicts how much each position is used as a splice donor or acceptor, how much each splice junction is used, and the most likely complete transcripts. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate alleles gives a score for how strongly a variant changes splicing.
profile.summary_source_locator: Manuscript: Main 'Hierarchical model of RNA splicing'; Methods 'Variant effect prediction'; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input is 196,608 bp of genomic sequence on the gene's sense strand, one-hot encoded, plus a one-hot code for the species (ten channels). A dense layer projects it to 256 channels, and 20 MetaFormer blocks follow, each with a depth-wise dilated convolution and a feed-forward network, at progressively coarser pooling. Each block's output feeds a splice site head over the central 65,536 positions. The 1,024 positions with the highest splice site usage are then paired by a query-key product to give a 1,024 by 1,024 matrix of splice junction usage. Sites and junctions form a splice graph, and Viterbi decoding finds the highest scoring paths, which are the predicted transcripts. The model was trained end-to-end on splice site, junction and transcript usage, with the three losses summed.
sections.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'SpliceAI2 model' (Inputs, Architecture, Outputs, Training); 'Transcript prediction'

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code is package version 2.0 (this page read commit 1dcd2a18 on main). The released model is an ensemble of two checkpoints trained with identical settings, held on Hugging Face as spliceai2_multispecies_13M_01 and spliceai2_multispecies_13M_02, each with a model.ckpt; the README's commands pass both folders. Illumina also publishes precomputed scores for all possible single nucleotide variants and observed indels in protein-coding genes (GENCODE v48, GRCh38). The manuscript also describes a tissue-specific model conditioned on RBP expression; the files read do not show it as released. A result should name the package version, both checkpoint folders and the Hugging Face revision (55948bae read here).

strengths.text: It predicts splice junctions and whole transcripts as well as splice sites, so a variant's effect can be read as a change in transcript structure, not only a site score.
Long context: each prediction sees 196,608 bp of sequence.
Precomputed scores cover all possible single nucleotide variants and observed indels in human protein-coding genes, and the output keeps SpliceAI-compatible columns and threshold equivalents.
The authors report improved detection of splice-altering variants and better quantification of their effects across cryptic splicing, sQTL and MPRA benchmarks; this is their claim.

limitations.text: Restrictive licence: non-commercial organisations only, no redistribution, no use to train other models, research use only and not for diagnostic procedures. This applies to the code as well as the weights.
A CUDA-capable GPU is required.
Weights are gated on Hugging Face and need a manual access request with academic details.
The user must supply the gene strand for each variant; if it is unknown, both strands have to be scored and combined.

profile.summary: AbMPNN designs antibody sequences for a given antibody structure. It is ProteinMPNN, an inverse folding model that proposes an amino acid sequence for a supplied backbone, fine-tuned by its authors on antibody data so that it does better on antibodies, in particular on the hypervariable CDR-H3 loop. The input is a backbone structure, optionally the antibody in complex with its antigen, and the output is one or more sequences for the positions being designed. The authors published the fine-tuned weights as a Zenodo deposit; there is no separate AbMPNN codebase, since the weights load into the ProteinMPNN code.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and section 1; arXiv abstract page; Zenodo record description

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Inverse folding asks, given a backbone structure, which sequences would fold into that shape. ProteinMPNN factorises the sequence probability autoregressively: at each step it predicts one residue given the structure and the residues already decoded, with the order chosen at random rather than left to right, so context on both sides is available. The encoder takes distances between the N, CA, C, O and virtual CB atoms of the 48 nearest residues in space, decomposed into Gaussian radial basis functions, plus a relative positional encoding of the separation in the sequence and a token marking whether two residues are in different chains; node features start as a zero vector and are updated by a three-layer message passing network, with the edge features also updated. AbMPNN keeps this architecture and changes only the weights, by fine-tuning on antibody data.
sections.source_locator: Paper: section 2, Inverse folding with ProteinMPNN

sections.title: How it was fine-tuned
sections.body: Training starts from the published ProteinMPNN weights and proceeds in two stages: first on antibody structures predicted by ABodyBuilder2 from paired sequences in the Observed Antibody Space, then on antigen-binding fragments in complex from the Structural Antibody Database. Both stages use Adam, starting at a learning rate of 5 times 10 to the minus 4 for the OAS stage and 10 to the minus 4 for the SAbDab stage, with the rate cut tenfold when the validation loss has not improved for 10 epochs, or 5 epochs in the OAS stage. Each epoch consists of 1000 randomly selected antigen binding fragments. Clustering gives 107961 clusters for OAS and 1701 for the SAbDab complexes, and the authors place any SAbDab sequence that would have clustered with an OAS training or validation cluster into the SAbDab training set to avoid leakage. The OAS structures are modelled and hold no antigen, so epitope context is present only in the SAbDab stage.
sections.source_locator: Paper: section 3, data and training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One set of weights is published: the Zenodo deposit 10.5281/zenodo.8164693, dated 19 July 2023, holding abmpnn.pt together with oas_splits.csv and sabdab_splits.csv, under CC BY 4.0. The deposit is a dataset record with no version string, and its description says the model is based on ProteinMPNN and can be run with that code. There is no AbMPNN repository, so a result should name the Zenodo DOI for the weights and the ProteinMPNN commit used to run them; this page read ProteinMPNN at commit 8907e6671bfbfc92303b5f79c4b5e6ce47cdef57. Sampling is stochastic, so the sampling temperature and seed also belong in any report; the paper used a sampling temperature of 0.2 for its SAbDab test set.

strengths.text: The weights are published openly under CC BY 4.0, and they drop into the existing ProteinMPNN code, so no new software is needed.
strengths.source_locator: Zenodo record metadata and description; ProteinMPNN README.md

strengths.text: The authors report the largest gains on CDR-H3, the loop they describe as the most diverse and usually the most important for antigen recognition; that is their claim about their own model.
The dataset splits used for fine-tuning are published with the weights, so a comparison can respect the same train, validation and test division.
strengths.source_locator: Zenodo record metadata: files and description

strengths.text: Order-agnostic decoding suits antibodies: the framework regions can be held fixed while the CDR loops are designed with context on both sides.

limitations.text: It designs sequences for a structure you already have: a backbone must be supplied, from experiment or from a structure predictor, so the quality of that model limits the design.

Most of the fine-tuning data is predicted, not experimental: the OAS stage uses ABodyBuilder2 models that contain no antigen, so antigen context enters only in the smaller SAbDab stage of 1701 clusters.
There is no AbMPNN software release and no model card: the deposit is a dataset record with a weights file, so loading it means matching the ProteinMPNN code version yourself.

The paper is a workshop paper (ICML 2023 Workshop on Computational Biology), and its evaluation is computational: sequence recovery, self-consistency RMSD from a structure predictor and physics-based scoring, with no experimental validation reported.

run_guide.summary: Download the AbMPNN weights from Zenodo, get the ProteinMPNN code, and design sequences for the chosen chains of a PDB file with those weights.
prerequisites: Python 3 or newer, PyTorch and NumPy, which is what the ProteinMPNN README asks for.
A GPU is used by the example script, which requests one in its scheduler header; the README gives no CPU-only statement.
A backbone structure file for the antibody, and the AbMPNN weights file abmpnn.pt from Zenodo.
Attribution under CC BY 4.0 for the weights, and the MIT terms of ProteinMPNN for the code.

steps.title: Download the weights
steps.shell:
mkdir -p abmpnn_weights
curl -L -o abmpnn_weights/abmpnn.pt https://zenodo.org/records/8164693/files/abmpnn.pt
steps.explanation: The Zenodo record holds abmpnn.pt alongside the dataset split files. The download command is composed here from the record's file name and the Zenodo file address pattern; check the record page if the address changes.

steps.title: Get the ProteinMPNN code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/dauparas/ProteinMPNN.git
cd ProteinMPNN
git checkout --detach 8907e6671bfbfc92303b5f79c4b5e6ce47cdef57
steps.explanation: The weights are run with the ProteinMPNN code, as the Zenodo description states. The checkout of the commit this page read was added here.
steps.source_locator: ProteinMPNN README.md: opening lines; Zenodo record description

steps.title: Create the environment
steps.shell:
conda create --name mlfold
source activate mlfold
conda install pytorch torchvision torchaudio cudatoolkit=11.3 -c pytorch
steps.explanation: The three commands the ProteinMPNN README gives as its example conda environment.

steps.title: Design sequences with the AbMPNN weights
steps.shell:
python protein_mpnn_run.py \
        --path_to_model_weights ../abmpnn_weights \
        --model_name abmpnn \
        --pdb_path ./inputs/PDB_complexes/pdbs/3HTN.pdb \
        --pdb_path_chains "A B" \
        --out_folder ./outputs/abmpnn_example \
        --num_seq_per_target 2 \
        --sampling_temp "0.2" \
        --seed 37 \
        --batch_size 1
steps.explanation: This is the repository's example 3 command with two flags added from the README's flag list so that the AbMPNN file is loaded instead of a bundled ProteinMPNN checkpoint: --path_to_model_weights selects a weights folder and --model_name a model name. The README documents --model_name only with the bundled ProteinMPNN names such as v_48_020, so a human must check how the loader resolves abmpnn.pt before relying on the command. Replace the PDB path and chains with your antibody structure. The sampling temperature 0.2 is the value the paper used for its SAbDab test set; example 3 itself uses 0.1.
steps.source_locator: examples/submit_example_3.sh; ProteinMPNN README.md: input flags; Paper: section 4

outputs: FASTA output in the out_folder with the designed sequences, each carrying a score, a global score, the designed and fixed chains, the model name, the code git hash, the seed, the sampling temperature and a sequence recovery figure.
limitations: These commands were read from the sources and have not been executed by Rewire.

The final command is a composition: the example script it is based on does not select external weights, and the two weight flags come from the README's flag list, so the exact file naming the loader expects was not verified.
No AbMPNN-specific instructions, model card or compatible code version are published, so the weights may need a ProteinMPNN version close to the 2023 release.
Design is stochastic: the number of sequences, the sampling temperature and the seed all change the output.
