profile.summary: FlowPacker predicts the side-chain conformations of a protein when the sequence and the backbone coordinates are already known, a task called side-chain packing. It treats the four chi torsion angles of each residue as the only degrees of freedom and generates them with torsional flow matching over an equivariant graph attention network, then writes out the all-atom structure. Two trained checkpoints are published with the code, along with a confidence model that scores several samples so the best can be chosen. It can also fill in only part of a structure, which the authors call inpainting, and works on multi-chain complexes although it was trained on single chains.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Introduction; README.md: Inference

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is built on the Equiformerv2 architecture with maximum degree 3, channel dimension 256 and 4 blocks, giving 18.0M trainable parameters. Node features are the amino acid identity, the backbone torsion angles and a timestep embedding; the chi angles are produced by flow matching on the torus rather than in Cartesian space, which keeps the side-chain geometry valid by construction. The authors report no gain from raising the maximum degree to 6, and no gain from higher-order solvers such as Heun or RK45 over the plain solver, which cost more runtime. A separate confidence model of 2.2M parameters, trained to regress residue-level side-chain RMSD, is used to pick the best of several samples: unless stated otherwise the authors generate four samples per test case and keep the one with the lowest predicted RMSD.
sections.source_locator: Paper: sections 2.3.2, 2.3.6 and 2.3.7, and Figure 2 caption

sections.title: What it was trained on
sections.body: Two training sets were used, each giving one published checkpoint. BC40 is a set of representative PDB structures clustered at 40 per cent sequence identity, released on 28 July 2020 and used by earlier work; after filtering it gives 36 451 training examples. PDB-S40 is a PDB snapshot clustered the same way, giving 23 191 clusters containing 309 467 structures. Filtering removes structures with more than a quarter of residues unknown, residues with missing backbone coordinates or overlapping alpha carbons, and proteins shorter than 40 residues. The test set is 99 structures: 20 from CASP13, 34 from CASP14 and 45 from CASP15. The authors report that the larger PDB-S40 data improves most metrics over BC40, and the README recommends the cluster.pth checkpoint for most cases.
sections.source_locator: Paper: section 2.3.1 and Results; README.md: checkpoints paragraph

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds three checkpoints: bc40.pth, cluster.pth and a confidence model checkpoint, which is switched on or off by setting its path in the config file. The README says checkpoints with other ablations can be provided on request, so only these are public. A result should name the checkpoint, whether confidence sampling was on, how many samples were drawn, and the commit; this page read commit 03421c7fdda73862994aa54fb3077f3f6561408c. Two run options change the output: by default the model masks according to coordinates missing from the input PDB, which suits benchmarking, while the use_gt_masks flag generates all chi angles regardless. The README also warns that its preprocessing may cause minor differences from the input structure.

strengths.text: The model is small, 18.0M parameters, and the authors report better runtime than the baselines they compared against, which is their own claim.
Part of a structure can be packed and the rest left alone: the inpaint flag takes residue ranges per chain, which the authors say is not readily available in other packing methods.
Both the code and the two trained checkpoints are in the repository under MIT, with no gate or request step.
The authors report that it transfers to antibody-antigen complexes, with improvements on CDR-H3 and the full variable domain, despite being trained on single chains.

limitations.text: It needs a backbone: the model predicts side chains for a supplied sequence and backbone, so it cannot produce a structure on its own.

Inputs must be cleaned first. The README says unknown or nonstandard amino acids are ignored, overlapping alpha carbons are dropped, and its own preprocessing can introduce minor differences from the input structure.

Long chains run out of GPU memory: the README's tested limit is about 1000 residues on a 12 GB card, and inference is batch-only over a folder, with single-file runs done by putting one PDB in a folder alone.
The model was trained on single-chain proteins, so multimeric and antibody-antigen use is transfer beyond the training distribution, as the authors state themselves.

profile.summary: IgLM is a generative language model for antibody sequences. Given an antibody heavy or light chain variable sequence with one span replaced by a mask, together with tags for the chain type and the species of origin, it generates replacement spans of variable length using the sequence on both sides of the mask, and it can also generate a whole chain from a short prompt or score an existing sequence. Its purpose is to build synthetic antibody libraries, for example diverse CDR loop libraries, from sequences that look like natural antibodies.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Methods: Infilling formulation; README: Command line usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: IgLM is a transformer decoder based on a modified GPT-2. A span of the antibody sequence is replaced by a single mask token, the remaining sequence is concatenated with a separator and then the span itself, and two conditioning tags for chain type and species are prepended, so an ordinary left-to-right language model learns to produce the missing span with the sequence on both sides available as context. In training the masked spans were ten to twenty residues long, chosen at random, so that spans of any position and length can be re-designed at inference. The released configuration is a 4-layer model with embedding size 512, 8 attention heads and a vocabulary of 33 tokens.
sections.source_locator: Paper Methods: Infilling formulation and Model implementation; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two sizes were trained: IgLM and IgLM-S, which the paper describes as 13M and 1.4M trainable parameters; its hyperparameter table gives total parameters of 12,889,600 and 1,439,616. Both checkpoints are bundled in the Python package, which selects them by name, and IgLM is the default. A result should name the checkpoint, the package version (setup.cfg declares 0.1.0) or the commit, and the sampling settings, because generation is stochastic and the paper varies temperature and nucleus probability.

strengths.text: Generation is conditioned on chain type and species, so human heavy chains, camel nanobodies and other combinations can be requested with a token.

strengths.text: It is small and self-contained: the largest checkpoint has about 13M parameters, both checkpoints ship inside the pip package, and the dependencies are PyTorch and Transformers with no data download needed for inference.

The authors report that infilled libraries were more human-like than their parent antibodies by OASis identity and had better in silico developability profiles; these are their measurements, not ours.

limitations.text: The licence is non-commercial: use is granted to non-profit academic and research institutions only, and research use by a for-profit entity needs a separate written agreement from Johns Hopkins.

It is an antibody-only model trained on the Observed Antibody Space: six species, heavily skewed towards human heavy chains, so other species and other protein families are out of its training distribution.
The context is 512 positions and the package generation call stops at 150 tokens, so it works on single variable domains rather than paired or full-length chains.

The authors note that antibody-specific language models have been found to underperform universal protein models on antibody fitness prediction, so this is a library design tool rather than a binding predictor.

steps.title: Re-design a CDR H3 span
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from iglm import IgLM

iglm = IgLM()

parent_sequence = "EVQLVESGGGLVQPGGSLRLSCAASGFNIKEYYMHWVRQAPGKGLEWVGLIDPEQGNTIYDPKFQDRATISADNSKNTAYLQMNSLRAEDTAVYYCARDTAAYFDYWGQGTLVTVS"

species_token = "[HUMAN]"
infill_range = (98, 106)
num_seqs = 100

generated_seqs = iglm.infill(
    parent_sequence,
    chain_token,
    species_token,
    infill_range=infill_range,
    num_to_generate=num_seqs,
)
print(generated_seqs[:3])
PY
steps.explanation: The README's package example for infilling, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It loads the default IgLM checkpoint and generates 100 unique variants of the 1JPT heavy chain with a re-designed span from position 98 to 106. steps.title: Score a sequence
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import math
from iglm import IgLM

iglm = IgLM()

sequence = "EVQLVESGGGLVQPGGSLRLSCAASGFNIKEYYMHWVRQAPGKGLEWVGLIDPEQGNTIYDPKFQDRATISADNSKNTAYLQMNSLRAEDTAVYYCARDTAAYFDYWGQGTLVTVS"
chain_token = "[HEAVY]"
species_token = "[HUMAN]"

log_likelihood = iglm.log_likelihood(
    sequence,
    chain_token,
    species_token,
)
perplexity = math.exp(-log_likelihood)
print(log_likelihood, perplexity)
PY

profile.summary: GPN-Promoter (Hugging Face name gpn-animal-promoter) is a DNA language model trained on promoter sequences from animal genomes. It was released with TraitGym, a benchmark of causal regulatory variants in human genetics. Given a DNA window, it predicts masked nucleotides; the GPN tools turn this into a variant score, the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele, or into sequence embeddings.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN-Promoter belongs to the GPN (GPN-SS) family: single-sequence genomic language models trained on unaligned genomes with masked language modelling. The published config uses the GPN model type with a ByteNet-style convolutional encoder of 64 layers and hidden size 1024, a first kernel size of 9 and later kernel size of 5, with dilation base 2 cycling every 8 layers. The vocabulary has 7 tokens, from the tokenizer gonzalobenegas/tokenizer-dna-mlm named in the training script. The archived training command used a dataset version called v6/512, 64 layers and hidden size 1024, with a total batch size of 2048. For variant scoring, the GPN package compares the model's likelihood of the alternate and reference alleles, averaged over both strands.

profile.summary: BACPI predicts how a small molecule and a protein relate, from sequence alone. It takes the SMILES string of a compound and the amino acid sequence of a protein, and returns either a binary interaction label or a continuous binding affinity value, depending on which of the two tasks it is trained for. A graph attention network encodes the compound, a convolutional network encodes the protein, and a bi-directional attention module combines the two representations before the prediction layer.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstractText, Results; README.md: Example usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The compound is turned into a molecular graph with RDKit and a 1024-bit Morgan fingerprint, and the protein sequence is cut into overlapping 3-mers that are mapped to learned embeddings. Atom embeddings pass through several graph attention heads; the protein embeddings pass through a stack of convolutional layers. A bi-directional attention block then scores every atom against every residue, pools both sides with the resulting attention weights, and feeds the combined compound and protein vectors to the output layer. The output layer has one unit for the affinity task and two for the interaction task, trained with mean squared error and cross entropy respectively.

sections.body: The repository ships its own data. Four affinity archives, named Ki, IC50, Kd and EC50, are unpacked by a preparation script that reads BindingDB column names and keeps the ligand SMILES, the target chain sequence and the chosen measure. Two interaction sets, human and celegans, are shipped as plain train and test text files. sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one artefact: the source code in the repository. No trained weights are published, and the two lines in the training loop that would save a checkpoint are commented out, so every result starts from a fresh training run. A result should therefore name the task, the dataset, the git commit and the hyperparameters used, since the command line exposes learning rate, batch size, epochs, hidden sizes and the convolution window. The defaults in the entry point are a learning rate of 0.0005, batch size 16 and 20 epochs, and the training script splits 10 per cent of the training data off as a development set.

profile.summary: Protein-RAG is a family of retrieval-augmented protein language models from GenBio AI, published under the names AIDO.Protein-RAG and AIDO.RAGPLM and now served as GB.Protein-RAG. Each model takes a protein sequence together with a retrieved multiple sequence alignment of homologues and, in the larger versions, per-residue structure embeddings, and it predicts masked residues. The embeddings and logits are used for contact prediction, structure prediction and fitness prediction. The models are released on Hugging Face and run through the ModelGenerator framework.
profile.summary_source_locator: 16B card: introduction; 3B card: introduction; preprint abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The models are transformer encoders trained with masked language modelling on a query sequence concatenated with its retrieved homologues. Two-dimensional rotary position embeddings let the model tell which chain a token belongs to and which residue index it holds. Masking is applied by column: when a residue of the query is selected, the aligned residues in every homologue are masked too, which stops the answer leaking from the alignment. The 16B models add structure: per-residue embeddings of dimension 384, produced by GenBio's structure tokenizer, are projected to the model width and added to the query token embeddings, and the loss is a weighted sum of a sequence term and a structure term. The 3B model uses dense MLP blocks; the 16B models replace them with sparse mixture-of-experts layers that route each token to two experts.
sections.source_locator: 16B card: Model Architecture Details, Pre-training, Sequence Masking, Positional Embedding, Loss Function; 3B card: Model Architecture, Training Details

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are published: GB.Protein-RAG-3B, GB.Protein-RAG-16B and GB.Protein-RAG-16B-proteingym-dms-zeroshot. The 3B model is the one the preprint names; it was fine-tuned from a 3-billion-parameter masked language model on 100 billion tokens of alignment data. The 16B model was built from GB.Protein-16B in three stages: position embedding fine-tuning on 10 billion tokens, 100 billion tokens of UniRef50 and UniClust30 alignments, then 80 billion tokens of AlphaFold Database alignments and structure tokens. The zero-shot checkpoint follows the same recipe but with 23 billion tokens in the third stage and a structure loss weight of 0.025 instead of 0.01. The models were first published under AIDO names; the old Hugging Face address for the 3B model now serves the repository named GB.Protein-RAG-3B, and the ModelGenerator backbone registry maps aido_protein_rag_16b and aido_protein_rag_3b to the gb_ names. A result should name the checkpoint, its revision and the backbone name used.

import random
import numpy as np
import torch
from modelgenerator.tasks import Embed

profile.summary: CARP is a family of protein language models built from convolutions rather than attention. Each model reads an amino acid sequence and was pretrained to fill in masked residues, on the March 2020 release of UniRef50. It returns a representation for every residue, plus per-residue logits that can be used to score sequences. Because it is a convolutional network, cost grows linearly with length rather than quadratically.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Convolutional autoencoding representations of proteins (CARP); abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each CARP model is a ByteNet encoder: stacked convolutional layers with growing dilation, so a residue's representation takes in a widening window of neighbours without attention. Pretraining masks residues and asks the model to predict them, as in BERT and ESM-1b. The loader reads the width, depth, kernel size and dilation factor from the checkpoint and builds a ByteNetLM over the protein alphabet, then wraps it so padding is masked. Forward returns per-residue representations; with repr_layers and logits you also get intermediate layers and the vocabulary logits.
sections.source_locator: README: CARP; ByteNet; pretrained.py load_carp and class CARP

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four sizes are released and are chosen by name in load_model_and_alphabet: carp_600k, carp_38M, carp_76M and carp_640M. The loader fetches each from one Zenodo deposit, so a result should name the checkpoint and that deposit (record 6564798, dated 2022-03-18). The same loader also serves MIF, MIF-ST and BiGCARP from other deposits; MIF-ST pulls carp_640M in as its sequence model, so a MIF-ST result is not a CARP result.

profile.summary: DeepSequence learns a generative model of one protein family from a multiple sequence alignment, with no labels and no experimental measurements. It is a variational autoencoder: the alignment is compressed to a small latent space and decoded back to a distribution over sequences. Once fitted, it scores the effect of a mutation by how much less probable the mutated sequence is than the wild type, and it can also supply features for supervised learning or generate new sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: first paragraph; paper abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A model is fitted to one alignment at a time. The training example builds a VariationalAutoencoder over the alignment: an encoder of two layers of 1500 units, a latent space of 30 dimensions, a decoder of 100 then 500 units, a convolutional final layer of width 40 with 4 patterns, and a sigmoid output with a learned scale. Sequence weights are computed from the alignment before training. The example runs 300,000 stochastic variational inference updates. The published idea is that this nonlinear latent variable model captures dependencies among many residues at once, where pairwise models capture only covariation between pairs.
sections.source_locator: examples/run_svi.py: model_params and train_params; README.md: first paragraph; paper abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is no versioned release and no checkpoint family. The repository holds one implementation, read at commit fd5c272b, and the fitted parameters are per protein family: the example script downloads pretrained parameters for beta-lactamase, a PDZ domain and PABP. A result must therefore name the alignment, the random seed and the number of updates, not a checkpoint name. The example fixes the seed at 12345 and trains for 300,000 updates on the BLAT_ECOLX alignment.
sections.source_locator: examples/README.md: Predicting mutation effects; examples/run_svi.py: data_params and model_params

name: ESCOTT
description: Missense effect predictor that ProteinGym lists with multiple sequence alignment and structure inputs under the PRESCOTT reference, which describes an epistatic and structural model of missense effects that also uses population allele frequencies; scored as a zero-shot substitution baseline.

profile.summary: ESCOTT predicts how damaging each possible amino acid substitution in a protein would be. It is not a trained network: it scores mutations from a multiple sequence alignment the user supplies, using the evolutionary distances between natural sequences to capture epistasis and conservation, together with a model structure such as one from AlphaFold. The output is a complete matrix of predicted effects for the protein. ESCOTT is one of two programs in the PRESCOTT package; the other, PRESCOTT, adjusts these scores with population allele frequencies from gnomAD for clinical classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Background; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESCOTT scores a missense mutation from two sources of information. The first is evolutionary: the distances between natural sequences in a multiple sequence alignment, which carry both epistatic information and the conservation of each position, following the GEMME approach. The second is structural: a model structure, in practice from AlphaFold. The score combines an epistatic term and an independent term, with a linear coefficient set to 0.6 by default in favour of the epistatic term. Without a structure file the program still produces a full mutational matrix, which the paper says then corresponds to iGEMME, their improved version of GEMME. ESCOTT is the part of the PRESCOTT package that does not use allele frequencies; PRESCOTT then adjusts ESCOTT scores using gnomAD population frequencies.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Background and Methods; README: A quick introduction to PRESCOTT

sections.title: What it needs and what it gives back
sections.body: ESCOTT takes a multiple sequence alignment in FASTA format, with the query protein as the first sequence and no gaps in it, and optionally but preferably a structure in PDB format. By default it predicts the effect of every possible single substitution at every position; a mutations file can restrict that, and multiple substitutions can be combined on one line. The developers warn that an alignment from ColabFold may contain gaps in the query sequence that have to be removed first, and that each alignment needs enough sequences.
sections.source_locator: README: Input Data Requirements, Running the escott program; paper: Methods, docker note

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: ESCOTT is distributed as part of the PRESCOTT package rather than as a model checkpoint. The paper's software citation gives PRESCOTT source code version v1.6.0 under GPLv3, including iGEMME and ESCOTT, with a Zenodo deposit at 10.5281/zenodo.10442848 and a Docker image on Docker Hub. The repository read here is the LCQB GitLab project, pinned at commit 46fecb55 of the master branch, whose own commit date is 8 June 2025. A result should name the package version or commit, and the alignment and structure used, since both are user supplied and change the score.
sections.source_locator: Paper: references to the software and Availability of data and materials; GitLab commit metadata; README: Cite

sections.title: How this record was benchmarked
sections.body: The record comes from ProteinGym, whose README lists ESCOTT among the substitution benchmark baselines with multiple sequence alignment and structure as its input modalities, cites the preprint of this work, and names the LCQB GitLab project as the repository its code came from. ProteinGym's release notes record ESCOTT as one of the baselines added in version 1.2 of the benchmark. The paper reports the whole ProteinGym dataset of about 1.5 million mutations completing in 6.16 hours.
sections.source_locator: ProteinGym README: baseline table, Acknowledgements and release notes; paper: Computational time performance of ESCOTT

description: Deep contextual protein language model trained without labels on 250 million protein sequences, whose learned representations support mutational-effect prediction; ProteinGym scores it as a zero-shot single-sequence substitution baseline.

profile.summary: ESM-1b is a protein language model from Meta's FAIR protein team. It reads a single amino-acid sequence and was trained without labels to predict masked amino acids from their context. Its per-residue and per-sequence representations are used as features for structure and function prediction, and its masked-token scores can be used to score the effect of sequence variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: introduction, Model description; paper: abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESM-1b is a 33-layer transformer based on the RoBERTa architecture, with pre-activation layer normalisation. It was trained with the masked language modelling objective: 15% of amino acids are masked and the model predicts them from the rest of the sequence. The training data are raw protein sequences only, with no structure or function labels. The authors found the hyperparameters by a search on 100M-parameter models and scaled them to a model of about 650M parameters trained on UniRef50 representative sequences (UR50/S). The representations can be read out per residue or averaged per sequence, and the attention maps give unsupervised contact predictions.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one ESM-1b checkpoint, esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S, released with the Rives et al. paper in a December 2020 update. It is distributed as a PyTorch file through the fair-esm package and as a Hugging Face transformers checkpoint at biohub/esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S. The earlier ESM-1 checkpoints and the later ESM-1v and ESM-2 models are separate models. The model card says ESM-2 will usually perform better and recommends it unless the goal is to compare against ESM-1b. A result should name the checkpoint and, for Hugging Face use, the revision; this page read revision 7b37824b.

steps.title: Load ESM-1b and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import esm

model, alphabet = esm.pretrained.esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S()
batch_converter = alphabet.get_batch_converter()
model.eval()  # disables dropout for deterministic results

data = [
    ("protein1", "MKTVRQERLKSIVRILERSKEPVSGAQLAEELSVSRQVIVQDIAYLRSLGYNIVATPRGYVLAGG"),
]
batch_labels, batch_strs, batch_tokens = batch_converter(data)
batch_lens = (batch_tokens != alphabet.padding_idx).sum(1)

with torch.no_grad():
    results = model(batch_tokens, repr_layers=[33], return_contacts=True)
token_representations = results["representations"][33]

sequence_representations = []
for i, tokens_len in enumerate(batch_lens):
    sequence_representations.append(token_representations[i, 1 : tokens_len - 1].mean(0))
PY
steps.explanation: The README's quick-start example, wrapped in a shell heredoc, with the ESM-2 loader replaced by the ESM-1b loader named in the README's model table, one input sequence kept, and the plotting lines removed. ESM-1b has 33 layers, so layer 33 is the final layer as in the README example.

name: EVE
description: Deep generative model of sequence variation across organisms that predicts the effects and pathogenicity of protein variants without labels; ProteinGym scores it as a zero-shot alignment-based substitution baseline.

attributes.source_locator: Pinned ProteinGym Spearman CSV header: EVE (single)

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.
review.reviewer_note: role: experimental use-case curation

attributes.identity_scope: Family/method identity only; no undocumented checkpoint equivalence.

profile.summary: EVE (evolutionary model of variant effect) predicts whether a single amino acid change in a human protein is likely to cause disease, without training on clinical labels. For each protein it learns from a multiple sequence alignment of that protein's family across organisms. The output is a score per missense variant giving the probability that it falls in the pathogenic cluster, with an uncertainty on that assignment.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README: Overview, Data requirements

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: EVE has three steps. First, a Bayesian variational autoencoder (VAE) is trained on a re-weighted multiple sequence alignment for one protein family and learns a distribution over its sequences. Second, the trained VAE gives each single amino acid mutation an evolutionary index, which approximates the log-likelihood ratio of the mutant against the wild type. Third, a global-local mixture of Gaussian mixture models splits the variants into a benign and a pathogenic cluster on that index, and the EVE score is the probabilistic assignment to the pathogenic cluster. In the default settings the encoder has hidden layers of 2000, 1000 and 300 units, the latent space has 50 dimensions, and the decoder is Bayesian.
sections.source_locator: README: Overview, Usage; EVE/default_model_params.json

sections.title: Alignments and precomputed scores
sections.body: The developers built each alignment with five Jackhmmer iterations against UniRef100 (downloaded on 20 April 2020), using EVcouplings, and chose a bit score threshold per protein to balance coverage and depth. This gave training data for 3,219 clinically relevant proteins. The paper reports predictions for more than 36 million variants across 3,219 disease genes. Precomputed EVE scores, alignments and ClinVar labels for all proteins are offered on evemodel.org; the repository itself ships alignments and labels for four proteins (P53, PTEN, RASH and SCN5A).
sections.source_locator: README: MSA creation, Usage, Example scripts; paper abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: EVE is a method, not one pretrained network: a separate VAE is trained for each protein, and the repository releases no trained VAE weights. A result should name the code commit, the alignment used (its bit score threshold and preprocessing), the VAE settings file, the number of samples used for the evolutionary index (20000 in the example) and the GMM parameters (the repository ships default GMM parameters). This page read the repository at commit 460d70ef.

No trained model weights are released; only code, four example alignments and the precomputed scores on evemodel.org.

name: FLARE
description: Contrastive spectrum-to-molecule retrieval model that follows MVP with a stronger spectra encoder using subformula peak annotation and a richer similarity; it needs the target's molecular formula.

attributes.source_locator: Table 3 source column FLARE; Section 5.1 Baselines

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.

attributes.identity_scope: Family/method identity only; no undocumented checkpoint equivalence.

profile.summary: FLARE (Fine-grained Learning for Alignment of spectra-molecule REpresentations) annotates metabolites from tandem mass spectra by retrieval. It embeds an MS/MS spectrum, written as chemical formulas for each peak, and candidate molecular graphs in a shared space, then ranks the candidates by similarity. The similarity is built from peak-to-atom and atom-to-peak matches, so the matches can be inspected.
profile.summary_source_locator: Space README: Overview; paper abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Peaks are first given chemical formulas by a MIST-style subformula assigner. Each formula peak is projected by a shallow MLP and contextualised by a transformer encoder, giving one embedding per peak. The molecule is a graph whose nodes carry atom features, encoded by a graph convolutional network into node embeddings. Training uses a fine-grained contrastive loss (filipContrastive): the similarity of a spectrum and a molecule averages the maximum peak-to-node and node-to-peak cosine similarities, with a temperature-scaled loss. At test time candidates are ranked by this similarity.
sections.source_locator: Paper Methods; Space README: Overview, Model (default stack)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Code and the released checkpoint (pretrained_models/flare.ckpt) are distributed in the Hugging Face Space HassounLab/FLARE, which the paper names as the code location; no separate GitHub repository is named. Paper recipes are in run_scripts: the main FLARE model with candidates by mass or by formula, a global pooling baseline, and an evaluation with msbuddy-predicted formulas. The evaluation scripts use the released checkpoint by default. The Space was last modified on 2026-10-22. A result should name the Space revision, the candidate setting (mass or formula) and the formula source (ground-truth subformulae or msbuddy predictions).
sections.source_locator: Space README; run_scripts/README.md; Space API; paper Code Availability

sections.title: Use in benchmarks
sections.body: The MSAlign benchmark paper (an existing source on this record) ran FLARE as a retrieval baseline and describes it as a follow-up to MVP with a stronger spectrum encoder that uses subformula peak annotation and a richer, more interpretable similarity. MSAlign groups baselines by whether they need the target's molecular formula; the record description says FLARE does.

facts.value: Spectrum encoder: MLP plus transformer over formula-annotated peaks (Transformer_Formula). Molecule encoder: GCN (DGL and dgllife) giving node embeddings. Loss: fine-grained contrastive (filipContrastive).

name: FramePool
description: Neural network with frame pooling that predicts mean ribosome load, a proxy for translation efficiency, from 5' UTR sequences of any length.

attributes.source_locator: S1/S4 Table; Methods Framepool model and Model training; S7–S8 figure captions

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.
review.reviewer_note: role: experimental use-case curation

attributes.identity_scope: Family/method identity only; no undocumented checkpoint equivalence.

profile.summary: FramePool predicts how strongly a 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) drives translation, measured as mean ribosome load, directly from the 5' UTR sequence. It is a convolutional network trained on a massively parallel reporter assay, made to accept 5' UTRs of any length by pooling motif detections separately in each of the three reading frames. Through Kipoi, it takes variants from a VCF file and reports the predicted log2 fold change in mean ribosome load for each affected 5' UTR.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README; Kipoi model.yaml: info.doc

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: FramePool adapts the published MPRA model of Sample et al. That model used a dense layer, so it only worked for the sequence lengths it was trained on. FramePool keeps three convolutional layers (kernel size 7, 128 filters each, with residual skip connections) and replaces the position-specific dense input with global max and average pooling, done separately for each of the three frames relative to the start codon. The pooled values (a vector of 768) go into a dense layer of 64 neurons and a final linear output. Each model has 282,625 learnable weights; the combined model has 4 more in a scaling layer. The model was trained with the Adam optimiser and a mean squared error loss.
sections.source_locator: README; Paper: Methods, Framepool model; Model training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper trains three models: FramePool50 on 50-nucleotide MPRA sequences, FramePool100 on 25 to 100 nucleotide sequences, and FramePoolCombined on both, with a scaling layer for the two libraries. The paper names FramePoolCombined as the model for variant effect prediction from VCF files. The Kipoi zoo entry downloads the weights file Framepool_combined_residual.h5 from Zenodo record 3584238 with a fixed md5 checksum. A result should name the Kipoi model (Framepool), the weights checksum and the kipoi/models commit; this page read commit 770dcaf2.

strengths.text: Works on 5' UTRs of any length, unlike the fixed-length Optimus models it was adapted from.
Packaged in Kipoi, so variant effects (SNVs and indels) can be scored from a VCF, BED and FASTA with a fixed environment, a test command and Docker images.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Kipoi section; Kipoi page: CLI, docker

strengths.text: Small model: 282,625 learnable weights. On the 20,000 held-out 50-nucleotide MPRA sequences, the authors report a Pearson correlation of 0.964 for FramePool50 against 0.966 for Optimus50.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Results, Evaluating frame pooling on MPRA data

limitations.text: Cannot reliably detect upstream open reading frames longer than 19 nucleotides, and cannot model the order of upstream start sites, so leaky scanning is only partly captured.
Trained on reporter assay data from one cell line (HEK293T, eGFP library), so it predicts the effect of 5' UTR sequence only, without coding sequence or 3' UTR context.
The Kipoi environment pins an old stack: Python 3.7, TensorFlow 1.13.1, Keras 2.2.4 and h5py 2.9.0.

Variant scoring through Kipoi expects a single-sample VCF: the BED and VCF must be sorted with a tabix index, chromosome naming must match across files, and a VCF that mixes patients gives results that are not meaningful.

name: JESTR
description: Contrastive model that matches MS/MS spectra to candidate molecules for metabolite retrieval, pretrained with batch InfoNCE and fine-tuned with candidate InfoNCE.

profile.summary: JESTR (Joint Embedding Space Technique for Ranking) annotates metabolites from tandem mass spectra. It embeds a query MS/MS spectrum and each candidate molecule into one shared space and ranks the candidates by cosine similarity, without predicting a fingerprint or simulating a spectrum. The candidates are typically molecules from PubChem with the right mass or formula.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: Data Preparation

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The molecule encoder is a graph convolutional network over atom and bond features, followed by max pooling and two fully connected layers. The spectrum is binned into 1 Da bins up to 1000 Da (peaks above are dropped), intensities are normalised and log-transformed, and the 1000-dimension vector is passed through a three-layer MLP. The two encoders are trained with a contrastive InfoNCE loss so that a spectrum and its molecule are close. Late in training the model is regularised with candidate molecules that share a formula with training molecules, which the authors report improves rank@1.
sections.source_locator: Paper Section 2.1 Encoders; abstract; Methods on regularisation

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository releases pretrained weights for two training sets, each as three files: a molecule encoder, a spectrum encoder and a third model file named pretrained_inter_model: NPLIB1 (run id 1707829192911) and MassSpecGym (run id 1741546103623). The NPLIB1 data is included, with large files on Zenodo; NIST and other licensed datasets used in the paper are not released. The released weights are for GPU-trained models. A result should name the weight set (NPLIB1 or MassSpecGym) and whether candidate regularisation was used.

name: Jores plant promoter CNN
description: Convolutional neural network that predicts plant core promoter strength, measured by STARR-seq in tobacco leaves or maize protoplasts, directly from promoter sequence.

profile.summary: The Jores plant promoter CNN is a pair of convolutional neural networks that predict how strongly a plant core promoter drives gene expression. Each model takes a 170-base promoter sequence (from 165 bases upstream to 5 bases downstream of the transcription start site) and outputs a single number, the promoter strength measured by STARR-seq. One model was trained on measurements in tobacco leaves and the other on maize protoplasts, using promoters from Arabidopsis, maize and sorghum.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, Computational modelling of promoter strength; Methods, Library design and construction; notebook: Build the models; README: folders

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence is one-hot encoded and passed to two forward- and reverse-strand scan layers, adapted from DeepGMAP, with 128 filters of width 13. These feed a standard convolutional layer (128 filters, width 13, ReLU). Each convolutional layer is followed by dropout at rate 0.15. A dense layer of 64 units with batch normalisation and ReLU leads to a final dense layer with one output. The first convolutional kernel is initialised with clustered transcription factor and core promoter element motifs. The models are trained as regressions with mean squared error loss on the measured enrichment, with Adam, early stopping and learning-rate reduction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Computational modelling of promoter strength; notebook: Build the models

sections.title: Use for promoter design
sections.body: The authors used the models for in silico evolution. In each round, every single-nucleotide variant of a promoter is scored and the best is kept for the next round. Scoring can use the tobacco model, the maize model, or the mean of both. The authors synthesised and tested promoters after three and ten rounds. They report a large rise in measured strength after three rounds and a smaller further rise after ten, and that the averaged score gave promoters active in both systems.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Computational modelling of promoter strength; Methods, In silico evolution of promoter sequences

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two trained models are committed to the repository as TensorFlow SavedModel folders: CNN/model_leaf (tobacco leaf) and CNN/model_proto (maize protoplast). The training and test tables used are in the same folder. The notebook loads a saved model if its folder exists and trains a new one otherwise. A result should name the model (leaf or proto) and the repository commit; this page read commit ace4ead5.

profile.summary: MIF (masked inverse folding) reads a protein's backbone structure together with a partly corrupted sequence and predicts the missing amino acids. It is a protein masked language model built as a structured graph neural network over the backbone. Its per-residue representations or amino acid predictions are used for protein engineering tasks such as variant effect prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: Abstract; README: Masked Inverse Folding (MIF) and Masked Inverse Folding with Sequence Transfer (MIF-ST)

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is a masked language model built as a structured graph neural network that reconstructs corrupted sequences given the backbone. In the released loader it is a bidirectional Struct2Seq decoder with hidden size 256, four decoder layers and MPNN message passing, and each residue is joined to 30 neighbours. The structure reaches the network as inter-residue distances and the omega, theta and phi angles computed from the N, CA and C coordinates of a PDB file. For MIF the sequence enters as a one-hot encoding. MIF-ST, in the same repository, instead feeds in the outputs of CARP-640M.

steps.title: Load MIF and encode one protein with its structure
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from sequence_models.pretrained import load_model_and_alphabet
from sequence_models.pdb_utils import parse_PDB, process_coords

model, collater = load_model_and_alphabet('mif')
coords, wt, _ = parse_PDB('examples/gb1_a60fb_unrelaxed_rank_1_model_5.pdb')
coords = {
        'N': coords[:, 0],
        'CA': coords[:, 1],
        'C': coords[:, 2]
    }
dist, omega, theta, phi = process_coords(coords)
batch = [[wt, torch.tensor(dist, dtype=torch.float),
          torch.tensor(omega, dtype=torch.float),
          torch.tensor(theta, dtype=torch.float), torch.tensor(phi, dtype=torch.float)]]
src, nodes, edges, connections, edge_mask = collater(batch)
rep = model(src, nodes, edges, connections, edge_mask)
print(rep.shape)
PY

profile.summary: MIST (Metabolite Inference with Spectrum Transformers) is a neural network for untargeted metabolomics. It takes a tandem mass spectrum (MS/MS) of an unknown small molecule, labels each peak with a chemical formula, and predicts a molecular fingerprint. A second, contrastively trained model embeds spectra so that candidate structures from a reference list can be ranked for annotation.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; Nature Machine Intelligence abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each MS/MS peak is assigned a candidate chemical formula (subformula labelling), and a transformer encodes the set of formula-labelled peaks rather than a binned spectrum. The paper describes encoding peaks by their formula, implicitly featurising pairwise neutral losses, and training the network to also predict substructure fragments (the training command shows an auxiliary MAGMa loss). The fingerprint model predicts a 4096-bit Morgan fingerprint in the README example. A contrastive model is then trained on top of the fingerprint model with decoy molecules, so that spectra and candidate molecules can be compared by distance. Training also uses simulated spectra from a separate forward model (ICEBERG, from the ms-pred repository) as data augmentation.
sections.source_locator: README.md: introduction, Training models, Change log; article abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The default branch, main_v2, is an updated version of MIST, not the code of the published paper. Its change log lists model changes (internal subformula labelling, sinusoidal formula embeddings, a simplified architecture, Adam instead of RAdam, augmentation moved to the external ms-pred repository) and analysis changes (worst-case tie handling in retrieval, no ensembles). The quickstart downloads two pretrained checkpoints trained on the public canopus_train (NPLIB1) data: mist_fp_canopus_pretrain.ckpt and mist_contrastive_canopus_pretrain.ckpt, from Zenodo record 8316682. That record is titled v2.0.0, but its related identifier points to the v1.0.1 tag, and the record is not flagged as the last version; the sources do not explain this. A result should name the branch or commit, the checkpoint file, and the split file used.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Update, Change log; quickstart/00_download_models.sh; Zenodo record metadata

sections.body: The MSAlign benchmark paper (an existing source on this record) ran MIST as a retrieval baseline and describes it as pretraining with fingerprint prediction, fine-tuning with contrastive learning, and augmenting data with a forward model.

name: MSA Transformer
description: Protein language model that takes a multiple sequence alignment as input, interleaving row and column attention, trained by masked language modelling across many protein families; ProteinGym scores it as a zero-shot alignment-based substitution baseline.

profile.summary: MSA Transformer is a protein language model that reads a whole multiple sequence alignment rather than one sequence. Attention runs twice in each layer, once along the rows (the residues of a sequence) and once down the columns (the same position across the aligned sequences), and training was masked language modelling across many protein families. It is used to embed an alignment, to predict residue contacts from its attention maps, and to score variants zero-shot. It is published inside Meta's ESM repository as ESM-MSA-1b, a 12 layer model of about 100M parameters.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: Main models you should use; Pre-trained Models table

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input is a set of aligned sequences. Each layer applies attention along a row and then down a column, so a residue is informed both by the rest of its own sequence and by what sits at the same alignment position in the family. Training masks residues and predicts them, across many families at once, rather than fitting one model per family. For contact prediction the tied row attention maps are read by a logistic regression, the same method used for the single-sequence ESM models. For variant scoring the repository's program masks each position of the first sequence in the alignment in turn and reads the log probability of each amino acid there, a strategy it calls masked marginals, which is the only strategy it allows for this model.
sections.source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: Unsupervised contact prediction; predict.py: MSATransformer branch

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints exist. ESM-MSA-1 was released with the February 2021 preprint. ESM-MSA-1b followed in July 2021 with what the developers call a minor fix in the row positional embeddings, and is the one the README recommends. Both are 12 layers, about 100M parameters, embedding dimension 768, trained on UR50/S with alignments from the 2018_03 release. A result must name which of the two was used, and also the alignment and how deeply it was sampled, because the scoring program takes only the first 400 sequences of the alignment by default.
sections.source_locator: README.md: News, Pre-trained Models, Release Notes; predict.py: --msa-samples default

sections.title: The alignment is part of the input
sections.body: Because the model reads an alignment, the result depends on which sequences are in it and how many. The scoring program reads an a3m file, strips insertions and takes the first n sequences, 400 unless told otherwise. The repository publishes a3m alignments for the structural split dataset, and the README notes that in its own structure comparison the alignment-based methods, ESM-MSA-1 among them, used the trRosetta alignments while the single-sequence models had none.

limitations.text: An alignment must be supplied in a3m format, so the model cannot be used on a protein with no relatives, and the result depends on the alignment.

name: MULAN
description: Multimodal protein language model that fuses a pretrained sequence encoder with a parameter-efficient adapter for angle-based structure encoding, scored in ProteinGym as a zero-shot substitution baseline from sequence and structure.

attributes.source_locator: Pinned ProteinGym Spearman CSV header: MULAN

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.

attributes.identity_scope: Family/method identity only; no undocumented checkpoint equivalence.

profile.summary: MULAN is a protein language model that reads a protein's sequence together with its three-dimensional structure, and returns per-residue or whole-protein embeddings. The structure enters as backbone and side-chain torsion angles, handled by a small added module called the Structure Adapter, whose output is added to the embeddings of a pretrained ESM-2 model that is then fine-tuned. The embeddings are meant to be used as features for downstream predictors.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and section 2.1; README: Overview

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MULAN keeps a pretrained ESM-2 encoder and adds a Structure Adapter: an MLP that turns each residue's torsion angles into an embedding, followed by one Transformer layer with rotary position embeddings. Each residue is described by the backbone angles phi and psi and up to five side-chain chi angles, with missing values filled by a reserved padding value. The angle embeddings are added to ESM-2's residue embeddings and the whole model is fine-tuned with the masked language modelling objective of ESM-2, masking 15% of tokens, and masking angles along with their residues. For AlphaFold2 structures, angles of residues with low confidence are masked.
sections.source_locator: Paper: sections 2.1.1, 2.1.2 and 2.1.3

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are released on Hugging Face: MULAN-small, MULAN-ESM2-35M and MULAN-ESM2-650M. The paper names them MULAN S, M and L and gives 9M, 37M and 652M parameters, initialised from ESM-2 8M, 35M and 650M; the Hugging Face parameter counts of the files read here are 9,077,010, 36,769,870 and 672,047,862. The Hugging Face listing for this author holds only these three models, so the SaProt-initialised variants the repository describes are not published there. The README records a change on 31/03/2025 that added the medium and large checkpoints, updated MULAN-small and moved the code to rotary position embeddings, so a result should name both the checkpoint revision and the code commit.
sections.source_locator: README: Pre-trained models and News; Paper: section 2.2; Hugging Face API responses and author listing

sections.title: What it is for
sections.body: MULAN produces embeddings, not scores. The repository extracts residue-level embeddings from the last layer and suggests mean pooling for a protein-level embedding; downstream predictors are then trained on those embeddings. The authors evaluate on nine downstream tasks and report the largest gains for protein-protein interaction prediction.
sections.source_locator: README: Quick start step 5; Paper: Abstract

strengths.text: Cheap to produce and to run: the structure module adds about 0.3% of the parameters of the large model, and the authors report fine-tuning in up to three days on one GPU.
Structure enters as torsion angles, which the authors note are rotation and translation invariant and therefore easy to use inside a transformer.
Code and all three checkpoints are MIT licensed and not gated, and the repository ships an inference notebook.
strengths.source_locator: LICENSE; Hugging Face cardData; README: Quick start

limitations.text: Every protein needs a structure file; experimental structures must first be repaired with pdbfixer in a separate conda environment.
SaProt-initialised MULAN also needs the Foldseek binary, which the README says must be downloaded from a third-party link.
It returns embeddings only: a downstream model must be trained for any prediction task, and the repository's own evaluation scripts expect precomputed embeddings.
Angles of low-confidence residues are masked for AlphaFold2 structures but not for experimental ones, so the same protein is handled differently depending on where its structure came from.

steps.title: Extract embeddings for a folder of structures
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from mulan.dataset import ProteinDataset, data_collate_fn_dynamic
from mulan.model import StructEsmForMaskedLM
from mulan.model_utils import auto_detect_base_tokenizer

protein_data_path = './example_structures'
saved_dataset_path = './example_dataset'
is_experimental_structure = False
use_foldseek_sequences = False

dataset = ProteinDataset(
    protein_data_path=protein_data_path,
    saved_dataset_path=saved_dataset_path,
    use_foldseek_sequences=use_foldseek_sequences,
    is_experimental_structure=is_experimental_structure,
)

model = StructEsmForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    'DFrolova/MULAN-small',
    device_map="auto",
)
device = 'cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
model.to(device)

esm_tokenizer = auto_detect_base_tokenizer(model.config, use_foldseek_sequences)

def data_collator(x):
    if use_foldseek_sequences:
        one_letter_aas = esm_tokenizer.all_tokens[5:]
    else:
        one_letter_aas = dataset.tokenizer.one_letter_aas

    return data_collate_fn_dynamic(x,
        esm_tokenizer=esm_tokenizer,
        nan_value=np.deg2rad(dataset.tokenizer.nan_fill_value),
        mask_inputs=False,
        all_amino_acids=one_letter_aas,
        use_foldseek_sequences=use_foldseek_sequences)

dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=1, shuffle=False, collate_fn=data_collator)

with torch.no_grad():
    for i, (batch, batch_names) in enumerate(zip(dataloader, dataset.protein_names)):
        struct_inputs = [struct_input.to(device) for struct_input in batch['struct_inputs']]
        embeddings = model(
            input_ids=batch['input_ids'].to(device),
            attention_mask=batch['attention_mask'].to(device),
            struct_inputs=struct_inputs,
            output_hidden_states=True
        )['hidden_states'][-1]
        embeddings = embeddings[0][1:-1]
        protein_embedding = embeddings.mean(dim=0)
        print(batch_names, embeddings.shape, protein_embedding.shape)

description: Contrastive spectrum-to-molecule retrieval model that extends JESTR with multiple views (fingerprint, graph, spectra and consensus spectra); it needs the target's molecular formula.

profile.summary: MVP (MultiView Projection) ranks candidate molecules for a tandem mass spectrum to annotate metabolites. It learns one embedding space for four views of the same compound: the molecular graph, the molecular fingerprint, a single spectrum and a consensus spectrum built from several spectra of that compound. A query spectrum or consensus spectrum is then compared with candidate molecules in that space.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MVP has one encoder per view and a contrastive loss over every pair of views. The molecule encoder is the same as JESTR's: a 3-layer graph convolutional network, a pooling layer and two fully connected layers. Spectra and consensus spectra are sets of peaks; by default each peak is represented by its chemical formula (FormSpec), encoded by a 3-layer MLP and then a transformer encoder with 2 attention heads. A binned-spectrum variant (BinnedSpec) is also provided. At inference any molecule view can be paired with any spectrum view; the authors report the graph to consensus spectrum view (mol-cs) as best.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Overview, Encoders, Comparative Study on Spectra Representation

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained checkpoints trained on MassSpecGym are distributed in the Hugging Face Space HassounLab/MVP: msgym_formSpec.ckpt and msgym_binnedSpec.ckpt. At the reviewed GitHub commit, the GitHub repository holds the code and params files but no checkpoint files, although the paper says pretrained models are available there. The GitHub repository and the Space carry no licence. A result should name the variant (FormSpec or BinnedSpec), the ranking view and whether consensus spectra were used.

name: Optimus 5-Prime
description: Convolutional neural network that predicts mean ribosome load from 5' UTR sequence, trained on massively parallel reporter assays of random 5' UTRs and limited by position-specific weights to the lengths seen in training.

profile.summary: Optimus 5-Prime is a convolutional neural network that predicts how well a 5' UTR sequence drives translation, measured as mean ribosome load (MRL). It reads a one-hot encoded 5' UTR, 50 nucleotides in the main model, and outputs a single MRL value. It was trained on polysome profiling of 280,000 random 5' UTRs placed in front of an eGFP reporter, and the authors also used it with a genetic algorithm to design new 5' UTRs.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Modeling 5' UTRs and ribosome loading; Fig. 2 legend

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The authors built a library of 280,000 reporter constructs with random 5' UTRs and a constant eGFP coding sequence and 3' UTR, measured ribosome loading by polysome profiling and RNA sequencing, and trained a CNN on 260,000 of them, holding out 20,000 for testing. The chosen architecture, from a 10-fold cross-validated grid search, has three convolution layers of 120 filters with filter length 8 and ReLU activation, a 40-node dense layer with 20% dropout, and one linear output. It was written in Python 2.7 with Keras on a TensorFlow backend and trained for three epochs. A separate model with the same layout predicts the full polysome profile, and a generalised version reads 5' UTRs of 25 to 100 nucleotides, zero-padded to 100.
sections.source_locator: Paper: MPRA design and validation; Online Methods, Convolution Neural Network, Polysome Profile Model, Generalized CNN

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds several saved Keras models in modeling/saved_models: the main MRL model (Figure 2), a retrained main model (Figure 4), a model for the genetic algorithm and its retrained version, and the polysome distribution model. The same folder also holds Varying_length_25to100_model.hdf5, whose name matches the paper's generalised 25 to 100 nucleotide model. Six further .h5 models (e1, e2, ep1, ep2, emp1, emp2) sit in modeling/cds_modification_comparisons/saved_data; the paper describes models trained on chemically modified RNA, but the sources read do not explain these file names. A result should name the saved .hdf5 file and the commit; this page read commit d53df410. Training data are on GEO (GSE114002).

name: PoET
description: Autoregressive transformer that models whole protein families as sequences of sequences and scores or generates variants conditioned on homologous sequences, scored in ProteinGym as a zero-shot substitution baseline.

attributes.source_locator: Pinned ProteinGym Spearman CSV header: PoET (200M)

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.

attributes.identity_scope: Family/method identity only; no undocumented checkpoint equivalence.

profile.summary: PoET (Protein Evolutionary Transformer) is a generative protein language model that treats a whole protein family as one long sequence of related sequences. Given a set of homologous sequences for a protein of interest, it scores variants of that protein or generates new family members. The released code scores a list of variants against a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of homologues and writes one fitness score per variant.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README: Scoring variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PoET is a stack of Tiered Transformer decoder layers with causal self-attention. Each layer works in two phases: it first attends within each sequence, then attends across the whole set of sequences joined together. Tokens are modelled in order within a sequence, while the order of sequences in the set does not matter. Training used 29 million sets of homologous sequences, one set per UniRef50 (version 2103) sequence with its UniRef50 homologues found by Diamond. To score variants, PoET conditions on homologues retrieved for the wild-type sequence (the final method uses the ColabFold protocol) and averages the conditional log-likelihoods over 15 subsamples of those homologues.
sections.source_locator: Paper: section 3.1.2, section 3.2, section 4

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper trained 57M, 201M and 604M parameter models and chose the 201M version as the standard PoET model. The repository releases one checkpoint, poet.ckpt (403,195,613 bytes on Zenodo, record version 1.0.0, published 2023-11-01), which the README describes as about 400MB. The sources read do not state which of the three sizes this file is. A result should name the Zenodo record and the commit of the scoring code, and also the homologue set used, because PoET scores depend on the MSA it is given.

profile.summary: ProGen2 is a suite of autoregressive protein language models released by Salesforce Research, in sizes from 151M to 6.4B parameters. Given a start token or the beginning of a sequence, a model generates amino acids one at a time, so it can write new sequences; the same model also scores an existing sequence by its log-likelihood, which the authors use to predict protein fitness without any fine-tuning. The checkpoints differ in the sequence database they were trained on, which includes genomic, metagenomic and immune repertoire sources.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: title, Models, Setup

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each ProGen2 checkpoint is a decoder-only transformer trained to predict the next token in a protein sequence. The configuration class in the repository sets the shape of a model: vocabulary, context positions, embedding width, number of layers and number of attention heads. Generation is done by the sampling script, which encodes a context string with the model's tokenizer and samples continuations with a temperature and nucleus (top-p) setting. The repository also ships a likelihood script that scores a given sequence. In the README's examples, a sequence is written between the tokens 1 and 2, and free generation starts from the token 1 alone.
sections.source_locator: configuration_progen.py: ProGenConfig; sample.py: argument defaults, sample(); README: Setup

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Seven checkpoints are published: progen2-small (151M), progen2-medium, progen2-oas and progen2-base (764M each), progen2-large and progen2-BFD90 (2.7B each) and progen2-xlarge (6.4B). They are downloaded as tar.gz archives from a Google Storage bucket; there is no official Hugging Face repository in the sources read, and the archives are not versioned by a revision hash. A result must therefore name the checkpoint, and should also record the sampling settings, because the script's defaults (temperature 0.2, top-p 0.95, max length 256, fp16 on GPU) differ from the values in the README's example command.

strengths.text: Code and models are BSD-3 licensed, and the weights download directly from a public bucket without an account.
Four sizes from 151M to 6.4B let a user trade accuracy against hardware.
The same checkpoint does both jobs: the repository ships a sampling script for generation and a likelihood script for scoring an existing sequence, with no fine-tuning in between.
Checkpoints trained on different databases are published side by side, including an immune repertoire model (progen2-oas), so a user can pick the one matching their protein family.

limitations.text: The pinned dependencies are old: torch 1.9.0+cu111, transformers 4.16.2 and tokenizers 0.10.3, and the setup uses python3.8.
The weights are plain tar.gz archives on a storage bucket with no revision hash, so a run can only be pinned by checkpoint name, not by a verified version.
The scripts assume a CUDA device and fp16 by default, falling back to CPU and fp32; the sources read do not state the GPU memory needed for the 6.4B checkpoint.
The authors ask for care in how generated sequences are used, and for oversight during design and deployment.

profile.summary: ProGen3 is a family of generative protein language models released by Profluent. Given a direction marker and an optional partial sequence, a model writes amino acids one at a time, in either the N-to-C or the C-to-N direction, and it can also fill in a span in the middle of a given sequence. The same models score an existing sequence by log-likelihood and perplexity, which is how the repository evaluates them on ProteinGym assays. Six checkpoints are published, from 112M to about 3B parameters, under a non-commercial weights licence.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: introduction, Models Available, Scoring CLI, Generation CLI; Hugging Face API response

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProGen3 is a sparse mixture-of-experts transformer. The 3B configuration has 24 layers, hidden size 1280, 16 attention heads, 8 experts with 2 chosen per token, SiLU-gated feed-forward blocks, RMS normalisation and rotary position embeddings. It is trained in both reading directions: a prompt starts with 1 for N-to-C or 2 for C-to-N, so the same model can extend a sequence from either end. A separate [GLM] prompt form asks the model to replace a named span of a given sequence with a chosen average number of residues, which is how infilling is done. Scoring averages the log-likelihood of the forward and reverse directions.
sections.source_locator: progen3-3b config.json; README: Interactive Usage, Prompt File Format, Info on GLM prompt preparation

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Six checkpoints are on the Hugging Face hub: progen3-112m, progen3-219m, progen3-339m, progen3-762m, progen3-1b and progen3-3b. Hugging Face counts their weights as 112,456,320, 219,677,184, 339,245,568, 762,885,888, 1,355,871,232 and 2,989,920,000 parameters, so the names round the true counts (the 1B checkpoint is about 1.36B and the 3B about 2.99B). None is gated. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision, and for generation also the temperature and top-p, since the README's example sets 0.85 and 0.95 rather than relying on defaults. This page read the 3B checkpoint at revision f2c6b565.

run_guide.summary: Install the repository on a GPU machine and score one protein sequence with the 3B checkpoint.
prerequisites: At least one GPU. The developers tested only A100 or H100 cards with at least 40GB of VRAM, and say earlier GPUs may not work because bf16 and flash attention kernels are needed.
The install script builds megablocks 0.7.0 and flash-attn 2.7.4.post1 from source, so a CUDA toolchain is needed. A prepared Docker image is offered instead.
The weights are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: non-commercial use only. They are not gated.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/Profluent-AI/progen3.git
cd progen3
git checkout --detach 5c8c88c10b369a8c3044e11d586266f68dfca0bf
steps.explanation: The README says to clone the repository but gives no clone command; these three lines get it at the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: bash setup.sh
steps.explanation: The README's install step. The script installs the package, then megablocks and flash-attn without build isolation.

steps.title: Score one sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch

from progen3.modeling import ProGen3ForCausalLM
from progen3.batch_preparer import ProGen3BatchPreparer
from progen3.scorer import ProGen3Scorer

model = ProGen3ForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Profluent-Bio/progen3-3b", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
model = model.eval().to("cuda:0")
batch_preparer = ProGen3BatchPreparer()

sequence = "MALWMRLLPLLALLALWGPDPAAAFVNQHLCGSHLVEALYLVCGERGFFYTPKTRREAEDLQVGQVELGGGPGAGSLQPLALEGSLQKRGIVEQCCTSICSLYQLENYCN"

scorer = ProGen3Scorer(model=model)
scores = scorer.score_batch(sequences=[sequence])
print(scores["log_likelihood"][0])
PY
steps.explanation: The README's interactive example, wrapped in a shell heredoc and reduced to the scorer part. It downloads the 3B weights from Hugging Face on first use. The README's logits example is left out.

torchrun --nproc-per-node=gpu -m progen3.tools.score \
--fasta-path sequences.fasta \
--output-path scores.csv \
--model-name Profluent-Bio/progen3-3b \
--fsdp
steps.explanation: The README's scoring command, unchanged. It needs a FASTA file whose sequences each have a unique id and at most 8190 residues, and writes sequence_id, log_likelihood and perplexity to scores.csv.

profile.summary: ProSST is a protein language model that reads both a protein's amino acid sequence and its 3D structure. The structure is first converted into a sequence of discrete structure tokens, one per residue, and the model is pretrained to predict masked residues. Its main use in the repository is zero-shot prediction of the effect of amino acid substitutions, scored on the ProteinGym benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Abstract; README: 4 Zero-shot mutant effect prediction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProSST has two parts. The structure quantization module serialises a protein structure into residue-level local structures, embeds each one as a dense vector, and assigns it to a cluster of a pretrained clustering model; the cluster index is the residue's structure token. A Transformer then reads the residue tokens and the structure tokens together. Its disentangled attention learns the relationship between the two token sequences explicitly; the config lists attention terms between residues, positions and structure tokens. The model is pretrained with masked language modelling on millions of structures.
sections.source_locator: Abstract; config.json pos_att_type

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The checkpoints differ in the size of the structure vocabulary K (20, 128, 512, 1024, 2048 or 4096). The notebook and the ProteinGym command pair ProSST-2048 with structure tokens made at vocabulary size 2048. Because the checkpoints differ in K, a result should name K and the Hugging Face revision. This page read ProSST-2048 at revision e94ffee7. The repository's ProteinGym script also needs precomputed structure tokens; the README links them on Google Drive, made from the same PDB set as ProtSSN.

steps.title: Score mutants on one protein
steps.shell:
cd zero_shot
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer
from prosst.structure.get_sst_seq import SSTPredictor
from Bio import SeqIO
import torch
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

prosst_model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("AI4Protein/ProSST-2048", trust_remote_code=True)
prosst_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("AI4Protein/ProSST-2048", trust_remote_code=True)
predictor = SSTPredictor(structure_vocab_size=2048)

residue_sequence = str(SeqIO.read('example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.fasta', 'fasta').seq)
structure_sequence = predictor.predict_from_pdb("example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.pdb")[0]['2048_sst_seq']
structure_sequence_offset = [i + 3 for i in structure_sequence]

tokenized_res = prosst_tokenizer([residue_sequence], return_tensors='pt')
input_ids = tokenized_res['input_ids']
attention_mask = tokenized_res['attention_mask']
structure_input_ids = torch.tensor([1, *structure_sequence_offset, 2], dtype=torch.long).unsqueeze(0)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = prosst_model(
        input_ids=input_ids,
        attention_mask=attention_mask,
        ss_input_ids=structure_input_ids
    )
logits = torch.log_softmax(outputs.logits[:, 1:-1], dim=-1).squeeze()

df = pd.read_csv("example_data/GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021.csv")
mutants = df['mutant'].tolist()
vocab = prosst_tokenizer.get_vocab()
pred_scores = []
for mutant in mutants:
    mutant_score = 0
    for sub_mutant in mutant.split(":"):
        wt, idx, mt = sub_mutant[0], int(sub_mutant[1:-1]) - 1, sub_mutant[-1]
        pred = logits[idx, vocab[mt]] - logits[idx, vocab[wt]]
        mutant_score += pred.item()
    pred_scores.append(mutant_score)

print(spearmanr(pred_scores, df['DMS_score']))
PY

profile.summary: ProtGPT2 is a protein language model for designing new protein sequences. It reads amino acid sequence text and generates further sequence, either from a start token alone or continuing a fragment the user supplies. The developers report that the sequences it writes keep the amino acid composition and secondary structure content of natural proteins while sitting in parts of protein space that known proteins do not cover. The same model can score an existing sequence by perplexity, and ProteinGym lists it as a single-sequence baseline in its zero-shot substitution benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; model card: introduction and How to select the best sequences; ProteinGym README: substitution benchmark baseline table

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtGPT2 uses the GPT2 Transformer architecture. It is a decoder-only model with 36 layers and a model dimension of 1280. It was trained with a causal language modelling objective: predict the next token from the tokens before it. Sequences are split into tokens by a byte pair encoding vocabulary trained on Swiss-Prot, so one token is a short run of amino acids rather than a single residue, and the card gives an average of four amino acids per token. Pre-training used the raw UniRef50 sequences with the FASTA headers removed.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model description; paper: Methods, Vocabulary encoding

sections.title: What the developers use it for
sections.body: The card describes three uses. The first is generation with no further training: give the start token or a fragment and sample continuations. The second is fine-tuning on a user's own sequence set with the Hugging Face run_clm.py script, so that generated sequences follow that set. The third is ranking candidate sequences by perplexity. The developers report that perplexity values correlate with AlphaFold2 pLDDT, and advise sampling many sequences and keeping those with the lowest perplexity. They state that they have no threshold separating a good from a bad perplexity value.
sections.source_locator: Model card: How to use ProtGPT2; Example 2; How to select the best sequences

profile.summary: ProtSSN scores the effect of amino acid substitutions on a protein without any experimental training data for that protein (zero-shot). It takes a protein sequence together with its 3D structure as a PDB file and returns a fitness score for each listed mutant. It combines a protein language model for the sequence with a graph neural network over the structure, and needs no multiple sequence alignment.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Introduction; Prepare Your Own Dataset. Paper: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein is turned into a k-nearest-neighbour graph over its residues. A frozen ESM2-t33 language model supplies the node features, and a six-layer equivariant graph neural network (EGNN) learns from the structure. Pre-training is a denoising task: residues are randomly mutated at each epoch to imitate natural mutation, and the model learns to recover the wild type. Variant effects are then scored from the model's fitness for the mutated sequence. The authors describe the method as an adapter that strengthens a language model, and the language model can be swapped.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Training setup; AA perturbation strategies. README.md: Start Training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Nine checkpoints are released, one for each combination of graph size k (10, 20 or 30 neighbours) and hidden size h (512, 768 or 1280). They are named k10_h512 to k30_h1280. They can be used alone or averaged as an ensemble; the developers recommend k20_h512 when using one model. A result should name the checkpoint, or the list of checkpoints in the ensemble. The Hugging Face repository was at revision cb2d622f when read.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Download Pre-trained Checkpoints; Hugging Face API sha

sections.title: Inputs and data preparation
sections.body: Each protein needs a folder with its PDB structure and a TSV file of mutants. Multiple mutations in one variant are joined with a colon, for example M1V:A2V. The developers suggest predicting the structure with AlphaFold or ESMFold, or downloading it from the AlphaFold database. A helper script builds all single-point saturation mutants for a protein that has no experimental data.
