name: RhoMax
description: Graph neural network that predicts the maximum absorption wavelength of a microbial rhodopsin from its AlphaFold2-predicted 3D structure.

attributes.source_locator: Table 1; Comparison to Previous Methods; Network Architecture

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.
review.reviewer_note: role: experimental use-case curation

attributes.identity_scope: Family/method identity only; no undocumented checkpoint equivalence.

profile.summary: RhoMax predicts the wavelength of light a microbial rhodopsin absorbs most strongly, from its amino acid sequence alone. The sequence is first folded by AlphaFold2, then the 24 residues that line the retinal binding pocket are cut out and turned into a graph: one node per atom, an edge between atoms within 2 Angstrom. A small graph neural network reads that graph and returns one number, the absorption maximum in nanometres. The purpose is to find red-shifted rhodopsins for optogenetics without measuring each candidate.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Method Summary

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence is folded with AlphaFold2, run with default parameters and without templates, and the highest-ranked model is kept; the authors measure a median RMSD of 1.08 Angstrom against the crystal structures they could check. A multiple sequence alignment picks out the 24 binding pocket residues. Each atom of those residues becomes a node with a feature vector of spatial and chemical properties, and atoms within 2 Angstrom are joined by an edge whose features come from the distance. The network is four graph layers: graph convolution, two graph attention layers, then graph convolution, each without self-loops and with one attention head, followed by batch normalisation and an ELU activation, with mean aggregation at the end to give a single number. It is designed to be invariant to rigid motions of the structure.

profile.summary: RITA is a family of four generative protein language models that read a protein sequence one amino acid at a time, left to right. They were trained on over 280 million sequences from UniRef-100 to predict the next amino acid. They can generate new sequences from a prompt, and the likelihood they assign to a sequence can be used as a zero-shot fitness score for mutants.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Usage; compute_fitness.py

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each RITA model is a decoder-only transformer trained as a causal language model: given the residues so far, it predicts the next one. The four sizes share this design and differ in width and depth, from 768 dimensions and 12 layers (Small) to 2048 dimensions and 24 layers (XLarge). The paper studies how next amino acid prediction, zero-shot fitness and enzyme function prediction change with model size. For fitness, the repository's script scores each mutated sequence by its log-likelihood under the model, summed over the sequence read forwards and backwards.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: model table; config.json; compute_fitness.py

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are four checkpoints, each a separate Hugging Face repository. The README reports a language-model loss on UniRef-100 that falls with size, from 2.31 (Small) to 1.70 (XLarge). A result should name the size and the Hugging Face revision. This page read RITA_s at revision 818eb05a; the API revisions for the others are in the saved responses. Weights are stored in float16.

profile.summary: S2F (Sequence-Structure Fitness model) predicts how amino acid substitutions change protein fitness without training on any fitness data. It feeds per-residue outputs of the ESM-2-650M protein language model into a graph network built over the protein backbone structure. The input is a wild-type sequence, its predicted structure (AlphaFold2 in the paper) and the substitutions to score; the output is one score per mutant.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Overview; Paper: Abstract, section 1, section 4.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: S2F builds a radius graph over alpha carbons (edges under 10 Å) and runs Geometric Vector Perceptron (GVP) message passing, starting from ESM-2-650M embeddings as node features. The paper gives 5 GVP layers with 100 scalar and 16 vector hidden features; the released s2f.yaml config sets node_h_dim to [256, 16]. Pre-training predicts masked residue types on 30,948 CATH v4.3.0 structures with ESM-2-650M frozen, so only the GVP layers are trained. At inference, mutation sites are masked; for residues with AlphaFold2 pLDDT below 70 the ESM-2-650M score is used instead.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository and Zenodo record 14257708 (published 2024-12-02) provide two checkpoints: s2f.pth (2,684,305,563 bytes) and s3f.pth (2,844,210,889 bytes). S2F uses s2f.pth. Both also need the ESM-2-650M weights (esm2_t33_650M_UR50D.pt). A result should name the checkpoint file, the commit of the code and the structures used.

profile.summary: S2F-MSA is not a separate network: it is S2F ensembled with predictions from EVE, an alignment-based model, by adding the two models' z-scores. S2F (Sequence-Structure Fitness model) predicts how amino acid substitutions change protein fitness without training on any fitness data. It feeds per-residue outputs of the ESM-2-650M protein language model into a graph network built over the protein backbone structure. The input is a wild-type sequence, its predicted structure, and the mutants to score; the EVE part also needs a multiple sequence alignment. The output is one score per mutant.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: S2F builds a radius graph over alpha carbons (edges under 10 Å) and runs Geometric Vector Perceptron (GVP) message passing, starting from ESM-2-650M embeddings as node features. The paper gives 5 GVP layers with 100 scalar and 16 vector hidden features; the released s2f.yaml config sets node_h_dim to [256, 16]. Pre-training predicts masked residue types on 30,948 CATH v4.3.0 structures with ESM-2-650M frozen, so only the GVP layers are trained. At inference, mutation sites are masked; for residues with AlphaFold2 pLDDT below 70 the ESM-2-650M score is used instead. profile.summary: S3F (Sequence-Structure-Surface Fitness model) predicts how amino acid substitutions change protein fitness without training on any fitness data. It combines per-residue outputs of the ESM-2-650M protein language model with a graph network over the protein backbone structure and a second network over the protein surface, represented as a point cloud. The input is a wild-type sequence, its predicted structure (AlphaFold2 in the paper) and the substitutions to score; the output is one score per mutant.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Overview; Paper: Abstract, section 1, section 4.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: S2F builds a radius graph over alpha carbons (edges under 10 Å) and runs Geometric Vector Perceptron (GVP) message passing, starting from ESM-2-650M embeddings as node features. The paper gives 5 GVP layers with 100 scalar and 16 vector hidden features; the released s2f.yaml config sets node_h_dim to [256, 16]. S3F adds a surface encoder: dMaSIF generates a surface point cloud from the backbone, each point is linked to its 16 nearest surface neighbours, and residue and surface features are exchanged through the 20 nearest surface points of each residue. Pre-training predicts masked residue types on 30,948 CATH v4.3.0 structures with ESM-2-650M frozen, so only the GVP layers are trained. At inference, mutation sites are masked; for residues with AlphaFold2 pLDDT below 70 the ESM-2-650M score is used instead.

run_guide.summary: Install the S3F code at a pinned commit, download ProteinGym data, the ESM-2-650M weights and the S3F checkpoint, and score all ProteinGym substitution assays.
prerequisites: Python 3.7 or 3.8 and PyTorch 1.8.0 with CUDA 11.1, as the README states.
One GPU; evaluation is single-GPU only and the README reports about 20 hours for all 217 assays on one A100.
Code is MIT; the Zenodo checkpoint record is CC BY 4.0.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/DeepGraphLearning/S3F.git
cd S3F
git checkout --detach 2efab6adfb27b8b36f99059a355125ce181fdaf0
steps.explanation: The README gives no clone command; these lines fetch the repository at the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Install dependencies (pip route)
steps.shell:
pip install torch==1.8.0+cu111 -f https://download.pytorch.org/whl/lts/1.8/torch_lts.html
pip install torchdrug
pip install easydict pyyaml
steps.explanation: The README's pip installation. It also gives a conda alternative.

steps.title: Download ProteinGym data
steps.shell:
wget https://marks.hms.harvard.edu/proteingym/DMS_ProteinGym_substitutions.zip -O ./dataset
unzip DMS_ProteinGym_substitutions.zip -d ./dataset/DMS_ProteinGym_substitutions
wget https://marks.hms.harvard.edu/proteingym/ProteinGym_AF2_structures.zip -O ./dataset
unzip ProteinGym_AF2_structures.zip -d ./dataset/ProteinGym_AF2_structures
steps.explanation: Copied as the README prints it. As written, -O ./dataset saves each zip to a file named dataset while unzip expects the zip in the current folder, so the download target may need adjusting.

steps.title: Get the surface graphs
steps.shell:
wget https://zenodo.org/records/14257708/files/processed_surface_proteingym.zip -P ./dataset
unzip ./dataset/processed_surface_proteingym.zip -d ./dataset
steps.explanation: Downloads the pre-processed ProteinGym surface graphs. The README's evaluation command reads ./dataset/processed_surface_gym/; check the folder name the archive unpacks to and pass that to --surfdir. Alternatively build them with script/preload_dataset.py and script/process_surface.py.

steps.title: Download the ESM-2-650M weights
steps.shell:
mkdir -p ~/scratch/protein-model-weights/esm-model-weights/
wget https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/fair-esm/models/esm2_t33_650M_UR50D.pt -P ~/scratch/protein-model-weights/esm-model-weights/
steps.explanation: The model is built on ESM-2-650M. The path must match task.model.sequence_model.path in the config.

steps.title: Download the S3F checkpoint
steps.shell: wget https://zenodo.org/api/records/14257708/files/s3f.pth/content -O s3f.pth
steps.explanation: The README links the Zenodo record without a file URL; this address is the s3f.pth download link in the Zenodo record metadata, and -O names the file.

steps.title: Run S3F on ProteinGym
steps.shell: python script/evaluate.py -c config/evaluate/s3f.yaml --datadir ./dataset/DMS_ProteinGym_substitutions --structdir ./dataset/ProteinGym_AF2_structures --surfdir ./dataset/processed_surface_gym/ --ckpt s3f.pth
steps.explanation: The README command with <path_to_ckpt> replaced by the downloaded file. To score a subset of assays, the config has an id_list option.

outputs: Score files in ~/scratch/proteingym_output, the output_dir set in the config.

profile.summary: SaProt is a protein language model whose vocabulary covers structure as well as sequence. Each position is a single token that pairs the amino acid with a Foldseek structure token derived from the 3D structure, so one input string carries both. It was trained by masked language modelling on about 40 million protein sequences and structures. It is used for zero-shot variant effect prediction, for embeddings, and as a starting point for fine-tuning on supervised tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: title and Load SaProt

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is an ESM-style masked language model: the 650M checkpoint has 33 layers, hidden size 1280, 20 attention heads and rotary position embeddings. The difference is the vocabulary of 446 tokens, one per pair of amino acid and Foldseek structure letter, so the string M#EvVpQpL# is read as the tokens M#, Ev, Vp, Qp and L#. A helper calls the Foldseek binary to turn a PDB or mmCIF file into the structure letters. The hash character marks a position whose structure is left out, which the developers advise for AlphaFold2 regions with pLDDT below 70.
sections.source_locator: config.json; README.md: Hugging Face model; Convert protein structure into structure-aware sequence

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four checkpoints are listed: SaProt_35M_AF2 (35M parameters, 40M AF2 structures), SaProt_650M_AF2 (650M, 40M AF2 structures), SaProt_650M_PDB (650M, the same first phase plus 60K PDB structures in a second phase) and SaProt_1.3B_AFDB_OMG_NCBI (1.3B, AF2 structures plus 200M OMG_prot50 and 150M NCBI sequences filtered at 70% identity). A 35M residue-sequence-only version and an inverse folding checkpoint are also published. The README says the ProteinGym checkpoint was trained in September 2023. A result must name the checkpoint and the Hugging Face revision, and say whether structure tokens or amino acids alone were used, since the two modes behave differently.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model checkpoints, News, ProteinGym benchmark; Hugging Face API sha fields

sections.title: Structure tokens or sequence alone
sections.body: The choice of input mode matters. The developers state that the 35M and 650M models need structure tokens for their best results: the amino acid only mode works but should be fine-tuned, and their frozen embeddings are meant for structure-aware input, not plain sequences. The 1.3B models are said to work well either way. Where a structure is predicted rather than measured, the developers report lower numbers with ESMFold structures than with AlphaFold2 structures, for example 0.455 against 0.478 Spearman on ProteinGym. These are the developers' figures and have not been reproduced by Rewire.

python3 - <<'PY'
from model.saprot.saprot_foldseek_mutation_model import SaprotFoldseekMutationModel

config = {
    "foldseek_path": None,
    "config_path": "weights/PLMs/SaProt_650M_AF2",

name: SiteRM
description: Independent-sites phylogenetic model that estimates an amino acid substitution rate matrix for each column of a multiple sequence alignment and uses it for variant effect prediction, scored in ProteinGym as a zero-shot substitution baseline.

attributes.source_locator: Pinned ProteinGym Spearman CSV header: SiteRM

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.

attributes.identity_scope: Family/method identity only; no undocumented checkpoint equivalence.

profile.summary: SiteRM is a phylogenetic model, not a neural network. Given a multiple sequence alignment of a protein family, it fits a separate 21 by 21 amino acid substitution rate matrix for every column of the alignment, with the classical LG rate matrix as a prior. For variant effect prediction it scores a mutant by the log probability of mutating away from the wild-type residue at each site after one unit of evolutionary time, summed over sites. It is distributed inside the CherryML Python package, together with FastCherries, the fast tree estimator that makes the fitting practical.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and section 4; README: Introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SiteRM extends the LG model of amino acid evolution by giving each alignment column its own rate matrix. Fitting runs in two steps: FastCherries estimates the cherries of the tree and the per-site rates from the alignment alone, then CherryML's optimiser estimates a rate matrix per site, regularised towards a prior matrix. The authors use the LG matrix as the prior with regularisation strength 0.5, so half the counts come from pseudocounts, and they treat the gap as a 21st state. A variant is scored as the sum over mutated sites of the log transition probability from the wild-type residue to the mutant residue at evolutionary time t = 1, which makes it an independent-sites model with additive per-site effects conditioned on the wild type.
sections.source_locator: Paper: sections 3.4 and 4; README: Introduction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are no weights: the model is fitted from the alignment each time it is used, so a result is defined by the alignments, the code version and the settings. The settings that matter are the prior rate matrix, the regularisation strength, the number of rate categories, the alphabet used for site rates against the alphabet used for the rate matrices, the evolutionary time, and the number of epochs. The ProteinGym scoring script fixes regularisation strength 0.5, evolutionary time 1.0, the lg.txt prior for tree estimation and lg_with_gaps.txt for regularisation, and device cpu. The package is on PyPI as cherryml, so a result should also name the package version or the commit used.
sections.source_locator: README: SiteRM/FastCherries Python API; ProteinGym scoring script

sections.title: Why an independent-sites model
sections.body: The authors argue that the gain over models that learn interactions between sites comes from conditioning on the wild-type residue, which the competing approaches do not do, and from being able to fit family and site specific matrices on very large alignments without overfitting. The largest alignment they processed had about 454,000 distinct sequences of length 364, which took FastCherries about 1,000 seconds on one CPU core, plus about one second per site for the rate matrices.
sections.source_locator: Paper: sections 4 and 5

strengths.text: Runs on CPU and scales to very large alignments: the authors report about 1,000 seconds on one core for an alignment of roughly 454,000 sequences, and FastCherries is 10 to 100 times faster than FastTree.
The whole ProteinGym substitution benchmark is reported to take about two hours on eight CPU cores of a laptop.
The authors report an AUC of 0.911 on the human clinical benchmark and say SiteRM beats ESM1v and ESM-IF1 on Spearman, AUC, MCC and NDCG in their table; these are the authors' own claims.
No weights to manage: the model is fitted from the alignment, so there is nothing to version except the code and the settings.

limitations.text: An alignment is required for every protein, and the quality and depth of that alignment set the result.
Sites are modelled independently, so interactions between positions are not represented; the authors present this as a deliberate choice.
The method assumes time-reversible evolution and carries a small asymptotic bias, which the authors list as limitations.
Installation has system dependencies (compilers, Boost, GSL, MPI) and was tested on Ubuntu 20.04 with Python 3.10; third-party phylogenetics tools are built locally if missing.

steps.title: Fit SiteRM on one protein alignment
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from cherryml import learn_site_specific_rate_matrices
from cherryml import io as cherryml_io
from cherryml.utils import get_amino_acids

msa = cherryml_io.read_msa("tests/data/Aln0037_txt-gb_phyml.txt")
res_dict = learn_site_specific_rate_matrices(
    tree=None,
    msa=msa,
    alphabet=get_amino_acids(),
    regularization_rate_matrix=cherryml_io.read_rate_matrix("data/rate_matrices/equ.txt"),
    regularization_strength=0.5,
    alphabet_for_site_rate_estimation=get_amino_acids(),
    rate_matrix_for_site_rate_estimation=cherryml_io.read_rate_matrix("data/rate_matrices/equ.txt"),
    num_epochs=30,
)
print(res_dict["learnt_rate_matrices"].shape)
print(len(res_dict["learnt_site_rates"]))
PY
steps.explanation: The repository's own test function test_learn_site_specific_rate_matrices_real_vectorized_GOAT_with_fast_cherries_proteins, wrapped in a shell heredoc and run from the repository root. name: TranceptEVE
description: Hybrid of a family-agnostic autoregressive transformer and family-specific alignment-based models that relies more on the alignment models as alignment depth grows, scored in ProteinGym as a zero-shot substitution baseline.

attributes.source_locator: Pinned ProteinGym Spearman CSV header: TranceptEVE S

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.
review.reviewer_note: role: experimental use-case curation

attributes.identity_scope: Family/method identity only; no undocumented checkpoint equivalence.

profile.summary: TranceptEVE predicts the effect of mutations in a protein without training on any experimental measurement of that protein. It combines two kinds of model: Tranception, an autoregressive transformer trained across protein families on unaligned sequences, and family-specific models built from a multiple sequence alignment of the protein in question, namely weighted pseudocounts and a trained EVE model. The input is a wild-type sequence, an alignment of its family and a list of variants; the output is one fitness score per variant. The three parts are combined with weights that follow the depth of the alignment, so a protein with a shallow alignment leans on the transformer.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract of PPR582395; score_trancepteve.py argument list; scoring_TranceptEVE_substitutions.sh

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Three sources of evidence are combined at scoring time, not during training. The first is Tranception, an autoregressive transformer with attention heads specialised for contiguous subsequences, which scores a mutated sequence in both directions by default. The second is retrieval from the alignment: weighted pseudocounts at each position, computed with the sequence weighting procedure of Hopf et al. The third is EVE, a family-specific alignment model, whose log probabilities are estimated by sampling and averaged over several trained seeds. The scoring script exposes the combination as two coefficients, alpha for the alignment pseudocounts and beta for EVE, and can rescale the alignment and EVE log probabilities to match the temperature of the transformer.
sections.source_locator: score_trancepteve.py argument list; scoring_TranceptEVE_substitutions.sh; Tranception README, Tranception section

sections.title: What a run needs
sections.body: TranceptEVE is not a single downloadable model. A run needs a Tranception checkpoint, an alignment of the protein family, redundancy-based sequence weights for that alignment, and one or more trained EVE models for the same family. The alignments and weights for the ProteinGym proteins are published by the ProteinGym project, 5.2 GB of alignments and 200 MB of weights; the EVE models themselves are not in that list of downloads, and the scoring script takes a path to a folder holding them. The reference settings the maintainers used draw 200,000 samples for each EVE log probability and average five EVE seeds, 0 to 4.
sections.source_locator: scoring_TranceptEVE_substitutions.sh; score_trancepteve.py argument list; ProteinGym README Resources table; Tranception README

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The variants are named after the Tranception checkpoint they use: TranceptEVE S, M and L, over Tranception Small, Medium and Large. The published script has all three output paths written out, with Medium left active. A result must name which of the three it used, and also the EVE models, because those are trained per family and are not part of a published checkpoint: different EVE training runs give different numbers. The probability recalibration flags and the alpha and beta coefficients are also part of the setting, and the script runs with recalibration of the EVE probabilities switched on and the coefficients left at their defaults of 0.5.

profile.summary: Tranception is an autoregressive transformer language model for protein fitness prediction, from the Marks lab and the OATML group. It scores a mutated protein sequence by how likely the model thinks that sequence is, and it can optionally blend that score with counts from an alignment of homologous sequences retrieved at inference time. It handles substitutions, multiple mutants and insertions or deletions, and it was published together with the ProteinGym benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: title, Abstract, Tranception; model card: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tranception is a decoder-only transformer built on two ideas: making attention heads specialise, and reading patterns from contiguous subsequences. The published configuration uses a squared-relu activation, grouped ALiBi position embeddings and a 25-token vocabulary. At inference the model's own autoregressive log-likelihood can be combined with weighted pseudocounts computed at each alignment position, using the sequence weighting procedure of Hopf et al. with the default thresholds. The configuration file carries the retrieval weight for that blend. Scoring insertions and deletions with retrieval also needs Clustal Omega, because the mutated sequence has to be realigned.
sections.source_locator: README: Setup, Tranception, retrieval paragraph; Tranception_Large config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are published: Small, Medium and Large, downloadable as zip archives from the Marks lab server (about 400MB, 1.4GB and 3.1GB unzipped) and also on the Hugging Face hub. They differ in depth and width: 12 layers and width 768 (Small), 24 and 1024 (Medium), 36 and 1280 (Large). All three use a context of 1024 positions. A result must say which checkpoint was used and whether retrieval was on (the --inference_time_retrieval flag), and with retrieval it must also name the alignment and the weights file. This page read the Hugging Face revisions d1ef6271 (Large), 96f42978 (Medium) and 303ff126 (Small).

profile.summary: UniRep is a protein sequence representation model: a multiplicative LSTM trained on unlabelled sequences from UniRef50, which turns an amino acid sequence into a fixed length vector. Simple models fitted on that vector predict protein properties, and the same model can also generate sequences, which the developers call babbling. Three sizes are released with trained weights, 64, 256 and 1900 hidden units, together with the evotuned weights that come from further unsupervised training on one protein family.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header and Description of files in this repository

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UniRep is a multiplicative LSTM trained on unlabelled protein sequences, which the repository calls a babbler. Running a sequence through it gives a fixed length representation, and simple models fitted on that representation predict properties such as stability or mutant function. The repository provides three sizes, 64, 256 and 1900 hidden units, each with trained weights, and the same interface supports inferring representations, further training and generating sequences. The 1900 unit model is the full one. The custom model file in the repository holds the GRU, LSTM and mLSTM cell implementations used for the representation training on UniRef50.
sections.source_locator: README: header and Description of files in this repository

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Several weight sets are published on a public S3 bucket, each as its own directory: trained weights for the 1900, 256 and 64 unit models; the random initialisations that were used to begin evotuning, which the README says are provided to make that reproducible; the evotuned 1900 unit weights from the pretrained model; and the evotuned 1900 unit weights from a random start. A result should name which of these directories it used, and whether any further evotuning was done by the user, since the developers publish only the fluorescent protein evotuning.
sections.source_locator: README: header and Obtaining weight files

sections.title: Running it in practice
sections.body: The developers recommend their Docker environments, one for CPU and one for GPU, both built on a TensorFlow 1.3 image over Ubuntu 16.04, which launch a Jupyter notebook tutorial. The weight files are fetched from a public S3 bucket with the AWS command line tool and no credentials. The README warns that back propagation through an mLSTM of this size is memory hungry and that the main driver is the maximum input sequence length rather than the batch size: they fine tuned on fluorescent proteins of about 120 to 280 residues on a 16 GB GPU instance, and they note the full model needs more than 16 GB of RAM while the 64 unit model runs anywhere.
sections.source_locator: README: Quick-start, Obtaining weight files, and the note on memory

sections.title: How this record was benchmarked
sections.body: ProteinGym lists one Unirep baseline, citing the Alley et al. paper, with single sequence input and a multiple sequence alignment used for evotuning, and names the UniRep repository among the repositories its own code borrowed from. The companion record for the evotuned variant covers that step.

strengths.text: Three widths are released with trained weights, so a small model can be used where memory is tight and the full one where it is not.
The weights are on a public S3 bucket that needs no account, and the repository ships Docker images and a tutorial notebook for both CPU and GPU.
It needs only a sequence: the representation is produced without an alignment or a structure, and simple downstream models are fitted on it.

strengths.text: The developers also release the evotuned weights and the random initialisations behind them, so the fine tuned variant can be used or reproduced rather than rebuilt.

limitations.text: The weights are non-commercial: CC BY-NC 4.0 covers all of them, while the code is GPL v3, so neither is a permissive licence for a product.
Memory use is driven by sequence length, not batch size, and the full model needs more than 16 GB; the developers' own fine tuning was on proteins of roughly 120 to 280 residues.
The environment is dated: the Docker images pull a TensorFlow 1.3 image over Ubuntu 16.04, and the GPU route lists CUDA 8.0 and cuDNN 6.0.21 as system requirements.

limitations.text: It is a representation, not a predictor: a downstream model has to be fitted on the features before anything is predicted.

profile.summary: Evotuned UniRep is the UniRep protein representation model after extra unsupervised training on sequences related to the protein of interest, a step its developers call evotuning. The starting point is the pretrained 1900 unit multiplicative LSTM; the published evotuned checkpoint was made with 13,000 unsupervised weight updates on fluorescent protein homologues found with JackHMMER. The result is a representation, or a sequence likelihood, tuned to one protein family rather than to all of UniRef50. For a different family the evotuning has to be repeated with that family's sequences.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Evotuned UniRep is the UniRep multiplicative LSTM after further unsupervised training on sequences related to the target protein, a step the developers call evotuning. The released evotuned weights are a TensorFlow checkpoint taken after 13,000 unsupervised weight updates on fluorescent protein homologues found with JackHMMER, starting from the globally pretrained 1900 unit UniRep. A second checkpoint is released for the same procedure starting from random weights instead of the pretrained model, so the two can be compared. In ProteinGym the method is listed as single sequence with a multiple sequence alignment used for the evotuning step, and the second repository ProteinGym names gives a script that evotunes UniRep with an alignment file as input and another that computes log likelihoods from the evotuned model.
sections.source_locator: README: Obtaining weight files; ProteinGym README: baseline table; chloechsu README: UniRep

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Several weight sets are published on a public S3 bucket, each as its own directory: trained weights for the 1900, 256 and 64 unit models; the random initialisations that were used to begin evotuning, which the README says are provided to make that reproducible; the evotuned 1900 unit weights from the pretrained model; and the evotuned 1900 unit weights from a random start. A result should name which of these directories it used, and whether any further evotuning was done by the user, since the developers publish only the fluorescent protein evotuning.
sections.source_locator: README: header and Obtaining weight files

sections.title: Running it in practice
sections.body: The developers recommend their Docker environments, one for CPU and one for GPU, both built on a TensorFlow 1.3 image over Ubuntu 16.04, which launch a Jupyter notebook tutorial. The weight files are fetched from a public S3 bucket with the AWS command line tool and no credentials. The README warns that back propagation through an mLSTM of this size is memory hungry and that the main driver is the maximum input sequence length rather than the batch size: they fine tuned on fluorescent proteins of about 120 to 280 residues on a 16 GB GPU instance, and they note the full model needs more than 16 GB of RAM while the 64 unit model runs anywhere.

sections.title: How this record was benchmarked
sections.body: ProteinGym lists one Unirep baseline, with single sequence input and a multiple sequence alignment used for evotuning, citing the Alley et al. paper, and names two repositories for it: the UniRep repository and chloechsu/combining-evolutionary-and-assay-labelled-data. The second one documents downloading the pretrained 1900 unit weights from the UniRep repository, evotuning them with an alignment, and then computing log likelihoods from the evotuned model, and states that UniRep mLSTM needs a GPU for training and inference.

strengths.text: Three widths are released with trained weights, so a small model can be used where memory is tight and the full one where it is not.
The weights are on a public S3 bucket that needs no account, and the repository ships Docker images and a tutorial notebook for both CPU and GPU.
The developers publish the random initialisations used to begin evotuning, which they say is to make that step reproducible, and a second evotuned checkpoint from a random start for comparison.
The evotuning route is scripted outside the original repository too: the repository ProteinGym names gives one script to evotune from an alignment and another to compute log likelihoods.

limitations.text: The weights are non-commercial: CC BY-NC 4.0 covers all of them, while the code is GPL v3, so neither is a permissive licence for a product.
Memory use is driven by sequence length, not batch size, and the full model needs more than 16 GB; the developers' own fine tuning was on proteins of roughly 120 to 280 residues.
The environment is dated: the Docker images pull a TensorFlow 1.3 image over Ubuntu 16.04, and the GPU route lists CUDA 8.0 and cuDNN 6.0.21 as system requirements.

limitations.text: The published evotuned weights are specific to fluorescent proteins: for any other protein family the evotuning has to be redone, and the sources give no cost for that beyond the 13,000 update figure.
Evotuning needs a GPU: the repository ProteinGym names states that the UniRep mLSTM requires a GPU for training and inference, and its GPU code was tested on one specific card.

name: VenusREM
description: Retrieval-enhanced protein language model that captures local amino acid interactions for mutation effect prediction, scored in ProteinGym as a zero-shot substitution baseline from alignment and structure inputs.

review.scope: Primary-source transcription and catalogue applicability audit; not human scientific review or independent experimental reproduction.

profile.summary: VenusREM predicts how single or multiple amino acid substitutions change a protein's fitness, without being trained on any measurements of the protein in question. It takes three inputs for the wild-type protein: its amino acid sequence, a structure in PDB format, and a set of homologous sequences found by alignment. A pretrained language model turns the sequence and the local structure around each residue into per-residue logits, a separate module turns the alignment into evolutionary logits, and the two are combined into one fitness score per mutant. The authors report Spearman correlations on 217 assays of the ProteinGym substitution benchmark and also test the model on a VHH antibody and on phi29 DNA polymerase mutants made in the laboratory.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: Abstract, Section 2.1 Model overview, Section 2.4.3.1; README: Zero-shot Prediction for Mutants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence and the structure of the wild-type protein are first turned into tokens. The sequence uses a vocabulary of the 20 standard amino acids plus five special characters. For each residue the local structure, defined as up to 40 neighbouring residues within 10 angstroms, is embedded by a pretrained geometric vector perceptron trained as a denoising autoencoder on 4,735,677 local-structure graphs from CATH43-S40, and the resulting 256-dimensional vector is mapped by K-means into a codebook of 2048 structure tokens. A BERT-style protein language model combines the two token streams through disentangled multihead cross-attention to produce native logits for each residue and amino acid type. In parallel, homologous sequences retrieved by alignment are converted into evolutionary logits by a module that needs no extra training. A mutant's fitness score compares the logits of the mutant residues with those of the wild type, mixing the native and evolutionary terms; the mixing weight is the script's alpha option, which defaults to 0.8.
sections.source_locator: paper: Sections 2.2.1.1, 2.2.1.2, 2.3.1, 2.3.2, 2.3.3; compute_fitness.py: argument definitions

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: VenusREM is a scoring pipeline rather than a single downloadable checkpoint. The pretrained weights it loads are frozen and live in a separate Hugging Face repository, AI4Protein/ProSST-2048, which the inference script loads by default; a result should name that revision as well as the commit of this repository. The repository's news list records later work under the same name: VenusREM2 reported at 0.556 on the ProteinGym substitution leaderboard through a separate VenusREM-Harness repository in September 2026, and an integration into VenusFactory2 in April 2026. Neither is described here as a checkpoint of its own. The score also depends on which homology search produced the alignment, since the repository offers prepared EVcouplings a2m files and ColabFold a3m files for ProteinGym and a Jackhmmer route for new proteins.
sections.source_locator: compute_fitness.py: argument definitions; paper: Section 2.4.2; README: News and Downloads

The default retrieval method (EVcouplings) and the retrieval ratio of 0.8 were chosen on a validation subset made of 10% random samples from each of the 217 ProteinGym assays.

strengths.text: The homology part is added at scoring time and needs no training, so a new alignment can be swapped in without refitting anything.
Inference does not need a forward pass per mutated position: the authors say their input preparation avoids mutating each position according to the DMS data or applying mask operations.
The hardware bar for inference is low by the authors' own account: they recommend at least 10 GB of graphics memory, such as an RTX 3080, and they ran the work on four of those cards.
The authors tested the predictions outside high-throughput benchmarks, on 31 VHH antibody mutants from the literature and on ten phi29 DNA polymerase mutants they made and measured.

limitations.text: The code is released under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, a non-commercial no-derivatives licence. Commercial use and modified redistribution are not permitted by it.
A structure is required as well as a sequence. For a protein with no experimental structure the authors point to prediction servers, and warn that wet-lab work needs the best structure available.

profile.summary: VESPA predicts the effect of single amino acid substitutions in a protein from the sequence alone, with no multiple sequence alignment and no structure. It embeds the sequence with the ProtT5 protein language model, predicts how conserved each residue is, extracts the language model's log-odds ratios for each substitution, and feeds all of that together with BLOSUM62 substitution scores into a logistic regression ensemble that outputs an effect score for every possible substitution. The authors report it as competitive with alignment-based predictors on deep mutational scanning data, although it was fitted without any such data.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header; paper: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: VESPA runs a pipeline of four steps. First it embeds the sequence with ProtT5. Second it predicts per-residue conservation in nine classes from that embedding, as defined by ConSurf-DB. Third it extracts per-variant log-odds ratios of masked marginal probabilities from ProtT5. Fourth it feeds the conservation prediction, BLOSUM62 substitution scores and those mask reconstruction probabilities into a balanced logistic regression ensemble, which outputs the effect score. The ensemble is ten logistic regressions trained on rotated cross-validation splits of Eff10k, a set of 100,737 binary variant effect annotations from 9,594 proteins, sharing one set of hyper-parameters. No deep mutational scanning data was used to fit it.

profile.summary: VespaG predicts the effect of missense single amino acid substitutions in a protein from its sequence alone. It embeds the sequence with the protein language model ESM-2 and passes the per-residue embedding through a feed-forward network with one hidden layer of 256 units, which outputs a score for each of the 20 amino acids at each position. Because experimental variant data is scarce, the network was not trained on measurements: it was trained to reproduce the scores of the alignment-based predictor GEMME on 39 million variants of the human proteome. The authors report a mean Spearman correlation of 0.48 plus or minus 0.02 on the 217 assays of the ProteinGym substitution benchmark, and say the whole mutational landscape of a proteome can be predicted in under 30 minutes on a 12-core laptop with 16 GB of memory.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: Abstract and Section 3; README: header paragraphs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input sequence is embedded by a frozen protein language model. The default is ESM-2, specifically esm2_t36_3B_UR50D as the README names it; the pretrained language models were used as is, without fine tuning. Each residue's embedding goes through a feed-forward network with one hidden layer, 256 hidden units and dropout of 0.2, which outputs a substitution score for every amino acid at that position. The training target was not experimental data. For about 5000 human proteins, homologous sequences were aligned with the MMseqs2-based strategy of ColabFold, GEMME was run on each alignment to produce a complete substitution matrix of size L by 20 with scores from minus 10 to 2, and the network was trained to map embeddings to those scores. The authors describe this as a student learning from an expert teacher, and compared the one-hidden-layer network against a linear regression, a two-layer network and a small convolutional network before settling on it.
sections.source_locator: paper: Sections 2.1, 2.2 Model specifications and 3; README: header and predict options; utils.py: DEFAULT_MODEL_PARAMETERS

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The weights ship inside the repository, not on a model hub. At the commit read here model_weights holds three files: v1/esm2.pt, v2/esm2.pt and v2/prott5.pt. The code sets the model version to v2 and loads model_weights/v2/<embedding type>.pt, with esm2 as the default embedding type, so a plain run uses v2/esm2.pt. The package version in pyproject.toml is 0.1.0. A result should therefore name the commit, the weight version folder and the embedding type, and also the language model used for the embeddings, since embeddings are either supplied by the user or generated at run time. What differs between v1 and v2 is not stated in the sources read. Retraining is possible: the repository drives it with DVC and offers precomputed embeddings and GEMME scores on Zenodo.

strengths.text: Fast and light once embeddings exist: the authors report predicting all mutational landscapes of a proteome in under 30 minutes on a 12-core laptop with 16 GB of memory.

strengths.text: The authors say the setup is easily retrainable with a new or updated language model, and the repository ships a DVC pipeline plus Zenodo embeddings and GEMME scores so that retraining can be repeated.

limitations.text: GPL-3.0 is copyleft. Code that includes VespaG and is distributed must carry the same licence, which matters for closed products.

The predictions are only as good as the teacher: the labels are GEMME scores, not measurements, and the authors flagged landscapes built from fewer than a couple of hundred homologous sequences as low confidence.
The speed claim assumes the ESM-2 embeddings already exist. If none are supplied they are generated first, and the README warns that generating them on CPU can be slow.
The authors warn about the state of the codebase themselves: it began as a Bachelor's thesis and they say design choices were never fixed, although the project is still supported.
It scores missense single amino acid substitutions. The sources read describe no handling of insertions or deletions.

profile.summary: This is the autoregressive sequence model released as SeqDesign by Shin and colleagues, which ProteinGym lists as WaveNet. It learns the probability of a protein sequence residue by residue from a set of unaligned family sequences, using a dilated convolutional network rather than a recurrent one. Because it needs no alignment it can score insertions and deletions as well as single substitutions, by comparing the log probability of a mutant sequence with the wild type, and the same trained model can generate new sequences. There is no pretrained checkpoint: a model is trained for each protein family.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header; paper: Abstract and Methods

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model learns the probability of a protein sequence one residue at a time, from unaligned sequences of a protein family. Instead of a recurrent network it uses a residual causal dilated convolutional network: six blocks of nine dilated convolutional layers, with weight normalisation and layer normalisation, dropout at 0.5 after each block and L2 regularisation on the weights. The authors say the number of blocks and layers was chosen to cover protein sequences of any length. To score a variant, the model gives the log probability of the mutant sequence; because no alignment is needed, insertions and deletions can be scored as well as substitutions.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results and Methods, model architecture; README: header and Mutation effect prediction

sections.title: How a model is trained and used
sections.body: A model is fitted per protein family: the training input is a FASTA file of that family's sequences, with an optional weight appended to each header, and the README's single command trains it. Prediction then scores a FASTA of variants into a CSV. The README offers two prediction settings: deterministic, with dropout kept at 1.0 and one sample, or an average of 500 samples at dropout 0.5. The same trained model can also generate new sequences. In the paper, six models are built for each family, three replicates in each of the two reading directions, each trained for 250,000 updates with Adam, batch size 30 and channel size 48.
sections.source_locator: README: Usage; paper: Methods, training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code has several versions and no single pretrained checkpoint. The branch read here is v3, which the README says works with Python 3 and TensorFlow 1; the v2 branch holds the Python 2.7 code used in the preprint, and a separate PyTorch port is linked. The paper's code availability note gives the repository and a Zenodo deposit. Because a model is trained per family, a reported result has to name the training sequence set, the branch or commit, the reading direction and replicate, and the prediction setting (deterministic or the 500 sample average).
sections.source_locator: README: header and Usage; paper: Code availability

sections.title: How this record was benchmarked
sections.body: The record comes from ProteinGym, whose README lists a baseline called WaveNet, citing this paper, and gives its input modality as MSA. The developers' own sources do not use the name WaveNet: the paper calls the architecture a residual causal dilated convolutional network and the released code is called SeqDesign, which the README describes as learning from unaligned sequences. So ProteinGym gives the input modality as MSA while the developers describe the model as alignment free. The sources read here do not say how ProteinGym prepared that input.

profile.summary: xTrimoPGLM is a family of protein language models that handles both understanding and generation. One pretraining framework combines a masked (autoencoding) objective with an autoregressive one, so the same design yields masked models that embed and classify sequences and causal models that write new ones. The published family runs from 1 billion to 100 billion parameters, the largest trained on 1 trillion tokens. A masked model takes an amino acid sequence and returns per-residue embeddings or mask predictions; a causal model continues a sequence prompt.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: Introduction to xTrimoPGLM Family Models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The family is built on the GLM transformer design, as the ProteinGLM model and config classes show: the released 1B masked model has 24 layers, hidden size 2048, 32 attention heads and a vocabulary of 128 tokens. The contribution the paper claims is joint optimisation of two pretraining objectives, autoencoding and autoregressive, in one model. In the released code a single configuration flag, is_causal, switches a checkpoint between masked use and causal use, and the loading class decides whether the output is mask predictions, a sequence label, per-token labels or generated text.
sections.source_locator: Paper abstract; config.json; README.md: How to use

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists seven downloads: 1B, 3B and 10B masked models, 1B, 3B and 7B causal models, and the int4 quantised 100B model that serves both uses. When read on 26 November 2026, the three masked repositories and the int4 100B repository answered, each redirected to a proteinglm name (for example xtrimopglm-1b-mlm answers as proteinglm-1b-mlm), and the model card is titled ProteinPGLM-1B-MLM and credits Tsinghua University alone. The Hugging Face API returned the error 'Invalid username or password.' for the three causal repositories on 26 November 2026. A result must name the size, the objective and the Hugging Face revision, because the naming has changed since the paper.

sections.title: What the developers report
sections.body: The README reports out-of-distribution perplexity on two held-out sets of about 10,000 sequences each, one below 0.9 and one below 0.5 sequence identity to the training data, and compares with ESM2 and ProGen2-xlarge. The developers' own figures put the masked 1B model behind ESM2 3B (9.3 against 7.7 on the set below 0.9 identity) and the 100B model ahead of both (6.7). The paper's abstract claims better results than other baselines on 18 protein understanding benchmarks. These are the developers' claims and have not been reproduced by Rewire.

run_guide.summary: Load the 1B masked checkpoint and get per-residue embeddings for one sequence.
prerequisites: Python with transformers and torch; the loader needs trust_remote_code because the model class ships with the checkpoint.
A CUDA GPU: the example moves the model and the inputs to the GPU. For the int4 100B model the README states a single A100 or A800 with 80GB.

steps.title: Install the Python packages
steps.shell: pip install transformers torch accelerate
steps.explanation: The README's example imports transformers and torch, and names accelerate for the dispatch load path. Rewire wrote the pip line; the sources name the packages but give no install command.

steps.title: Get residue embeddings from the 1B masked model
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch

tokenizer  = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm", trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=True)
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm",  trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    model = model.cuda()
model.eval()

seq = 'MILMCQHFSGQFSKYFLAVSSDFCHFVFPIILVSHVNFKQMKRKGFALWNDRAVPFTQGIFTTVMILLQYLHGTG'
output = tokenizer(seq, add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors='pt')
with torch.inference_mode():
    inputs = {"input_ids": output["input_ids"].cuda(), "attention_mask": output["attention_mask"].cuda()}
    output_embeddings = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_last_hidden_state=True).hidden_states[:-1, 0] # get rid of the <eos> token
print(output_embeddings.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: Copied from the model card's How to use block, which loads Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm. Rewire wrapped it in a shell heredoc and added the final print so the step shows a result. The repository README runs the same code against biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4, which needs an 80GB GPU.

steps.title: Generate a sequence with a causal model
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, AutoConfig
import torch

tokenizer  = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4", trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=True)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4",  trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=torch.half)
config.is_causal=True
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4", config = config, torch_dtype=torch.half,trust_remote_code=True)
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    model = model.cuda()
model.eval()

gen_kwargs = {'max_length': 256, 'top_p': 0.8, 'temperature':0.9, "num_beams": 1}
prompt=['', 'MLFVVL', 'LDL', 'VTQA']

for idx, each in enumerate(prompt):
    print(f"Begin generating idx: {idx} with prompt {each}")
    output = model.chat(tokenizer, each, **gen_kwargs)
    print(f"\nEnd generation with length: {len(output.split())} - seqs: {output}\n")

name: HelixFold 3
description: PaddleHelix model built to replicate AlphaFold 3, predicting the structures of proteins, nucleic acids and ligands, with an open-source release for academic research.

profile.summary: HelixFold3 is the PaddleHelix team's open reimplementation of AlphaFold3. It takes a JSON description of the molecules in a complex, where proteins, DNA and RNA are given as sequences and ligands as a SMILES string or a Chemical Component Dictionary code, builds multiple sequence alignments with the usual search tools, and predicts one all-atom structure of the assembly. The output is a set of mmCIF files with confidence metrics, ranked by those metrics. Code and parameters are published for non-commercial use only.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md opening section, Understanding Model Input and Understanding Model Output; technical report Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HelixFold3 follows AlphaFold3 as described in that paper rather than from released code, and is built in PaddlePaddle on the team's earlier HelixFold, HelixFold-Single, HelixFold-Multimer and HelixDock work. Prediction has two parts. First the pipeline searches genetic databases with jackhmmer, hhblits, hhsearch, nhmmer and hmmsearch to build alignments and finds structural templates up to a template date cutoff. Then the model runs, with a number of recycling passes and a diffusion module that samples several structures for the same input. By default each inference does 5 diffusion samples, and the report's own evaluation used 5 random seeds, 5 diffusion runs per seed and 200 sampling steps, keeping the predictions with the best confidence score.
sections.source_locator: README.md opening section, Running HelixFold for Inference and Resource Usage; technical report Section 1 and Section 2

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The first release accompanied a technical report dated August 2024, posted to arXiv on 30 August 2024 and last revised on 23 December 2024. The repository then announced HelixFold3.2 on 23 July 2025, reporting gains on protein tasks in FoldBench and fewer atomic clashes. The parameter file the README links is named HelixFold3-params-20250714.zip, so a result should name the parameter file as well as the repository commit. The README also states the environment it was validated in, Python 3.10, CUDA 12.0, cuDNN 8.4.0, NCCL 2.14.3 and Paddle 3.1.0, and says these settings are needed to reproduce the reported results. Output is not deterministic by default: the number of inference rounds, the diffusion batch size and the random seeds all change the structures produced.
sections.source_locator: README.md Updates, Environment, Usage and Running HelixFold for Inference; arXiv 2408.16975 abstract page dateline

sections.title: Licence and the hosted server
sections.body: This is not an open-source licence in the usual sense. The code, the parameters and their outputs may be used only by individuals and non-commercial organisations, or for journalism, and a commercial licence has to be negotiated with the authors. The terms also forbid building the code into unauthorised automated systems, naming screening and biomolecule design workflows as examples, and require derivative works to carry the same terms. There is a hosted alternative on the PaddleHelix website with an interactive interface and an API; the free tier of that server is restricted to non-commercial use and a paid tier allows commercial use.

strengths.text: Covers a whole assembly in one prediction: proteins, DNA, RNA, ligands as SMILES or CCD codes, ions, and modified residues.

The inference code and parameters are published, which AlphaFold3 itself was not when this work started. The authors say their accuracy on conventional ligands, nucleic acids and proteins is comparable to AlphaFold3; that is their own claim.
strengths.source_locator: Technical report Abstract and Section 1; README.md opening section

strengths.text: A hosted server is offered as well as the code, with an interactive interface and an API for high-throughput runs, which avoids the 530 GB database download.

limitations.text: Non-commercial licence, and the terms go further than that: the code may not be built into unauthorised automated systems, with screening and biomolecule design workflows named as examples, and derivative works must keep the same terms.

Heavy setup. The reduced database preset alone is about 190 GB to download and 530 GB unzipped, and full_dbs is not supported yet. The alignment tools jackhmmer, HH-suite and kalign must be installed as well.

Input size is limited by GPU memory: about 1,200 tokens on an A100-40G at bf16 and up to 1,000 on a V100-32G at fp32, with nucleic acids and other entities costing more memory per token than protein residues.

Not for clinical use, and tied to a specific software stack: the authors state the release is for theoretical modelling only and that reproducing the reported results needs Python 3.10, CUDA 12.0 and Paddle 3.1.0.

name: Protenix
description: ByteDance biomolecular structure predictor built as a comprehensive open-source reproduction of AlphaFold 3, with released weights and training data pipeline.

profile.summary: Protenix is an open-source biomolecular structure predictor from ByteDance, built as a reproduction of AlphaFold3. It takes a JSON description of the molecules in a complex, such as protein chains, ligands and nucleic acids, optionally with multiple sequence alignments and templates, and predicts the all-atom three-dimensional structure of the complex. It is run through a command-line tool that also prepares the alignment and template inputs.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; README: introduction, Quick Prediction; instructions: Inference and CLI Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Protenix follows the AlphaFold3 design: a diffusion model that samples atom coordinates, with recycling over a pairformer trunk and a confidence head. Inference is controlled by the number of recycles and the number of diffusion steps: the base checkpoints use 10 recycles and 200 diffusion steps, while the mini and tiny checkpoints use 4 recycles and 5 steps to run faster. Most checkpoints take multiple sequence alignments; the v1.0.0 checkpoints also take RNA alignments and structural templates, the constraint checkpoint takes pocket and contact restraints, and the ESM and ISM checkpoints add single-sequence protein language model embeddings from ESM2-3B (standard ESM2 embeddings for ESM, ISM embeddings for ISM) and do not use alignments by default.
sections.source_locator: supported_models.md: Model Detailed Descriptions; instructions: Key Inference Flags, Inference Cost

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository lists nine named checkpoints. Their names follow the pattern protenix_{model_size}_{features}_{version}, with sizes base, mini and tiny. The base v1.0.0 checkpoints hold 368.48 M parameters; protenix-v2 holds 464.44 M, mini 135.22 M or 134.06 M, and tiny 109.50 M. Two training data cutoffs exist: 2021-09-30, chosen to match AlphaFold3, and 2025-06-30 for the applied checkpoint. A result must name the checkpoint, because accuracy, cutoff and inference settings all differ between them, and should also name the number of seeds and samples, since the README reports accuracy rising with the sampling budget.

profile.summary: GPN-Star is a DNA language model that predicts how strongly each position of a genome is constrained by evolution, and so how damaging a single-nucleotide variant there is likely to be. It reads a window of a whole-genome alignment of many species with their species tree, predicts masked nucleotides of the target genome, and scores a variant by how much less likely the alternate allele is than the reference. Human models exist at vertebrate, mammal and primate timescales, and further models cover five model organisms.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Main; docs/models/gpn-star.md: opening paragraph and Models; cli.md: GPN section on the output score

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN-Star is an encoder-only Transformer trained to predict masked nucleotides. Each input is a window of a whole-genome alignment and its species tree. The alignment is split into target sequences and source sequences. Source species that are closely related are pooled into clade-level representations. Each encoder block has self-attention along the target sequence, a phylogeny-informed cross-attention module that reads the source sequences weighted by evolutionary distances from the species tree, and a feed-forward network. The published vertebrate human checkpoint has 16 layers, hidden size 1024 and 16 attention heads.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Main, Fig. 1 legend and model description; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Eight checkpoints are published. Three are human (hg38) models of 200M parameters each, trained on a 100-way vertebrate, a 447-way mammalian and a 243-way primate alignment; the paper calls them GPN-Star (V), (M) and (P). Five are for model organisms: mouse and chicken (85M parameters), fly (85M), worm and arabidopsis (25M). Each checkpoint needs the alignment it was trained on, with matching assembly, species set, species order and evolutionary scale. Genome-wide scores are published, so many uses need no inference. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision, whether published scores or new inference were used, and the window size.

strengths.text: Training cost is modest by the authors' account: the 200 million parameter models were trained for several days on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

Separate human models at three evolutionary timescales let a user choose; the authors report that deeper timescales better capture coding and highly constrained regions, and shallower ones better inform fast-evolving regulatory elements.
Code and weights are MIT licensed, and the package supports both inference and training on prepared alignments.

limitations.text: Inference needs a whole-genome alignment that matches the checkpoint. The human vertebrate archive is about 42 GB compressed, more once extracted, and the command-line tool does not download it.
Variant scoring covers biallelic single-nucleotide variants. The authors say the fixed alignment format makes the model less suited to indels and structural variants.
Scores from the command-line tool are raw and uncalibrated. The paper's results use mutation-rate calibrated scores, so raw output is not directly comparable to them.
The model is trained on DNA sequence alone and is not specific to any tissue.

profile.summary: LOL-EVE (Language Of Life for Evolutionary Variant Effects) scores the effect of insertions and deletions (indels) in human gene promoters without task-specific training. It is a conditional autoregressive transformer trained on 13.6 million mammalian promoter sequences, each tagged with its gene, species and clade. A variant is scored by comparing how likely the model finds the reference and the variant promoter sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Abstract; Using Hugging Face Model. Model card: Key Features

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LOL-EVE is a causal language model based on the CTRL architecture, with 12 transformer layers, hidden size 768 and 12 attention heads. Each input starts with control codes for the gene, species and clade, followed by the promoter DNA between [SOS] and [EOS] tokens; training sequences were up to 1000 base pairs. The developers describe adaptive local position embeddings and say the model uses pretrained ESM protein embeddings for gene context. To score a variant, the reference and variant sequences are each run through the model with the same control codes, the summed cross-entropy of each is computed, and the score is the variant's minus the reference's, with higher meaning more deleterious.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, Marks-lab/LOL-EVE on Hugging Face; this page read revision 397bbb87. Its custom model code describes itself as a simplified wrapper that builds a standard CTRL language model with the configured sizes, and its comments say that in practice this would load the actual trained model. The wrapper does not refer to ESM embeddings or adaptive position embeddings. The repository's example_usage.py uses the same wrapper and only prints the shape of the output logits. The repository's own scoring script takes a local checkpoint, tokeniser, genome and embedding file instead. A result should state which route was used (the Hugging Face wrapper or the repository script), the Hugging Face revision, and the control codes given. The paper is the MLCB 2025 work; the model card links a bioRxiv preprint and says the link is to be updated.

steps.title: Score example variants
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
import torch
import pandas as pd

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('Marks-lab/LOL-EVE')
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained('Marks-lab/LOL-EVE', trust_remote_code=True)

def score_variants_hf(variants_df, gene, species, clade):
    scores = []
    for _, row in variants_df.iterrows():
        ref_seq = f"{gene} {species} {clade} [SOS] {row['sequence']} [EOS]"
        var_seq = f"{gene} {species} {clade} [SOS] {row['variant_sequence']} [EOS]"
        ref_inputs = tokenizer(ref_seq, return_tensors="pt")
        var_inputs = tokenizer(var_seq, return_tensors="pt")
        with torch.no_grad():
            ref_outputs = model(**ref_inputs)
            var_outputs = model(**var_inputs)
            ref_logits = ref_outputs.logits[0, :-1]
            var_logits = var_outputs.logits[0, :-1]
            ref_tokens = ref_inputs['input_ids'][0, 1:]
            var_tokens = var_inputs['input_ids'][0, 1:]
            ref_score = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(ref_logits, ref_tokens, reduction='sum')
            var_score = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(var_logits, var_tokens, reduction='sum')
            score = (var_score - ref_score).item()
            scores.append(score)
    variants_df['score'] = scores
    return variants_df

variants = pd.DataFrame({
    'sequence': ['ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA', 'ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA'],
    'variant_sequence': ['ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA', 'ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA']
})

scored_variants = score_variants_hf(variants, gene='brca1', species='human', clade='primate')
print(scored_variants)
PY

description: Deep learning model that predicts the impact of promoter variants on gene expression. Scores range from -1 to 1 (negative for under-expression, positive for over-expression); the README recommends thresholds of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 in absolute value. Supports single nucleotide variants and left-normalised indels.

profile.summary: PromoterAI is a deep learning model from Illumina that predicts how a variant in a gene promoter changes that gene's expression. It takes a list of variants (chromosome, position, reference and alternative allele, strand) and a reference genome, and adds a score between -1 and 1 to each variant: negative values mean lower expression and positive values mean higher expression. The authors built it to find noncoding promoter variants that may explain rare genetic diseases.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Variant effect prediction; Europe PMC abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PromoterAI is a convolutional network written in TensorFlow and Keras. The code first projects one-hot DNA (4 channels) with a 1-wide convolution, then stacks blocks that each apply a dilated depthwise convolution and a two-layer dense step, with batch normalisation and residual connections. The README's training command uses 24 blocks of width 1024, a 20,480-base input and a 4,096-base output. The model is first trained to predict regulatory profiles stored as bigWig tracks around transcription start sites, optionally across several species, and is then fine-tuned on a GTEx variant file. For variant scoring, a twin wrapper runs the model on the reference and the alternative sequence and averages the difference between the two predictions.
sections.source_locator: promoterai/architecture.py; README.md: Model training and fine-tuning; setup.py; issue 3 collaborator reply

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The Python package is at version 1.0rc6 in the repository read here. In June 2025 the authors said they had released the code and precomputed scores but not the model weights. In September 2025, answering an issue titled 'Pretrained model weights release', they said the download link is sent by email after the licence agreement linked from the README is completed. The sources read do not name or version the distributed weights, so a result should name the package version, the repository commit, the model folder used and the input length (the README uses 20480).
sections.source_locator: setup.py; issue 3 and issue 10 collaborator replies; README.md: Variant effect prediction

sections.title: Scores and thresholds
sections.body: Scores run from -1 to 1. The README recommends cut-offs at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 in absolute value. Because a promoter variant acts through one gene's strand, each variant row needs a strand; if it is unknown, the README says to score both strands as separate rows and combine the results. Precomputed scores for all human promoter single nucleotide variants are available for academic and non-commercial research after the licence agreement.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: 1D convolutional network: a 1-wide input convolution followed by blocks of dilated depthwise convolution and a dense layer pair with batch normalisation and residual connections; output heads average dense layers taken every fourth block. The README training command uses 24 blocks with model dimension 1024.

strengths.text: Works from plain variant coordinates and a reference genome, and handles both single nucleotide variants and left-normalised indels.
Gives a signed score, so a user can tell predicted loss of expression from predicted gain, and the README gives thresholds to apply.

The authors report that variants it flags show outlier RNA and protein expression and strong negative selection, and that they confirmed effects with reporter assays (the authors' claims, from the paper abstract).
Training, preprocessing and fine-tuning code is included, along with the benchmark and training annotation files, so the model can be retrained.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Model training and fine-tuning; issue 3 collaborator reply

limitations.text: Not open source: the code is under the PolyForm Strict licence (noncommercial, no distribution, no derivative works), and commercial use of scores and models must be bought from Illumina.
The weights are not downloadable directly. They are sent by email after a licence agreement, and the scoring command cannot run without a model folder.
limitations.source_locator: issue 10 collaborator reply; README.md: Variant effect prediction

limitations.text: Each variant needs a strand. If the strand is unknown the user must score both strands and combine the results themselves.
Tied to TensorFlow 2.13 to 2.15 and Keras 2; GPU testing covers H100 and A100 only.

run_guide.summary: Install PromoterAI and score a small variant file against a reference genome, using a model folder obtained under the licence agreement.
prerequisites: Python 3.8 or later, with TensorFlow 2.13 to 2.15 and Keras 2 (installed by pip).
CPU or GPU; tested on H100 and A100 GPUs.
A trained PromoterAI model folder, sent by email after completing the licence agreement linked from the README. Noncommercial use only under the PolyForm Strict licence.
A reference genome FASTA file matching the variant coordinates.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/Illumina/PromoterAI
cd PromoterAI
git checkout --detach ce9fcd080556d7e962a5946327fe8fd1a04e272b
steps.explanation: Clones the official repository. The checkout line, added here, pins the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: pip install -e .
steps.explanation: Installs the package and the promoterai command. For scoring only, the README also allows pip install promoterai.

steps.title: Prepare a variant file
steps.shell:
printf 'chrom	pos	ref	alt	strand
chr16	84145214	G	T	1
chr2	55232249	T	G	-1
' > variants.tsv
steps.explanation: Writes two of the README's example variants to a tab-separated file with the required columns. Coordinates must match the reference FASTA used in the next step.

steps.title: Score the variants
steps.shell:
promoterai \
    --model_folder path/to/model \
    --var_file variants.tsv \
    --fasta_file path/to/genome_fa \
    --input_length 20480
steps.explanation: Runs the scoring command from the README. Replace path/to/model with the model folder received under the licence agreement and path/to/genome_fa with the reference FASTA.

outputs: A copy of the variant file with a new score column, named by appending the model folder name to the variant file name.
